Counselor: Hi, Janice. How are you doing today?
Client: Good. I'm good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm good. I'm really impressed that you came back for a second session.
Client: Oh, no, I'm really glad to, I'm really glad to come back because meeting with you last week really helped me to really think about why I want to do this. So I'm really happy to be back. Yeah.
Counselor: Good. Good. So as we met last week, we talked about a few things. And to recap, we talked about alcohol dependency, anxiety, feelings of hopelessness and failure and the impact that alcoholism has had on you and your ability to perform your schoolwork.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I really want to work on my addiction and I feel like it's really effective, my schoolwork.
Counselor: So how has the last week been there for you?
Client: Um, last week, I think, um, I was thinking about what we talked about last week and I try to, you know, think about some things I want to work on and so it was better than before, but I still had a difficult time managing my work and my time and. Yeah.
Counselor: So have you, did you have any drinks last week?
Client: I had a couple of drinks, yeah, I went out with my friend a couple of times and even at home, you know, I felt kind of anxious because deadlines are coming up and my assignments are coming up, so I feel really anxious. So, yeah, I had a couple of drinks at home by myself.
Counselor: Good. So one of the things that we talked about was meeting with your professor or sending out an email to tell them how you, you need some assistance in completing your work because you have missed a lot of days from school.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, yeah. So I actually talked to my professor and asked him if I could get any extra help and he suggested to kind of reach out to the tutoring center that they, they have on campus. So I email them and I'm in the process of setting up some time where I could get extra help. And I'm also talking with my tas to meet for office hours.
Counselor: That's great. That's awesome. And I think that's part of your goals that you've already achieved.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. So I'm really glad that we were able to talk last week because that really helped me to kind of plan ahead.
Counselor: Yeah, that's good. That's good. So let's talk about a little bit more of the schoolwork and the anxiety that you experienced during that time. So you said that whenever those schoolwork accumulates, you find yourself getting anxious and resolving to drinking. And you mentioned that you've been out a few times last week. Yeah. So in terms of anxiety, one of the things I've used with my clients when they experience anxiety, it's kind of a relaxation tool that will help them to stop and relax and get their focus back and come back and be able to complete whatever activity that they working on. So what stop is it really? It's a point for you to reflect.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So from the time you start experiencing the anxiety, you stop. You put everything down, put all the papers, push them aside, and you just take a deep breath, breath in, and you breathe out. You could do it a few times and really reflect on what you want to achieve and how your feelings are impacting the way that you accomplish those goals. So you need to complete your assignment, but being anxious, you get worked up, and you cannot finish those assignments. So what this activity does is help you to relax. You can practice breathing techniques. You could put your arms on the, like, put your arms under your legs, or you could practice just stretching. Whenever you feel worked out, you could do it to the back, and that really helps to calm the nerves in the body and help you to relax a little bit. And then you can really gain your focus and come back to look at whatever you were doing, whatever assignment that you were trying to complete. So you could do this exercise as often as you feel any type of anxiety coming on. And I think that would really help to, like, relax.
Client: Yeah, I think it's gonna help.
Counselor: Breathing exercise, especially the stretching, will get you, when you get worked up to, you know, like, take out all the tension in your body.
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: So another thing we could touch on now that we've talked about an activity or something you can do to relieve anxiety, another thing I see that's been affecting you is the expectations from your family.
Client: Yeah. I mean, they really want me to do well, but whenever I feel like I'm, like, I don't pass my classes, I just fail one of the tests, and I just feel like I'm a failure. And I don't want to be a failure. I don't want to do that to my parents.
Counselor: I know that's a big expectation for you, to have that placed on you and knowing that if you fail that you will bring disappointment to your family.
Client: And, like, if I fail the school, that I'm just gonna fail for my life. I don't know what to do.
Counselor: So do you think that's positive thinking? Do you think that is true?
Client: I mean, I'm not going to fail my life, but I just feel like, you know, I'm a failure because I cannot even finish school.
Counselor: So let's try to restructure that thinking because I think probably that thinking is 40, so probably to think of it in another way. Okay, how about you try thinking about times that you've been successful?
Client: Hmm? Yeah, actually I, well, until last semester I did pretty well in my classes. And so far it's just this last semester I just have a lot of things to do. But so far I did pretty well and I'm pretty involved in school and I am involved in student council, so I do a lot of activities and you know, I work too, so. And people, people like me, I think so, yeah.
Counselor: So that's good. You have a lot of things here that you should be positive about, especially being part of an organization, being part of student council. It shows that you're responsible and you're capable of handling your task. So what really is taking the best of you is like the last semester and I being overwhelmed with the papers that are coming to you. So I think thinking positive about being capable and using positive self talk and telling yourself that you're able to complete your assignments, you have done this before and you've been reliable and responsible. So using those things, at least try using them throughout the day to motivate you to keep up the good work and believe in yourself that you can complete your assignments. And you know, just take the focus of the negative thinking and think positive about yourself and think positive that you will complete your assignments because you've done it before and you're capable of doing it again. So I think that would work for you. Probably using that as a tool.
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: And we also mentioned about quitting. I think that's one of your top goals you already discussed.
Client: Yeah, I wanted to stop thinking.
Counselor: Yeah. So I think stopping can be dangerous sometimes. I'll more likely influence you to think of it as minimizing your drinking and dealing with all the soft goals. And then I think that would really help you. And another way to do that is I found this agency that started a clinic that I have researched as we talked about the last time, and they're starting a session next Saturday at twelve.
Client: How does that look for you to schedule next Saturday? I think, I think at twelve I think I can make it. Yeah.
Counselor: So we have the intake form, so what we could do, we could fill that out and I could call and make the appointments for you. And it is a, it is a five session, it's within a group. So you have other people who also struggle in dependency. So you get to meet with others and talk about your feelings and probably that would help you to cope with it and find ways to deal with that. How is that?
Client: Yeah, I like that.
Counselor: So good. I glad that we're making some steps. So what we've discussed overall, just to do a recap, we talked about the, the school, like reaching out to your professors and you said that worked for you. We talked about the techniques, the coping skills. You could do some breathing techniques or exercise and stretching and also the clinic dependency clinic that's setting up. So I think we on a good start.
Client: Yeah, I'm excited to start the therapy and I'll definitely try the stop method that you're telling me about.
Counselor: That's good. All right.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Nice meeting you again.
Client: See you next week. Okay, bye. Hi, Janice. Hi. Welcome back.
Counselor: Thank you.
Client: It's really good to see you again. I'm really glad that you're able to come back this time.
Counselor: Yeah, I really want to do this and I thought about it and I think that in order to reach my goals I need to participate and do something about it. And I'm glad that you going to help me.
Client: Okay. I'm here to help you. I'm really glad that you're able to really make your time and come.
Counselor: Thank you.
Client: So today what we're going to do is you shared with me last time how you are feeling anxious about not being able to finish school because of your alcohol dependency. Am I correct?
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Okay. So how was that for the last, last week after we met? Yeah.
Counselor: I've been drinking a lot because I've accumulated a lot of papers. I work full time and I really don't have the time to do my assignment. So whenever I feel overwhelmed I just want to feel better and relax. So I have a few drinks, probably too many, and try to resume assignments. And then I find myself not going to class because I just can't make it and my assignments are not complete. So I just feel like hopeless and I drink some more in the mornings and that's just my days.
Client: So it sounds like you're not able to finish a lot of work because of the stress, but at the same time, whenever you try to cope with that stress and drink, that also makes you not be able to go to class and that just cycle, just repeats.
Counselor: Yeah, that's exactly my problem.
Client: Yeah. Okay. So, you know, it sounds like a lot, you work full time and you have a lot of courses especially this is your last semester. I'm sure you have a lot things that are due. So how do you, how do you keep up with all this work. Do you have, like, a planner? Do you have a calendar that you use? How do you. How do you manage all.
Counselor: I have a planner, but I don't really use it. I put everything down in that planner, but I just never get to it.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Every time I look at it, it's just a bunch of work that needs to be completed and just can't get done.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So.
Client: So you know, what's are done, but it just. You just need to prioritize.
Counselor: Yeah, I think that's one of my problems.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Prioritizing which ones that needs to be done immediately, the due dates, and keeping up to date with that. Not just, you know, just.
Client: Just doing it.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Okay, so how about. How about this? Next time that we meet, I want you to kind of get in the habit of writing your assignments down according to the due date so that, you know, we have a clear idea of what to expect for the next days or next two days so that you're not overwhelmed with all the things that you do. How about. How's that sound?
Counselor: That sounds good.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I haven't tried that.
Client: Yeah. Before.
Counselor: I think that would be good.
Client: Right. So by kind of listing out what things are due in next two days or next three days, you know, what to expect so that you feel more control of your time and your assignments. Yeah, I think we could try that.
Counselor: I think trying. That would probably help me a lot.
Client: Okay. Okay. Yeah. I'm glad to hear that you're open to that idea. And also going forward, you also. We talked about last week about asking for professor for help. How did that go?
Counselor: Well, that went well. My professor actually reached out.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And have extended some of my assignments. So that's really. Yeah. So I'm happy about that. But I still have to complete them.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So this. I still feel a lot of anxiety.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Because one of my problems was that I missed a lot of classes, and I really don't know what I should be doing. And I think that's the worst of my problems, like, not being able to understand the material and, you know, do an effective paper. So I'm pretty anxious about that.
Client: But, I mean, you missed the class, but from now on, you have more opportunity to make up for the courses through the tutoring help. And.
Counselor: Yeah, my professors have given me that time to actually make up so I could come to tutoring and that's helpful. So I could catch up a bit on the work that I've missed.
Client: Okay. And when is that gonna start?
Counselor: He's told me you see, that's my problem. I can't remember things.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: I think it's next week.
Client: Next week? Okay.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Okay. So when you're writing down your, all the things that you need to do, I think if you include going to a training session, it will definitely help you to come to catch all your assignments.
Counselor: I think that planner would really work for me.
Client: Yeah. And you remember, you remember to talk to your professor, which is a good sign that you are getting things done in your list.
Counselor: Yeah, that's a start because I really want to finish. And I think that's one of my biggest goals, to finish. Apart from alcohol dependency, I would really like to finish my schoolwork.
Client: And what, what makes you, how does it make you feel when you do not complete something or when you, you're afraid that you're not gonna finish school? And how does that make you feel? I feel.
Counselor: I feel very hopeless because my family have a lot of expectations and not being able to meet those expectations are depressing. And I feel hopeless. Sometimes I just feel like I can't. I just can't do it. And those expectations, I think are getting the best of me. So when I sit down and I think about those assignments and I just think about doing good with not concentrating on what I need to get done or just doing good with that expectation that you have to do good, you have to finish school. And I think that's just depressing. It makes me feel I just can't do it.
Client: So it sounds like whenever you have a lot of things to do, a lot of things to do on your face, then you know, all those things make you anxious.
Counselor: Yes.
Client: And feel hopelessness, feel overwhelmed and start.
Counselor: Getting the feeling and the cravings of drinking.
Client: Right. And that causes to crave in alcohol. And I want you to kind of see that pattern, how it goes. And so if you could kind of start another technique that kind of change your thoughts and your reaction. So what I suggest is, how about we start like a journal. So whenever you feel anxious, or whenever you feel you have a lot of things that you need to do and that resource you to drink when you're drinking or go to resort to alcohol, I want to kind of write down your thoughts and your feelings whenever you have those cravings.
Counselor: Do I do that? Like in the, like in the midst of thinking or after the day or at the end of the day?
Client: I think whenever you have that cravings.
Counselor: Whenever you just write it down.
Client: Yeah. Whenever you have the think of, oh, I wanna have some drink. And kind of, I want you to kind of think about what makes you want to have a drinking.
Counselor: So I bring. I do this on a daily basis or just on.
Client: Yeah. Whenever you have a cravings, it's up to you. Whatever that makes you feel comfortable. I'm sure it's really hard to begin in the first, in the beginning to start journal and remembering all the journals. But I think, yeah. Just kind of writing down your feelings and thoughts.
Counselor: Sometimes I get so stunned. I don't remember anything. Yeah, I don't think I remember journaling.
Client: Right. So if you forget it, that's fine. But I think for you to kind of be aware of, you know, your thoughts, your thought process, and how, what. What makes you really go to alcohol. And also, another thing we mentioned last time was that you're interested in group therapy. Are you still interested in that?
Counselor: Oh, yes, I am.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: I really like to meet with, because you told me from the last time, it's group sessions with individual that are suffering from alcohol dependency. So I really like to share that atmosphere with others and be able to relate and be able to. For someone to be able to understand what I'm going through.
Client: Yeah. So I researched some of resources that you could attend for the group therapy. There's a alcohol dependency clinic right down the street, and I found out that they have Saturday classes. I think the time was at 12:00 p.m. did you be able to make on Saturdays at 12:00 p.m. for the session?
Counselor: Yeah, Saturdays at 1212. I think I'll be able to make it because I start work later in the evening, so. And how long is the session?
Client: It's about hour. An hour? Yeah, hour.
Counselor:
output: It's about an hour. And you said it's near campus?

Counselor: Not like she did.

Client: It was my mistake. It was in it. It makes me a worse person for doing it.
Counselor: So you see how you're being a little. Well, it'd be quite a bit rougher on yourself. Like, your evaluation of yourself is. Is fairly harsh. You mentioned loser earlier and ashamed. Whereas you wouldn't necessarily evaluate someone else that way. How would you evaluate your behavior? How would you judge your behavior of taking that first drink?
Client: Shameful. I mean, irresponsible, bad overall.
Counselor: So bad, irresponsible, shameful. Is there a way to separate that behavior in terms of your thinking, in terms of the way you evaluate it from yourself? Like, are you into behavior together, enmeshed, or can you be separated?
Client: Um, I think we could be separated, but it. It feels like we're, like I am.
Counselor: That behavior in that moment, it's very congruent for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. The shame matches the behavior. The behavior matches shame like it's there one at that moment. But really, logically, rationally, you're you. Right? Your identity and values and your behavior is something you do, but in the moment, it's hard for you to see that. Looking back on it now, are you able to see the distinction between what people do and what they are?
Client: Yeah. I mean, just because you have one drink doesn't make you a horrible person, I don't think. Right.
Counselor: No, certainly not. No. And you were clean for three weeks, and you had one drink. So really, your behavior was a slip, right? It was. And irresponsible in relationship to your goals, I suppose, but still a slip. And you could have stopped, but that shame got ahold of you, right? That thought, well, now I've done it.
Client: I blew it.
Counselor: Yeah. So with that mentality, you kind of set yourself up for drinking more. So I think this is important because we've seen this cycle, like, where you have weeks of sobriety, and then you'll drink a bit and then have weeks of sobriety. And I'm wondering if part of the difficulty you're facing is you're not coping with the slips as just slips.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: You're allowing them to be gateways into a lot more drinking than a slip. Does that make sense?
Client: That sounds pretty accurate.
Counselor: And you see how the shameful feelings kind of just interfere with the behavior that you really. That's really consistent with your goals, which would be to not continue drinking. Another piece of this, too, is the associating with friends who drink. You're putting yourself in a treacherous situation. And again, that's a behavior, right? That doesn't make you one way or the other. It's a behavior. How would you judge that behavior, going out with friends?
Client: I don't know. I mean, difficult, because I like being around those people, but I guess it would be. It's risky.
Counselor: Risky? Okay. It's a risky behavior. And what does it make you? Who are you? Because you do that behavior. Like, how do you feel about yourself when you take that risky behavior?
Client: Guilty.
Counselor: Okay. So you have guilt when you go out with your friends, and then you have shame if you drink. And both, in this case, both emotions that kind of point you in the direction of more drinking. So part of this behavioral strategy here is to avoid those circumstances. Like, to recognize that's a risky behavior, which you have. And the other part would be to deal more effectively if you do slip.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: Right. Does that separation of what we do and who we are make sense to you rationally? Kind of feels a little unnatural, though.

Client: Right. It used to be so easy for me to do what my teachers expect and to get good grades. Now I feel like it's really a struggle and I'm not doing as well as I need to. Constantly worried about not doing as well.
Counselor: Have you been getting any feedback from professors or your classmates about your performance?
Client: My teachers all seem to think I'm doing well. I seem to get good feedback on my assignments, but I feel like. I feel like I. Counselor: All right, so before, when you got A's, you were working hard to do a good job, but not to the level of precision in terms of, like, the detail of the assignment that you are now. You're trying to get more information about the assignments. You're working harder to get the same grade that you used to get before.
Client: Right? Like, I find myself, like, emailing the teacher, like, almost, like, obsessively, like, trying to clarify the assignment and to make sure do they think I'm doing well in class and whatnot.
Counselor: So when you're having this feeling that I guess it's a feeling of anxiety or stress.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going through your mind? What are you thinking about?
Client: Well, I guess I'm just feeling that, you know, I've worked really hard this whole program, and I don't want to mess it up now or, you know, because if I don't get these grades, then I feel like, what was the use? If I met, then I'm going to be ruining all this hard work that I've done, this whole program. If I kind of. If I don't maintain that level of, you know, like you said, precision, I feel like. Like that I've let myself down or that I'm a failure because I'm. I just slacked off at the end of the program, and it's so close to being done.
Counselor: So what grade would you have to receive for you to feel like you have failed?
Client: Probably less than an a. Anything other than an a.
Counselor: And right below an a is an a minus.
Client: I mean, I guess I would be okay with that, but I wouldn't be really happy with it.
Counselor: How about a b?
Client: I wouldn't be that excited about that.
Counselor: A b.
Client: I wouldn't be happy with that.
Counselor: No, that would be worse. Okay, so an a, you can tolerate an a minus. You're not exactly sure, but you think you could.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But a b plus and a b, to me, like.
Client: Like a a minus, I would maybe be okay with. But, like, below that, like, to me, like, a b is a b, whether it's, like, a b minus, a b, a b plus, it's all a b, and that's not an a.
Counselor: So what would it mean to you if you received a bde that I.
Client: Didn'T try hard enough? That there's something else I could have done to do better? That I was, like, slacking or I didn't read the directions right or I didn't have enough responses or make my paper long enough. I just didn't do enough.
Counselor: That you didn't try hard enough. That you didn't do enough. What would it mean if that were true?
Client: If I didn't try hard enough? That I was lazy.
Counselor: You were lazy?
Client: Yeah. Then I could have tried harder, and I didn't. So why didn't I try? Maybe I didn't care. I was lazy. Kind of like, what's the use? If you're not gonna try your best, then why try it all?
Counselor: Okay. And we've talked before about automatic thoughts and cognitive distortions, right? In other sessions. And one of the cognitive distortions is this idea that an unuseful type of thinking and error in thinking is when you think of everything in terms of, like, black or white, all or nothing. So it sounds like you have a little tolerance for, like, an a minus, so you're not completely there. Generally, it's kind of an a of some type or you're not interested. Right. It would get down to you didn't try hard enough, and if that were true, then you would be lazy.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Which, you know, having seen you in these last few sessions is clear to me. You're not lazy, but that's the thought you're having.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Now, it seems that earlier, in your earlier years in the program, the A's were not effortless for you, but you didn't have to work as hard for them.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you think has changed?
Client: I'm not quite sure. Like, it didn't stress me out as much in the beginning of the program, I really like school, but now I feel like I almost dread it because it's anxiety producing for me because I'm constantly worried.
Counselor: You mentioned part of it was you're getting close to the end. Right. So is there anything else?
Client: Well, the only thing I can think of is we have the same students throughout our program, but I guess this semester there's a new student in the program. And now that you mention it, it seems like she's kind of really stressing me out.
Counselor: How so?
Client: Well, see, throughout the program, I kind of considered myself, like, to be the student who got the best grades. And there's this award at the end of the program for doing really well. And I kind of made it a goal of mine to get this award at the end because I felt like that would show that I really tried hard. Program really meant a lot to me. It would show people who viewed it that I really busted my butt and did a good job in this program. And for the whole program so far, that was me. I was kind of the front runner, I guess, for this award. And this semester there's a new student and then come to find out, like, she had a 4.0 in her other program. So.
Counselor: So if I'm reading you right, you. You really didn't have any competition for this award that you were aware of, right? And now you feel like you really do, right?
Client: Like, I feel like the pressure's on. Like, I felt like I tried so hard this whole program, and now, like, this new person comes in and she might win it over me. So I really need to go above and beyond to make sure that I'm still on track. So when that's the word.
Counselor: And paradoxically, that's caused you to be more anxious and more stressed. And you're performing well. You're still getting the A's, but you're working harder to get the A's right.
Client: And it's causing me a lot of anxiety with school, where it's not as enjoyable for me as it once was.
Counselor: So what would it mean if you couldn't get the award? If you didn't win the. What's the name of the news? What's the first name of the new student? Joyce. Joyce. Okay. What if Joyce won this award and you didn't? What'd that mean?
Client: I guess part of me feels like, then why did I do the program? If, you know, part of me feels like, if you're not gonna be the best, why try? So if she got the award over me, then it's kind of like, why did I work so hard this whole time? Like, I could have been slacking this whole time and just skated by. So why did I bust my butt if it was all for nothing? I don't have anything to show for it.
Counselor: So it's all for nothing if you don't win the award?
Client: I mean, I guess it's not the only thing that matters, but part of me feels that way sometimes, that I have these. These thoughts that if I don't try my hardest and do well and win this award, then why did I try so hard the rest of the time? Like, it negates all the positive things that this. You know, kind of like the end result. Like, if you tried hard the whole race, and then you lose, you know, at the end.
Counselor: Right. But you're not really losing the whole race because you would still graduate.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. You're. You're just not getting an award, which you would like and which would be great and certainly an accomplishment. But the reason you came to the program was to get the degree, right.
Client: I didn't even know about the award until probably, like, the second year anyway. So that wasn't the reason I entered. But.
Counselor: But it's now. It's now taken on some importance for you. Winning this award has been a real goal. So with the new student, Joyce, coming in, they have this increased competition, and it's causing anxiety. It's causing you to work harder for the same grade. All right. So, as we talked before, you have a tendency to be. I mean, this is a compliment. A little perfectionistic. Right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I don't think it's necessarily a bad thing if it's taken too far. It can be right. It can be not useful. You ever hear the phrase perfect is the enemy of good?
Client: No.
Counselor: Does that make sense, what that might mean?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So this desire to be perfect or to win the award is potentially causing you not even to perform well. Right?
SPK_3: Right.
Counselor: You're still getting the a's, but it's causing the anxiety and you're working hard.
Client: Right. And I'm not even. I feel like when I read, like, I'm so stressed with it, I'm reading the right thing and memorizing every word that I'm not retaining all the information. So it could. And it's starting to, like, impact school.
Counselor: So is there any way that you cannot win the award and still walk away having accomplished worthy goals? Or does it have to be the award or none of this was worth it?
Client: I mean, it kind of sounds silly when you're reflecting it back to me, how you know, that I have to earn the awards. Like, I think that it makes sense, you know, that wasn't my goal going into it. You know, why does it matter so much to me that there's different degrees of success? I think, as you've said before, that it's not all about the award. And I think I would be happy with just, you know, getting the degree and all the stuff that I've learned, and I would feel like it was if I didn't get the award, rather, I would have feel like it was still a worthwhile journey, but in the moment, sometimes it's really upsetting at the thought of not getting the award. But that's a possibility.
Counselor: The award validates all the hard work you've done, right?
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: And in your mind, losing the award invalidates all the hard work you've done, right. But in reality, there's probably a between ground there, a shade of gray where you're still an excellent student, you still graduate, you just don't have an extra plaque to hang on the wall. Whatever the award is, that's really all you'd be missing, right? Would this award have any impact on employment?
Client: I don't think so. I don't think in the long term many people would know about it besides me or if I put it, you know, on a resume or something, but I don't think it would make that much of a difference.
Counselor: And you didn't even know about it when you first came in.
Client: You were already working hard right at the beginning. I didn't even know about it.
Counselor: So in a sense, and of course, we can't do this, but in a sense, if you could forget about the award, you'd probably win it.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Right. Because you were already doing so well. What is the thought of this potential failure not wearing the word that's holding you back?
SPK_3: Right.
Client: It makes me paranoid to make mistakes or to try and take risks or to really, you know, do well because I'm so worried about judgment, like, from my teachers, if I'm doing well or not.

Client: Right.
Counselor: So now that this award's out there, you really feel like you can't make any type of mistake or you just go right to a catastrophe.
Client: Right. Like I'm walking on eggshells and I'm just expecting my grades to tank if I. If I kind of, like, deviate from that line.
Counselor: So for you to feel better about this one way, I guess, right. Would be to not have to not place so much value in winning.

What's the automatic thought that comes to mind?
Client: If I'm. You mean if I'm. When I'm just doing the work.

Counselor: Expected of me to ensure that you're going to get that award. So at a higher level, one of your thoughts is, I must win that award.

Counselor: Does that make sense? I mean, that's probably in there somewhere.
Client: I'm thinking.

Client: Did I miss win the award? Do you believe that adaptive response is true?

Counselor:

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Samantha. How you doing today?
Client: Good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm doing all right. How have things been since last week?
Client: Things? You know, I've been really sort of preoccupied and anxious a lot this weekend. My daughter got sick, so I had to take three days off of work to take care of her. And I'm starting to worry. She's been sick a lot since I've gone back to work, and she's in daycare, and I've had to take a lot of time off work, and I'm getting close to going over my allotted amount of days. And so I'm finding myself being very anxious about that and then feeling guilty because when I'm trying to take care of her, I'm always worrying about work. So.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a couple things may be going on. Child. Child's been sick, so you're taking off days. So you're a little worried about your relationship with your employer. At the same time, you want to make sure you're taking good care of your child, so you're having trouble reconciling those two.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. What was the last time it happened? Can you describe what happened the last.
Client: Time I had to take off work? It was just this week. She woke up one morning with a really high fever, so I had to call out that day, and then she still had a fever the next day, and then I had to take a third day because she has to be fever free before she can go back to daycare. So the first day was, I was okay with that. But then, like, the second. And then when I started realizing that I was going to have to take a third day, then I really start to get kind of panicky and worried about it.
Counselor: All right, so let me see. Let's go through each day. So the first day when you discovered that she was sick, right. What were you thinking then when you had to call out of work?
Client: Well, because she's been sort of sick a lot lately, I was a little bit worried, and I was sort of, you know, I have this number, ten, because I only have ten days for the whole year. So I have this number in my head, and I just thought, well, there's one more day I gotta take away from that ten that I have. And. But I was able to sort of think about. I was a little worried about any work that I would miss, you know, keeping up with my caseload and stuff at work, so. But I was able to kind of figure out that I would be okay for a day. And I can kind of make up for that when I get back.
Counselor: Okay, so your thinking was, this isn't ideal, but I can live with it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just one day, right? How about on day two when you realize that you're going to have to take a second day?
Client: Then I got a little bit more worried. And then I did start to also, you know, add the worry of I was going to start to get behind at work. Not only was I missing more time, but I was also going to be behind on my work. So then I started thinking, when I go back, it's going to be a mad scramble to kind of catch up and keep up with everything and, you know, so then it became worrying about my workload and worrying about taking more time.
Counselor: Okay, so a little more stressful version of what happened on day one. And then how about when you discovered that you had to take a third day off?
Client: I was. Then it was just more amplified, you know, amplified worry. And it was a lot harder for me to let it go. I just kept thinking. I kept going back to it. And then I started feeling guilty because I was so preoccupied, worried about that. And I was trying to answer emails and do some stuff and send out some emails to people that I work with to try to help me out with things at work since I wasn't there. And then I felt guilty because I wasn't really caring for my child as best as I felt I should have been. You know, I started feeling kind of like a bad mom.
Counselor: So, so guilty and a bad mom. And that was mostly on the third day? That was the worst of it, yes. Now, did this go up against the weekend? It was the third day, Friday. So then you kind of knew that by Monday things would be able to return to work. So tell me what happened when you returned to work on Monday.
Client: Well, I checked in with the main office and, you know, I just said, I'm really, you know, I'm starting to worry. I'm getting. I know I had to take a lot of time, but you. I've done the best I can to try to make other arrangements, but just starting back in, starting in daycare, she's just been sick a lot and I can't control it. I'm doing the best I can. I asked them if there was anything I needed to do as far as providing doctor's notes and stuff, and they said, no, they don't need a doctor's note since it was my daughter that was sick. They said there's nothing, nothing that I really can do and just try to not have it happen much more if I can just do what I can to not miss more.
Counselor: So they said that to you?
Client: Yeah, but. Yeah.
Counselor: How did they frame that?
Client: They kind of just said, you know, do what you can to not have it happen, but if it, you know, if it has to happen, you know, what can I do about it? It's kind of. They were saying.
Counselor: So they were understanding.
Client: I didn't feel like they were that understanding, but I also didn't feel like they were gonna take any punitive action against me. Right. Right then and there or anything.
Counselor: Did you anticipate a worse reaction than you experienced?
Client: Yeah, I did. And I also anticipated that they would maybe have more of a procedure for how to handle it, and they didn't have a procedure, which also made me feel a little worried. I can't imagine I'm the first mom that has had to deal with this. And they kind of talked like it's never happened before, so I kind of felt anxious because I thought, am I really the first mom that's had to take a lot of time off because their child's sick? They didn't give me the impression that they had sort of a protocol or like they had dealt with this before.
Counselor: Right. So sort of like it took them by surprise.
Client: Yeah. Or they just didn't have a plan for what to do about it.
Counselor: They weren't investing a lot of energy in thinking about that?
Client: No. No, I guess nothing.
Counselor: And when was this again? How long ago?
Client: Just this past week.
Counselor: So how has this week been? Bag of work?
Client: Oh, it's been very busy because I'm trying to catch up and get everything handled, but that's the way it always is. So nobody has said anything to me or anything about the absences other than that first, yeah.
Counselor: And there have been no more absences. Okay. Earlier you mentioned being a good mom. What does a good mom look like?
Client: Somebody who takes care of their child and puts them. Makes them a priority, like their first priority, and, you know, does the things that they need to do to make sure they're child is taken care of.
Counselor: And you're a little worried through this last experience you were telling me about that you didn't rise to the level of good mom.
Client: Yeah, I felt like I wasn't being a good mom because I was preoccupied and making work a bit of a bigger priority than taking care of my kidney.
Counselor: Okay. So good mom's more about. More than just rather your behavior, what you're doing. It's about what you're also thinking. So you took care of your child.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But your mind, your thoughts were somewhere else some of the time, and that's where you feel like you've wandered out of the good mom area. Okay, how about on the other side? How about a good employee? Did you mention that you want to be a good employee?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. What's that look like?
Client: Well, somebody that, you know, takes care of all of their workload and handles all of the tasks that they have each day, and someone that's consistent and reliable and, you know, puts effort into what they're doing and gets their job done, really, you know, reliably.
Counselor: And that's where you feel like with this. So the last eight work days you missed. You missed three. Okay, how about in the last year, how many days have you missed?
Client: Well, I missed a lot for maternity leave, certainly.
Counselor: Understandable.
Client: But excluding that I've missed since the school year started, I've missed. If you include the three, I've missed nine days. But some of those were half days. They add up to nine days.
Counselor: Okay, total nine days?
Client: Yeah. And you're allowed ten per school year? For school year, it's only January and I'm already at nine.
Counselor: I can see where that would cause worry. What happens if you go over the.
Client: I don't know. I mean, I think that they would dock my pay for those. If I was there a day and I didn't have any more sick days left, they would just dock my pay for that day. But outside of that, I don't know what else would happen.
Counselor: Is there anybody that you work with that you could ask that question to, like an HR department?
Client: Yeah, I guess I could contact the HR department.
Counselor: I'm just thinking. Cause you're just one day away from being at that number, might be prudent just to talk with them and see. So you know what to expect.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So this is this whole thing, though, the missing days cause you anxiety, frustration?
Client: Yeah, a little bit, yeah.
Counselor: How about any type of feeling down at all?
Client: A little bit. Sometimes when I start feeling like I'm a bad mom.
Counselor: Okay, so as far as your child is concerned, your relationship with your child, you have some anxiety, relationship at work, some anxiety. But the sadness mostly surrounds how you feel you're treating your child. Of all the emotions, frustration, anxiety, what I'll refer to as depression, let's just say sadness. What's bothering you the most? What emotional response does bother you most?
Client: Probably sort of the guilt and the feelings of not being able to be the best mom.
Counselor: How would you rate yourself right now as a mother if, say, ten was the best mother you could imagine. Right. And one was the absolute worst.
Client: Probably like, I don't know, an eight.
Counselor: An eight? Okay. That's pretty good, right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What would be the cutoff to where. What's the cutoff score in that little scale I just gave you for good mother and not good mother?
Client: I guess, like halfway, like.
Counselor: So five is good enough?
Client: Yeah, I don't feel like it's good enough for me.
Counselor: Okay. Okay.
Client: I wouldn't be okay with that.
Counselor: So if you looked at somebody else, another person in a similar situation, a five would be acceptable, right?
Client: Probably, yeah.
Counselor: But how about for you specifically?
Client: Yeah, that's not.
Counselor: That's not gonna cut it. What would cut it?
Client: Um. I don't know. At least a seven.
Counselor: At least a seven, yeah. And you're an eight?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Sure.
Client: No, not sure.
Counselor: Okay. So you're close to the border. I feel like you're close to the border and you're.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Out of your value system of being not a good mother.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: What happens if you.
Client: Well, as good a mother as I want to be.
Counselor: Okay. How good do you want to be?
Client: Yeah, I want to be like an eight or higher.
Counselor: Eight or higher. Well, you are an eight, you said.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so you want to be a ten, sounds like.
Client: Well, yeah. Doesn't everybody want to be the best at what they do?
Counselor: I mean, I think people are driven to do their best, but is it crucial to be perfect? Is it crucial to be a tendency.
Client: No, there's some leeway. I guess you have to allow for that.
Counselor: Remember before, in other sessions, for other situations you've brought in here, we talked about dysfunctional thinking, irrational thinking. How does when you reflect on that, like, the usefulness of these thoughts, that other mothers can be a five and be. And that's good, right. You need to be an eight or higher. Eight, nine or ten. Does this seem useful, like a useful way of thinking?
Client: In some ways it's useful because it keeps me. It keeps me on track, if that makes sense. It keeps me pushing to keep doing the best I can. Driven.
Counselor: Motivated.
Client: Yeah, motivated.
Counselor: So it does have a useful side. Does it have an unuseful side, a less than useful side?
Client: Well, yeah, I guess it does. In the sense that if I become too worried about it, then I'm wasting energy on worry instead of being able to put that energy into being a good mom.
Counselor: Yeah. So I guess one of the things I'm getting at here is has the worry. Has the anxiety and the worry paid off for you?
Client: Probably not.
Counselor: Probably not. So you're suffering with it. It might make you a little more vigilante, but mostly it's just causing you to suffer.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So at the heart of it, you're not a bad mom. You're in the good mom category. You're a good employee. But your way of valuing yourself, your perception, is that you're not doing a great job at either one.
Client: Mm hmm. Exactly.
Counselor: And that's the thinking I'm getting at. It's not, you know, it's not necessarily irrational. I'm thinking it's just less than useful. Right. It's dysfunctional.
Client: Yeah, I can see that.
Counselor: Yeah. We're talking about that third day, right? The third day of work you had to. You had to call off. And do you remember any of the specific thoughts that were going through your mind on that? Was that a morning when you figured it out? Like a Friday morning?
Client: Yeah. No, it was really the night before. But, you know, I went as far as to think, am I going to get fired? You know, I had to kind of think about that.
Counselor: So your thought was, am I going to get fired?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And then what was the feeling that came right after that?
Client: Um. Panic.
Counselor: Panic?
Client: Worry. Oh, yeah.
Counselor: Maybe some anxiety.
Client: Some anxiety, yeah.
Counselor: Were you able to do anything to address that panic or your anxiety at that time? Like, did you tell yourself anything or did you take some action?
Client: I did tell myself that I didn't go over yet, and, you know, hopefully I won't. You know, there's still a chance that I'm not going to go over all my days, and hopefully it won't go so far as to fire me, you know?
Counselor: And how'd you feel after you consciously had that thought?
Client: A little bit better, but the thought still kept hovering around. Yeah.
Counselor: The whole time. Probably all the way till Monday. Right. When you return to work.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Like, I wanted to call somebody at work and talk to them about it and make sure it was okay, but, you know, it was the weekend, so I couldn't do any of those things. I just had to wait it out. Yeah.
Counselor: So we've talked before about self talk. You might remember me saying the phrase adaptive response. Right. So it's the kind of pre packaged response we have to thoughts that we've identified is not so useful.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So would you agree to those thoughts, like, am I gonna get fired and all that? Not very useful in that moment.
Client: Yes. Not useful in that moment.
Counselor: Understandable. Right. But not useful. So what's now? You had sort of some self talk that you applied on your own. What's some other self talk. What's some other. Another thought that you could think or something you can said yourself that could counter an automatic thought like that? Like specifically that I'm gonna lose my job.
Client: Well, I guess I could say, you know, I didn't, you know, I'm not, I haven't had any conversations with anybody that have indicated that. So sort of like maybe I just need to not worry about it or cross that bridge when I come to it kind of thing. Like, hopefully it won't, I don't know if it will happen or not, and hopefully it won't happen.
Counselor: So the self talk there is, there's no clear indication that it's going to happen.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So why borrow the worry? Right. How about other, how about adaptive behaviors? We talked about the importance of support systems before in other sessions. Is there anybody else that could watch your child if you were really running up against that?
Client: Yeah, my mom can sometimes. I did call her this, this week to see if she could take one of take a day, but she couldn't because of what she had going on. But in another time she might be able to take a day and stay home or my sister can do that as well and my husband can sometimes it depends on what is going on that week for him at work. So there are some options there.
Counselor: Did you explore those options for this last time?
Client: I did, I did. But just the circumstances didn't work out.
Counselor: So none of those individuals were available.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Is there any other options you have for care? Is that it?
Client: That's really it. You know, when she's sick, that's really it. Because I don't want to put her around any other kids, which is why I wouldn't send her to daycare.
Counselor: So that seems reasonable. Okay. There are some things you've already done right. And I think at this point, since to address, I know this is the lesser of your worries, which is your employer. You're more worried about being a good mom. But to go look at the employer side for a second, you can talk to HR, you can try to understand what the consequences are for going over, explain that it doesn't appear to be your fault. And I don't know what you can do in terms support. Maybe try to get a better awareness of the schedules when they're available or convey the nature of your problem to them to get some more support.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So that was one issue. Now you highlighted more prominently, though, the good mother. I want to touch on that as well. You did everything you had to do to care for your child?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Are you sure?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. 100%.
Client: Except for my thinking I was maybe a little not as present as I should have been.
Counselor: Okay. And we'll get to that. But your behavior.
Client: But behavior. Yeah.
Counselor: You did everything a good mom would do.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So is it okay if you're doing everything you need to do to think thoughts that don't seem congruent with that, you know, that distract you away from that?
Client: I guess it's not ideal, but it's okay.
Counselor: It's not ideal. So you'd really rather have the ability to be really focused on what's going on with your child to the exclusion of what's going on in other circumstances?
Client: Yeah. Or at least be able to put my worry about the other circumstances aside for that time period.
Counselor: So by addressing the employer issue, that might give you a little relief on the good mom issue. So here's another opportunity to talk about dysfunctional thoughts. I think that as you reflect on whether you're a good mom or not, you're really basing it on this idea that if I'm thinking about something other than my child, I'm in the wrong place in terms of being a good mom, you're only being distracted.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So that pushes you on that one to ten scale.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: The more thoughts you have like that, you think of it as, like, pushing you down toward five.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So when you have those thoughts, what's an adaptive response or, you know, self talk? What can you tell yourself in those moments.
Client: That I'm doing? I'm behaving, doing the behaviors that I need to do. And the baby doesn't know what I'm thinking, so probably not. She doesn't know whether I'm distracted or worried, so I'm not doing any harm to her.
Counselor: Who does know you're distracted or worried?
Client: I guess just me. Yeah.
Counselor: So the self talk there would be, I'm doing what I have to do to be a good mom, and that's what my child sees. But I have these understandable thoughts that come in where I worry about other things and more or less just is what it is. I mean, you're permitted to worry about things. Life isn't going to be worry free.
Client: True.
Counselor: But we can. We can work to not suffer more than we have to.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Does that kind of make sense?
Client: Yeah, it makes sense. And, you know, when you say it back to me, the things that I'm saying, it does sound a little bit irrational or unhelpful.
Counselor: Less than useful?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Yeah, a little less than useful. It's not, you know, I want. And this is an important distinction. It's not good or bad, and those words have a function in our lives, but they're a little dangerous when applied in terms of mental health. When they're applied to things like good mom, bad mom, it doesn't leave a lot of gray area to talk about improvement. Also, it seems like from what you're describing, you're way into the good mom category anyway. If you're an eight, a ten, I think most people would be happy with an eight out of ten.
Client: True.
Counselor: So it's not like you've drifted down toward five or four somewhere. Okay, so there's a couple different. I know we talked about two different subjects, right. But they're related. The work situation and the situation of caring for your child. But those are some self talk strategies. So what I'd like you to do when you go home today, and I would. I would ask that you do it today if you can. I think it's important that it stays in terms of time near when we're having this conversation.
Client: Right.
Counselor:
output: If you could try to document some of those automatic thoughts. I remember I gave you a worksheet before. Right. And then work on some of your own. We'll call them adaptive responses.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Andrew. How you doing today?
Client: Hey, Doug. Nice to see you.
Counselor: Nice to see you. It's been about a week since I seen you last. I know you're having some different difficulties, particularly at work.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Any changes there?
Client: Not really. I mean, it's pretty much the same pace. I'm very frustrated with the whole system. I'm working with inner city kids, african american kids, males in particular. And, you know, I sit and talk with these kids and I realize that there's not much I can do for them. You know, for the most part, we're talking about, you know, criminal arrest, drug abuse, you know, no education. And, you know, I don't know what I can really do for them anymore. I mean, you know, I sit and talk to them, but really, in terms of their statistics, it's looking pretty bad for them. So, you know, I get pretty frustrated and it's kind of depressing to do this every day.
Counselor: All right, so as you're working with these use, you're looking at their circumstances and you're saying the odds just don't look good for major improvement. That's leading you to lose hope in your ability to help them into different circumstances.
Client: Absolutely, yeah. I mean, it's just their reality. A kid comes in and mom is either dad's incarcerated, rotted, a picture. Mom is either on drugs or not fully engaged. And this kid has absolutely no life skills. None. He's self medicating or smoking marijuana. At the very least, it's marijuana. And he is just totally convinced that, you know, this is who he is the rest of his life. And he's sitting in front of me looking for answers, and I don't know if I have him.
Counselor: What kind of questions do they ask you?
Client: It's not even questions as more as it is just statements of, you know, this is my life, you know, the struggle is real. This is what I do, this is where I am. And, you know, anything other than this is not even, you know, I didn't fathom. So I'm sitting here, just kidding, I'm trying to draw him out of that whole mindset. But we're talking about years of social conditioning, years and years and years of it. And I just don't know if, you know, I have the skills and the tools to really break through that way of thinking.
Counselor: All right, so can you think of a particular case, particular youth that you're working with that, where you're finding the struggle. I just think of one particular individual where you're frustrated, you're making these statements that kind of. This is the way it is. They don't seem like they have much hope. You don't seem like they have much hope for them. Right. So you have one in mind.
Client: Yes, they do.
Counselor: Okay, so what's his self statement? What's he saying to you that you think is getting a reaction from you?
Client: That he's a drug dealer. He's going to continue to be a drug dealer. He's not going to stop. And that he's involved with gang activity, and that's his family. It's the only family he's ever known, and he's loyal to them. And that loyalty is deep. And he has absolutely no. Even the thought of going back to prison doesn't shape this kid.
Counselor: Not afraid of that.
Client: Not afraid of it for them. Gerald is like going to the school courtyard. There's all his boys in jail. So I'm sitting here like, what in the hell am I doing here with this kid? You know, what kind of options do I give him when I don't even believe he has any at this point?
Counselor: So that's really your automatic thought, is I don't believe he has any options. That's what's going through your mind when he says things like he's involved in gang activity and wants to continue dealing drugs? That's your thought?
Client: That's my thought, yeah.
Counselor: There's no way out for him.
Client: I don't see it. I just don't. I really don't see it for him. You know, he's self medicating. He's giving dirty urine to the probation office. He doesn't care. The judge has given them pass after pass after pass. But the kid just seems intent to, you know, to live this life.
Counselor: So in a sense, your mood, the sadness, the frustration is linked to, for example, this use statements and his philosophy. So he's saying that success is not an option, as you would think of success.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And you're reacting to that, and your mood is moving because of that.
Client: Yes. Yes. And I mean, to a certain degree, I understand where he's coming from. I mean, I was raised with the understanding that you were born black. That's one strike. You were born male. That's two strikes. A criminal arrest record, that's it. Life is over. So to a certain degree, his perception is reality. So I can't disagree with him. But at the same time, this is my job. And I'm having a very difficult time trying to give this kidde any glimpse of hope, which I don't even think he really wants.
Counselor: So it's hard for you to give the hope, and I'm sure he's looking for the hope. And you can understand his situation in terms of being african american, being male and having the criminal record and how that seems to stack the deck severely against him.
Client: Severely, yeah. And that's nothing. I mean, there's some truth to that. I don't know. That criminal arrest record, a conviction in this country pretty much relegates you to a certain level of society, in my.
Counselor: Opinion, in terms of employment opportunities.
Client: In terms of employment opportunity and things like that. So to a certain degree, I understand where he's coming from. It's just an absolute sense of hopelessness that comes from this kid. He'll sit in front of me and he'll just laugh. He'll laugh about it like, Mister D, this is my life. Why are you tripping? Why do you care so much? So I'm just starting not to carry.
Counselor: So you're starting to mirror that approach, the approach he's using.
Client: Yes, I am.
Counselor: So what's bothering you in all this? Not only the circumstances, the racism, the discrimination, the circumstances in with the criminal record, that all bothers you, but also you're bothered because you're losing hope for him.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And for others like him.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: Have you expressed that thought? Sentiment?
Client: No, I haven't. Not in so many words. Not, you know, because to do that, I think, gives the kid credibility. I don't want to increase to his way of thinking if I, you know, agree with him on doing that, giving him a license to be an asshole, so to speak.
Counselor: You don't want to let on that his loss of hope is really. You kind of share that, in a way. You get it. You understand that.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: His lack of hope is grounded in a lot of reality.
Client: Yes, exactly.
Counselor: At the same time, you do this work every day. Do you believe there's hope at some level?
Client: Absolutely. I do believe at my core, I do believe there is hope at some level. I believe in resilience. I think once you tap into it, you can pretty much achieve anything. But it's just hard to peel back so many different layers with this particular generation of kids. It really takes a lot out of you.
Counselor: It's hard to get through.
Client: Hard to get through. Hard to penetrate that shell. So I leave work someday saying, I'm not coming back. We've had enough, you know, and it's depressing after all.
Counselor: So let's go back to that automatic thought. When a youth like the one that you were talking about makes a statement like, you know, their life is essentially defined in this and these narrow parameters, drug dealing and maybe other criminality or other behaviors that aren't productive, and you're kind of thinking there's some truth to that and you're kind of thinking there may not be hope. That's kind of the automatic thoughts or something close to the automatic thoughts. You're having much?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Your reaction to that is to not help them or to not say what you feel to them. What's going on?
Client: I don't want to say what I feel because I think they don't possess the filter to be able to understand it, to understand it. So I think for them it's going to be a license to continue the behavior. So I just hit them bullshit for half an hour, 45 minutes. Because what I really want to say, I don't think it would be beneficial to him.
Counselor: Partially because of the message, but partially because of how they would interpret the message.
Client: Very good.
Counselor: There's two levels to that.
Client: Right? That's how they would interpret the message. I think the message is, you know, for the right person with the right kind of filter would be receivable. But I think how they interpret it is going to be the issue.
Counselor:
output: Right. So what is the message? Tell me what you would want to say to them.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Now, one thing I thought we might do today is to get an example of one of these situations in which you get really anxious and try to see if we can understand more about how you think and how you feel when you're in the middle of one of those situations. So can you think of an example of something that's happened recently?
Client: Yeah. My daughter has been. She's actually been sick, and so she had a fever yesterday, and they started her on an antibiotic, and I had to go pick it up from the drugstore, and that's like, I don't usually go there. It's hard to get there. Like, it's not right in the neighborhood.
Counselor: Any expressways or bridges to get there?
Client: Not expressways, but it's busy. It's busier. It's like in a mall.
Counselor: So, you know, any four lanes or six lane?
Client: Four lanes
Counselor: Yeah, four lane.
Client: So it just. It's not someplace I usually would go. And if I was gonna go, usually I would either have her go with me or my husband go with me. But she was sick, and he was at work, and so to try to.
Counselor: Understand what goes through your mind, let's try to take you back. And now you know that the prescription's there, and your daughter's sick, and I guess you don't want to ask her to drive over there.
Client: I sort of did, yeah.
Counselor: Probably not the wisest idea. So you're thinking about doing the drive, and what's going through your mind? What are the thoughts that are turning inside?
Client: I'm just, you know, I'm sort of thinking about going there, and I'm already starting to think, well, you know, what if. You know, what if I'm driving and somebody crashes into me? What if I'm driving and I can't do it? What if I just have to stop because I can't do it anymore? And it was raining, and I'm sort of like. I've got this picture of myself out in the middle of the road, you.
Counselor: Know, what's the picture look like? You're out in the middle of the.Road, and it's raining,
Client: it's stranded, and it's dark, and my, you know, my shoes are gone. I'm just like. It's like it would be a million miles to get back home.
Counselor: Pretty miserable.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: Pretty scary.
Client: Oh, terrifying.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: And I just. It's so hard to get there.
Counselor: And, Kate, as you put yourself back into that situation and have those thoughts going through your mind, what kinds of feelings go along with it? By feelings, I mean things that are inside, like, physical, like the physical anxiety. Physical things are going on.
Client: Well, fear and anxiety. And I just feel really shaky and I feel really, like, lightheaded and dizzy, and I just don't feel like I can breathe very well. And I feel like I'm gonna, like, fall over.
Counselor: Is this a panic attack? Now, you told me about having some panic attacks.
Client: I've had worse ones, but it's getting there.
Counselor: Not quite to a panic, but, you know, it's brewing.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah, it feels like it might.
Counselor: Yeah. Yeah. What I think we might do to try to move things along toward getting a plan of attack on this is to actually sketch this out and see if we can figure out some things we might be able to start doing to give you a better handle on it that you have right now.
Client: Okay
Counselor: so let's put some boxes here. And one of them is going to be event. These are the things that trigger your anxiety. And in this case, the event was.
Client: Having to drive to the pharmacy.
Counselor: Drive to pharmacy. And then this next box, I'm going to label something we call automatic thoughts. And by automatic, I mean that they occur relatively automatically. They just sort of pop into your mind and you don't stop to check them out. And we all have these kinds of automatic thoughts. You know, I have them. Everybody I know has them. They're inner thoughts. In fact, if you think about it for a minute, we probably have a lot more thoughts. We don't speak out loud that are part of our inner dialogue than thoughts. We actually end up speaking aloud to other people. And I suspect that you have lots of those thoughts, and you just gave me some examples of them. So that's why we call them automatic.
Client: So, like the what ifs.
Counselor: Yeah. So let's put a couple of those down in this box.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: In the automatic thought box. And they are.
Client: What if someone runs into me?
Counselor: Yeah, what if. What else?
Client: What if I get stranded?
Counselor: Get stranded? Uh huh.
Client: Um. I can't do it.
Counselor: I can't do it. And then there was this image about the rainstorm, and you don't have your shoes on and so forth. What should we put down for that?
Client: I think, what if I. What if I can't get back home?
Counselor: I can't get back on sort of lost.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. What if I end up on this road forever?
Counselor: And then we're going to put another box. There's a sort of a chain of events here. The event can make you think in ways that stir up feelings of anxiety and so forth. So if you're thinking like this, it makes sense that you'd be feeling pretty nervous inside, and you might have some of these physical reactions. So let's put those in here. This is the emotions box, and they are much shaky, you said?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: A lot of fear.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: If we're going to rate that fear on a zero to 100 scale, and zero is none at all and 100 is the maximum anyone could ever get, where would you be at this point?
Client: Oh, I'd say about an 80.
Counselor: 80? Pretty high.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: It's gone higher, though, I suspect I. Oh, yeah, yeah. But at this point, it's an 80. Okay. And then you had some other feelings inside.
Client: Well, yeah, I sort of felt like I might fall over. What else? My heart was pounding and I didn't feel like I could breathe.
Counselor: How about your stomach?
Client: Any flip flops in your stomach or anything like that?
Counselor: So a lot going on here and a pretty high level of distress.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. And then we're going to complete this loop by putting a box we're going to call behavior. This is how you actually acted when you were in this situation. So what did you do after you had these thoughts and you had these feelings?
Client: Went to the pharmacy.
Counselor: You did do it.
Client: I had to.
Counselor: Okay. And what was it like for you when you were going to the pharmacy and driving there?
Client: It was so bad. I just, you know, I think I left permanent marks on the steering wheel because I was holding onto it, gripping tightly.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: So in this case, you actually did go to the pharmacy, but maybe did some damage to the steering wheel.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, Ed, do you want to tell me a little bit about what's going on?
Client: Well, everything changed.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: It changed. This last Friday or Saturday was my birthday. 13th birthday.
Counselor: Happy birthday.
Client: Well, it wasn't a happy birthday.
Counselor: What happened?
Client: We had a little party at my house. My cousin came, and then my cousin said that somehow joking around said, you're lucky, man, and that they adopted you.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And then I just found out on my 13th birthday that I was adopted.
Counselor: Okay, so you had no idea before that.
Client: And that was. I just feel. I've never been. I just don't feel the same. I don't feel the same about my parents. I don't know. They're not really my parents, but I call them Ruth and Abe.
Counselor: Wait, what? What? Okay, hang on. You found out you were adopted and you were upset. Upset, I understand. Upset because you didn't know. Is that. That's part of it?
Client: Yeah. And then I. Then I wonder what's the matter with me.
Counselor: What's the matter? Okay, I got three I'm gonna write on this board. Are you okay with that?
Client: Sure.
Counselor: You have three things that are. Okay, so give me the right word. Upset. Angry. Mad that you didn't know, mad that.
Client: I. Mad that I didn't know and.
Counselor: Mad I didn't know. Okay. And then you said, they're not my parents anymore, so I'm gonna. So that's. That's sort of one thing. And then not my parents.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And then you said something else.
Client: That I. Well, I want to know what's wrong with me.
Counselor: What's wrong?
Client: That's probably the biggest thing. Do you think something's wrong with me?
Counselor: No. I want to help you. So these are just three sentences that you said that I think if we look at each one of them, we could get you feeling a little better by the time you look. Leave today. Okay. What's wrong with me? Okay, so the first one, feeling angry, not knowing that seems like a pretty normal feeling to me. You know, if I thought that I was my kids biological parent, and I found out that I wasn't, I can understand that. Okay. As a counselor, and I'm a mom. As a mom, I get that. All right? Not my parents. Help me understand that. Why aren't they your parents anymore?
Client: Well, because I have other. Two other parents, obviously.
Counselor: Right.
Client: That didn't want me.
Counselor: Well, we. I mean, do you know the circumstances of the adoption? Did your parents share that with you?
Client: Well, they just said they got me when I was about two days old, that my mother was a 16 year old.
Counselor: Okay, so your biological mother was really young?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And she couldn't. Wasn't able to care for you.
Client: I figured something was wrong with me.
Counselor: Well, how old are you?
Client: I'm 13. I was just 13 Friday.

Client: Right.

Client: Yes.

Client: That all this, that what you said is real, that, you know, with a criminal arrest record, you know, your circumstances growing up in the city, broken homes, racism. It's real. Client: Yes.

Client: Yeah.

Client: It was. It was a family member, but I don't really like talking about it.
