Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. As a child, you know, sometimes parents aren't very available, don't provide basic food, clothing, shelter, that kind of thing. Did you ever have that experience of being neglected? Hmm? What's going on, Tricia?
Client: I don't like all these questions.
Counselor: Yeah? Starting to get uncomfortable, huh? You feel that somewhere in your body, you're feeling that in your. Your body? Yeah. Sometimes these questions can bring up very difficult things. I know. Sorry. When you're feeling like this, what helps you?
Client: My cat.
Counselor: Hmm. Tell me about your cat.
Client: She's a jerk. She's a jerk? Yeah. She's not very friendly. Um, she's friendly to me, though, when I'm really upset. She, uh, she'll, like, cuddle with me on the bed and stuff, so she knows when I'm really upset. But it's great that she knows. Yeah.
Counselor: That's pretty amazing.
Client: She's just kind of a jerk. She'll bite and scratch it, whoever she wants to. She wants to be snuggled until she doesn't want to be snuggled.
Counselor: What's her name?
Client: Persephone.
Counselor: Persephone. That's a great name for a cat.
Client: She came with it, and I decided to just leave it.
Counselor: Wow. I like it a lot.
Client: Great.
Counselor: It's wonderful to have a cat named Persephone who's good at helping you when your feelings are difficult. That's really good. That's, you know, that's a blessing there. Can we go on with the interview now?
Client: Yeah, I guess.
Counselor: Okay. About continuing. Okay. I'm going to ask you some different questions. I want to ask you a little bit about your living situation. So what kind of housing do you live in?
Client: I have an apartment.
Counselor: Mm hmm. And how long have you lived there?
Client: Almost a year.
Counselor: So not that long. And who do you live with?
Client: Just the cat.
Counselor: Just per second. Okay. Do you feel safe where you live?
Client: Safer than when I was homeless.
Counselor: Mm hmm. Safer, but maybe not entirely safe.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. What makes you not feel that safe where you live?
Client: I've kind of a. Have a landlord situation. Mm.
Counselor: Difficult relationship with your landlord?
Client: You could say that.
Counselor: Can you tell me about it?
Client: I don't. I don't make a lot of money, and my hours got cut at work recently, and he said he was going to evict me, and I really didn't want to be homeless again, so he said if I had sex with him that I wouldn't have to pay my rent.
Counselor: Wow. That's really hard. It makes sense. So you agreed to that I didn't.
Client: Want to be homeless again.
Counselor: That's right. And in order to survive, anyone is going to do what they have to do. Right.
Client: But it sounds like that's what I keep telling myself.
Counselor: Mm hmm. But it's also upsetting you a lot.
Client: I just keep thinking, like, what if somebody finds out? And now I told you so, obviously people are gonna find out.
Counselor: Well, what do you mean people?
Client: Well, I mean, don't you have to tell people when stuff like that happens?
Counselor: No, actually, what you and I discuss is between us, and you'll get to decide what you want to do about that situation so we can talk about it. But you get to decide. I only have to disclose if you're going to kill yourself or someone else to somebody else. Those are, you know, or if you're abusing an elder. Those are the circumstances under which I have to let other people know. So this is something that's just for you and I to talk about. And as part of, you know, our work together, we can decide what's the best way to take care of yourself going forward. So it's entirely up to you what we do from here. And I totally appreciate the courage it took to let me know that that was happening. And I'm happy to be with you as you sort out what's really the best path for you going forward for your own well being. We'll work on that together. Does that make sense to you?
Client: Kind of. No one's ever said it to me like that before, so I thought you had to tell people. But no. If not, but no.
Counselor: And I should tell you that. Remember how I said earlier in the interview that people who've had adverse experiences like sexual abuse in their past or physical abuse in their past, that sometimes that's connected to what happens going forward?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Well, it's not. It's really common for girls who've experienced sexual abuse later in life to end up using or being in a position where they end up using that for survival purposes. So what you're experiencing is actually probably a lot more common than you think. But just like you didn't want to talk about it, you know, the reason you don't know that other people are doing that is because they don't have often talk about it. So that way you think you're the only one in the world who ever ended up in this position. But in reality, lots of girls who've experienced sexual abuse grow up and it changes something that then they end up putting themselves, they end up in situations. Now, obviously you didn't create this situation. Your landlord is the one who is proposing to use his position of power to get you to do something that isn't what you want to do. And you're not responsible for his doing that. You're not. You're just doing what you've learned to do to help you survive. And we can work together for you to figure out what other options you have and what else you can do. Do.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Good. Thanks. Thanks for being so open. So are you ready to continue with the rest of the interview?

Client: Well, maybe I should have come to.

Counselor: And maybe this is good, you know, for something for the future, you know, that will help you think. Okay, a few alarm bells are ringing here. Maybe I'm just going to go by my own instincts and have a chat with them, rather. And, okay, you talk to Laura and Bob and whoever else you spoke to, and they gave you your opinion, their opinion, you know, and ultimately it is up to you how far you want to take something. But, you know, if things don't work out as you expected, you shouldn't take it to heart and blame yourself because, you know, this world is not made for perfectionists.
Client: No, no, I suppose not. I just. I don't know, I just thought I'd have maybe more time to talk to him or. I suppose I just hoped that he would come to me. But, you know, I really hate to fail my students.
Counselor: Let's look at that one. You hate to fail your students? What does it mean to fail your students?
Client: Well, you know, to let something like this happen. You know, I want my students not just to learn English, but to grow and mature and be happy. I hate to think of them being miserable and not being able to talk to someone. I want to be that person for them.
Counselor: So let's review what you mean when you say that you had something like this happen. What do you mean that, you know, you shouldn't let something like this happen?
Client: Well, you know, to care for our students.
Counselor: Yes.
Client: To help them through difficult times. Right.
Counselor: You know, and how do you envisage doing that when you barely know a child and you don't? You see them three times a week and he's only been at the school for a few. A few weeks. So I suppose, really, how logically is it for you to take that all on board?
Client: Well, I suppose I want them to know that they can talk to me.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I mean, that's not my job. You know, you're the counsellor, but I'd like to be able to let them know that there's help for them.
Counselor: Sure.
Client: And guide them towards you. Maybe not do it all myself, but, you know, I don't like to think that I just send them on their way, not caring about them.
Counselor: But you. You know yourself that you do care about them. Yeah. And, you know, building a relationship with students does take time. So, you know, in the situation with you and Vince, you know that that wasn't going to happen when he needed it because he barely knew you. And his structures around the school where you only see him three times a week, you know, that doesn't support. That doesn't support a relationship building approach either. So how can you blame yourself for not having that opportunity to build that relationship, to let them know that you are there, to listen, you know, lots of other factors in play here, Liz.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So, you know, let's think about what you were talking about before, you know, how you led this to happen. Do you still think you. You led this to happen?
Client: Well, no. I mean, I still kind of feel like I should have done something and maybe he still would have tried to kill himself, but, you know, I just feel that, you know, what if I had taken a moment to talk to him, okay? You know, just to let one. Him know that one person noticed, and it might not have changed anything, but it might have.
Counselor: And it might have. You're absolutely right. It might have. But we'll never know that. And there's your shoulds and what ifs. We can't change the past, but we can use the past to help us in the future. All right?
Client: Yeah. And.
Counselor: But I know. I'm still really concerned that you might think that you had at least something to do with this. But when you first came in here, you were really distressed. All right? Like, so on a scale of one to five, you were a five.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Now, how are you feeling now?
Client: I don't know. I mean, you know, talking about it does sort of put things into perspective. I mean, that. That's been great, you know?
Counselor:
output: Yeah.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good. How about you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How did you do this week?
Client: Better. Well, last time we talked about that postpone gratification. Yeah, that, and I think you wanted ten minutes for me to put it off.
Counselor: Ten minutes, yeah.
Client: So I did better. I think I ended up only doing, like, a joint a half instead of two. I was able to put it off for, I think, the ten minutes a couple times. And then I. There was, I think, one or two days where I went out for a walk because I was tired of staring at the clock, waiting for the ten minutes to pass. So I got up, went for a walk, and then I passed one of my friends, so I ended up walking with her. And I actually didn't get back to my house for, like, an hour, so I kind of put it off for, like, an hour because then I came home and took a couple hits.
Counselor: All right, so it sounds like. It sounds like you were able to maintain waiting ten minutes to smoke marijuana, at least in most cases. It was rough.
Client: It was rough, yeah.
Counselor: So it was difficult for you, but in most cases, you're able to hold off the ten minutes, and it sounds like there was a few instances where you're able to hold it off longer because something else kind of.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Came up.
Client: Yeah, I found I actually, like, talked to a couple people on the phone. Before I knew it, like, a half hour had gone by.
Counselor: So another activity presented itself. And you forgot about the marijuana?
Client: Kind of, yeah. Yeah, I guess I just wasn't thinking about it.
Counselor: So has your. Have your feelings about marijuana changed since we last talked?
Client: No, not really.
Counselor: Tell me about that.
Client: I mean, it's. I don't see it as a problem. It's legal in a lot of states now, and, I mean, it's not that bad for you. It doesn't really endanger me much.
Counselor: So you still. You still believe you should have the right to smoke marijuana?
Client: Yeah, I mean, I'm not hurting anybody.
Counselor: Else, but at the same time, you want to go back to work, and if I remember right, you're the person that you could go work for. I guess you know them, right?
Client: Yeah, it's my uncle.
Counselor: Your uncle. And you need to be clean for, what was it, about two months?
Client: Yeah, I think two to three months.
Counselor: So you have kind of opposing forces here, right? You have your enjoyment of marijuana, and then you. That's something you, like. You don't want to give up, and you believe you should have a right to do that, but then there's that job.
Client: Yeah. I mean, my parents are pretty cool with it. Like, they know, but, I mean, I'm at the point now where they kind of want me to move on and move out. But I don't know. I mean, I just. It'd be nice to have that job. Like, it's a really good job, but at the same time, like, I don't see why I have to sacrifice something that I like.
Counselor: So it doesn't seem fair to you, but she recognizes the reality of your situation. Yeah, it really does come down, in your instance, to marijuana use or employment.
Client: Yeah, it's pretty accurate.
Counselor: Okay, so you're not happy about that choice?
Client: Not at all.
Counselor: Yeah. And kind of what we did with the postponed gratification was just. I mean, I really just ask you to wait ten minutes, and you were able to do that and more. Although it was difficult.
Client: It was difficult.
Counselor: It was difficult for you. So I asked you to track the number of times you smoked marijuana. Did you. Were you able to track that over the last week?
Client: Yeah, for the most part.
Counselor: Do you remember how many times that was?
Client: I think. I think I did, like, 15.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Between 15 and 20.
Counselor: Between 15 and 20. And how many times did something kind of get in the way? Did something else come up in that ten minute span that distracted you or that you enjoyed?
Client: Like, almost closer to 20 times, I guess. Otherwise I probably would have kept going, smoked more. I mean, there were a couple times where, like, somebody would call me or somebody would text me, and that kind of distracted me, so I was able to put it off for a little bit.
Counselor: So you can see in that ten minutes, things can happen. Things can happen that can help you to avoid the marijuana. Sometimes nothing does, and after the ten minutes you use it, and sometimes something does kind of get in the way with the marijuana, like, distract you or you have another activity that you enjoy and then you didn't use. So with that in mind, you found the experience rough. But was it tolerable?
Client: Yeah, it wasn't bad.
Counselor: Was it bad? Do you think for this next week we could try postponing that gratification from ten minutes to 20 minutes?
Client: I don't know. That seems kinda. Yeah, that seems like a longer time.
Counselor: That is definitely. That is a longer time.
Client: I don't know about that.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Maybe like 15 minutes.
Counselor: No, a compromise. Is 15 okay. Yeah. Do you think you could maintain 15 minutes weighing 15?
Client: I think I could try a little bit more than 20.
Counselor: Be a loser than 20. All right, so let's go with 15. Minutes. So 15 minutes is compared to ten. That will give you five extra minutes that something could happen that could distract you and you wouldn't use in that instance. Right. There's also to constructively use that time. You could consider alternatives. Like you mentioned walking. You could use that time and start walking.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Anything else that you like? Maybe in the past, on occasion when you wanted to use marijuana, but you didn't have anything available, what would you.
Client: Do instead, if anything, binge watch tv.
Counselor: Watch tv. Okay, well, so perhaps in that 15 minutes time period that that time you're delaying using marijuana, you could start watching a show that you like.
Client: Yeah, I can do that.
Counselor: At the end of 15 minutes, you might end up using marijuana, or you might want to continue watching the show. So do you see kind of how it works? Is it making sense to you, the postponing?
Client: Yeah, it doesn't make it any easier.
Counselor: But it's tough for you.
Client: Yeah, no, I definitely see how it helps.
Counselor: And maybe if we're successful with the 15, who knows? We can move it up from there.
Client: Maybe. We'll see how the 15 goes.
Counselor: We'll see how it goes with the 15. We'll see how that goes. I'm hoping, and I hope this kind of makes sense, that there'll be a point where you'll be really interfering with the vast majority of the times that you use marijuana because you're giving yourself that many more opportunities. The longer you wait. Right. The more minutes you wait, the more opportunities for something else to get in the way, so to speak. And probably what you'll see, just like you saw this last week, is you used marijuana less frequently just by waiting the ten minutes, even though you described as difficult, and I'm sure it was, but there were a few times where it kind of worked out.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I think that planning something for that time would be helpful. Try to plan something 15 minutes. Even if you fully intend at the end of the 15 to go write and use, I think it's still useful to plan something in there. And you never know where that might take you. You might end up walking or watching tv or doing something else that would distract you or pull you away from the marijuana use.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Does that sound like a plan?
Client: Yeah, I think I can give that a try.
Counselor:
output: Good. And if you do the same thing, if you could kind of write down the number of times that you used, like mark each time you used and kind of what happened in terms of the 15 minutes wait.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Michelle. How you doing today?
Client: Um, I'm kind of doing. I'm feeling a little bit stressed out.
Counselor: Stressed?
Client: Yeah. I feel like I have a lot on my plate. I have this test that I have to take for work.
Counselor: What kind of test?
Client: It's like an aptitude test. It has, like, math problems on it and, like, scenarios in order for me to move up to the assistant manager. Precision.
Counselor: That's a job that you've been interested in for a while?
Client: Yes, it is. Yes. So I've been just feeling a lot of anxiety about taking the test, and then they actually scheduled for me to take the test, and I went and I just got really overwhelmed, and I started, like, I felt my heart was racing. I felt like I wish my hands were shaking. And I just really couldn't concentrate on the test, even though the night before, me and my friend did practice problems and I knew all the answers with no problem, like, I didn't miss any of the questions.
Counselor: So you know the material on this test pretty well.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: But the feelings and that physiological response to heart rate and sweating, that the feelings of anxiety plus those physiological responses, they got in the way of you completing it. Like, you weren't able to complete it?
Client: No, I wasn't able to complete it. And thankfully, they gave me a chance to come back. I just told them I didn't feel well, so they rescheduled. So now I'm feeling a lot of anxiety because I'm scared the same thing's gonna happen when I go back.
Counselor: All right, so you weren't. You weren't feeling great about taking the test in the first place?
Client: The day, the night before, I felt like, I know all the answers, but the minute I walked into the room, all of a sudden, all these fears kind of took over.
Counselor: But did you know that was coming?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You did? Okay.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you had some anxiety in advance. Yes or not? You did? Okay.
Client: I had some anxiety the day before, but when I reviewed it with my friend, I'm like, oh, I know the answer. So I thought that would kind of push it down. But I think once I got there, it all came back up to the surface.
Counselor: It erupted in that moment. And that prevented you. What do you think is leading to this?
Client: Well, I've always kind of struggled with tests. Like, I can remember when I was in third grade, I had to take this test because I was really struggling in math, and I had to pass this test in order to move to the next grade. And I thought, just like this test, that I was ready for it. I had a tutor, and I felt really prepared for it. And then when I took it, I failed and I was held back. And I feel like, you know, that was so. It was. It was really embarrassing for me to be held back. And I felt like. I don't want to say, but I did feel like a failure at the time because I felt like I really did know this. So I don't know why I couldn't pass the test.
Counselor: And since that you said this was third grade?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And since that bad testing experience, have you had trouble with tests since?
Client: Yes, I always feel really anxious. I mean, I'm able to pass tests, obviously, because I graduated from grade school and went on to high school. But it's so hard for me because of this anxiety that I feel that even though I may think I know it, I may still fail the test anyway. Maybe like a repeat of what happened.
Counselor: All right, so in third grade, you had a really bad testing experience, and as you moved forward from there, you've never really been thrilled about taking tests.
Client: No.
Counselor: But you've been able to adapt. You've been able to take them and still, like, pass them.
Client: Yeah. I mean, sometimes I get an a. So that's.
Counselor: That's good, right? Yeah.
Client: I mean, yeah, it is good. Yeah, it's good.
Counselor: But with this particular test, which is not for school, which is for work.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: This one. This is more of a stomach block for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You have any ideas as to what may be making this test such a point of anxiety for you?
Client: I think it's just the fact that it's this promotion, it's almost like the same thing. Like, if I fail, I'm being held back, and I feel like it's reliving that moment of being held back. And that's like, a fear that I have, that by not being able to pass these tests, they're holding me back.
Counselor: So, really, that same feeling you had in third grade that's coming up with this test now, right?
Client: Yeah. I mean, I didn't put them together until now, but, yeah.
Counselor: And the other tests you've taken throughout the rest of grade school and high school, they didn't have that same value attached to them?
Client: No, because they didn't have all that pressure that it was either win or lose.
Counselor: Basically, you could take them again or take that course again, or I could.
Client: Take another test to raise the grade if I didn't do good on that test.
Counselor: So you maybe had more options in school.
Client: Yes. It wasn't fail, pass or fail.
Counselor: It's the pressure. It's the pressure of you need to get through this. And you don't have the safety nets that you had in school.
Client: Yeah. If I fail it, then I'm not going to be able to get the promotion. I would have to wait just like I did. I'm going to have to wait a certain amount of time, I think, an ear before I could take it again.
Counselor: So that is a lot of pressure.
Client: Yeah, it is.
Counselor: So is there any time limit to this tests for work?
Client: No, there isn't.
Counselor: There's no time?
Client: No.
Counselor: How many? Is it like a. Like a multiple choice?
Client: Yes, it is.
Counselor: Okay. And you seem like. Like you said you study the night before with your friend.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You're really well prepared for it.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I have a few thoughts about this.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: One is I'm wondering, you know, we've talked before about cognitive therapy, about the core beliefs. So I'm curious as to what you think about, like, what core belief may be operating for you now with this.
Client: Test, this work test that I could fail, and then if I fail, I could end up being a failure at all, you know, the things that I try.
Counselor: So something like I am a failure, or I'm. I'm bound to be a failure. I'm destined to be a failure.
Client: I would say, like, I'm destined to be a failure.
Counselor: Okay, so I'm destined to be a failure. So that. So that potentially is a core belief, right? That's operating?
Client: Yeah. I mean, that's what scares me. That's exactly the thought that I'm thinking when I'm about to take the test. And if I don't pass it, it's just going to have, like, this dominant effect of failure.
Counselor: Okay. So it could be a core belief, but it also seems like it's the automatic thought. Like, as you get ready to take that test, you're thinking I'm destined to be a failure.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you're having what sounds like a panic response with the heart racing.
Client: Yeah. My hands.
Counselor: My hands shaking. Are you in the room alone when you're taking the test? Yes, you are. So no one's really seeing you have this? I wouldn't want to call it a panic attack yet. We haven't really gotten that far into it. But it sounds like a. It has some panic like features. Yeah, because it's not. It's interfering with you thinking clearly enough to get through the items. So. Okay, so one thought I have is you've. Have you ever had panic attacks in the past or anything like this? The third grade thing?
Client: No. Not really. I mean, sometimes I get worked up when I'm about to take a test, but it's only around tests.
Counselor: And what happens once you get worked up? Like, once your heart rate increases and you have the other physiological symptoms?
Client: When I actually do take the test, I kind of try to work through it and start trying to answer one question at a time to get to the last question.
Counselor: So, one possible strategy here is we talked about the adaptive response. Right. So which is that thought that you say to yourself, that self talk. I wonder if your adaptive response couldn't be, I can ride this out. Like, you have no time limit test.
Client: Yeah, that's true.
Counselor: I mean, the panic responses only maintained for so long.
Client: And I could also choose, like, maybe questions that I know the answer to automatically. So that could help maybe relieve some.
Counselor: Of that stress to get some, in a sense, to get some minor victories under your belt by, like, answering those. Right. You know you're closer to achieving your goal.
Client: Yes. And then I feel like I know. At least I know that. Like, they'll validate the feeling that I. Maybe I can pass this test.
Counselor: Mm hmm. So the more items you. You answer correctly, the less anxious you're gonna feel because you're closer to the end of.
Client: Yeah, definitely. Because then I start to feel more calm because I know that. I know these questions are definitely going to be right.
Counselor: So that's. So that's one. Well, that's a cognitive and behavioral strategy. Right? Like, you can. You can wait out the. The panic. I mean, you're in the room alone.
Client: Yeah, that's true. Nobody's there. Nobody's gonna see me. I'm kind of trying to get myself together.
Counselor: Yeah. Now, the panic's painful. Right? The panic symptoms are painful. So what you could tell yourself is, yeah, this is unpleasant, but I can ride out these symptoms because they only last so long.
Client: Okay. I could use, like, self talk.
Counselor: Exactly.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Yeah. Cause usually panic symptoms can run five minutes, ten minutes, 15 minutes, but you have no time limit.
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: So if you can just kind of use that time to focus on the items, as you mentioned, that you could get. Right. And kind of, at the same time, be telling yourself, I can ride this out.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I've done that in the past, so I can apply it to this test.
Counselor: So that's worked for you?
Client: Yes, that has worked for me in the past.
Counselor:
output: So that's certainly. That's certainly one adaptive response to try. Right. Another one could be that, although it wouldn't be great to fail, you can retake the test in a year, right? You could try again.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So, good morning.
Client: Good morning.
Counselor: What would you like to work on in this session?
Client: I would like to work on my avoidance behavior. I actually have an opportunity which I was looking for from a very long time to give a presentation. And now that I have this opportunity in front of me, I'm trying to avoid it.
Counselor: So you were looking forward to this opportunity for a long time?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And then now you are avoiding it. Right. And what you would like to do?
Client: I would not like to. I would not. I would like not to avoid it.
Counselor: So you would like to go ahead with the presentation?
Client: I would like to go ahead with the presentation.
Counselor: So how do you feel when you're about to avoid? In the sense, like what kind of feelings are making you avoid this?
Client: Rather whether I'll be able to do it or not, whether it will go well, like whether all the students or the people who are listening to the presentation will like it or not. What if I forget? Or what if I do a mess?
Counselor: Now, these are your thoughts. How do you feel when you think like this?
Client: I don't feel good.
Counselor: Can you label that feeling? When you. When you think like this, you don't feel good. And which is what feeling?
Client: I feel anxious.
Counselor: You feel anxious? Right. And instead of feeling anxious, how would you like to feel so that you go ahead with the presentation?
Client: Rather not anxious, but at least some little anxious.
Counselor: Little anxious. You would like to reduce your anxiety?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you wouldn't want to get rid of the anxiety completely?
Client: Yes, I want to get rid.
Counselor: You want to get rid of the anxiety.
Client: Anxiety completely.
Counselor: So how about feeling concerned but not anxious? So you're careful about your presentation. You also work towards the presentation well and you're not ignorant or you're not indifferent towards the outcome. Would that make sense?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you don't want to be indifferent and feel nothing about the presentation, but you would like to feel concerned and not anxious about it.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Do you also think there is a connection between your anxiety and your avoidance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: If you were concerned and not anxious, would you continue to avoid or you would probably go ahead?
Client: I would go ahead.
Counselor: You would go ahead?
Client: I always wanted to do this, so I would go ahead.
Counselor: You would go ahead. Right. So can we set that agenda for today's session is to feel concerned and not anxious about the upcoming presentation?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay, fine. So now to help you reach this goal, we will have to examine one specific incident where you know you felt anxious. And then you will understand how you get anxious and how to shift your feelings from anxiety to concern. So would you mind me telling me a specific incident where you had a chance to go ahead with, you know, preparing for the presentation, but you didn't.
Client: Recently, I have a social group where there was a chance that they wanted a presentation regarding a particular topic, and they have asked me for the dates to give me my dates when I would be presenting, and I have been just postponing it. Postponing it and not giving them the dates.
Counselor: Is this the same presentation that you are postponing, or this is different one?
Client: This is, again, a different one.
Counselor: This is a different one. But this is a specific example.
Client: Yes, this is a very specific example, which I always like. On the back of my mind. This example is always disturbing me or just always coming to my mind that I did that postponing thing.
Counselor: All right, so let's take this incident where, you know, there was a social group, and they asked you about a date for presentation. And in this situation, do you remember the incident clearly?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So when you chose to avoid it, can you remember that in that moment?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: What was going through your mind that made you avoid it?
Client: Whether I will be able to do it properly or whether they will like it or not. Am I that qualified to give the presentation now?
Counselor: These are the doubts that you had in your head. Could you convert them into statements?
Client: I'm. I'm not qualified.
Counselor: I'm not qualified.
Client: I am. People will not like it.
Counselor: People will not like it, and I.
Client: Will not be able to deliver it.
Counselor: And when you thought these, how did you feel?
Client: I didn't. I was feeling nervous. Rather nervous and not happy.
Counselor: Even not happy. Nervous and anxious. Also anxious on a zero to 100, how distressing was this anxiety?
Client: It was very distressing, I think. 80.
Counselor: 80. So that was pretty intense, right?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: It is like death anxiety. Something is gonna happen to me.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: 70 rather than, I would say.
Counselor: Okay. What was your natural intention to do at that time when you felt so anxious?
Client: I just told them, I'm busy for a while, and I will just let you know the dates when I am free and when can I take up the presentation.
Counselor: So this is what you did?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay. Was there anything else going on in your mind? That I want to do this?
Client: No.
Counselor: And what, in this entire incident was most anxiety provoking for you?
Client: Whether I will be able to give the presentation or not. Whether the presentation would go well or not.
Counselor: So having to make a presentation was the trigger?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Your thoughts were, I won't be able to make the presentation well, I am not qualified, and these people will not like it. These were the thoughts that were going through your head. And then you felt anxious about it. You felt nervous about it. You also escaped. Or you bought time by, you know, telling them, I'll get back to you. So you postponed accepting the invitation. Is that correct?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So did I summarize that well?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So we'll go ahead with finding out where your anxiety comes from. So when you thought these three thoughts, you felt very anxious. Out of these three thoughts, which was most important thought for you, that made.
Client: You anxious whether I will be able to do it or not.
Counselor: So your prediction that you will not be able to do it well?
Client: Yes. That I will not be able to do it well.
Counselor: Do it well, right. Okay. Let's assume for the sake of therapy that you know, you do not do it well. We are trying to find out where your anxiety comes from. Are you with me?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So if you don't do it well, what does that mean to you?
Client: That I am not competent enough.
Counselor: You are not competent enough?
Client: Yes. I am incompetent.
Counselor: You are incompetent and therefore you are not able to do it well.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. So do you think that this label and the rating you have attached to it has something to do with your anxiety? I am incompetent. How?
Client: When I say I am incompetent, how.
Counselor: Do you feel then?
Client: I feel anxious as well as I feel very disappointed.
Counselor: So it's usually self doubting when you say that I am incompetent. You might feel depressed or ashamed when you say this. Depressed. And when you have to present a presentation, you will feel anxious because the underlying thought is I am incompetent. Do you see the connection between your depression and your anxiety? Let's double check it. Right. Let's assume that you do make a very bad presentation. You do not live up to the mark or you do not. Your presentation is not up to the mark. In spite of this, you don't believe that you are incompetent. Let's say in spite of this, you don't believe that you are incompetent. You say that just my presentation was bad, but you don't believe that you are incompleted. Would you be anxious in the first place before the presentation began?
Client: Can we do that?
Counselor: Let's assume, hypothetically, that you make a very bad presentation. And even in this situation, you don't call yourself incompetent. You are a person. You are a kind of a person who does not call herself incompetent. Even in case of a bad presentation. Imagine yourself a person who does not label herself as incompetent even if things go wrong. And still then would you be anxious about a presentation?
Client: No. Then why?
Counselor: That's what I'm saying. So if you were not to label yourself as impedance, you would not be anxious in case of a presentation where there are chances that it may go wrong?
Client: Yes. If I am. If I do not label myself incompetent, then I would not be anxious.
Counselor: You would not be anxious. So the possibility of a presentation going wrong, does that make you anxious or your own belief that you are incompetent in such a case makes you anxious?
Client: I am incompetent. The possibility of presentation going wrong would make me incompetent.
Counselor: That would only make you.
Client: Not a good presenter.
Counselor:
output: This is what you think. My point is, does this possibility lead to your feelings or your own? Labelling leads to your feelings.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how are you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well, thank you.
Counselor: Doing well.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: I have family coming into town and I have to go to the airport to pick them up.
Counselor: So you have family flying in?
Client: Yes. That's something that I get very anxious about, having to cross the bridge. I have to cross the Ben Franklin bridge and then get over the bridge that goes to the airport by the stadium. I think that's the Girard point bridge. Yeah. That's two levels there. I have to do that both ways.
Counselor: Going and coming both ways. You have to cross four times?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So what kind of feeling is this bringing up for you?
Client: I get very anxious even just thinking about it right now.
Counselor: So you're anxious right here with me?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I want to try to scale this. We talked about this before with cognitive therapy. So let's say that ten is really the most anxious you're felt about crossing bridges, and one is no anxiety. Where would you be right now?
Client: Right now, probably an eight. Yeah.
Counselor: I don't love anxiety.
Client: Yes. It's worse when I'm at that point on that day, but right now, I think just knowing that I have to do that. Yes.
Counselor: And what's it on that day?
Client: A ten.
Counselor: It reaches a ten, definitely.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. So. But even now, how far away is the. Until they.
Client: Oh, it's a week.
Counselor: So even now, a week out, it's. Nate, this is really hurting.
Client: Yes. I don't like that at all.
Counselor: So for your job and local travel, you don't really have to cross any.
Client: Ten minutes to work every day. And banks. So 20 minutes, shopping centers and everything is just within the vicinity. I don't have to cross any bridges.
Counselor: So no bridges?
Client: No, not at all. I probably planned it that way, too.
Counselor: That worked out well.
Client: That worked out very well.
Counselor: All right. But coming up, pick up the family you will be crossing. So let's look at this at each stage. So, I mean, you're clearly anxious now, as you mentioned. But let's go to, let's try to move forward a week to the day that they'll be flying, what time they fly in.
Client: It's going to be a 04:00 flight. In the afternoon.
Counselor: In the afternoon. So about what time would you have to leave to?
Client: I would have to leave probably at 03:00 because it's only about 20 minutes to the airport. Really?
Counselor: Really.
Client: But I would like to leave earlier. They'll probably take them time. By the time they land and go through, you know, getting their luggages, they probably won't even come out till maybe 430, but I'd like to make sure I'm there at around 334 o'clock.
Counselor: All right, so let's go to that day. Let's go to that day and to that afternoon. So you're still at home. And let's say we're about 15 minutes before you have to get in the car. Car. What are you thinking then?
Client: I have to do this. I have to get up and go. They need me to be there this week. It's my parents coming in and they're elderly, so I don't want them to be stuck at the airport. There's no one else that actually can go pick them up. So I have to get up and go and pick them up.
Counselor: That's what's going through your mind?
Client: That's what's going through my mind. So, you know, there's nobody else that can do this. I mean, it's cheaper than there's no. I probably can't even afford to get a taxi for them because you'd have to cross that's from Philly to. Into New Jersey. So that's going to be very expensive. I can't afford that. When all I'd have to do is pay $5 for the tow and maybe gas up my car for $10 or something. But, um, I. Yeah, I'll be thinking about, I have to do this.
Counselor: I have to do it.
Client: I can do it. Something that I can save money that way. And I don't want to leave them stranded. Definitely someone else can. I mean, they'd be lost. They're not familiar with the airport. And Philly airport is crazy to me.
Counselor: Yeah, it's a big place. A lot going on. So. So you're sitting at home in 15 minutes before getting the cardinal and you're thinking, I have to do this. But your reasons are positive. Like you save money and protect your parents from having to be there alone. So when does the anxiety come in?
Client: Just the thought of the bridge, it's just. I could drive off the bridge. I can fall off. Usually what I do is try to stay in the middle lane. I can't do more than 40 miles an hour. And I just. I'm shaking. I have the radio on and windows down because I can't swim. So if for any reason I'm to fall off, I mean, that's it for me. I even have a little metal one of those. I think it's an instrument that you use in the house for, I don't know, plier or something. Something real hard that I can hit the ground with. It sits right there on my door, on the side of my door. So I'm already, I planned, I have that. I planned ahead of time. I know what I'm going to do as soon as I approach the bridge, but I still feel anxious.
Counselor: So you're anxious before you leave and you're starting to think about the bridge at that point. You already think about it. How about when you get in your car, you start driving toward the bridge?
Client: I say a prayer. I am still anxious. I turn on the radio and the closer I get to, especially the toll point, and I know it's at me. And you see those lights flashing. Last exit before the, you know, the.
Counselor: Toll, you know you're going over once.
Client: Yeah, there's no turning back. There's no turning back.
Counselor: So before that, when you can still exit, what's your anxiety level?
Client: Before, when I can still exit?
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: It'S probably still high. It's probably at a nine or so.
Counselor: It's still high, but it's not maxed out yet. But it's pretty bad.
Client: Yeah, I think it's pretty bad at that point.
Counselor: And how about when you cross through the.
Client: That's when it's at a ten.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yes, yes.
Counselor: So your specific fear as you start to cross, this is the Ben Franklin would be the first bridge. Right. You can go across. Is that your car will go off the bridge?
Client: Yes, definitely.
Counselor: And when does that, so that's a ten anxiety. When does that anxiety start to go away?
Client: As soon as I'm getting close to getting off the bridge, I'm now leaving a little sigh of the, there's a little release there. And I know that I've been able to manage those two, three minutes of cross. I don't know how many minutes it takes actually crossing the bridge. I start feeling a little bit of relief, but then again, I know I have to take that exit and there's another one coming right up, so starts all over again.
Counselor: All right, so then you cross the second bridge, the Gerard point bridge, you go to the airport. Does your anxiety drop, any of those points?
Client: Oh, as soon as I'm descending from the Gerard Point bridge, there's less, you know, it's almost reduced. I come, you know, really low.
Counselor: It's almost gone.
Client: Yes. It's almost gone. Yes.
Counselor: And when do you start thinking about that? You're going to have to cross them again?
Client: As soon as I'm exit, I'm getting back on 95 going north. And I know, here we go again. And cars are zooming by and you.
Counselor: Know, because you're not going very quickly.
Client: No, no, I'm that person. The middle lane doing 40 miles an hour. Yes.
Counselor: All right. So you're doing everything you can to keep your car on the bridge, but you're still feeling anxiety, like you're going to go off the bridge.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: The whole time. Until you start really descending.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: And then you feel like you made it.
Client: Especially when there are those big trucks.
Counselor: Tractor trailers coming because the air.
Client: Yes, yes. Or if it's also in bad weather or at night, it's worst because on the bridge, especially the top one, you kind of see the sky and there's nothing else you see. So it's like you're gonna fall off. Yes.
Counselor: So in the lower level it's not as bad.
Client: On the lower, lower level, coming back it's not as bad because you're kind of like protected here and there. So it's not as bad, but going it's definitely worse. Yes.
Counselor: Are you aware of any time a car would have gone off the bridge?
Client: I hear on the news once in a while you'll hear something happen, or sometimes in movies you see things happen. I think it's possible.
Counselor: It's possible?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You think it's a high risk?
Client: No, maybe not on that Gerard bridge. Because I noticed. I was checking it the other day, I had to go to the airport and I was trying to measure the distance between the metal poles just to see if a car could fit there. Really? And I think a car could fit there, but, you know, it just depends on the angle you were hit or something or if you flew. So, yeah.
Counselor: Done some thinking, she's done some calculations, geometry. And you've concluded that it's not really likely, but it could. It could fly off the. Alright, but either way, your anxiety is maxed out on each bridge.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Now when you get home, get your parents back to take them back to your home.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: How do you feel then?
Client: I don't even recall all the anxiety. Why it was such a big deal anyway. I don't think about it at all.
Counselor: All right, so when you arrive home, you're down to one.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. So going back to the. The first stage, like when you're getting ready, you were thinking that you have to go.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And it would save your parents money?
Client: It would save me money. I would be the one calling the cat.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: But I would be the one to pick them up and save them from being stranded at the airport and being in a land that they're not familiar with an area they're not familiar with. Make sure that they're safe.
Counselor: How important is their safety to you?
Client: Oh, very important.
Counselor:
output: Very important?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how you doing today?
Client: Good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How has the anxiety been going since last session?
Client: It seems to be in check. Nothing really major has been going on with it. So I think I'm getting to a point where it's under control.
Counselor: It subsided a bit. That's good. That's good. How's things been going at work lately?
Client: So work's a little bit of a different story. We have our daily meetings, and. I. Actually had to pull, like, one of my coworkers aside because I feel like they undermine me all the time, and they, like, they don't give me the respect, basically, that I deserve. So I took her outside after the meeting and leaned into her about it. And afterwards, I mean, the next day, because we have these meetings every day, she, like, she came back and came at me again, but it was worse even after talking to her.
Counselor: So talking to her, that didn't improve your situation?
Client: No.
Counselor: So you have these. Someone understands. You have these daily meetings, and you mentioned that she's not showing you respect and that you deserve respect, something to that effect. So tell me about that belief. Remember we talked about ABC before, activating events and beliefs and consequences in rabt. Tell me about that belief.
Client: Well, I just feel that I do a good job and I deserve to be respected by my coworkers. Yeah, it just.
Counselor: Are there levels of respect? Is there a certain level of respect that you demand or need?
Client: I don't know if there's a certain level, but I feel just like I deserve it. Mm hmm.
Counselor: You know, and what did she do that kind of convinced you that she wasn't meeting that level of respect?
Client: Well, she was, like, shooting down my ideas and just kind of made me feel like a fool, basically. So I just. I didn't understand.
Counselor: All right, so she had criticisms of your ideas, right? A few of them, it sounds like. So that would upset anybody. But were those criticisms unusual, given the tone of these meetings? Like, is this a type of meeting where people criticize each other or attempt to in a constructive way?
Client: I mean, I guess.
Counselor: Have you criticized other coworkers?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you think that her criticism was within normal limits, like, within the. What you've kind of seen there regularly?
Client: I mean, now that you pointed out? I mean, I guess I can view it in that way that it wasn't.
Counselor: It wasn't too far out of line the first time. Right. But then after you talked to her, you said that it got worse.
Client: Yeah. So it just felt like she was purposely trying to nitpick, if you will.
Counselor: Trying to get at you a little bit.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So maybe the second time around, correct me if I'm wrong, maybe she was actively showing you disrespect just because of what you had done, because you came after her. Or was that with the normal limits, too? I don't know.
Client: I mean, I. I guess I may have gone at her a little harshly, but I felt at the time that.
Counselor: It was reasonable at the time when you were.
Client: When I was talking to her outside of the meeting.
Counselor: All right, so you felt that she was a bit harsh. You talk to her about it, but then she's become more harsh. So where do you stand with her now, like, with the meetings?
Client: Well, I've just been trying not to talk to her, and obviously in a work situation, doesn't really help.
Counselor: That's not convenient. Yeah, it might not help. All right, so let's work this through. Using the ABC model, like we used for the anxiety that you had before that was troublesome to you before. What would the activating event be here in this situation?
Client: So I guess the confrontation I had with her.
Counselor: Well, you could look at that as an activating event. Another way to look at it is her criticism of you could have been the activating event, and your conversation with her could have been the consequence. But these things are cyclical, so it's sometimes hard to know where to cut in and put the a and the b and the c. But let's just work it through with the activating event being what she said. Let's just try that, okay, and see how that works out. Would that be reasonable? That could have been kind of what started it was this criticism.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: All right. So then what would the belief. So all activating events, right, are filtered through our belief system. So what would your beliefs be in that scenario?
Client: So she criticized me, and I felt disrespected.
Counselor: That's a feeling.
Client: And I feel, or my belief is that I deserve respect.
Counselor: Right. And that came first. Right. So you have the activating event, which is her criticism, processed through your belief, which is that you. You must have respect. You deserve respect. You mentioned the feeling. So tell me what the feelings.
Client: So that being upset and disrespected and aggravation.
Counselor: It was aggravation. Frustration.
Client: Frustration.
Counselor: So that would be one of the consequences of how you processed her behavior. Does that make sense? The feeling. The frustration feeling would be one of the consequences. Like an ABC.
Client: Gotcha.
Counselor: So you have the activating event. She criticizes you. Your belief is that you deserve respect. And that clearly she violated that belief. Right. She didn't show you the respect that you deserved according to your belief system. And then one of the consequences, therefore, was this feeling of frustration. Were there any other consequences?
Client: Well, if we, like, go forward, it's the kind of disarray or the tension, I guess, now in the office.
Counselor: So you get. That's definitely a consequence. I'm thinking there's an intermediate consequence, though. So you had that feeling of frustration, and what's the next thing you did after that meeting was over?
Client: Oh, well, I confronted her.
Counselor: You confronted her. Right. So you have kind of those two consequences. And that confrontation, it would appear, has led her to kind of come on more strongly with her criticisms, which is another activating event you could also think of as a consequence. But like I said, this is cyclical. So you see how the a and the B and the c, that paradigm can fit in to what happened here at work for you. Does that make some sense?
Client: It does, yeah. And, I mean, when you put it that way, and then you say it's cyclical, then you just. I can see, I can visualize it going around like carousel.
Counselor: Sure. Exactly. So it helps you to kind of see what caused what and maybe what could have been changed or could be changed in the future. Right. Because we can't go back and change that, but we can work on the future. So her criticism of you, there's no direct way to change that. The consequence is a consequence. So that leaves the belief system, which is the deserving respect. One of the things we try to do in Rebt is help people move from rigid thinking to more flexible thinking. So kind of a rigid belief system would be, and not that you said it in this way, but I demand and deserve respect. Right. At this particular level, and people aren't meeting it. Would you say that's a fair.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Okay. Maybe a more flexible way of thinking would be that you'd like respect. Right. Respect. Respect's good, respects healthy and work environments, certainly. But if you don't get it, you can still function. It's tough for you. I can see that's tough. Tell me about that.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Terry. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay, I think.
Counselor: You okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know when we talked last time, you were having a rough time dealing with the passing year, Sister Sheila.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you're kind of a point where we were talking about emotional consequences, but also some of the thinking that's going on. Have you been processing that?
Client: Yeah, I've been thinking about some of that and, you know, trying to kind of work through it a little bit. So I think I'm kind of ready to kind of work through it and talk about it a little bit now.
Counselor: So, feeling a little less emotional and feeling a little more thinking about it. And, like, on the rational side, like we talked about rational and irrational beliefs.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: A little more focus there or more ability to focus there today.
Client: Yeah, I think I'm ready to think about it more.
Counselor: I know the emotional part was tough for you, and I'm sure it still.
Client: Is, but I think I've kind of got through some of that, and I'm ready to kind of get through the way I'm thinking about some things.
Counselor: Ready to look at through the thinking lens.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So to speak. All right. So what are some of the thoughts or beliefs that you've been having, you think maybe part of what's affecting your mood?
Client: Well, I've been. I've been thinking about it, and, you know, I just. I just feel like I don't. I don't have anybody that I can talk to. I mean, I just. I keep thinking about it. I don't have anybody to talk to. She was the only one I had to talk to.
Counselor: So in your relationship with her, you guys talked a lot. She was an important person in your life for a variety of reasons, but including that she was easy to talk to.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And that you could talk to her?
Client: I. Yes.
Counselor: So the thought is you have nobody to talk to.
Client: I just, you know, she was just everything to me. I talked to her about everything, and, you know, she was just always gave me good advice, and she could always work, you know, talk me through anything that I needed to talk about, and I just don't feel like I have that anymore. Since she's going, I don't have anybody like that anymore.
Counselor: That relationship is valuable to you, and you've lost that, and you feel like you've lost having anybody that you could talk to. Is that. Is that close?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right, so let's look at that thought. Let's break that down. Certainly you were able to talk to her, as you mentioned, and you have lost her.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. So you have lost someone that you could talk to that was very valuable to you, and that's understandably painful. The question would be, have you lost everybody that you could talk to? Is there anyone else in your life, for instance, currently, that you regularly speak with?
Client: Well, you know, since you said that, you know, maybe I do have some people that I can go to. They're not her. But, you know, you know, I have a couple of people that I can talk to that they're willing to talk to me about certain things. I guess if I give them the chance, you know, I'll be able to talk to them.
Counselor: So there are some people in your life that you can talk to. They certainly don't replace your sister, but you have people you can't communicate with, and that can be helpful for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So as we build kind of a rationale, self talk to replace the irrational thinking that you brought in.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Which was that you have no one to talk to. Could the replacement be something like, I had my sister to talk to, and she was really good at that, and it's painful to have lost her, but I gained something from that experience, and I do still have some people to talk to now.
Client: Yeah, that sounds about right.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Yeah, yeah. Yeah. Because nobody's gonna replace my sister. But, you know, I do think that there's other people that can. Could help me and what I need to talk. Yeah.
Counselor: And maybe one thing that you can. You can take away from this as well is that because of the way you could talk to your sister, you are a more effective communicator now, and you can make the most out of the relationships that you have now with people currently. Another rational thought kind of honors her contribution to you.
Client: Right? Yeah, because, you know, she is, like, the only one that believed in me. I mean, she just, you know, she always, you know, pushed me to go higher and, you know, on my job. She always said that, you know, that you can do it, you know, just believe in yourself. She always, you know, encouraged me to. To go back to school and, you know, I'm, you know, I have done that and, you know, continually doing that, you know, but, you know, she was a big motivator for me. And, you know, since she's gone now, you know, I don't feel like that I have anybody else that gives me that push that she did.
Counselor: So. So the thought would be, I've lost the only person that would believe in me. Yes, something like that. Okay, so she was a great positive force, great positive presence and contributor in your life, in part because she believed in you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And now that's gone, and you feel like no one else will believe in you in that way.
Client: Not like she did.
Counselor: Not like she did.
Client: No. No.
Counselor: Which could be true. Right? There may be no one else that ever believes in you that same way, but similarly, like we were doing before, can you think of some people now that believed in you, maybe in a different way that's still helpful? It doesn't replace her, but it might still be helpful to you?
Client: Well, I do have very encouraging parents. They've always, you know, been, you know, somewhat of encouraged encouragement, but, you know, they just didn't have that extra push that she did. But, you know, they are very encouraging, and I have encouraging friends. You know, some of my friends, you know, want to see me succeed, and they give me encouraging words and tell me to, you know, to keep going. So, you know, she stopped at nothing to make. Make me go, you know, she just didn't take no for an answer. And, you know, you know, if she had to go with me to do something, she would, you know, that's why, you know, I just felt like, you know, I wasn't gonna make it, you know, without her, you know, pushing me.
Counselor: Her level of belief in you was higher or different or better than what you have now? In some ways, yes. Like, she was really committed to her belief in you, it sounds like.
Client: Yes.
Counselor:
output: So some people currently do believe in you, and that's good. It doesn't replace her level of belief, her type of belief in you. I also wonder if by her believing in you, you mentioned that it helped you with all kinds of accomplishments.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Michelle. How you doing today?
Client: Um, I'm kind of doing. I'm feeling a little bit stressed out.
Counselor: Stressed?
Client: Yeah. I feel like I have a lot on my plate. I have this test that I have to take for work.
Counselor: What kind of test?
Client: It's like an aptitude test. It has, like, math problems on it and, like, scenarios in order for me to move up to the assistant manager. Precision.
Counselor: That's a job that you've been interested in for a while?
Client: Yes, it is. Yes. So I've been just feeling a lot of anxiety about taking the test, and then they actually scheduled for me to take the test, and I went and I just got really overwhelmed, and I started, like, I felt my heart was racing. I felt like I wish my hands were shaking. And I just really couldn't concentrate on the test, even though the night before, me and my friend did practice problems and I knew all the answers with no problem, like, I didn't miss any of the questions.
Counselor: So you know the material on this test pretty well.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: But the feelings and that physiological response to heart rate and sweating, that the feelings of anxiety plus those physiological responses, they got in the way of you completing it. Like, you weren't able to complete it?
Client: No, I wasn't able to complete it. And thankfully, they gave me a chance to come back. I just told them I didn't feel well, so they rescheduled. So now I'm feeling a lot of anxiety because I'm scared the same thing's gonna happen when I go back.
Counselor: All right, so you weren't. You weren't feeling great about taking the test in the first place?
Client: The day, the night before, I felt like, I know all the answers, but the minute I walked into the room, all of a sudden, all these fears kind of took over.
Counselor: But did you know that was coming?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You did? Okay.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you had some anxiety in advance. Yes or not? You did? Okay.
Client: I had some anxiety the day before, but when I reviewed it with my friend, I'm like, oh, I know the answer. So I thought that would kind of push it down. But I think once I got there, it all came back up to the surface.
Counselor: It erupted in that moment. And that prevented you. What do you think is leading to this?
Client: Well, I've always kind of struggled with tests. Like, I can remember when I was in third grade, I had to take this test because I was really struggling in math, and I had to pass this test in order to move to the next grade. And I thought, just like this test, that I was ready for it. I had a tutor, and I felt really prepared for it. And then when I took it, I failed and I was held back. And I feel like, you know, that was so. It was. It was really embarrassing for me to be held back. And I felt like. I don't want to say, but I did feel like a failure at the time because I felt like I really did know this. So I don't know why I couldn't pass the test.
Counselor: And since that you said this was third grade?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And since that bad testing experience, have you had trouble with tests since?
Client: Yes, I always feel really anxious. I mean, I'm able to pass tests, obviously, because I graduated from grade school and went on to high school. But it's so hard for me because of this anxiety that I feel that even though I may think I know it, I may still fail the test anyway. Maybe like a repeat of what happened.
Counselor: All right, so in third grade, you had a really bad testing experience, and as you moved forward from there, you've never really been thrilled about taking tests.
Client: No.
Counselor: But you've been able to adapt. You've been able to take them and still, like, pass them.
Client: Yeah. I mean, sometimes I get an a. So that's.
Counselor: That's good, right? Yeah.
Client: I mean, yeah, it is good. Yeah, it's good.
Counselor: But with this particular test, which is not for school, which is for work.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: This one. This is more of a stomach block for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You have any ideas as to what may be making this test such a point of anxiety for you?
Client: I think it's just the fact that it's this promotion, it's almost like the same thing. Like, if I fail, I'm being held back, and I feel like it's reliving that moment of being held back. And that's like, a fear that I have, that by not being able to pass these tests, they're holding me back.
Counselor: So, really, that same feeling you had in third grade that's coming up with this test now, right?
Client: Yeah. I mean, I didn't put them together until now, but, yeah.
Counselor: And the other tests you've taken throughout the rest of grade school and high school, they didn't have that same value attached to them?
Client: No, because they didn't have all that pressure that it was either win or lose.
Counselor: Basically, you could take them again or take that course again, or I could.
Client: Take another test to raise the grade if I didn't do good on that test.
Counselor: So you maybe had more options in school.
Client: Yes. It wasn't fail, pass or fail.
Counselor: It's the pressure. It's the pressure of you need to get through this. And you don't have the safety nets that you had in school.
Client: Yeah. If I fail it, then I'm not going to be able to get the promotion. I would have to wait just like I did. I'm going to have to wait a certain amount of time, I think, an ear before I could take it again.
Counselor: So that is a lot of pressure.
Client: Yeah, it is.
Counselor: So is there any time limit to this tests for work?
Client: No, there isn't.
Counselor: There's no time?
Client: No.
Counselor: How many? Is it like a. Like a multiple choice?
Client: Yes, it is.
Counselor: Okay. And you seem like. Like you said you study the night before with your friend.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You're really well prepared for it.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I have a few thoughts about this.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: One is I'm wondering, you know, we've talked before about cognitive therapy, about the core beliefs. So I'm curious as to what you think about, like, what core belief may be operating for you now with this.
Client: Test, this work test that I could fail, and then if I fail, I could end up being a failure at all, you know, the things that I try.
Counselor: So something like I am a failure, or I'm. I'm bound to be a failure. I'm destined to be a failure.
Client: I would say, like, I'm destined to be a failure.
Counselor: Okay, so I'm destined to be a failure. So that. So that potentially is a core belief, right? That's operating?
Client: Yeah. I mean, that's what scares me. That's exactly the thought that I'm thinking when I'm about to take the test. And if I don't pass it, it's just going to have, like, this dominant effect of failure.
Counselor: Okay. So it could be a core belief, but it also seems like it's the automatic thought. Like, as you get ready to take that test, you're thinking I'm destined to be a failure.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you're having what sounds like a panic response with the heart racing.
Client: Yeah. My hands.
Counselor: My hands shaking. Are you in the room alone when you're taking the test? Yes, you are. So no one's really seeing you have this? I wouldn't want to call it a panic attack yet. We haven't really gotten that far into it. But it sounds like a. It has some panic like features. Yeah, because it's not. It's interfering with you thinking clearly enough to get through the items. So. Okay, so one thought I have is you've. Have you ever had panic attacks in the past or anything like this? The third grade thing?
Client: No. Not really. I mean, sometimes I get worked up when I'm about to take a test, but it's only around tests.
Counselor: And what happens once you get worked up? Like, once your heart rate increases and you have the other physiological symptoms?
Client: When I actually do take the test, I kind of try to work through it and start trying to answer one question at a time to get to the last question.
Counselor: So, one possible strategy here is we talked about the adaptive response. Right. So which is that thought that you say to yourself, that self talk. I wonder if your adaptive response couldn't be, I can ride this out. Like, you have no time limit test.
Client: Yeah, that's true.
Counselor: I mean, the panic responses only maintained for so long.
Client: And I could also choose, like, maybe questions that I know the answer to automatically. So that could help maybe relieve some.
Counselor: Of that stress to get some, in a sense, to get some minor victories under your belt by, like, answering those. Right. You know you're closer to achieving your goal.
Client: Yes. And then I feel like I know. At least I know that. Like, they'll validate the feeling that I. Maybe I can pass this test.
Counselor: Mm hmm. So the more items you. You answer correctly, the less anxious you're gonna feel because you're closer to the end of.
Client: Yeah, definitely. Because then I start to feel more calm because I know that. I know these questions are definitely going to be right.
Counselor:
output: So that's. So that's one. Well, that's a cognitive and behavioral strategy. Right? Like, you can. You can wait out the. The panic. I mean, you're in the room alone.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Samantha. How you doing today?
Client: Good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm doing all right. How have things been since last week?
Client: Things? You know, I've been really sort of preoccupied and anxious a lot this weekend. My daughter got sick, so I had to take three days off of work to take care of her. And I'm starting to worry. She's been sick a lot since I've gone back to work, and she's in daycare, and I've had to take a lot of time off work, and I'm getting close to going over my allotted amount of days. And so I'm finding myself being very anxious about that and then feeling guilty because when I'm trying to take care of her, I'm always worrying about work. So.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a couple things may be going on. Child. Child's been sick, so you're taking off days. So you're a little worried about your relationship with your employer. At the same time, you want to make sure you're taking good care of your child, so you're having trouble reconciling those two.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. What was the last time it happened? Can you describe what happened the last.
Client: Time I had to take off work? It was just this week. She woke up one morning with a really high fever, so I had to call out that day, and then she still had a fever the next day, and then I had to take a third day because she has to be fever free before she can go back to daycare. So the first day was, I was okay with that. But then, like, the second. And then when I started realizing that I was going to have to take a third day, then I really start to get kind of panicky and worried about it.
Counselor: All right, so let me see. Let's go through each day. So the first day when you discovered that she was sick, right. What were you thinking then when you had to call out of work?
Client: Well, because she's been sort of sick a lot lately, I was a little bit worried, and I was sort of, you know, I have this number, ten, because I only have ten days for the whole year. So I have this number in my head, and I just thought, well, there's one more day I gotta take away from that ten that I have. And. But I was able to sort of think about. I was a little worried about any work that I would miss, you know, keeping up with my caseload and stuff at work, so. But I was able to kind of figure out that I would be okay for a day. And I can kind of make up for that when I get back.
Counselor: Okay, so your thinking was, this isn't ideal, but I can live with it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just one day, right? How about on day two when you realize that you're going to have to take a second day?
Client: Then I got a little bit more worried. And then I did start to also, you know, add the worry of I was going to start to get behind at work. Not only was I missing more time, but I was also going to be behind on my work. So then I started thinking, when I go back, it's going to be a mad scramble to kind of catch up and keep up with everything and, you know, so then it became worrying about my workload and worrying about taking more time.
Counselor: Okay, so a little more stressful version of what happened on day one. And then how about when you discovered that you had to take a third day off?
Client: I was. Then it was just more amplified, you know, amplified worry. And it was a lot harder for me to let it go. I just kept thinking. I kept going back to it. And then I started feeling guilty because I was so preoccupied, worried about that. And I was trying to answer emails and do some stuff and send out some emails to people that I work with to try to help me out with things at work since I wasn't there. And then I felt guilty because I wasn't really caring for my child as best as I felt I should have been. You know, I started feeling kind of like a bad mom.
Counselor: So, so guilty and a bad mom. And that was mostly on the third day? That was the worst of it, yes. Now, did this go up against the weekend? It was the third day, Friday. So then you kind of knew that by Monday things would be able to return to work. So tell me what happened when you returned to work on Monday.
Client: Well, I checked in with the main office and, you know, I just said, I'm really, you know, I'm starting to worry. I'm getting. I know I had to take a lot of time, but you. I've done the best I can to try to make other arrangements, but just starting back in, starting in daycare, she's just been sick a lot and I can't control it. I'm doing the best I can. I asked them if there was anything I needed to do as far as providing doctor's notes and stuff, and they said, no, they don't need a doctor's note since it was my daughter that was sick. They said there's nothing, nothing that I really can do and just try to not have it happen much more if I can just do what I can to not miss more.
Counselor: So they said that to you?
Client: Yeah, but. Yeah.
Counselor: How did they frame that?
Client: They kind of just said, you know, do what you can to not have it happen, but if it, you know, if it has to happen, you know, what can I do about it? It's kind of. They were saying.
Counselor: So they were understanding.
Client: I didn't feel like they were that understanding, but I also didn't feel like they were gonna take any punitive action against me. Right. Right then and there or anything.
Counselor: Did you anticipate a worse reaction than you experienced?
Client: Yeah, I did. And I also anticipated that they would maybe have more of a procedure for how to handle it, and they didn't have a procedure, which also made me feel a little worried. I can't imagine I'm the first mom that has had to deal with this. And they kind of talked like it's never happened before, so I kind of felt anxious because I thought, am I really the first mom that's had to take a lot of time off because their child's sick? They didn't give me the impression that they had sort of a protocol or like they had dealt with this before.
Counselor: Right. So sort of like it took them by surprise.
Client: Yeah. Or they just didn't have a plan for what to do about it.
Counselor: They weren't investing a lot of energy in thinking about that?
Client: No. No, I guess nothing.
