Counselor: And when was this again? How long ago?
Client: Just this past week.
Counselor: So how has this week been? Bag of work?
Client: Oh, it's been very busy because I'm trying to catch up and get everything handled, but that's the way it always is. So nobody has said anything to me or anything about the absences other than that first, yeah.
Counselor: And there have been no more absences. Okay. Earlier you mentioned being a good mom. What does a good mom look like?
Client: Somebody who takes care of their child and puts them. Makes them a priority, like their first priority, and, you know, does the things that they need to do to make sure they're child is taken care of.
Counselor: And you're a little worried through this last experience you were telling me about that you didn't rise to the level of good mom.
Client: Yeah, I felt like I wasn't being a good mom because I was preoccupied and making work a bit of a bigger priority than taking care of my kidney.
Counselor: Okay. So good mom's more about. More than just rather your behavior, what you're doing. It's about what you're also thinking. So you took care of your child.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But your mind, your thoughts were somewhere else some of the time, and that's where you feel like you've wandered out of the good mom area. Okay, how about on the other side? How about a good employee? Did you mention that you want to be a good employee?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. What's that look like?
Client: Well, somebody that, you know, takes care of all of their workload and handles all of the tasks that they have each day, and someone that's consistent and reliable and, you know, puts effort into what they're doing and gets their job done, really, you know, reliably.
Counselor: And that's where you feel like with this. So the last eight work days you missed. You missed three. Okay, how about in the last year, how many days have you missed?
Client: Well, I missed a lot for maternity leave, certainly.
Counselor: Understandable.
Client: But excluding that I've missed since the school year started, I've missed. If you include the three, I've missed nine days. But some of those were half days. They add up to nine days.
Counselor: Okay, total nine days?
Client: Yeah. And you're allowed ten per school year? For school year, it's only January and I'm already at nine.
Counselor: I can see where that would cause worry. What happens if you go over the.
Client: I don't know. I mean, I think that they would dock my pay for those. If I was there a day and I didn't have any more sick days left, they would just dock my pay for that day. But outside of that, I don't know what else would happen.
Counselor: Is there anybody that you work with that you could ask that question to, like an HR department?
Client: Yeah, I guess I could contact the HR department.
Counselor: I'm just thinking. Cause you're just one day away from being at that number, might be prudent just to talk with them and see. So you know what to expect.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So this is this whole thing, though, the missing days cause you anxiety, frustration?
Client: Yeah, a little bit, yeah.
Counselor: How about any type of feeling down at all?
Client: A little bit. Sometimes when I start feeling like I'm a bad mom.
Counselor: Okay, so as far as your child is concerned, your relationship with your child, you have some anxiety, relationship at work, some anxiety. But the sadness mostly surrounds how you feel you're treating your child. Of all the emotions, frustration, anxiety, what I'll refer to as depression, let's just say sadness. What's bothering you the most? What emotional response does bother you most?
Client: Probably sort of the guilt and the feelings of not being able to be the best mom.
Counselor: How would you rate yourself right now as a mother if, say, ten was the best mother you could imagine. Right. And one was the absolute worst.
Client: Probably like, I don't know, an eight.
Counselor: An eight? Okay. That's pretty good, right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What would be the cutoff to where. What's the cutoff score in that little scale I just gave you for good mother and not good mother?
Client: I guess, like halfway, like.
Counselor: So five is good enough?
Client: Yeah, I don't feel like it's good enough for me.
Counselor: Okay. Okay.
Client: I wouldn't be okay with that.
Counselor: So if you looked at somebody else, another person in a similar situation, a five would be acceptable, right?
Client: Probably, yeah.
Counselor: But how about for you specifically?
Client: Yeah, that's not.
Counselor: That's not gonna cut it. What would cut it?
Client: Um. I don't know. At least a seven.
Counselor: At least a seven, yeah. And you're an eight?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Sure.
Client: No, not sure.
Counselor: Okay. So you're close to the border. I feel like you're close to the border and you're.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Out of your value system of being not a good mother.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: What happens if you.
Client: Well, as good a mother as I want to be.
Counselor: Okay. How good do you want to be?
Client: Yeah, I want to be like an eight or higher.
Counselor: Eight or higher. Well, you are an eight, you said.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so you want to be a ten, sounds like.
Client: Well, yeah. Doesn't everybody want to be the best at what they do?
Counselor: I mean, I think people are driven to do their best, but is it crucial to be perfect? Is it crucial to be a tendency.
Client: No, there's some leeway. I guess you have to allow for that.
Counselor: Remember before, in other sessions, for other situations you've brought in here, we talked about dysfunctional thinking, irrational thinking. How does when you reflect on that, like, the usefulness of these thoughts, that other mothers can be a five and be. And that's good, right. You need to be an eight or higher. Eight, nine or ten. Does this seem useful, like a useful way of thinking?
Client: In some ways it's useful because it keeps me. It keeps me on track, if that makes sense. It keeps me pushing to keep doing the best I can. Driven.
Counselor: Motivated.
Client: Yeah, motivated.
Counselor: So it does have a useful side. Does it have an unuseful side, a less than useful side?
Client: Well, yeah, I guess it does. In the sense that if I become too worried about it, then I'm wasting energy on worry instead of being able to put that energy into being a good mom.
Counselor: Yeah. So I guess one of the things I'm getting at here is has the worry. Has the anxiety and the worry paid off for you?
Client: Probably not.
Counselor: Probably not. So you're suffering with it. It might make you a little more vigilante, but mostly it's just causing you to suffer.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So at the heart of it, you're not a bad mom. You're in the good mom category. You're a good employee. But your way of valuing yourself, your perception, is that you're not doing a great job at either one.
Client: Mm hmm. Exactly.
Counselor: And that's the thinking I'm getting at. It's not, you know, it's not necessarily irrational. I'm thinking it's just less than useful. Right. It's dysfunctional.
Client: Yeah, I can see that.
Counselor: Yeah. We're talking about that third day, right? The third day of work you had to. You had to call off. And do you remember any of the specific thoughts that were going through your mind on that? Was that a morning when you figured it out? Like a Friday morning?
Client: Yeah. No, it was really the night before. But, you know, I went as far as to think, am I going to get fired? You know, I had to kind of think about that.
Counselor: So your thought was, am I going to get fired?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: And then what was the feeling that came right after that?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Jordan. How you doing today?
Client: Could have been better.
Counselor: Could be better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: Um, well, you know, I have two jobs.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: And I lost one of them.
Counselor: You lost your job? Yes. Which one did you lose?
Client: I lost one at the grocery store.
Counselor: That was your part time?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I'm sorry to hear that.
Client: Me too. And I'm just. It's all I think about now.
Counselor: And when did this happen?
Client: It happened about two, three days ago.
Counselor: Two, three days ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if I remember right, you took that job not too long ago to kind of supplement your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So certainly that would be upsetting, but I know that's not a major part of your income.
Client: It's not, but, I mean, I'm still very worried about it.
Counselor: Tell me about the worry.
Client: I mean, I worry that, you know, I'm. Now I only had so much money, and now I have less than that. I mean, without my money, you know, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: So before you had the job, you were paying all your bills. You want some extra income, you've lost that extra income. And I can certainly understand how that would be disturbing. But as I understand that you were doing okay before with your full time job.
Client: I was doing okay, but, I mean, I got comfortable with that extra income, and so now my fear is that I've gotten too comfortable with it, and now that it's not there anymore, it's going to affect the fact I'm not going to be able to pay for food or my rent.
Counselor: Okay, so you adjusted to the new income level with the full time and the part time job together, and you're worried you can't adjust back?
Client: I'm worried that, I mean, things are just gonna get worse from here. I mean, it's a big deal, losing your job. Even if it was part time, I've gotten comfortable from having so much money, from the money I had to. Now that's, you know, been divided and, I mean, God knows how many things, like I said, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: Well, what. What can happen? So you have that income, your income is reduced now to just your full time job. What can happen from this point on?
Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. So, I mean, if I can't, if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not gonna have insurance on my cardinal. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work, and then I'll get fired there too.
Counselor: All right, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something the police officer could see, don't have insurance, give you a ticket, which is just money. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?
Client: Because I wouldn't be able to get to work.
Counselor: So it'd be. So the ticket would be so expensive, you would lose your.
Client: Well, the ticket would be expensive, so I wouldn't be able to try to pay the next month's insurance. So I just wouldn't have insurance on my car. So I.
Counselor: So you'd lose your insurance?
Client: I'd lose my insurance.
Counselor: And then by losing your insurance, you lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive that insurance. And then you lose your job.
Client: Mm hmm. I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car, and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times.
Counselor: No, that's serious. Yeah. You wouldn't want to do that.
Client: I wouldn't go to jail.
Counselor: So there's two. You have two kind of causal change. One is losing your job. And now even just the idea you can end up incarcerated.
Client: Yes. I mean, which I definitely lose my.
Counselor: Job if I'm in jail, I would imagine.
Client: And so that would have. So then I wouldn't even have, like, any money to help me through jail. Like, to. For the commissary and stuff.
Counselor: Because you would have no income.
Client: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm. No one's gonna hire me.
Counselor: Because you have a criminal record.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances. So what's happened is kind of in your mind, and we've talked about how thoughts work and beliefs work, is you, in reality, you've lost this part time job. And as I said, that's certainly. That's understandable that you'd be upset about that. I doubt many people would be happy about losing additional income, but you move from there, from losing additional income, which is what has actually happened to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this. So I remember maybe last week. Week before, you're talking about the. The letter that you received from. It was like a late notice. It wasn't. Turned out wasn't.
Client: Yeah, it was sent to me, but it was somebody else's credit card mistake. Yeah.
Counselor: Do you remember the conclusions you drew from when you believe that was actually for you, that late notice, that my.
Client: Credit score was gonna go down, that I would. I'd be stuck in that apartment, and then I'd go into depression. I wouldn't be able to do anything.
Counselor: Yeah. So you ended up in that scenario. You end up in a situation where you just couldn't function at all. And you moved there from a letter that you believe was addressed to you, saying you were one month or six days late or something on a credit card, which, of course, you don't want to be late on a credit card, but you move from there to being so depressed you couldn't work, couldn't function, I think, is how you put it. Couldn't function. Do you see, kind of, given how we've talked about cognitive behavioral strategies and concepts, do you see a pattern that's emerged over the last few times I've seen you?
Client: I mean, I've seen that, you know, sometimes I can. I can think the worst, and then. And I know it didn't happen last time, but that was, you know, a stroke of good luck.
Counselor: That it wasn't you.
Client: Yeah. That it was, you know, it wasn't me. And, you know, that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part time job anymore.
Counselor: You've lost real income.
Client: I mean, this isn't a mistake. This isn't a. We fired the wrong person. You know, this is real. So there's real concerns here.
Counselor: I.
Client: Unlike last time, where I was lucky.
Counselor: So this. This situation, you see, is different than the first situation because the first situation was more. You were perceiving something was wrong that wasn't wrong because you weren't the intended recipient of the letter.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But in this situation, it's different because it's real. You really lost your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And, of course, keeping in mind that this job, again, only a few months old, and you survived well before that, is it reason to believe you could survive well again, that you could adapt to this lost income?
Client: Well, I suppose there is, but I'm concerned about whether I'm not, whether I won't adapt.
Counselor: Well, let's look at this in terms of probabilities, right. You've had several jobs throughout your career. You've had some of them worked out. You've lost other ones. You're still paying your bills. So in terms of probabilities, how many times have you, how many times have you ended up in jail or losing your full time job?
Client: I mean, they haven't happened yet.
Counselor:
output: It hasn't happened.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, Marsha, so how can I help you today?
Client: Well, I'm working full time. I'm a part time student. I've just gotten engaged, and I live at home. There's just so much stress in my life. I have everything happening all at once. Just to top it all off, I failed an exam, a really big exam, and I just feel like I can't do anything anymore. I can't do anything right. I've just got so much stress, and I feel like such a disappointment, such a failure. And I've embarrassed my family by failing. I just don't know what to do anymore. I guess I've come here today to tell you, like, I want to leave uni, and I guess that's why I've come here to you today.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a whole lot of stuff's on top of you at the moment.
Client: Yeah, just so much. Just all parting on. Yeah.
Counselor: So you're working full time, plus part time study. Part time study. And then you've got your wedding preparation.
Client: Yeah, just got engaged, and weddings just a month away now, so, yeah, so I've just got so much happening. Work is really, really demanding and. Yeah, just fail this exam. It's just. Yeah, don't know what to do all too much.
Counselor: So imagine you've been sweating on this for a while, and it's all been swirling around in your head.
Client: Just been building up and building up and so much pressure with everything. And I'm living at home, so my parents, you know, a lot of pressure, need to do everything right. And. Yeah, by failing this, I feel like I've just embarrassed and disappointed them, and I just don't feel like I'm good enough, you know, to go on studying.
Counselor: Okay. And have they said much to you about failing your exam?
Client: They haven't said much. I was really scared to tell them, actually, because I knew they'd just be so disappointed and just embarrassed by the fact that I did fail. Yeah. I've never failed anything before. And so, yeah, really hard.
Counselor: Yeah. So it's new and you don't like it at all?
Client: Not at all, no. And I think leaving uni will just be the way out, just so I don't have to go through it again.
Counselor: Right. Okay. Well, I'm glad you've come to counselling, because it's good for us to get an outsider's opinion when we've got so much on our plate and we're confused as to what to do and our emotions can get in the way. And you've just said earlier that a whole lot of stuff's on your plate at the moment. Okay. So I'm glad you've come here. Here at the clinic, we use the ABC model, which is a cognitive behavioural therapy model. So, Marsha, some counsellors have put together a list of beliefs that we often use and we don't realise that we're using those beliefs and they tend to be faulty ones. Here's the list. Here, have a look through that to see if there are any beliefs that you might be operating on at the moment.
Client: I think number two.
Counselor: Okay, read that one out for me.
Client: That it's necessary to have a high degree of order uncertainty in order to be happy and perform well.
Counselor: Yeah, yeah, you mentioned that earlier.
Client: Number four, that it's necessary to be competent and successful in all those things which are attempted.
Counselor: Yeah, that's an expectation from your family.
Client: Yeah, possibly. Number eight, that life should be entirely pleasant and enjoyable and that any frustration, discomfort or pain would be unbearable.
Counselor: Which one of those stands out the most for you at the moment?
Client: Um, probably number four.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How would you put that in your own words?
Client: That I need to be successful all the time in everything that I do. Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. And is that different from what's happening in your life at the moment?
Client: Well, failing that exam, I mean, I wasn't successful with that. So. Yeah, I mean, it just throws out, I guess, even number two because throws out all the order in my life. I need to have everything, you know? So I need to know what I'm doing, where I'm going. Yeah.
Counselor: So, okay, so if number four is an expectation that your family have and that you have of yourself, how do you measure up next to number four?
Client: I don't feel like I'm good enough.
Counselor: Okay. All right. I. Well, what I'd like to do is put some of those ideas on the board under the ABC and I'll explain as we go along.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. So what do you think the trigger point might be or the activating event for you at the moment?
Client: I mean, there are a lot of things, but I think obviously failing the exam was the main one.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. And the consequences. You thinking of leaving uni?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. And that statement you made earlier about.
Client: I'm not good enough?
Counselor: Yeah, that's. That's the b one. That's the crucial one. And I'll explain it shortly when I get up to the board.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right. Okay. I think I'll put it up there now for you so we can work through that. So, Marsha, the activating event, which is what you stated earlier.
Client: I failed my examined.
Counselor: That's right. And the kind of decision that you're thinking about is leaving uni. That's right. Yeah. Okay. So it's important that we consider the jump from here over to here. And the kind of thinking that you've been swirling around in your head affects the consequence. And you've mentioned earlier that number four seems to fit. And you put that in your own words. What were your words before?
Client: That I'm not good enough.
Counselor:
output: Yeah. Good. That's really important for us to consider that kind of thinking. Okay, Marsha, it's good that we've got those things on the board. And what I'd like to do now is focus. Stepping out a bit from your situation and looking at it from another point of view. To me, it sounds like you're doing a whole lot of things really well. Can you list all of the things that you're doing really well?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maury. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: You doing all right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?
Client: Yeah, yeah. I mean, you know, it kind of came up again. You know, every time my wife yells at me, you know, I feel like a failure, you know, like I told you last time, I just. I just feel like I can't do anything right, you know? Like everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling, and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.
Counselor: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So it's frustrating.
Client: Yeah, it definitely is.
Counselor: How is what's going on impacted your relationship with your wife?
Client: I mean, it's rocky, you know, because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that. And then, you know, we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad, and then it just keeps going like that.
Counselor: So when you. You mentioned you feel like a failure when she. When she yells at you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Can you think back to maybe the last time, one of the last times you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We've talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts. She starts yelling at you?
Client: I mean, she'll yell at me. I mean, I feel, you know, frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And. I don't know. I mean, as I was thinking about, like we were talking about it, and as I was thinking about it more this week, kind of felt like, you know, kind of like what happened with my dad, you know? I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. You know, like, if my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way. And it feels like the same thing. Yeah. It's kind of the first. I guess kind of the first thought that comes to mind.
Counselor: The first thought is I've been through something like this before, I guess.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like, you know? Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Like, it's like just a sense that this isn't brand new.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad. Yahweh. Yeah.
Client: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So, in a sense, these arguments are taking you back to another point in time.
Client: I guess so, in a way, that's distressing.
Counselor: Yeah, it is.
Client: I mean, it feels, you know, pretty crappy.
Counselor: Now, in these arguments, she yells at you. You mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own, you know, in the midst of all that. Right. How would you rate it in terms of, like, any physical violence? Nothing like that.
Client: No, it's just words. I mean, we're just, you know, just yelling.
Counselor: And what level, like, what level of yelling would you say? How severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?
Client: Yeah, I don't know. I mean, it's like, you know, sometimes it can get up to, like, the eight or nines, you know, but just, I guess generally it's, you know, down. Closer to a seven on scale, like one to ten. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So sometimes it's seven. That would be pretty bad.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But some other times it's not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you feel like your reaction is being frustrated is disproportionate to what's really going on or you feel like it's money?
Client: I don't know what else to do. You know? I mean, it's just. It's kind of my reaction, my gut reaction to it, you know? I think I'm justified in it because, you know, she just doesn't understand how much she yells at me, you know, and how much that hurts me. You know? I do feel justified. I mean, but it just. It just keeps going, though. And I feel justified, though. I don't know.
Counselor: Let's talk for a moment about, if you're okay with it, about your father and his yelling. You've discussed this with me a little bit before. In the past few sessions. I remember you saying that most. It was in the afternoon. Most of the yelling was when you were both home.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it was. I mean, mostly when I get home from school. I mean, I wasn't, you know, I was in high school, and then after that, you know, I went to college. And so I wasn't really home much during college, but, you know, I guess it'd be after I got home from high school. You know, I'd get home and he'd get home from work and, you know, just kind of be aggravated, whatever, just start yelling and. Yeah, usually when I got back from school, yeah.
Counselor: So he would get back from work, you would get back from school. And how long would that last? How long would the period where you were kind of vulnerable to being yelled at last?
Client: I don't know. I mean, sometimes about an hour, you know, and he'd be yelling because he's, you know, frustrated from work and he's frustrated from the drive home and whatever else, you know? And at some point, he would usually start drinking, you know, so maybe about an hour or so, you know, where that was. Like, you knew you were gonna get it.
Counselor: So kind of every day you could predict that between when you. Or between when he came home after you were already home from school and when he started drinking, you were gonna. He was gonna find something to yacht you about.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And, I mean, there were some days, like, I knew when he came home, he came home the same time every day. I knew I could get out of the house, you know? Cause at some point, I had a car, my friends had cars, you know, whatever.
Counselor: You had more freedom.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. You know, at some point, I had a job, so sometimes I'd work after school and stuff, so I knew I'd be able to leave the house at times, you know, like when I knew he was gonna start yelling and stuff. But, I mean, there was a period of time probably like my senior year of high school that I just didn't, you know, I just came home and, you know, it was gonna happen, you know, that's the way it happened.
Counselor: Even though you were able to escape it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. You could have stayed out long enough for him to start drinking. Yeah.
Client: Instead you stayed in the house.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I mean, it was pretty much my whole senior year come home. I knew what was gonna happen, and I just took it. You know, I just. I knew he was gonna yell. I just took it that.
Counselor: Was there ever a period when you first got your freedom that you tried, like.
Client: Oh, yeah, yeah, I did. And. I don't know. I don't know why I didn't just keep doing that. It probably would have been easier, but. I don't know. The whole senior year, I just started. I was just back there at the house when he came home from work.
Counselor: So in that period, were you. Were you. There's times when you did leave, what did he do instead of yell at you?
Client: I guess he had to yell at somebody else. I mean, my. My sister, my brother were home. I guess he probably yelled at them. I don't know. I mean, it felt good to not be there, but I guess he probably yelled at them, which just sucks. I mean, you know, I guess somebody had. Whoever was there was gonna take it, you know?
Counselor: Somebody was gonna get you out there.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, I guess it was them when I wasn't there. I don't know.
Counselor: And how do you think you took it. When you were there, how well did you respond?
Client: I just got used to it, you know, I knew what was gonna happen. I knew he was gonna yell. I knew that it was gonna make me upset. I knew that just those repeated times, just like now, you know, I'm gonna feel like a failure, which ultimately I did. You know, maybe I probably just became numb to it, you know, it happens so often and same thing every day. Probably just became numb to it and just kind of stopped caring and kind of stopped, I don't know, believing in myself or something, you know?
Counselor: Like you've just given up.
Client: Yeah, probably. That's probably. I don't know. Probably. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And how many years total did this experience go on? Do you endure the yelling?
Client: I mean, it would have been while I was in middle school and most of high school. I mean, I told you at some point I was able to leave, but probably all of middle school, most of high school, and I left, and then some, you know, for the rest of the senior year, I would be there. So, I don't know, quite a few years, I guess.
Counselor: A long time to suffer.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And now if we move back forward in time, you're in a relationship where you're getting yelled at a bit. Right. And that's sometimes quite a bit, and that's causing you distress.
Client: It's like the same thing. You're yelling a little bit and. Yeah.
Counselor: So you feel like you're back in the same place.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it does. Yeah. I mean, obviously, you know, she's. She's not doing anything like he was, you know, like drinking or anything like that, but it does. I mean, it's like the same thing that happened is happening again.
Counselor: So that's. In your opinion, that's the consequence of what happened to you. Like, all this yelling that you endured before in some way is significantly contributing to what you're going through now.
Client: Maybe. I mean, I guess it could, you know, because it is the same thing. So maybe it's.
Counselor: There could be some connection.
Client: Maybe. Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, maybe not 100% explain it, but it explains part of it.
Client: Yeah, it definitely could. I definitely could.
Counselor: So your functioning has been affected a bit. I mean, to the point where you're here with me now, we're talking about it, and you're frustrated, and it does sound painful. Now, I'm curious. You mentioned you had a younger sister and a younger brother, and they grew up in the same house. How are they doing?
Client: Well, my sister, she's three years younger than I am. She's doing great. I mean, she graduated from college, like, top of her class kind of thing, you know? And she's about to get married, too. That's cool. Got a really great guy, you know. She's doing great. She lives next town over for me. I get to see her a lot. Yeah, she's great, though. My brother, he's five years younger than I am. He's doing pretty good, too. He's just about to graduate from college. I think he gets really good grades, too, from what I hear, from what he tells me. I don't get to see him as much as I do her because she's in college, but I think he's doing really well, too. You know, they both. Yeah, they both do some really good stuff. They have really good goals and stuff like that.
Counselor: You seem like you have a good relationship with them. You're proud of them. Yeah, definitely.
Client: I'm definitely proud of them. I think they're doing some really good stuff, you know, really trying to make something of themselves. Yeah.
Counselor: So, you know, I wonder. They're doing pretty well. You're doing okay, but you're having a rough time right now. How would things have been if you had taken that? I know it's difficult to predict, but if you had taken that opportunity to not be there, if you had, like you said, you had a car, your friends had cars, you could have avoided. You could have avoided the situation directly between your dad and you.
Client: Yeah, I mean, yeah, I guess I could have. I don't know. I mean. I mean, I took the yelling and stuff, so, you know, it's obviously affecting me now.
Counselor: You took the brunt of the abuse.
Client: Yeah, I guess I did. I mean, you know, I bring it up to them sometimes and they're like, yeah, I mean, dad yelled sometimes, but, you know, it wasn't that bad. Definitely a different experience from what I had. You know, they don't see it like I do, you know? I don't know. Maybe things would have been worse for them.
Counselor: So, in a sense, your father verbally abused you. Nothing makes that right. But in a sense, you, because you were there and you were the target. And. Could ride it out, you shielded them from that abuse.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, you mentioned it would have been somebody else, right?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, it probably would have been them. Probably was them when I wasn't there, you know? Yeah, I don't know.
SPK_3: I guess you're probably right.
Client: I mean, they are doing pretty well, you know, I think probably they're doing better than I am, I guess.
Counselor: You know, probably no small part because of your protecting them.
Client: Right.
Counselor: I mean, you were in an impossible situation, and you made the choice to stay there.
Client: I guess I did. Right.
Counselor: There was some negative consequences for you, which we'll try to work through, but some really positive consequences for your siblings.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, I guess so. I mean, they, you know, I feel like a failure most of the time, but, I mean, they don't. They're doing good stuff, you know? Shoot, I guess you're right. I mean, that could have been it. I guess I'd love to ask them, like, what, you know, like, what they think would have happened if, you know, the yelling would have been more or something towards them, you know?
Counselor: And maybe you'll find out that when you weren't there, that is what would happen.
Client: Maybe.
Counselor: So you feel like a failure, but at the same time, you're happy for them and proud of all their accomplishments.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: It seems like you were a part of that success.
Client: Maybe. I mean, I guess that makes sense, you know? Yeah, maybe. I hope so. You know? I hope so.
Counselor: Well, in cognitive therapy, oftentimes, we try to do what we call reframing. Right? That's where we take. We take a situation and we don't change the facts. Like, we don't move from the truth, but we try to cast it in some different lights. So certainly being yelled at and abused, like I said, nothing makes up. Right. That's awful. And what you're going through now, possibly because of that, is awful, and that's a reality. But at the same time, it's a reality, perhaps that you protected your siblings. Both those things can be true at the same time.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, I guess so. I mean, I guess there's, like, a positive that comes out of that negative, maybe. Mm hmm. Yeah, I hope that's true. I'd like to think of this.
Counselor: So another thing that occurs to me is that you were mentioned how before, I think a few sessions ago, how you're being yelled at now, and you're having some strong reactions to that, just like you told me today. But also, you do some of the yelling, probably, yeah. You think some of that comes from what you learned from your father?
Client: Yeah. I mean, you know, I saw him do it for so many years. Probably all I know how to do, you know, if I'm trying to resolve something or whatever, you know, probably all I know how to do.
Counselor: Have there ever been occasions where your wife starts yelling at you and you don't respond with yelling?
Client: Yeah, I think so.
Counselor: I mean, that's happened a few times.
Client: I guess. I mean, I was trying to think of that this week, too. And, you know, I was trying to be more. A little bit more aware, like we were talking about before, you know, about my reaction to her and stuff. And, you know, I kind of started to realize a little bit more like maybe I'm yelling a little more than I think I do, or maybe a little bit more, like, intensely than I think I do. You know, that's probably the case. That's all I knew how to do. That's all I was taught.
Counselor:
output: That's what you learned. So again, just like your father yelling at you, your wife yelling at you isn't what we want. But maybe in that case, maybe your reaction to it is making it worse. Maybe you're contributing to an escalation again, because it's what you learned, which is understandable. But perhaps in that moment, and we can talk about your automatic thoughts around that, but perhaps in that moment, that automatic thought, whatever it is, is contributing to that behavior of yelling back. And we can get in there and try to interrupt that and maybe get your reaction to be. Maybe the more she yells, the more you calm down, because we know. We know what you're doing now is not working right. And that's not working, and you want to work right. You want your marriage to be successful. So for this week, I want you to reflect kind of on. Kind of on the reframe, you know, kind of how the past is connected to what's going on now, but also how things would have turned out if. If you had just left that whole situation, how it might not be as positive for your siblings. So you contributed some good to a situation that was really miserable for you. And I also want you to try to. I've given you the thought record to work on for homework and stuff. I want you to try to capture that automatic thought. And I know we talked about a little today in terms of your core belief, Andrew, automatic thought when she yells at you. But think about how you can respond to the variety of automatic thoughts that you're having when she is yelling at you and with adaptive responses with the self talk we talked about, and I know there's still from earlier today talk with you, there's still a real focus on the feelings, but in there is a thought. We talked about that before. Even though those feelings are strong, there's a thought in there that's, well, creating them. We believe that it directly leads to them. So what I want to work on with you is interrupting that process. Let's see what's actually happening at the cognition level before it gets to the feeling and see if we can get some self talk in there. So if you complete, you know, as many thought records on that, you know, say, one, one to three, depending on how many thoughts you can identify. So remember to ask yourself that question, what's going through my mind right now? So when that yelling starts, try to maintain focus and say, what's going through my mind right now? Try to think about that. Think about that thought that's automatically coming into your mind, and then we can build some adaptive responses and self talk.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: Been doing okay. It's been a while now. You've been practicing with the waiting after you wash your hands? Mm hmm. How's that been going for you?
Client: Well, I think it's been going pretty well. I've been able to, you know, wait pretty good. I'm gonna start it out slow like you suggested, with three minutes. Then I would wash my hands for five minutes. I would wash my hands, and I got up to about 15 minutes.
Counselor: That's great.
Client: And there were some times that I was really proud of myself that I actually forgot.
Counselor: You forgot to wash your hands entirely?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So when was the next time you washed them?
Client: When I would go to, like, eat. Dinner,
Counselor: which is when you normally wash your hands. So really, you touched something that had germs, and you had some anxiety as you had to get to that waiting period. But then the anxiety subsided to a point where I forgot about it just wasn't a priority. You just completely forgot and went on with your day?
Client: Yeah. I was really proud of myself, but I got really concerned because I got sick. I got sick recently, and I'm afraid it's from one of those times that I didn't wash my hands.
Counselor: Well, tell me about the sickness.
Client: Well, my throat started to get hurt real bad, and I was just really congested. And all I could think about was, it's because I didn't wash my hands when I went to the store or when I went to my car when I touched a jacket. That's, you know, been everywhere.
Counselor: How many times do you normally get it? Sounds like a cold.
Client: I mean, it was kind of a light cold.
Counselor: Light cold.
Client: I mean, we wouldn't wait in a.
Counselor: Few days, a couple days. So how long or how many times a year would you get something like that normally?
Client: I mean, I get sick. I mean, quite often because of my job. I'm around a lot of people, and hand sanitizer can only work so much. I do get sick.
Counselor: So it's been six weeks since you started waiting? Right. I think it was around session three where we talked about putting a gap between when you touch something, when you wash your hands, like a time gap, and you got a cold once. Would that be out of the ordinary to get a cold one time in six weeks this time of year?
Client: I suppose not. I mean, the rational part of me knows that I get sick, but just because I'm trying something new with the, you know, and then the waiting and then the not washing, I'm just afraid that there was, you know, you're afraid.
Counselor: They were linked at one cause the other that waiting to wash your hands got you sick. And that could have happened. I don't know. But let's talk about the cold. You said it was a couple days.
Client: It wasn't severe. I mean, I took some, you know, over the counter medicine, slept it off.
Counselor: So wasn't a catastrophe.
Client: No, I've definitely been sicker in my life. And I mean, it did seem like one of those ones that I get every now and then.
Counselor: So when we spoke, I remember before you had said that the kind of worst case scenario, the reason that you're thinking so much about the germs on your hands is that it could make you sick. But you did get sick and you were able to tolerated.
Client: Yeah, I was. Which I found kind of odd because I was. I was panicked at the beginning when I started to feel those first, you know, the itchy throat, the headaches.
Counselor: Sure, it's miserable, right? Nobody wants to get sick.
Client: And I got concerned, you know, that it was because of that. Then it just kind of subsided. I guess I felt a little better, you know, as the days went on, I felt better about it happening, about.
Counselor: The whole getting sick and you started to recover. So kind of the worst case scenario occurred and you survived. And again, we don't know if the, the amount of hand washing you were doing before the ERP exposure and response prevention, we don't know if that would have prevented the cold or not. Yeah, because you do get sick several times, several times a year, in a year. So there's a lot we don't know. But we do know that you survived it and it wasn't as bad looking back at it.
Client: I mean, in my head, not washing my hands and the sick that I would get is a lot worse. It's like hospital worthy. And this was, you know, like I said over the counter, you know, relax a little bit.
Counselor: So not pleasant, but survivable.
Client: It definitely wasn't pleasant, but it wasn't as bad as it could have gone in my mind.
Counselor: So presume for a moment that it was a consequence of not immediately rushing over and washing your hands. What would you rather have? The occasional cold like that or the excessive hand washing and anxiety?
Client: I mean, I definitely don't like the excessive hand washing. I don't. I mean, it ruins my skin and I. It's expensive and it makes me feel bad about myself. And I mean, I guess the trade off is if I get a little sick and that would be okay.
Counselor: Again, that's presuming that it did cause you to get sick, which it may not have.
Client: I suppose that's true.
Counselor: So I wanted to point out, too, that I remember when we, we first started the exposure response prevention exercise, we did it right here in session by touching the arms of the chair. And I can see now your arms are.
Client: Oh, I didn't even notice I was doing that. Oh, I don't, you know, even noticing it, I don't feel like I need to go, you know, wash my elbows or anything.
Counselor: You don't feel that compulsion?
Client: No, I don't. I mean, I know that it's dirty. I know that people sit here and people can be dirty, but I don't feel that need to go wash my hands right now.
Counselor: So your anxiety increased a little when I told you, I pointed out that you were touching it, but not as much as it did before.
Client: I mean, on that scale, I think it'd be about a two.
Counselor: Well, with one being the lowest anxiety and ten being the highest, you're about two.
Client: Well, when you pointed it out, I didn't notice before.
Counselor: So you were a one in anxiety before that. So now you're aware of it a little bit. Right. So your elbows. Your elbows have to touch the chair.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you're aware of it a little bit and you're a little anxious.
Client: I mean, not so much anymore. I mean, it's kind of. You mentioned it. I got anxious for a moment, and then it's just kind of like, oh, well, you're already doing it and nothing bad's happening right now.
Counselor: Well, good. You made a lot of progress.
Client: Thank you.
Counselor: A lot of progress. So you're still going to have, as we move forward, you're still going to have some anxiety, like when I mentioned that your arms are touching the chair. You're still going to have some anxiety from time to time. Anxiety is part of life.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: It's going to happen from time to time. So one of the things I hope that you've gained from this is that just like you tolerated being sick for those few days, right. Is to tolerate that anxiety. Right. To be able to be okay with having some anxiety in your life.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: In a sense, the fear of being anxious kind of causes a vicious cycle. Right. You have fear of being anxious. You'll do not anything, but you'll do many things to get rid of that.
Client: Anxiety because it gets really bad. It starts consuming me.
Counselor:
output: It's uncomfortable. I remember when you touched the chair before, right? Like many weeks ago, that you had the urge to go wash your hands right away, you were anxious.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Gabriella. I understand that you're here today because you've been experiencing some low mood.
Client: Yeah, I just. Recently, I'm just feeling down a lot and I can't really, like, snap out of it. Like, sometimes if it's happened before, I can just, like, get myself back on track, but recently I just find it really difficult to do.
Counselor: Hey, so it sounds like you've been experiencing some low mood and you're kind of struggling to get going a bit.
Client: Yeah, yeah, definitely.
Counselor: You've had low mood in the past, but it's kind of. You've been able to pull yourself out of it before, but more recently you found that harder. Okay, so I understand that you first went to your GP. He referred you here about two months ago. Can I ask what led you to go to the GP in the first place?
Client: My long term boyfriend broke up with me and it was such a shock. Like, I really wasn't expecting it and it just got me really down and I just felt really lonely and I didn't really want to see people and just wanted to be in my own space. And my mum told me I should probably go to the doctors. Oh. And he's referred me to you.
Counselor: Okay. So it sounds then like you had that breakup and you weren't expecting it, so it kind of came out of the blue a bit and that you've been on your own quite a lot, so you've not been seeing people as much. And it sounds like your mum noticed that there's been a bit of a change in you. Okay. And how have things been then, since then, since that happened and since you went to the GP?
Client: I just. Nothing's really changed. Nothing's really improved. I just feel down, like everything's an effort and just feel distant from things. And like I said, I can't snap out of it.
Counselor: Okay. And how did you feel about coming here today?
Client: I was kind of disappointed in myself because I feel like nobody else my age is doing this. Like, I should have been able to snap out of it. Like, it's just another thing that I've not really. It's another thing that's making me stand out for the wrong reasons.
Counselor: Okay. So you feel like it's kind of odd or unusual to be coming to see a clinical psychologist? I suppose I just want to reassure you that it's absolutely normal to have feelings of depression and anxiety. It's really very common and it certainly isn't odd or strange at all. So it sounds like it was actually quite hard for you to come here today?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So what, I guess led you to do that? Because it sounds like maybe there was a lot pushing you against coming here today, but you've managed to come anyway.
Client: I'm just hoping that it's gonna help, I think. I didn't really want to admit it because it's just another failure, but my mum was talking to me and I know she's not really happy with the way I'm behaving. I didn't really want to disappoint her again and so I thought there's no harm in it, so she thought it'd come.
Counselor: So it sounds like partly you're doing it then, for your mum because you're a bit worried that she isn't pleased with you at the moment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Well, I think it's great that you've come here and definitely there's a lot of evidence to suggest that psychological therapy can help depression and particularly the type of therapy that we're going to be doing, which is called cognitive behaviour therapy. And I'll tell you a bit more about that as we go on, but I'm just trying to find out a bit more about you today. So I saw from your notes that you're a medic student.
Client: Yeah, I'm not currently in uni at the moment, but, yeah, last year as a medic student.
Counselor: Okay. So I guess what's the reason that you're not in uni this year?
Client: It was pretty tough first year, so they then suggested that I took a year out. This is the break.
Counselor: Okay. So just thinking. So that would be about six months ago, was it that your year out started? Yeah. And it sounds then maybe like your first year was also quite tough.
Client: Yeah, it was. I thought it's tough for everyone, but obviously we all take it in different ways, don't we?
Counselor: And you're planning on. Are you planning on returning and.
Client: Yeah, I'm gonna have to. Really? So. Yeah.
Counselor: Don't sound too sure about that, though.
Client: I think returning is probably that's what's gonna make everyone happy. And I think, you know, at least I'll be able to finally achieve something and get something right, so. Yeah, like, next year I'm gonna. I'll get through it. Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So it doesn't. It doesn't sound like you want to go back.
Client: I do. I do enjoy it. I just don't feel like me at the moment and I just. It's a lot of work and it's a lot of pressure, but that's what comes of it. And, you know, it'll work out for the best if I go.
Counselor: Okay. So I guess then there's quite a lot of thoughts and feelings about going back at the moment. I'm just wondering, in the meantime, what are you up to? What have you been doing?
Client: Well, I've not really had much on the horizon. My mum, her friend, owns a restaurant and she suggested that I did a bit of waitressing there just for a bit of money and stuff, because obviously I'm not in uni, so I've done that.
Counselor: Okay. How many shifts have you done there?
Client: I've only done one so far. Yeah. I don't know whether it's something that I'd probably go back to, but.
Counselor: Okay. When was that shift?
Client: It was last week, actually. Okay.
Counselor: And how was it? I suppose I'm intrigued. Can you tell me a bit more about that?
Client: It was different, you know, because it was like, I could. I did enjoy it because there was like. It's just different aspect and I had to, like, speak to people and, like, try to get their orders and try to remember it and stuff. Like, I wasn't very good, but I suppose, like, it was handy to have some money and, like, get out the house.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you quite enjoyed that, then.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What makes you think you weren't very good?
Client: I just. I was just a bit slow and people sometimes didn't understand what I was saying, so I'd have to talk louder or quieter or slower. And I got a bit confused sometimes with the orders and I just don't really think that I'm not really, like, a friendly. Like, people don't really think that I'm a friendly person, so they didn't really want to talk to me and stuff. I felt like I was, like, inconveniencing them by, like, asking them things and getting things wrong. But, yeah, they said that apparently most people get, like, a few mistakes on their first shift. But then again, she's my mum's friend, so it's probably why she's saying it.
Counselor: So the person who owns a restaurant is your mum's friend?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So it says you're saying that you think you weren't very good and that's because you're a bit slow and you got confused with some orders.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is it? But you said it's common for people to do that on their first shift.
Client: That's what she said to us. But it's probably just. She's just trying to make me feel better. She probably felt sorry for me because I'm obviously not very good at it. Like, I'm not very good at any things. Recently, I think she just felt sorry for me.
Counselor: Okay. So I've just been noting down some of those thoughts that you've been having. You kind of say that you feel like you're not very good. You're slow, you're confused with the orders, and you feel like you're inconveniencing her and she feels. So for you. I suppose I'm wondering, I mean, what makes you think that she feels sorry for you?
Client: Well, like, like I said, she's my mum's friend, and she's obviously feeling sorry for my mum as well because she's got a daughter that's not like anyone else of her age, and she's just, like, all alone and she's not getting involved. So I think she just feels sorry for me and she doesn't want to say anything to upset me.
Counselor: But, yeah, when you're having these kind of thoughts, because that's quite a lot of negative thoughts you're describing, how do you feel?
Client: Empty? I don't. I'm just calling as it is. I'm just calling it as reality. And I feel like I'm being honest with myself by just voicing it and not trying to get around hiding it, because I know, like, I can say in myself.
Counselor: So it sounds like you feel like those thoughts are very true, then. I mean, if you were going to rate them, say, I'm going to pick out some of those thoughts you described. So you said I'm not very good and I'm inconveniencing them. How much would you say you believe those on a scale out of a hundred, where a hundred is like, I absolutely believe it and zero is like, I don't believe it at all.
Client: I'm about 80. Yeah.
Counselor: So you feel quite sure that you definitely believe those? Okay. And you said that when you're thinking those thoughts, you start to feel quite empty.
Client: I just feel distant. And like I said, I'm not really myself. I just. It's like I'm not really there, but when I am, I can't even do a good job.
Counselor:
output: Are there any other emotions that you experience?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Jordan. How you doing today?
Client: Could have been better.
Counselor: Could be better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: Um, well, you know, I have two jobs.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: And I lost one of them.
Counselor: You lost your job? Yes. Which one did you lose?
Client: I lost one at the grocery store.
Counselor: That was your part time?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I'm sorry to hear that.
Client: Me too. And I'm just. It's all I think about now.
Counselor: And when did this happen?
Client: It happened about two, three days ago.
Counselor: Two, three days ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if I remember right, you took that job not too long ago to kind of supplement your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So certainly that would be upsetting, but I know that's not a major part of your income.
Client: It's not, but, I mean, I'm still very worried about it.
Counselor: Tell me about the worry.
Client: I mean, I worry that, you know, I'm. Now I only had so much money, and now I have less than that. I mean, without my money, you know, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: So before you had the job, you were paying all your bills. You want some extra income, you've lost that extra income. And I can certainly understand how that would be disturbing. But as I understand that you were doing okay before with your full time job.
Client: I was doing okay, but, I mean, I got comfortable with that extra income, and so now my fear is that I've gotten too comfortable with it, and now that it's not there anymore, it's going to affect the fact I'm not going to be able to pay for food or my rent.
Counselor: Okay, so you adjusted to the new income level with the full time and the part time job together, and you're worried you can't adjust back?
Client: I'm worried that, I mean, things are just gonna get worse from here. I mean, it's a big deal, losing your job. Even if it was part time, I've gotten comfortable from having so much money, from the money I had to. Now that's, you know, been divided and, I mean, God knows how many things, like I said, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: Well, what. What can happen? So you have that income, your income is reduced now to just your full time job. What can happen from this point on?
Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. So, I mean, if I can't, if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not gonna have insurance on my cardinal. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work, and then I'll get fired there too.
Counselor: All right, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something the police officer could see, don't have insurance, give you a ticket, which is just money. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?
Client: Because I wouldn't be able to get to work.
Counselor: So it'd be. So the ticket would be so expensive, you would lose your.
Client: Well, the ticket would be expensive, so I wouldn't be able to try to pay the next month's insurance. So I just wouldn't have insurance on my car. So I.
Counselor: So you'd lose your insurance?
Client: I'd lose my insurance.
Counselor: And then by losing your insurance, you lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive that insurance. And then you lose your job.
Client: Mm hmm. I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car, and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times.
Counselor: No, that's serious. Yeah. You wouldn't want to do that.
Client: I wouldn't go to jail.
Counselor: So there's two. You have two kind of causal change. One is losing your job. And now even just the idea you can end up incarcerated.
Client: Yes. I mean, which I definitely lose my.
Counselor: Job if I'm in jail, I would imagine.
Client: And so that would have. So then I wouldn't even have, like, any money to help me through jail. Like, to. For the commissary and stuff.
Counselor: Because you would have no income.
Client: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm. No one's gonna hire me.
Counselor: Because you have a criminal record.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances. So what's happened is kind of in your mind, and we've talked about how thoughts work and beliefs work, is you, in reality, you've lost this part time job. And as I said, that's certainly. That's understandable that you'd be upset about that. I doubt many people would be happy about losing additional income, but you move from there, from losing additional income, which is what has actually happened to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this. So I remember maybe last week. Week before, you're talking about the. The letter that you received from. It was like a late notice. It wasn't. Turned out wasn't.
Client: Yeah, it was sent to me, but it was somebody else's credit card mistake. Yeah.
Counselor: Do you remember the conclusions you drew from when you believe that was actually for you, that late notice, that my.
Client: Credit score was gonna go down, that I would. I'd be stuck in that apartment, and then I'd go into depression. I wouldn't be able to do anything.
Counselor: Yeah. So you ended up in that scenario. You end up in a situation where you just couldn't function at all. And you moved there from a letter that you believe was addressed to you, saying you were one month or six days late or something on a credit card, which, of course, you don't want to be late on a credit card, but you move from there to being so depressed you couldn't work, couldn't function, I think, is how you put it. Couldn't function. Do you see, kind of, given how we've talked about cognitive behavioral strategies and concepts, do you see a pattern that's emerged over the last few times I've seen you?
Client: I mean, I've seen that, you know, sometimes I can. I can think the worst, and then. And I know it didn't happen last time, but that was, you know, a stroke of good luck.
Counselor: That it wasn't you.
Client: Yeah. That it was, you know, it wasn't me. And, you know, that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part time job anymore.
Counselor: You've lost real income.
Client: I mean, this isn't a mistake. This isn't a. We fired the wrong person. You know, this is real. So there's real concerns here.
Counselor: I.
Client: Unlike last time, where I was lucky.
Counselor: So this. This situation, you see, is different than the first situation because the first situation was more. You were perceiving something was wrong that wasn't wrong because you weren't the intended recipient of the letter.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But in this situation, it's different because it's real. You really lost your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And, of course, keeping in mind that this job, again, only a few months old, and you survived well before that, is it reason to believe you could survive well again, that you could adapt to this lost income?
Client: Well, I suppose there is, but I'm concerned about whether I'm not, whether I won't adapt.
Counselor: Well, let's look at this in terms of probabilities, right. You've had several jobs throughout your career. You've had some of them worked out. You've lost other ones. You're still paying your bills. So in terms of probabilities, how many times have you, how many times have you ended up in jail or losing your full time job?
Client: I mean, they haven't happened yet.
Counselor: It hasn't happened.
Client: Not yet. But I mean, I, I struggled a little bit when I lost a part time job or when I was younger and I had those little jobs.
Counselor: So you had to adapt.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And it was painful.
Client: I did struggle, yeah.
Counselor: You struggled.
Client: Yeah. I mean, but I'm older now. These are, you know, even though grocery stores, not a serious job. It was income.
Counselor: Sure. Yeah. And again, to lose income would be disappointing for just about anybody. Are there any upsides to not having that job?
Client: I suppose I have more time to focus on my full time job because, I mean, that is really intensive.
Counselor: Is there a possibility that you could find another part time job just as you found that one?
Client: I mean, because will somebody else take me because I was fired from that job? I mean, that's my concern, is that.
Counselor: Nobody, they're going to find out.
Client: Yeah. And then they're going to go, oh, she was fired, you know. No, we don't. We don't want her.
Counselor: But you've had other jobs that didn't work out before and that didn't affect you getting that job.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: So the worst case scenario, I guess what I'm getting at the worst case scenario is, in your case, ending up in jail or losing your full time job, which you've had for a while.
Client: Yeah, I really don't want to lose my job.
Counselor: And it seems like they like you there.
Client: I hope they do.
Counselor: Right? Yeah. So those scenarios, I guess, are possible, but they seem, based on what you're saying, is pretty unlikely. So I wonder how useful it is to invest a lot of energy in kind of tracking that causal chain to jail or prison or to unemployment when that's really not the most likely outcome. Sorry to interrupt you, but do you invest as much energy in tracking the positives or the probable outcomes?
Client: No, not even close. I know that I don't think about the positive things. I mean, I don't get fired and then go, what's good about this?
Counselor: Or get a letter in the mail and say, what's, you know, although I can see there's not much upside to that, although it turned out that was an error, so. But this has still been a theme that I've seen over the last eight to ten weeks, where you really have, you really emphasize the negative, possible, even unlikely outcomes, kind of expanding the negative as you move through. Like a causal chain.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Does that make sense? Yeah, but you don't do the same thing for the positive side. You don't look at how something could work out. Well, would you say it's fair assessment?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, no, that's. That's pretty accurate.
Counselor: But still, you're worried about this.
Client: I mean, yeah, I am worried. I'm not gonna be thrilled about it, but I suppose I don't have to go to when I'm gonna go to jail or I'm gonna lose my full time job.
Counselor: I think there's a lot of intervening factors that could occur before going to jail or losing your job. There's other things that you could do.
Client: I suppose I could get a family member to drive me or take the bus if I lost my insurance and lost my car.
Counselor: So, alternate forms of transportation. Yeah. There's adapting your spending back to where it was before.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: Part of your fear was that you wouldn't be able to adapt your spending. Right. But that's something you would have control over.
Client: I guess. I can keep, you know, better track of how much I do spend and, you know, keep track of my bank accounts and exactly how much money I have in them.
Counselor: So, having talked through this a little bit. Right. What I'm going to refer to, or is referred to as catastrophizing. Remember we talked about that when we reviewed the cognitive distortions.
Client: That sounds familiar. Yeah.
Counselor: Where a negative is taken and just making way more negative than it is at the moment. Right. Kind of knowing that, that tends to be what you do. It's what we call an error in thinking that you tend to make. Does that lower your anxiety about the situation? Does it change it in some way?
Client: I mean, knowing that I'm thinking about it wrong makes me feel a little better.
Counselor: I would say you're thinking about it in a way that's less than useful.
Client: Okay. That actually makes me feel better. Knowing that, you know, these things can happen, but it might not. There's other things that can happen before them.
Counselor: Yeah. I mean, I would even say probably not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So one way, potentially, and there's a few things we can review over the next few sessions. One way to address catastrophizing, in addition to the adaptive responses which we've talked about before, would be to find some sort of peace with the worst outcome, meaning you kind of take away the power of that anxiety over you. When you can accept worst possible outcomes doesn't mean you look forward to them or you think they're likely, or you dwell on them and ponder them. But I mean, obviously, being in jail, even though it's an extremely low probability event in your circumstance, being in jail would be survivable. Being unemployed would be survivable.
Client: People weaker than me have gone through jail.
Counselor: I guess a lot of people have been to jail. A lot of people lost their jobs. And while it's certainly a struggle, to use your word, right, I mean, that would be more than a struggle. It'd be quite unpleasant. It's at the point where you can accept that that could happen and that you would survive, that you could find some peace with the catastrophizing. Again, we'll have other routes. We'll attack these cognitive distortions from a few different angles. But one of the angles is reaching a point where you could accept that those things could happen. They're unlikely. They could happen, and you would survive.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: I mean, one thing you've shown throughout your. I mean, based on what you described to me, is that you're a survivor. You find a way to make it work.
Client: That makes me feel better. They're thinking about me as a survivor.
Counselor: Right. So in a sense, kind of reframing. We talked about that before, too. Right. Your circumstances as you're somebody that's surviving adversely losing a job is. We talk about negative things.
Client: I'm right in thinking that that's not a good thing, losing my job.
Counselor: It's certainly not ideal in your situation. So you can be defeated by it, right? That's one possibility, but you can survive. You can look at it in terms of, this is a challenge I will overcome, and I've overcome it before. And the advantage to try and look at it from the positive point of view, survivor angle is that you're going to be able to develop more solutions and kind of useful ways of thinking to overcome it. Whereas if you move from the other side, it's going to lead you down the road to worrying about ending up in jail or unemployed, which, again, although that could happen, it's unlikely. And focusing on it isn't going to change it. It's not going to change. It's not going to. It's not going to decrease its likelihood. Okay, does that make sense?
Client: Yeah, I think it does.
Counselor: In a way, it almost increases its likelihood because you're.
Client: I'm thinking about it too much.
Counselor: You're investing in the negative outcomes without really looking at the positive side. Okay, so that's kind of how cognitive distortions work, right? They're consistent errors in thinking, and we'll work on the helping you to reframe circumstances like this. Granted, this is certainly more distressing than receiving that letter that you received. Yeah, but I remember when you were talking about a while back, when you were talking about getting the part time job, you were unsure if you really wanted to take the time and do it. You were kind of on the fence back then about taking it because I.
Client: Wanted to invest all my time in my full time job. But it's always nice to have some extra spending money, especially with the holidays coming up.
Counselor: Sure. So you're on the fence, but you decided to go with it. It didn't work out. So you can revisit it and try to find another part time job, or you can go back to the other strategies you were looking at before. Invest more energy in your full time work. There's some things you want to do in your spare time. You had mentioned kind of recreationally, so it's not good news. But if you look at it in terms of the whole context, you weren't that thrilled about that job in the first place. You had other possibilities. Kind of investing in those could be a route. I'm trying to give you more options than just the catastrophic ones.
Client: I mean, it seems like that there's better ways to go about it than thinking, I'm going to go to jail, I'm going to be unemployed forever.
Counselor: Sure, there's ways that are more useful to you that'll probably help you dig out of this faster and either adjust to not having the income or replace the income.
Client: Yeah, I suppose it's not hard to get a grocery store job again.
Counselor: Well, you did it before. Right?
Client: That's true.
Counselor: And again, even if it is hard, it's a struggle. You survived in that other income for a long time without that. So when you have, and we'll talk about this next time, we can develop some adaptive responses for some of these automatic thoughts that are coming up. So we'll try to identify some of the automatic thoughts that are coming up around the job loss. But for now, I want you to try to get a general understanding of the theme, which is that you tend to catastrophize.
Client: Right.
Counselor:
output: And it is what it is, but it's not so useful for you in terms of your most efficient, productive functioning. It's not bad or good. It's just not useful.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jodie. Nice to see you again. How have you been since I saw you last?
Client: Yeah, I've been fine. Been sticking to the plan. So it's been going well?
Counselor: Oh, the plan that the hospital set you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, fantastic. And how have you been finding that?
Client: Yeah, it's been, it's been good. I've been trying to follow it, but last week wasn't very good. I had a bit of a bad day, but since then I've been fine, so it's okay.
Counselor: Okay, so tell me a bit more about that bad day. I mean, what did you eat on that day?
Client: I don't think I had anything.
Counselor: Okay, so you just ate nothing at all?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. I mean, tell me a bit more about why was that day difficult? Was there anything that had been happening around that time?
Client: It's been quite busy at school because we've got our exams and we had, like, a test the next day, so I think I was just a bit, like, worried about that, so I was trying to focus on that instead.
Counselor: So you were feeling a bit anxious about the exam that was coming up. Was there anything else that was worrying you?
Client: No, I think we had, well, we had 6th form applications due in and that was coming up in the next couple of days and I didn't really want to fill in my application.
Counselor: So it sounds like there was a couple of things that were worrying you that were on your mind.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Which thing was worrying you more, do you think?
Client: Probably the 6th form. Yeah, the 6th form one.
Counselor: Okay. What kind of. How did you feel about that? When, when we talk about that now and when that's brought up, what kind of emotions do you experience?
Client: I don't really want to start 6th form yet. It's quite soon. But I don't really want to. I mean, I've got exams first, so I've got to think about those. But I don't really want to go to 6th form at the minute.
Counselor: Okay. So what is it about sick form that makes you not want to go?
Client: I have to start over again and make new friends and like, a new routine and stuff, and I don't have, I don't really feel ready for that yet.
Counselor: What do you think might happen when you have to make new friends and start a new routine?

Client: Fear of being rejected. Yeah.

Client: Yeah, I think two to three months.
