Client: Yeah. I mean, my parents are pretty cool with it. Like, they know, but, I mean, I'm at the point now where they kind of want me to move on and move out. But I don't know. I mean, I just. It'd be nice to have that job. Like, it's a really good job, but at the same time, like, I don't see why I have to sacrifice something that I like.
Counselor: So it doesn't seem fair to you, but she recognizes the reality of your situation. Yeah, it really does come down, in your instance, to marijuana use or employment.
Client: Yeah, it's pretty accurate.
Counselor: Okay, so you're not happy about that choice?
Client: Not at all.
Counselor: Yeah. And kind of what we did with the postponed gratification was just. I mean, I really just ask you to wait ten minutes, and you were able to do that and more. Although it was difficult.
Client: It was difficult.
Counselor: It was difficult for you. So I asked you to track the number of times you smoked marijuana. Did you. Were you able to track that over the last week?
Client: Yeah, for the most part.
Counselor: Do you remember how many times that was?
Client: I think. I think I did, like, 15.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Between 15 and 20.
Counselor: Between 15 and 20. And how many times did something kind of get in the way? Did something else come up in that ten minute span that distracted you or that you enjoyed?
Client: Like, almost closer to 20 times, I guess. Otherwise I probably would have kept going, smoked more. I mean, there were a couple times where, like, somebody would call me or somebody would text me, and that kind of distracted me, so I was able to put it off for a little bit.
Counselor: So you can see in that ten minutes, things can happen. Things can happen that can help you to avoid the marijuana. Sometimes nothing does, and after the ten minutes you use it, and sometimes something does kind of get in the way with the marijuana, like, distract you or you have another activity that you enjoy and then you didn't use. So with that in mind, you found the experience rough. But was it tolerable?
Client: Yeah, it wasn't bad.
Counselor: Was it bad? Do you think for this next week we could try postponing that gratification from ten minutes to 20 minutes?
Client: I don't know. That seems kinda. Yeah, that seems like a longer time.
Counselor: That is definitely. That is a longer time.
Client: I don't know about that.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Maybe like 15 minutes.
Counselor: No, a compromise. Is 15 okay. Yeah. Do you think you could maintain 15 minutes weighing 15?
Client: I think I could try a little bit more than 20.
Counselor: Be a loser than 20. All right, so let's go with 15. Minutes. So 15 minutes is compared to ten. That will give you five extra minutes that something could happen that could distract you and you wouldn't use in that instance. Right. There's also to constructively use that time. You could consider alternatives. Like you mentioned walking. You could use that time and start walking.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Anything else that you like? Maybe in the past, on occasion when you wanted to use marijuana, but you didn't have anything available, what would you.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maury. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: You doing all right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?
Client: Yeah, yeah. I mean, you know, it kind of came up again. You know, every time my wife yells at me, you know, I feel like a failure, you know, like I told you last time, I just. I just feel like I can't do anything right, you know? Like everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling, and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.
Counselor: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So it's frustrating.
Client: Yeah, it definitely is.
Counselor: How is what's going on impacted your relationship with your wife?
Client: I mean, it's rocky, you know, because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that. And then, you know, we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad, and then it just keeps going like that.
Counselor: So when you. You mentioned you feel like a failure when she. When she yells at you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Can you think back to maybe the last time, one of the last times you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We've talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts. She starts yelling at you?
Client: I mean, she'll yell at me. I mean, I feel, you know, frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And. I don't know. I mean, as I was thinking about, like we were talking about it, and as I was thinking about it more this week, kind of felt like, you know, kind of like what happened with my dad, you know? I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. You know, like, if my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way. And it feels like the same thing. Yeah. It's kind of the first. I guess kind of the first thought that comes to mind.
Counselor: The first thought is I've been through something like this before, I guess.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like, you know? Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Like, it's like just a sense that this isn't brand new.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad. Yahweh. Yeah.
Client: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So, in a sense, these arguments are taking you back to another point in time.
Client: I guess so, in a way, that's distressing.
Counselor: Yeah, it is.
Client: I mean, it feels, you know, pretty crappy.
Counselor: Now, in these arguments, she yells at you. You mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own, you know, in the midst of all that. Right. How would you rate it in terms of, like, any physical violence? Nothing like that.
Client: No, it's just words. I mean, we're just, you know, just yelling.
Counselor: And what level, like, what level of yelling would you say? How severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?
Client: Yeah, I don't know. I mean, it's like, you know, sometimes it can get up to, like, the eight or nines, you know, but just, I guess generally it's, you know, down. Closer to a seven on scale, like one to ten. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So sometimes it's seven. That would be pretty bad.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But some other times it's not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you feel like your reaction is being frustrated is disproportionate to what's really going on or you feel like it's money?
Client: I don't know what else to do. You know? I mean, it's just. It's kind of my reaction, my gut reaction to it, you know? I think I'm justified in it because, you know, she just doesn't understand how much she yells at me, you know, and how much that hurts me. You know? I do feel justified. I mean, but it just. It just keeps going, though. And I feel justified, though. I don't know.
Counselor: Let's talk for a moment about, if you're okay with it, about your father and his yelling. You've discussed this with me a little bit before. In the past few sessions. I remember you saying that most. It was in the afternoon. Most of the yelling was when you were both home.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it was. I mean, mostly when I get home from school. I mean, I wasn't, you know, I was in high school, and then after that, you know, I went to college. And so I wasn't really home much during college, but, you know, I guess it'd be after I got home from high school. You know, I'd get home and he'd get home from work and, you know, just kind of be aggravated, whatever, just start yelling and. Yeah, usually when I got back from school, yeah.
Counselor: So he would get back from work, you would get back from school. And how long would that last? How long would the period where you were kind of vulnerable to being yelled at last?
Client: I don't know. I mean, sometimes about an hour, you know, and he'd be yelling because he's, you know, frustrated from work and he's frustrated from the drive home and whatever else, you know? And at some point, he would usually start drinking, you know, so maybe about an hour or so, you know, where that was. Like, you knew you were gonna get it.
Counselor: So kind of every day you could predict that between when you. Or between when he came home after you were already home from school and when he started drinking, you were gonna. He was gonna find something to yacht you about.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And, I mean, there were some days, like, I knew when he came home, he came home the same time every day. I knew I could get out of the house, you know? Cause at some point, I had a car, my friends had cars, you know, whatever.
Counselor: You had more freedom.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. You know, at some point, I had a job, so sometimes I'd work after school and stuff, so I knew I'd be able to leave the house at times, you know, like when I knew he was gonna start yelling and stuff. But, I mean, there was a period of time probably like my senior year of high school that I just didn't, you know, I just came home and, you know, it was gonna happen, you know, that's the way it happened.
Counselor: Even though you were able to escape it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. You could have stayed out long enough for him to start drinking. Yeah.
Client: Instead you stayed in the house.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I mean, it was pretty much my whole senior year come home. I knew what was gonna happen, and I just took it. You know, I just. I knew he was gonna yell. I just took it that.
Counselor: Was there ever a period when you first got your freedom that you tried, like.
Client: Oh, yeah, yeah, I did. And. I don't know. I don't know why I didn't just keep doing that. It probably would have been easier, but. I don't know. The whole senior year, I just started. I was just back there at the house when he came home from work.
Counselor: So in that period, were you. Were you. There's times when you did leave, what did he do instead of yell at you?
Client: I guess he had to yell at somebody else. I mean, my. My sister, my brother were home. I guess he probably yelled at them. I don't know. I mean, it felt good to not be there, but I guess he probably yelled at them, which just sucks. I mean, you know, I guess somebody had. Whoever was there was gonna take it, you know?
Counselor: Somebody was gonna get you out there.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, I guess it was them when I wasn't there. I don't know.
Counselor: And how do you think you took it. When you were there, how well did you respond?
Client: I just got used to it, you know, I knew what was gonna happen. I knew he was gonna yell. I knew that it was gonna make me upset. I knew that just those repeated times, just like now, you know, I'm gonna feel like a failure, which ultimately I did. You know, maybe I probably just became numb to it, you know, it happens so often and same thing every day. Probably just became numb to it and just kind of stopped caring and kind of stopped, I don't know, believing in myself or something, you know?
Counselor: Like you've just given up.
Client: Yeah, probably. That's probably. I don't know. Probably. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And how many years total did this experience go on? Do you endure the yelling?
Client: I mean, it would have been while I was in middle school and most of high school. I mean, I told you at some point I was able to leave, but probably all of middle school, most of high school, and I left, and then some, you know, for the rest of the senior year, I would be there. So, I don't know, quite a few years, I guess.
Counselor: A long time to suffer.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And now if we move back forward in time, you're in a relationship where you're getting yelled at a bit. Right. And that's sometimes quite a bit, and that's causing you distress.
Client: It's like the same thing. You're yelling a little bit and. Yeah.
Counselor: So you feel like you're back in the same place.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it does. Yeah. I mean, obviously, you know, she's. She's not doing anything like he was, you know, like drinking or anything like that, but it does. I mean, it's like the same thing that happened is happening again.
Counselor: So that's. In your opinion, that's the consequence of what happened to you. Like, all this yelling that you endured before in some way is significantly contributing to what you're going through now.
Client: Maybe. I mean, I guess it could, you know, because it is the same thing. So maybe it's.
Counselor: There could be some connection.
Client: Maybe. Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, maybe not 100% explain it, but it explains part of it.
Client: Yeah, it definitely could. I definitely could.
Counselor: So your functioning has been affected a bit. I mean, to the point where you're here with me now, we're talking about it, and you're frustrated, and it does sound painful. Now, I'm curious. You mentioned you had a younger sister and a younger brother, and they grew up in the same house. How are they doing?
Client: Well, my sister, she's three years younger than I am. She's doing great. I mean, she graduated from college, like, top of her class kind of thing, you know? And she's about to get married, too. That's cool. Got a really great guy, you know. She's doing great. She lives next town over for me. I get to see her a lot. Yeah, she's great, though. My brother, he's five years younger than I am. He's doing pretty good, too. He's just about to graduate from college. I think he gets really good grades, too, from what I hear, from what he tells me. I don't get to see him as much as I do her because she's in college, but I think he's doing really well, too. You know, they both. Yeah, they both do some really good stuff. They have really good goals and stuff like that.
Counselor: You seem like you have a good relationship with them. You're proud of them. Yeah, definitely.
Client: I'm definitely proud of them. I think they're doing some really good stuff, you know, really trying to make something of themselves. Yeah.
Counselor: So, you know, I wonder. They're doing pretty well. You're doing okay, but you're having a rough time right now. How would things have been if you had taken that? I know it's difficult to predict, but if you had taken that opportunity to not be there, if you had, like you said, you had a car, your friends had cars, you could have avoided. You could have avoided the situation directly between your dad and you.
Client: Yeah, I mean, yeah, I guess I could have. I don't know. I mean. I mean, I took the yelling and stuff, so, you know, it's obviously affecting me now.
Counselor: You took the brunt of the abuse.
Client: Yeah, I guess I did. I mean, you know, I bring it up to them sometimes and they're like, yeah, I mean, dad yelled sometimes, but, you know, it wasn't that bad. Definitely a different experience from what I had. You know, they don't see it like I do, you know? I don't know. Maybe things would have been worse for them.
Counselor: So, in a sense, your father verbally abused you. Nothing makes that right. But in a sense, you, because you were there and you were the target. And. Could ride it out, you shielded them from that abuse.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, you mentioned it would have been somebody else, right?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, it probably would have been them. Probably was them when I wasn't there, you know? Yeah, I don't know.
SPK_3: I guess you're probably right.
Client: I mean, they are doing pretty well, you know, I think probably they're doing better than I am, I guess.
Counselor: You know, probably no small part because of your protecting them.
Client: Right.
Counselor: I mean, you were in an impossible situation, and you made the choice to stay there.
Client: I guess I did. Right.
Counselor: There was some negative consequences for you, which we'll try to work through, but some really positive consequences for your siblings.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, I guess so. I mean, they, you know, I feel like a failure most of the time, but, I mean, they don't. They're doing good stuff, you know? Shoot, I guess you're right. I mean, that could have been it. I guess I'd love to ask them, like, what, you know, like, what they think would have happened if, you know, the yelling would have been more or something towards them, you know?
Counselor: And maybe you'll find out that when you weren't there, that is what would happen.
Client: Maybe.
Counselor: So you feel like a failure, but at the same time, you're happy for them and proud of all their accomplishments.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: It seems like you were a part of that success.
Client: Maybe. I mean, I guess that makes sense, you know? Yeah, maybe. I hope so. You know? I hope so.
Counselor: Well, in cognitive therapy, oftentimes, we try to do what we call reframing. Right? That's where we take. We take a situation and we don't change the facts. Like, we don't move from the truth, but we try to cast it in some different lights. So certainly being yelled at and abused, like I said, nothing makes up. Right. That's awful. And what you're going through now, possibly because of that, is awful, and that's a reality. But at the same time, it's a reality, perhaps that you protected your siblings. Both those things can be true at the same time.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, I guess so. I mean, I guess there's, like, a positive that comes out of that negative, maybe. Mm hmm. Yeah, I hope that's true. I'd like to think of this.
Counselor:
output: So another thing that occurs to me is that you were mentioned how before, I think a few sessions ago, how you're being yelled at now, and you're having some strong reactions to that, just like you told me today. But also, you do some of the yelling, probably, yeah. You think some of that comes from what you learned from your father?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Do you have on your presentation, do you have so many bullet points you want to cover?
Client: Yeah, like an outline sort of thing.
Counselor: Okay. Would it help to time the deep breathing with reviewing each one of those bullet points?
Client: I never thought about that.
Counselor: I don't know how many bullet points you'd have in a presentation. Maybe you'd have ten or 20, something like that. Yeah, depending on how long it is. So maybe you, as you start to review a certain bullet point, as you're trying to get it into your memory and think about it, you breathe in really deeply. And then as you continue on, you just let out that breath really slowly.
Client: Like a rhythm, sort of. Yeah, I can.
Counselor: And then you go to the next bullet point and do the same thing.
Client: Never thought about it that way.
Counselor: I'm just thinking it'd be some way to structure so you would get in so many breaths.
Client: So I wouldn't forget. Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Something that kind of becomes a habit.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Just make sure you keep your bullet points at a length, not a few paragraphs, but just a few seconds each, so you can get a good deep breath. Or you could, you know, if you did have a longer bullet point, you could have, obviously several breaths, but just some rhythm that you could kind of grab onto something concrete.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Because I know that in that moment, things are probably, like you mentioned, zoning out and it becomes very easy to lose your anchors.
Client: Yeah, exactly. And just get really foggy, almost dizzy.
Counselor: Yeah. So if you can remember for a particular bullet point that you want to take three deep breaths, and that might be something you can really grab onto.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And would kind of cut through that fogginess of something you could still do.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: When's the next presentation in that class?
Client: The next one, I believe, is next Friday.
Counselor: Is that the next presentation you have, like, in all the classes is the one?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. And that's next Friday. Do you know where you are in the order, like, for presenting?
Client: Um, I think I'm actually third in this one.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So not first.
Counselor: Not first. And this one's how many minutes?
Client: Um, like 15 or so.
Counselor: Okay. It's a little shorter than the 20 minutes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So 15 minutes. So you have about a half hour, maybe a little more if there's time to switch out of kind of sitting there.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And potential time where you could be anxious.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: But also potential time when you could be reviewing the notes, your bullet points and breathing.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And saying to yourself, that kind of self talk, that they're not really paying attention to me anyway.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Because that might help reduce that. That anxiety.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's one thing you could say to yourself when you're up there?
Client: I guess I could say that, you know, in general, do pretty well. You know, one bad grade isn't going to make me. Doesn't mean that I don't deserve to be here.
Counselor: Okay, so the. So the self talk up there could be. I deserve to be here.
Client: Maybe I've prepared enough. You know that. I know that I've prepared and I'm a good student.
Counselor: Okay. I've prepared enough. I'm a good student. I deserve to be here.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. Is that something it would be helpful to write down and have as part of your notes that you can.
Client: Yeah, I think it would actually.
Counselor: You can recite that.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Internally as you.
Client: Because it's not long. I think I could. It would be easy to remember and I could just like, maybe put it down on one of my note cards in front of me or something.
Counselor: And how much do you believe that those statements are true?
Client: I think, you know, sitting now. Sitting here now, I believe them in the moment. Sometimes it's a little hard to believe because I convinced myself otherwise, but I think I actually believe that that's true, that I do deserve to be in the program.
Counselor: Okay, so those self talk items, you believe them to be true.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But you recognize in the moment, and I want you to be aware of this. You might note, I believe them as much.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But remember that, you know, we worked on them, you came up with them and you believe them now.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So try to keep that in your mind as you start to doubt yourself.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And be ready to recite them. It's easy. I realize it's easy to form these plans.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But in the chaos of the anxiety and the worry, it's. It's harder. So the more tasks you can make concrete and that you can write down and you can rehearse, I think the better off you'll be.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: I would like to see you your presentations next Friday. I would like to see you right before that. So it'll be about a week before that. Do you have any questions? These are items you can rehearse still, even without the presentation, the self talk and the breathing and of course, preparing. But do you have any questions between now and then, do you think?
Client: I don't think so. I think it makes sense.
Counselor: You understand, kind of the plan to attack that anxiety symptom.
Client: And I think, you know what you kind of suggested before, like maybe practicing my deep breathing. Like maybe now, like, when I'm calm and getting into a habit of deep breathing, like, I'm more apt to also remember it then.
Counselor: All right, so, good. So you have some kind of behavioral pieces.
Client: Yeah. Right.
Counselor: The studying. The focus on studying the breathing and some cognitive pieces. The self talk we talked about.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: That you use when you're seated and that you use when you're at the podium.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And actually presenting. Alright, good. So I'm glad we have a plan going forward. I think that you did a really good job today helping kind of untangle all this and figure out what's going on. And I appreciate that you were able to really connect with the symptoms and the thoughts and kind. Kind of realize how they're related.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And I feel like this is something that's going to serve you well as you move through this.
Client: Thank you.
Counselor:
output: So I'll see you in a week.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Samantha. How you doing today?
Client: Good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm doing all right. How have things been since last week?
Client: Things? You know, I've been really sort of preoccupied and anxious a lot this weekend. My daughter got sick, so I had to take three days off of work to take care of her. And I'm starting to worry. She's been sick a lot since I've gone back to work, and she's in daycare, and I've had to take a lot of time off work, and I'm getting close to going over my allotted amount of days. And so I'm finding myself being very anxious about that and then feeling guilty because when I'm trying to take care of her, I'm always worrying about work. So.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a couple things may be going on. Child. Child's been sick, so you're taking off days. So you're a little worried about your relationship with your employer. At the same time, you want to make sure you're taking good care of your child, so you're having trouble reconciling those two.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. What was the last time it happened? Can you describe what happened the last.
Client: Time I had to take off work? It was just this week. She woke up one morning with a really high fever, so I had to call out that day, and then she still had a fever the next day, and then I had to take a third day because she has to be fever free before she can go back to daycare. So the first day was, I was okay with that. But then, like, the second. And then when I started realizing that I was going to have to take a third day, then I really start to get kind of panicky and worried about it.
Counselor: All right, so let me see. Let's go through each day. So the first day when you discovered that she was sick, right. What were you thinking then when you had to call out of work?
Client: Well, because she's been sort of sick a lot lately, I was a little bit worried, and I was sort of, you know, I have this number, ten, because I only have ten days for the whole year. So I have this number in my head, and I just thought, well, there's one more day I gotta take away from that ten that I have. And. But I was able to sort of think about. I was a little worried about any work that I would miss, you know, keeping up with my caseload and stuff at work, so. But I was able to kind of figure out that I would be okay for a day. And I can kind of make up for that when I get back.
Counselor: Okay, so your thinking was, this isn't ideal, but I can live with it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just one day, right? How about on day two when you realize that you're going to have to take a second day?
Client: Then I got a little bit more worried. And then I did start to also, you know, add the worry of I was going to start to get behind at work. Not only was I missing more time, but I was also going to be behind on my work. So then I started thinking, when I go back, it's going to be a mad scramble to kind of catch up and keep up with everything and, you know, so then it became worrying about my workload and worrying about taking more time.
Counselor: Okay, so a little more stressful version of what happened on day one. And then how about when you discovered that you had to take a third day off?
Client: I was. Then it was just more amplified, you know, amplified worry. And it was a lot harder for me to let it go. I just kept thinking. I kept going back to it. And then I started feeling guilty because I was so preoccupied, worried about that. And I was trying to answer emails and do some stuff and send out some emails to people that I work with to try to help me out with things at work since I wasn't there. And then I felt guilty because I wasn't really caring for my child as best as I felt I should have been. You know, I started feeling kind of like a bad mom.
Counselor: So, so guilty and a bad mom. And that was mostly on the third day? That was the worst of it, yes. Now, did this go up against the weekend? It was the third day, Friday. So then you kind of knew that by Monday things would be able to return to work. So tell me what happened when you returned to work on Monday.
Client: Well, I checked in with the main office and, you know, I just said, I'm really, you know, I'm starting to worry. I'm getting. I know I had to take a lot of time, but you. I've done the best I can to try to make other arrangements, but just starting back in, starting in daycare, she's just been sick a lot and I can't control it. I'm doing the best I can. I asked them if there was anything I needed to do as far as providing doctor's notes and stuff, and they said, no, they don't need a doctor's note since it was my daughter that was sick. instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Client: I want to go to go, but maybe not for six days. Maybe just like a long weekend.

Client: It's the same thing.
Counselor: The same thing. So mostly family and now some pets.
Client: Well, I had pets then, too.

Client: Yeah, like, I'm ready to come back, but then I'm missing home. Like, I want to go back to my family and everything's okay, but I miss, you know, where I just left because it's away from home. I know it sounds really conflicting and weird, but, you know, I like to get away. I enjoy being away from this small town.

Client: Absolutely.
Counselor: And right now, the feeling, the thought, anyway, of, you know, I would like to go on a trip is winning, but the fear thought is kind of dragging you down. So what's the sensation? Anxiety.
Client: Yeah. I get anxious. Yeah. My heart gets. Feels like it's heavy. My chest heavy. And I just. All these thoughts go through my mind, like, you know, I know my parents. Somebody can watch my pets, but they may not take care of them like I would. I don't know, it's just. I mean, you know, they've always. They'll take care of them. I know, but they'll miss me and they might tear my house up. I don't know. All these thoughts go through my mind that seem crazy to me.
Counselor: So it seems like an endless stream of worries.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Surrounding family and the pets and what might happen. So really, that's. That's it. Right. It's what might happen. It's the uncertainty.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So has anything ever happened?
Client: No. No.
Counselor: So, so far, all this worrying, anxiety really hasn't paid any dividends.
Client: No.
Counselor: Do you end up going on the trips anyway?
Client: Yes. And now that I'm older, when I was younger, I probably wouldn't like an overnight, but now that I'm older. Yes, I do. I just say I got to live my life and it'll be okay. Counselor: Right. So the problem really isn't when you're there leading up to the problem is now leading up to. Right.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: And maybe just the first half day or day when you're there. Maybe the last half day or day.
Client: You'Re there, it's like a plane. Like, I don't have a problem riding, like, flying out, but it's the thinking, like, while I'm waiting for the plane, like, what if a terrorist is on there? Client: Yes.
Counselor: But you'll probably still go.

Client: Yeah.

Client: Probably. Like, I want to. I want to say. I don't know. I really. It's kind of hard. Like, I want to. Counselor:
output: Right. Okay. Would you mind practicing this, what you have learned in this session in a real life situation?

Counselor: which is when you normally wash your hands. So really, you touched something that had germs, and you had some anxiety as you had to get to that waiting period. Client: I mean, we wouldn't wait in a.
Counselor: Few days, a couple days. So how long or how many times a year would you get something like that normally?
Client: I mean, I get sick. I mean, quite often because of my job. I'm around a lot of people, and hand sanitizer can only work so much. I do get sick.

I think it was around session three where we talked about putting a gap between when you touch something, when you wash your hands, like a time gap, and you got a cold once. Would that be out of the ordinary to get a cold one time in six weeks this time of year?
Client: I suppose not. I mean, the rational part of me knows that I get sick, but just because I'm trying something new with the, you know, and then the waiting and then the not washing, I'm just afraid that there was, you know, you're afraid.
Counselor: They were linked at one cause the other that waiting to wash your hands got you sick. And that could have happened. I don't know. But let's talk about the cold. You said it was a couple days.
Client: It wasn't severe. I mean, I took some, you know, over the counter medicine, slept it off.
Counselor: So wasn't a catastrophe.
Client: No, I've definitely been sicker in my life. And I mean, it did seem like one of those ones that I get every now and then.
Counselor: So when we spoke, I remember before you had said that the kind of worst case scenario, the reason that you're thinking so much about the germs on your hands is that it could make you sick. But you did get sick and you were able to tolerated.
Client: Yeah, I was. Which I found kind of odd because I was. I was panicked at the beginning when I started to feel those first, you know, the itchy throat, the headaches.
Counselor: Sure, it's miserable, right? Nobody wants to get sick.
Client: And I got concerned, you know, that it was because of that. Then it just kind of subsided. I guess I felt a little better, you know, as the days went on, I felt better about it happening, about.
Counselor: The whole getting sick and you started to recover. So kind of the worst case scenario occurred and you survived. And again, we don't know if the, the amount of hand washing you were doing before the ERP exposure and response prevention, we don't know if that would have prevented the cold or not. Yeah, because you do get sick several times, several times a year, in a year. So there's a lot we don't know. But we do know that you survived it and it wasn't as bad looking back at it.
Client: I mean, in my head, not washing my hands and the sick that I would get is a lot worse. It's like hospital worthy. And this was, you know, like I said over the counter, you know, relax a little bit.
Counselor: So not pleasant, but survivable.
Client: It definitely wasn't pleasant, but it wasn't as bad as it could have gone in my mind.
Counselor: So presume for a moment that it was a consequence of not immediately rushing over and washing your hands. What would you rather have? The occasional cold like that or the excessive hand washing and anxiety?
Client: I mean, I definitely don't like the excessive hand washing. I don't. I mean, it ruins my skin and I. It's expensive and it makes me feel bad about myself. And I mean, I guess the trade off is if I get a little sick and that would be okay.
Counselor: Again, that's presuming that it did cause you to get sick, which it may not have.
Client: I suppose that's true.
Counselor: So I wanted to point out, too, that I remember when we, we first started the exposure response prevention exercise, we did it right here in session by touching the arms of the chair. And I can see now your arms are.

Client: I mean, on that scale, I think it'd be about a two.
Counselor: Well, with one being the lowest anxiety and ten being the highest, you're about two.
Client: Well, when you pointed it out, I didn't notice before.
Counselor: So you were a one in anxiety before that. So now you're aware of it a little bit. Right. So your elbows. Your elbows have to touch the chair.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you're aware of it a little bit and you're a little anxious.
Client: I mean, not so much anymore. I mean, it's kind of. You mentioned it. I got anxious for a moment, and then it's just kind of like, oh, well, you're already doing it and nothing bad's happening right now.
Counselor: Well, good. You made a lot of progress.
Client: Thank you.
Counselor: A lot of progress. So you're still going to have, as we move forward, you're still going to have some anxiety, like when I mentioned that your arms are touching the chair. You're still going to have some anxiety from time to time. Anxiety is part of life.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: It's going to happen from time to time. So one of the things I hope that you've gained from this is that just like you tolerated being sick for those few days, right. Is to tolerate that anxiety. Right. To be able to be okay with having some anxiety in your life.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: In a sense, the fear of being anxious kind of causes a vicious cycle. Right. You have fear of being anxious. You'll do not anything, but you'll do many things to get rid of that.
Client: Anxiety because it gets really bad. It starts consuming me.
Counselor: It's uncomfortable. I remember when you touched the chair before, right? Like many weeks ago, that you had the urge to go wash your hands right away, you were anxious.
Client: Yeah, I remember that.
Counselor: So you become less anxious by waiting and kind of getting used to it. And with that remaining anxiety, what I'm getting at is that at some point you have to learn to tolerate that. And it sounds like that's kind of the direction you're moving that you're able to tolerate. Like, the anxiety is still unpleasant for you, but you're able to survive to.
Client: Kind of live through it. Yeah, yeah, I would really say that.
Counselor: So tolerating that degree of anxiety, is that better than the frequent hand Washington?
Client: I mean, the little bit of unpleasantness versus, you know, the depression and the anxiety that comes with washing my hands? I would really rather take the little unpleasantness, I guess, in the grand scheme of things. Yeah.
Counselor: So where are you now in terms of how many minutes do you wait after you touch something.
Client: On average? Because I write them down, on average, I wait a good seven minutes.
Counselor: So you've been averaging around seven minutes. So I want to continue ramping that up. So if you had no awareness of germs, how many times would you normally wash your hands in a day?
Client: You know, wash them after eating or before eating, touching anything, you know, like a toilet or stuff like that. I mean, so definitely a fraction of what I do.
Counselor:
output: So maybe in a day, ten times, a dozen times maybe would be normal.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.

Client: I guess, yeah.
Counselor: Not sure.
Client: I don't know, just the same.
Counselor: Yeah, still a little down.

Counselor: Past four months?
Client: Um, just the guy. I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.
Counselor: You still been working?
Client: Well, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But not much else?
Client: No, I usually just go to work and go home.
Counselor: Tell me what happens after you arrive at home, like after work?
Client: Um, well, my fiance tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep for just. I don't know. I tried, I tried reading the other day. Cause I used to like that and it's just, I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.
Counselor: What were you thinking when you put the book down?
Client: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.
Counselor: I. And before you were depressed, which is, I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading?
Client: Mm hmm. Oh, yeah, all the time.
Counselor: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?
Client: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up till like two in the morning just reading a book.
Counselor: Something you look forward to?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But not now?
Client: No, I just didn't really get any. I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like.
Counselor: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?
Client: Yeah, I used to be a runner and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I. I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.
Counselor: Alright, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running, like when you first started?
Client: Not really. I mean, it was a change to be outdoors and I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while, so. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run. I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route. And by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.
Counselor: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?
Client: Kind of a mix of, like, relief just because it was over, and then, I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.
Counselor: Sadness, maybe disappointment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I've seen you a few times now, and based on those conversations, and, of course, what you said today, it seems like you have, for a variety of reasons, given up on the activities that you used to enjoy, you're not motivated toward them anymore.
Client: Yeah, I guess you could say that.
Counselor: And that's a common symptom of depression. I think we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed. So we've been working with the cognitive piece. Right, like we did last time, we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self talk. I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. We'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle. And the technique is called behavioral activation. The theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, like with the running, that will connect to your mood. Right. Remember, we believe in cognitive therapy, that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood and what you do. Your behavior affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we talked about?
Client: It does, yeah.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Kathy. How you doing today? You okay? I know when you spoke last time, you had some goals that you want to talk about this time. Are you ready to do that?
Client: I need to. Yeah?
Counselor: Yeah. What do you have in mind?
Client: I just keep thinking about, you know, losing this weight, and I just. I really want to do it, and I just. I just can't get there, and I don't know why I.
Counselor: So you're frustrated.
Client: So ridiculous.
Counselor: Yeah, frustrated trying to lose the weight. Now, you'd said before that you had a specific number of pounds in mind, a specific amount of weight to lose. Do you still have that in mind?
Client: I would like 20 pounds.
Counselor: 20 pounds.
Client: I mean, I would like more, but I've tried to do more in the past, and I don't even get past a couple of days, so if I can do 20, that would be great.
Counselor: All right. And you tried before, and what do you think got in the way?
Client: I don't know. I guess it wasn't convenient. You know, I want to do it, and it means a lot, you know, for me and my family. I think I'd be a lot healthier.
Counselor: It's important to you. Yeah.
Client: But just, like, something always gets in the way, you know? And then I lose focus. I'm not very good at staying focused on stuff like that anyway, so.
Counselor: All right, so loss of focus. So you start trying to lose the weight, and your focus gets disrupted, and I forget.
Client: And then I make, you know, spaghetti casserole for six people, and then I eat a lot of it, and that's carbs and cheese and fat. And then I will eat what my kids don't eat. And then it's just like, I forget that I'm supposed to be making healthy choices.
Counselor: All right, so you know how to lose weight, and you know, you can lose weight, but your focus is a little off when you're, when you're trying, and that's. That's causing the problem.
Client: I think so, yeah.
Counselor: Could we break that goal of losing 20 pounds down into smaller units, like, say, five pounds, do you think?
Client: Well, maybe, yeah. Cause I've never. I always just keep, like, the chunk of weight, you know, ahead of me. I don't break it into smaller increments. That might work. I mean, I don't know how. I'd have to stay on top of it, though. Weigh myself every day.
Counselor: Is that something you can do.
Client: I'm so busy. I don't know.
Counselor: Or once a week.
Client: I probably do once a week. Put a sticky note somewhere or something, you know, maybe. Yeah. I mean, I want to try. I'm going to say yes because I want to try it, you know?
Counselor: So you mentioned the loss of focus is one problem. How about motivation? Do you feel motivated to move through all those steps, like five pounds and five pounds and so on.
Client: Right now? Yes. I think I would need a. Something to keep me going, you know.
Counselor: Week to week, a little bit of that. Something extra to help you stay motivated.
Client: Yeah. Like when you're. Sometimes when, you know, your kid does your homework early or does their homework early, and you can give them a special treat for dessert that helps, you know, keep it going.
Counselor: Okay. So some sort of activity or item that you enjoy that you could reserve for when you reach that goal of, say, the first five pounds.
Client: Right, right. I would love. I mean, I'm just. I've been so embarrassed, you know, lately. So I feel like I just. If I can find something that keeps me bone at me, keeps you motivated, that would be great.
Counselor: All right. Do you have an activity or item in mind that we could put in place as something you could reward yourself.
Client: With, like, after the first five pounds?
Counselor: Well, there's a few ways we could do it. We could do that. So you reach five pounds, and then you can give yourself that reward. Or it could be for something you do every day. If that day you're successful in eating the way you want to eat, what do you think would benefit you more?
Client: Maybe something every day. So I remember, you know, I just get so distracted by other stuff. So there was something every day that maybe I put out, almost like a goal at the end of the day or something.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: You know, if I made the right choices.
Counselor: Yes. So, you know, each and every day, as you're trying to lose weight, you're aware when that day comes to a close, if you had a successful day or a less than successful day.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And if you have a successful day, then you could engage in an activity or receive an item that we work out in advance that, you know, would motivate you.
Client: Right. And that could be, you know, maybe watching, like, a favorite tv show.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: You know, because I don't watch tv at night because I'm so busy, you know, cleaning up and everything. And maybe I could just take some time for myself because I did something good, you know, and just watch a tv show.
Counselor: All right, so let's do that on a day you know, towards the evening when, you know, you have had a successful day. By what time would you know in the evening?
Client: Probably as I'm preparing dinner. If I prepare a good dinner, or if I prepare fun food for my kids, but I don't eat it, like, chicken nuggets and french fries and stuff, I would know, you know, maybe by, like, six or seven. Okay.
Counselor: Say seven.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So by 07:00 p.m. at that point, in terms of the day being successful or less than successful, you know.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Right. By 07:00 p.m. you're aware. And at that point, if you have met your goal, then you have a tv show that you maybe have recorded on the DVR or something you would watch if you were not as successful. You wouldn't.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So that would be, like, something to keep you motivated throughout the day because you really want to watch that show.
Client: Right. It'd be a lot of fun.
Counselor: Do you think that structure, that kind of behavioral strategy, would give you enough motivation to have successful days through this process?
Client: I don't know, honestly, but it would probably beat the way I feel right now. Anything's kind of better than carrying this frustration around. So I'm willing to try anything, and I'll try to remember. Like I said, I'll write it down. I'll have it in the kitchen. Have it on a note. 07:00 p.m. how did I do today?
Counselor: Yeah. This is something you could also track. You could write down days that were successful, days that were less than successful, and we could look at if there's any patterns. Maybe weekends are harder, weekends are easier, or something where we can identify days that have maybe more triggers or where you're less motivated.
Client: Yeah, I didn't think about that because.
Counselor: Right.
Client: Every day would be different. Okay.
Counselor: There's a potential for every day to be different with what you're exposed to and what temptations in terms of different foods or what your schedule is like. Maybe if you're busier, it's easier. So we can look at those different patterns, and we can add levels to this plan. But for now, we'll go with the tv show that you'll watch sometime after seven. So at seven, you'll evaluate how you did and sometime after that, watch the show. That's like a plan.
Client: So that's leading up to the five pounds, right? Right. Okay. That's just day by day. Okay.
Counselor: Take this in five pound increments.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Four times to get to your goal of 20 pounds.
Client: Okay. Yeah.
Counselor: Does that sound good? So far, so good.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: We'll give that a shot. And we'll take a look at the pattern that emerges. So record everything. So write everything down. Probably at around seven is a good time when you know what kind of day you had. Write down kind of what happened that day and whether you had success or not, and bring that in. I'll see you again in a week. So I'll give you seven days to work with and we'll look at that log of events and we'll reevaluate each week.
Client: So I could start tonight?
Counselor: Start tonight.
Client: Okay. All right.
Counselor:
output: All right. So we'll give that a shot and I'll see you in a week.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Carlos. How are you feeling today?
Client: Feeling terrible. I had a wrestling match last night, and I lost my match again. I should just quit the team. I'm such a bad wrestler.
Counselor: What do you mean by again?
Client: I lost my match last week, too. I should just quit the team.
Counselor: You mean because you lost two matches, it automatically means you're going to lose your next match?
Client: Well, yes. I am clearly a bad wrestler.
Counselor: Okay, so losing is not fun. No one likes to lose. But it doesn't mean you're a bad wrestler.
Client: Yeah, I guess not. But all my other teammates won their matches. It made me feel dumb to be the only one who lost. Like I'm a terrible wrestler. I don't feel like I belong on the team anymore.
Counselor: Yes, losing is unpleasant. And those two matches weren't your best. Does that mean that you're a bad wrestler?
Client: Well, I don't know. Maybe not.
Counselor: How were you doing before you lost those two matches?
Client: We've only had four matches so far, but I won my first two matches.
Counselor: Okay, so you started off the season by winning two matches in a row, which means you do know how to wrestle. You just happened to lose two matches in a row, but that's all it was?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What else are you telling yourself about wrestling?
Client: Well, I just felt terrible after I lost those two matches, and I was thinking that if I lo. That if I lose my next match, I'm never going to be able to get a scholarship to college.
Counselor: Hold on a second, Carlos. Let me stop you right there. What if you do lose your next match? What is the worst thing that could happen? Would it be the end of the world?
Client: Um, no, I guess not. The season just started.
Counselor: How much longer do you have in the season?
Client: A few more months.
Counselor: A few more months? Which means you still have plenty of matches left. So, although losing your next match would be frustrating, you would be okay. The world would not end.
Client: Yeah, I guess you're right.
Counselor: Do you enjoy wrestling?
Client: Yes. Actually, I love wrestling. I've been wrestling since my freshman year.
Counselor: You've been wrestling for three years, and it is a sport you love participating in. Does it make sense that you said you were going to quit just a few matches into the season?
Client: No, it really doesn't.
Counselor: Are you starting to understand what you told yourself about the consequences of losing a few wrestling matches?
Client: Yes, I guess I am. I told myself that if I lost any matches this season, I'm a bad wrestler. That isn't true. Losing some of my matches doesn't automatically mean I'm a bad wrestler. It's also not the end of the world.
Counselor: Is that correct information to give yourself?
Client: No.
Counselor: Okay, I feel like you're starting to get it now. Let's look at the other things you've been telling yourself about wrestling. What else did you tell yourself?
Client: Said that if I lost any of my matches, I wouldn't get a wrestling scholarship for college.
Counselor: Is it a reasonable goal to say you're not going to lose any matches over an entire season?
Client: No, not really.
Counselor: You've lost before over the last three years, right? Have you had success in past seasons?
Client: Yes, I have. I lost a couple of matches last season, but I had a good season overall.
Counselor: Okay, so you know that losing several matches throughout the course of the season isn't the end of the world. What else have you been telling yourself?
Client: My parents don't really have the money to pay for my college, so I need to get good grades and do well with wrestling in order to have a better chance at getting a scholarship.
Counselor: How do you think all that pressure affects you?
Client: I think about it all the time, which makes it hard for me to focus.
Counselor: That is a lot to have to deal with. And all that pressure is leading you to tell yourself negative things.
Client: Yeah, I guess it is.
Counselor: Have you discussed how you're feeling with your parents?
Client: No, not really. I don't want to bother them with this.
Counselor: How does it make you feel to keep all this inside to yourself?
Client: Definitely not. Great.
Counselor: Well, of course, junior year is a stressful year. Do you think that all of this stress relates to wrestling at all?
Client: Yeah, it probably does. I guess I hadn't really thought about it that way. I was having a hard time concentrating during my last two matches. I think it's affecting my performance.
Counselor: So what are the real reasons you lost those two matches?
Client: Been under a lot of stress lately. Put more pressure on myself to perform perfectly in wrestling to help me get a scholarship for college. I got so mad about losing that I wasn't thinking straight.
Counselor: Striving for perfection is unrealistic. Making mistakes or losing a wrestling match in this case, is normal. You learn from it and you keep going.
Client: Yeah, I guess you're right.
Counselor: Well, Carlos, we're running out of time for today's session. Before we end, let's go over some of the bad messages you've been telling yourself.
Client: I lost two matches in a row and I told myself that I was a bad wrestler, that I should just quit the team, and that I wouldn't get a scholarship to college. I thought losing was the end of the world.
Counselor:
output: And do you still believe those things about yourself?

And if they were to be interested in me, I'm not allowed to date, you know, so the repercussion would just be, you know, I'd kind of be shunned for doing so. So it kind of just stayed with me, you know, now I'm 24 and I'm in school, and it's just so overwhelming. And I'm kind of envious of my girlfriends because they're able to do it, and I'm like, damn. Counselor: So that process is far from removed from you. You look at that and think, I don't even know how to approach it.
Client: It's like a foreign object. Like, yeah.
Counselor: So how would you say, how would you describe yourself? Like, how do you feel about yourself?
Client: I always do the right thing. I'm really studious, and I like to have fun. When I'm with my girlfriends, we have a great time, and I'm personable with them and my family, but it's just when it comes to interacting with male, it's just super difficult for me. And I can tell you why, but I can't tell you why. You know, it's kind of that, like, it's like a seesaw every time I'm with a male, you know, in a dating aspect anyway, so it's just difficult for me.
Counselor: Is there a particular outcome that you're afraid of? Like, when you're, well, you're in college now, right? So likely interact with males to some extent. Is there when an opportunity comes up when somebody's interested in you? Is there a particular fear that comes to mind?
Client: Yeah, like, I don't even know why you're talking to me. Like, why would you talk to me? I'm not pretty. I'm flipping awkward. Like, you know, why would you even be interested?

Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you question why they would be interested in you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So have you ever had evidence presented to the contrary, like, people who thought you were attractive and not awkward?
Client: Um, well, yeah, I mean, yeah, like, people have told me that I'm pretty and, um, you know, fun and stuff like that, so, yeah, I have.
Counselor: Yeah. But there's some, so they're telling you that? But there's something else telling you that you're not?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you think that's coming from?
Client: I guess just from my, you know, my mom and I think just her rules that I guess I just associated, you know, me not being able to date, that I wasn't presentable enough to date. And I just got this idea that that's the reason why she just didn't want me to date.

Client: I think it was much more strictly, yeah. Because it's so much so now that I can't even talk to a guy. It's just. I mean, the anxiety and the fear is so intense. I just can't explain it. Counselor: So the way you perceive yourself, the self image here is part of this?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, absolutely.
Counselor: So you have evidence that says that men would be interested in going out with you, dating you, but internally, these thoughts you're having say you're just not worthy.
Client: You know what I mean?
Counselor: That's kind of the theme of it, right?
Client: Yeah, absolutely. That's it.
Counselor: And maybe this is tied to a core belief. Like we talked about core beliefs before cognitive therapy. Are there any of those core beliefs in the list I gave you a few weeks ago kind of stood out that you think might be core beliefs you have?
Client: That I'm unlovable.
Counselor: Unlovable, yeah. Any others?
Client: Fear of rejection.
Counselor: So fear of being rejected?
Client: Fear of being rejected. Yeah.
Counselor: So unlovable. And a fear of being rejected. And then when you have interactions in the moment, like, say you're in class and there's a man sitting next to you in class, and they're interested in you, he's interested in you. He says something that expresses that he's interested. You're immediately suspect.
Client: Oh, yeah.
Counselor: That's what you're.
Client: Oh, yeah. That's like. It's like, what is it? Fight or flight kind of feeling like it really is. It's like, oh, you know. Yeah. Just something comes over me where, you know, it's kind of like I'm conditioned because I don't even live with my mom and my dad now, and I'm on my own, but yet I still hold their values. And not just. All I can just think of is being in high school and having. Being told I can't do that or just the rules and having to follow it. And that's really where I feel like I'm there. If someone says something to me, it.
Counselor: Takes you right back there.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. I. So how do your parents feel about now? Have they said anything like, your sisters are married and you're not? Have they pointed that out?
Client: No, they haven't. Not really. No. Because my mom really wants me. She. I guess. Well, maybe it has to do with that. Like, I'm smarter than my sisters, so she really wants me to be a doctor. And my sisters, they have, you know, they have great jobs, but, you know, they just stopped at a bachelor's degree, and I'm really working to be a doctor. And I always had straight a's in high school and my sisters didn't. So I think that my mom wants to hold on to that, you know, that hope that I'm going to be something great. So she doesn't really enforce the dating thing with me. I guess she's for fear that that's going to get in the way.

Client: I mean, I guess. Yeah.

But I'm not in high school anymore, so I don't know. I just. I honestly don't know what the conversation would be like if I talked to a guy that I was interested in or if a guy was interested in me. I mean, because I came to the realization, and my friends have helped me with this, that I am in college, I am an adult now. And, you know, what my mom thinks is what she thinks now. It's just me peeing in front of a male that I'm attracted to, that I want to go out with.

Client: Right? I don't know. I don't know if it's going to be bad, but you don't know if.
Counselor: It'S going to be good either.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a risk.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So in the situation you're in, if you can get through that anxiety and have a conversation, it could end up where things went very well or didn't. So what happens if it doesn't go well?
Client: Well, I mean, like I said, I think because my mom didn't let me date that it was sign that I was unattractive, so I could take it that way, that I was just unattractive, but that he wouldn't have initiated the date if I was unattractive.
Counselor: Good point.
Client: So for that, I was. It just didn't work. You know, there just wasn't anything in common with what I'm about. You know, that I have different hobbies and he has different hobbies, and maybe they just don't mesh well and I have to. That could be a reason why it didn't work. Not that I'm. I guess, nothing. I'm lovable. You know, I shouldn't take it that personal, but it's hard.
Counselor: It's difficult for you. This is painful for you.
Client: Yeah, it is.
Counselor: You're fighting through some strong feelings. If you try to look at the logical, right. If it's likely you just because of the way it works, you'd have to date several people to find somebody that was a match.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So some of those relationships you'll end, maybe some of the man will end, but eventually, one likely you would stumble on, or neither one of you would end it. So there's risk involved here. There's a risk of rejection. There's a risk of having to reject. That doesn't seem to be the risk you're most worried about, though. You're more worried about the risk of being rejected.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Because you're questioning their intent.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: So can you survive being rejected?
Client: I think. I think I can, you know. Yeah. I mean, because in essence, I was, you know, rejected by my mom, but I still moved forward with my life because since she didn't let me date, that's a rejection from her that I'm not worthy. So, yes, I think because my friends have helped me, so that's a step in the right direction.
Counselor: And you took that behavior from your mother as rejection. And it seems like that may not have been her reason for doing that. You don't know for sure.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But even if it was, which it seems unlikely it would have been, that's still just one person.
Client: Yeah, yeah. That is just one person.
Counselor: So if we just take it to the extreme and say for some reason.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: You know, she didn't think you were worthy. That's just one person opinion.
Client: Yeah, absolutely. Right. Because my friends think I'm worthy. Right.
Counselor: And their opinions are valid too.
Client: Right? They are.
Counselor: So if you really look at it and weigh the evidence and look at it logically, the imbalance of the evidence would say that you are worthy.
Client: Right.
Counselor: You're not unlovable. But still, in any type of relational situation, there's going to be rejection. So there's potential pain up ahead, but the reward could be you find somebody that you want to be with. And that's really your goal.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So really part of this is pushing through a good deal of uncomfortableness, discomfort, right?
Client: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. A lot of that. A lot of it, yeah, yeah. And I think that I'm willing. I'm willing to do it because I want it so bad that, you know, I have to. You don't know until you try it, and I have to try it. I have to.
Counselor: So what, kind of a behavioral experiment. Right. So let's. Let's take it one step at a time. Let's say that back to the situation I alluded to earlier. You're in class and there's somebody that's interested in you, sitting next to you or whoever they are, and they come and initiate a conversation. What's your reaction now? What do you do now?
Client: Well, I would introduce myself because I never. I have never done that before to a guy where I introduce myself. I wouldn't even make eye contact. So I think to just look up with them and just say, you know, hi, my name is, you know, Leia, and just see what that feels like because I don't know what to do.
Counselor: You've never reached that step?
Client: No. No, I haven't, because I wouldn't even, you know, I wouldn't even look them in the eye.
Counselor: Your current reaction is not look them in the eye. Not engaging in discussion.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just kind of shy away. So the. So the behavioral experiment is to nothing, do that, but instead proactively engage in another behavior, which would be to introduce yourself. So let's just make that the experiment. You seem like you're pretty comfortable and you have some confidence you could do that.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And that's not a particularly long amount of time. You just have to get through that introduction. And the worst that they could do if you introduce yourself, I mean, I guess they could reject you at that point, but that seems pretty unlikely. I mean, you're just introducing yourself.
Client: Right. Right. I mean, I guess that would be really shallow if they did that. So.
Counselor: Yeah. That's not a great indicator that there would be a suitable mate. Right.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you introduce yourself and you're open. I guess the second part would be you're open to whatever conversation comes next.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you're not committing to anything. Right. You're not committing to an engaged, long engaged social interaction. You're just saying, here's my name, what's your name? Or whatever, and just see where the conversation goes. So this is really all new?
Client: Oh, yeah, it's all new. And it's like. It's embarrassing, but I feel. I feel, like, safe with you, so I feel okay that I'm able to talk about it. And, like, my friends know, you know, like, 24 and never really introducing yourself to a guy is. It's embarrassing. It's embarrassing. Yeah.
Counselor: So not doing. That's embarrassing.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So by doing that, you can overcome that embarrassment, but you'll have some anxiety.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a trade off.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So my guess is the more you introduce yourself, the less that anxiety will be.
Client: Yeah, I think so. Absolutely. Yeah.
Counselor: So let's just start with that.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: Right. Let's start with that. And when's the next time you'll be in a class?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:

And anytime you have a question, if you have any comments, if you don't understand something, I want you to tell me so that I can make sure that you understand everything that we're doing, that we're talking about, and it will be actively. Yeah. Between both of us will be a team, if you want.
Client: Oh, I definitely ask questions. Trust me. I like to ask a lot of questions. I like to talk.
Counselor: Well, that's good. And then the other thing, we have an agenda that I'm going to try to stick by. We want to start off with a mood check. I'll just kind of see how you're feeling today. We'll talk about your presenting problems, and we'll go into making some goals, and I'll explain a little bit of the theory that I use for our sessions. Kind of do a little educational piece to make sure you understand what's going on, and we'll give a summary. And also, I may have some homework that we can talk about.
Client: Okay. Because I sure do have lots of problems. I can tell you about tons of problems.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: So I'm going to be talking your ears off.
Counselor: Well, we have approximately about 15 to 20 minutes today, and I'll let you know when the time starts to run short so you're not taken by surprise.
Client: Okay, that will be fine. But if I need more time, I'll just have to buy it, I guess.
Counselor: Well, we can work something out, I'm sure.
Client: Well, I'll try to keep it short.
Counselor: Okay. Well, the first thing I do want to do is check on your mood and just kind of see how you're feeling today.
Client: Well, today, I just tell you, that teenager of mine, I could just hang him up by his toes. That right there. If I could just get that settled for a while. I think I might have get some common ground with him. I think I might be okay.
Counselor: Okay. So you would say you're kind of feeling frustrated.
Client: I'm frustrated and stressed and can't sleep. Just, you know, really just snappy. I just snap at him all the time.
Counselor: Okay. And I guess the biggest thing would be your frustration. On a scale of one to ten with your frustration, how would you rate that?
Client: Why? Twelve, of course. Yeah. Frustration with a teenage boy. Have you ever said girls are hard to raise? Boys, they're hard to raise.
Counselor: Okay. So you're really having some frustration issues. And I noticed you mentioned your sleep that you're not sleeping very well.
Client: No, not sleeping well. I think I'm just stressed with him all the time and just, you know, just the day to day life stuff. And I'm just stressed. Just stressed. Not sleeping really good at all.
Counselor: And it seems like maybe not sleeping, you know, a lot of times that can also add to you're being more prone to de stressed. So that's something we need to kind of get balanced out. So you're getting the sleep that you need, but you're also able to, you know, deal with your teenager, deal with your child and kind of get to where you need to be.
Client: That would be great. That would be great. I've got to get some sleep.
Counselor: So you said that you're very frustrated or stressed out. And that kind of leads me right into, you know, the main reason that you're here today to presenting problems. And I know you didn't mention it has to do with your teenager, but can you clarify a little bit about what's going on with him?
Client: I think it's racing hormones.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: He just can't. Anything that I say, he just disagrees. You know, he's right, I'm wrong. We can't come to common ground on anything. Curfew. He's just, you know, I feel I give him everything and he feels that we're too strict, you know? You know, and he wants to do things that I don't feel that is appropriate. But who knows? Just, who knows? What is he, what is he really wanting? But we've got. We've got to come to some type of common ground to figure out what we can do. Just make our life just a little bit easier and not fight all the time.
Counselor: So it sounds to me y'all have a lot of little things that y'all disagree on, but it's all added up to be a very big stressor.
Client: Oh, yes. I could just hang him up by his toenails okay.
Counselor: Okay. Well, let me remind you that I am a mandated reporter. So anything that you say, if it is something that would leave me of concern, I do have to make a report.
Client: Well, hate him, but by his toenails. I'll just tell you what.
Counselor: Okay, so I know you said you have some communication problems. I believe I heard you say that.
Client: We do.
Counselor: Okay. And do you feel that maybe it's just he's not listening or that y'all just.
Client: We just can't agree.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: We just can't agree.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: We can't because he thinks that we're just so strict.
Counselor: Okay. Okay, well, and, you know, how old is he?
Client: He's 15.
Counselor: And that is very common for 15 year olds, for teenagers. They're going through the changes in the school and the peer pressure and friends. So that is something very common. But it can also be very frustrating. And I see where you're having some struggles with that, and that's perfectly understandable.
Client: We've got sexting going on. We have things that are going on on the computer, so we're having to watch that and leave at that.
