You're just having some issues right now dealing with, and that's. That's a positive thing.
Client: Yeah, I told him, you know, he can start considering doing these things when he's pretty white and 21.
Counselor: Yeah. Okay.
Client: Well, one thing that I would like.
Counselor:
output: For you to think about is some goals that we can set.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jesse. How you doing today?
Client: Not too good. Doctor Grande?
Counselor: Not so good.
Client: Nah. I just got into a. I got into a fight with my parents.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: Well, I. I've been doing heroin for a few months now, and I didn't think my parents knew, but I guess they. They found a needle in my room and, I mean, they knew what I was doing, and they. They told me that I have to start shaping up and I need to stop doing any kind of drugs because they said. They said the next time that they find any kind of drugs, then that's it, they're going to kick me out of the house.
Counselor: All right. So they're at the point where anything else happens and they discover it, and you're out in the street. Right. What are your feelings about being out in the street?
Client: I don't want to be out there. I don't know. I don't know who would be. I mean, it would be hard just to kind of stop cold turkey. I know a couple of buddies that did that, and it's not good when you get junk sick. And, I mean, I'm kind of stuck because. I don't know. I don't want to be out on the streets, but it's just going to be so hard, so hard to give it up.
Counselor: So there are conflicting feelings here. You don't want to be out in the street, but you don't want to give up the heroin at the same time.
SPK_3: Right. Right.
Client: I just. I mean, I don't want to give it up, but I mean, I kind of know I have to. I mean, I'm a young guy. I couldn't make it outside of my parents house, and I definitely don't want to be on the streets.
Counselor: You want to stop to avoid the consequences, what could happen, right. But to this point, you haven't been able to.
Client: I mean, I guess at this point, I really haven't had, like, something that would make me, like, I've been doing it for a while, and, I mean, it's been pretty great, but I, you know, I never really had any kind of, like, problem with it. And nothing too bad has happened. So this is kind of the first time I've been like, something's hit me where it's like, oh, man, I really gotta stop it.
Counselor: So this is the first consequence or potential consequence that's motivated you since you started using? How strong is the craving to use?
Client: I mean, when I first started, it was. I mean, it was pretty freaking great. I mean, the rush that you get from it. It's. It's just mind numbing. It's. It's just amazing. But I've. I've noticed recently that, like, the rush isn't as intense anymore, and it's even, like, it's even kind of started to backfire a little bit where, like, actually, I'll feel a little sick without using it. And that, I mean, that kind of scares me. But the crazies are definitely still there.
Counselor: All right, so when you try to cut back, have you tried to cut back?
Client: I had before, but, I mean, there was no reason to, so I didn't try very hard.
Counselor: But when you did try, did you have the feeling where you were getting sick?
Client: I did, yeah. It wasn't as bad as any of my buddies, but I definitely. I mean, I didn't feel well.
Counselor: Have your parents given you any options in terms of, like, do they understand that you're. It seems like you're a little dependent on.
Client: Yeah, I mean, they, they do. I definitely, like, I don't hold anything against my parents. Like, actually, I have a pretty good relationship with them. I know what I'm doing isn't good for me. And they said that they would completely support me. They told me that they have a place picked out where I can go and that they'd be willing to pay for it and everything. But they said if I don't meet them halfway, then it's just. That's it. They're done.
Counselor: All right, so they have a solution, in a sense, for what's going on, right? Like, it's like a detox.
SPK_3: It is.
Counselor: Okay, detox. So they have a. They have a solution to help get you off the heroin, but there's still. There's still part of you that doesn't want to go that route.
Client: I mean, I, you know, I think. I think I'm starting to come to terms, and it's. That. That it's time to stop. And it might be good that maybe I'm stopping so early. I know. I know my friends have been doing it for a lot longer than I have, but I just. I don't know if the detox is going to work. I mean, it's hard for me to focus on, like, anything until sometimes. Until I get my next fix.
Counselor: All right, so there's a few problems here. So one is, can you. Can you commit to going to detox? And the second is, even if you successfully complete that, when you come back out, you can avoid the heroin.
Client: Right. It's tough right now because, actually, my dealer lives in my neighborhood. I mean, he's, I mean, he's just, like, a few. A few houses down. My girlfriend lives in our community, too, and, like, he's. He's on the way to her house, so, like, I'll. I'll kind of just maybe pick it up on my way, throw him. Throw it in my book bag, and then get. Hang out with my girlfriend a bit, and then maybe on my way back home, I'll shoot up the buddy, so.
Counselor: Right, so really, you're running into him as you walk to your girlfriend's house, right?
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: And he's there, and the temptations is great. And.
Client: I mean, it's like, that house is kind of, that's where I shoot up a lot. So it's like, whenever in his house. Right, right. So it's like, whenever. Whenever I'm coming up to his house, I'm like, I start getting excited. You know, I started anticipating how. How great it's gonna feel the next time, and it's. I don't know. It's, like, stuck with me. I get excited when it's his house.
Counselor: So you have a feeling. So let's explore this. As you're walking up to the. Well, as you're getting ready to pass this house on your way to your girlfriend, you divert to kind of go to his house, and you have this feeling of excitement. What's the thought that's going through your mind?
Client: I kind of. I just can't wait for the next hit. Now I got past this house since my parents are giving me the ultimatum, and now it's kind of mixed. Cause I'm like, oh, man, if I go do that and somehow they find out, like, it's kind of all over for me. But on the other hand, I'm thinking about how great it's gonna be. I'm just kind of, like, I'm planning in my mind how much I'm going to do and, like, what kind of plans we'll have for the rest of the night.
Counselor: Okay, so you have a. You have a few things going on. Do you think, like, is your plan right now to go into the detox?
Client: It is. Yeah. It's. Yeah. I mean, my. My definite plan is to go in the detox. And if the detox works, like, I mean, I think I could be done with it, but it's just, I don't, I don't know if the detox can work. And, I mean, I've never. I only tried to cut back that one time. I mean, I don't know how good I'll be at it. You know, let's.
Counselor: Let's presume for a second that the detox would be successful and. And you wouldn't be. You wouldn't be on heroin coming out of detox. Right, right. You're worried at that point that you'll go right back?
Client: I don't know if I'll go right back. Like, I think if I can get off it, if the detox actually works like they say I do, I think I can stay off it. I think, like, my. I think my cravings will still always be there. But now that. It's, like, now that I've come to the realization of some of the stuff that I can lose if I get caught, I mean, if I can get off it for good, I don't. I don't think I'd go back. It might be hard, like, if I run into my buddy or something.
Counselor: That's the point of worry. Right.
SPK_3: Right.
Counselor: So there's. There is a concern that you'll. You could. You could go back if you run into them.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But if you could stay away from him, you think you'd increase your chances of being successful?
Client: Well, I mean, yeah, definitely. I won't. Like, there's so many, like, experiences in this house that kind of feed into the anticipation and the cravings. I mean, if that doesn't happen, you know, probably hope.
Counselor: When are your plans in terms of going into detox?
Client: Pretty soon, I think. I'm supposed to go on Monday, after the weekend, so, like, three days.
Counselor: Okay. So it actually sounds like what your parents have put in place, you believe will work. Right. You have confidence it'll work and that your worry is what worry you have is when you get out, can you avoid. Can you avoid your friend?
Client: Right.
Counselor: You don't buy from anybody else other than your friend.
Client: No. No.
Counselor: So that's really becomes the. Maybe one of your key goals here, since you're sound like you're committed to the detox part. Right. I'm reading that incorrectly. That seems to be something you're.
Client: No. Yeah. If it works, then I can try.
Counselor: So it's preparing for life after detox.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And avoiding. Well, you've heard the phrase people, places, things with the addictions or substance use. So in this case, you need to avoid, it would seem, your friend and where he lives, which is unfortunately not far from you and in between, like, his house is in between your house and your girlfriend.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So is there a way. This may seem a little odd. Is there a way to walk around the block where you can completely avoid this house and still get to your girlfriend's house.
Client: Yeah. I mean, there is. It's kind of out of the way, but I think, yeah, I could go. There's like a. Like a horseshoe path. I could. Yeah, I could. I could, like, go up the block and, like, around the horseshoe, and then. And then I could, like, turn right and get her house there.
Counselor: She would never even see his house.
Client: Right, right.
Counselor: How about other options as well? Like, so there's that option. How about her coming over to where your parents live? Is that ever happened before?
Client: I mean, yeah, she's come over. So maybe if, like, maybe if I tell her that it'll help me out, she can, like, she can make that walk, and it'll be like.
Counselor: It'll be easier because she can walk right by the house without a problem.
Client: Right, right. And, I mean, if I start walking out of the house, it'll be harder for me to actually do what I'm supposed to. So if I can't even leave and she comes, that might be best.
Counselor: And to get to work, do you have to pass this house?
Client: No, not at all. I work down the road, so I just drive. I drive the other way out of the community.
Counselor: So there's kind of some, like, really, there's a physical kind of slash behavioral strategy here, which is just physically keeping you away from having to go buy his house. And it sounds like the only reason, other than to buy and use drugs, is to see your girlfriend.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And there's an alternative strategy here. Right. She. She come to you. Or you could go all the way around and then all the way around back.
Client: Right.
Counselor: To return and to get back and forth to work. You don't have to go by his house at all.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, I could do that, actually.
Counselor: Is there ever a time where he comes to you?
Client: Honestly, not that much. Now. He obviously, he doesn't. He doesn't really like to leave his house much. He's kind of the only one who lives there. So that's kind of. He just deals out of there and then shoots up there. So he stays in his ass most of the time. So now he doesn't even come out.
Counselor: And we know that there's automatic thoughts. We talked about this before. Right. There's automatic thoughts that lead to feelings and behaviors.
SPK_3: Right.
Counselor: And can you identify a specific thought that may occur or maybe has occurred not related to walking by his house, but when you've been in your house like, that maybe has motivated you to go walk to his house.
Client: Right. I'm bored? Yeah, straight up. I mean, when there's nothing to do with the house, my parents are gone. It's the best way to have fun.
Counselor: So you've identified a thought that directly connects to a behavior you want to avoid. Right. So on board. So, on board leads to using the drugs, because that would alleviate the boredom. Right.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Is there an adaptive response that you can put in right there that you can interject right at that moment when you say, I'm bored? Is there an adaptive response you could apply? Let's assume this is post detox, right? Sounds like that's your plan. You're sitting in your house. Detox is done. There's no more, you know, we would hope, withdrawal type symptoms.
Client: Right.
Counselor:
output: The thought comes upon you on board. What's a self talk piece that could be interjected there?

Counselor: Okay.

Now you're thinking differently and your feelings are different, which means that what you think about the presentation going wrong has a huge role to play in your anxiety.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: What you think is you are incompetent in case the presentation goes wrong.

But how does that mean that you are an incompetent person?
Client: If I don't have the knowledge, if I don't have the skills, if I don't have the competencies, it will make me.
Counselor: That means you are a person who lacks these competencies.
Client: Yes. That means I am a person who lacks these competencies.
Counselor: Right. But how does that mean that you are an incompetent person?
Client: Yes. It does not mean that I am an incompetent person, but I am a person who lacks these competencies, the knowledge, the skill and the competencies which are required.
Counselor: So, competencies is not you. For instance, if you have a competency, it doesn't mean you are competent. Let me give an example. I have ring. I am not ring.

Counselor: All right. I have a phone. I am not phone. I have it or I don't. In a similar way, you have a competency, but you are not competent. So you lack or have an ability. You lack or have a skill. You lack or have a competency. Fine. I am with you on that.
Client: But that does not make me an incompetent person.
Counselor: It does not define you fully and accurately.
Client: My skills are different from a person.
Counselor: Absolutely. Absolutely. You are not your skill.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Skill is just a small part of the whole human being. You know, we are made up of so many complex attributes. Skill is just one of them.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And it would be a little too much to label a person based on their skill or behavior or knowledge or their finances or their looks or their materialistic possessions or, you know, their social status. I mean, like, these are few things that we define human beings on, but they are pretty inaccurate to label anyone as good or bad based on these things. So coming back to the point, how much are you convinced that lacking a competency does not make you incompetent?
Client: Yes, I am convinced that my skills and me is a. We are different. Skills can be learned and they can be learned over time. They can be mastered over time.
Counselor: Mastered over time?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you will have to do what to master them?
Client: I'll have to study more, practice more.
Counselor: To do that, and fail more, goof up with presentations more. So, you know, when you make mistakes, you learn best. So this is your conviction now. But as human beings, you know, conviction is very unstable. It goes up and down with adversities. So why don't you prepare yourself for an adversity and convince yourself in case of an adversity? Client: Right.
Counselor: If you are able to convince yourself in adversities. Excuse me. I think you will be able to manage your feelings better next time. Then when you are able to manage your feelings, you will also be able to get over the avoidance that you were talking about.

output: Okay. And how likely are you to avoid this presentation?

Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you've been feeling down, you've been feeling unmotivated, you feel like you want to be better. But actually it sounds like you feel like you can't reach out for help, you can't speak to anybody.

Counselor: Okay, so this would be like last March, last April?
Client: Yeah, I think so.
Counselor: Around that time. So about six months ish. And it sounds like a lot was happening. So you had a lot of uni pressure on and you said that your parents were having marital problems. Okay. And it sounds like that was a real shock to you.
Client: Yeah, I guess it was hard as well because I wasn't doing well at uni. I guess I just felt a bit guilty. I know it sounds silly, but I felt like maybe if I could do better, then they would get better, but it just wasn't really happening.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you were trying to work hard and be more successful because you thought that that would make them happier and try and fix things.
Client: Yeah, I wanted to make them feel better, but it just kind of backfired a little, I guess.
Counselor: How did it backfire?

Client: Yeah.

Counselor: So it sounds like you feel you should always do your best. Is that the word you used? Yeah. And that there isn't any kind of exceptions for that, but no. Okay. I mean, what's the situation with your parents at the moment?
Client: I think it doesn't sound good. I don't really talk to them a lot, but I don't think they're going through very good. I don't like to talk to them about it because it just makes me feel worse. But I don't think it's getting any better.
Counselor: Were you home over the summer?
Client: For a little bit, yeah.
Counselor: And how was that?
Client: Not very fun? No, it was quite tense all the time. Stress me out more than relaxed me over the summer, I guess.

And sounds like you feel like you can't really reach out to anyone. Like you can't understand, but you can't really reach out to your parents right now. You can't really confide in your friends. So I suppose I'm just wondering if you can tell me a bit more about how you've been feeling. I mean, say this past week.
Client: Really not good, to be honest. I actually. If I don't have to, then I don't really leave the house or get out of. But I just. I can't find the motivation for the things I used to join. I used to love doing sports or going out. And now I just prefer to lie in bed and not really do anything.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I missed a few lectures this week that I should have gone to.
Counselor: Right. So I suppose I'm just wondering then let's see if we can think about one thing. Say a lecture. What kind of thoughts do you have about going to that lecture before it happens?
Client: I don't really see the point anymore. If I can't do as well as I should be doing, then what's the point in putting myself in those positions? I can't be bothered anymore to try. It just stresses me out more than I need to.
Counselor:
output: Okay, so it sounds like the kind of thoughts you've got in your head are. It's pointless. It's not worth it.

Client: Yeah, I can do that.
Counselor:
output: At the end of 15 minutes, you might end up using marijuana, or you might want to continue watching the show. So do you see kind of how it works? Is it making sense to you, the postponing?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: You doing okay?
Client: I guess, yeah.
Counselor: Not sure.
Client: I don't know, just the same.
Counselor: Yeah, still a little down.
Client: Yeah, I've been sleeping a lot. Going to work is a struggle. I don't really ever want to go. Just I haven't been eating much, so I think I've lost like ten pounds since past, like four months or so.
Counselor: Past four months?
Client: Um, just the guy. I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.
Counselor: You still been working?
Client: Well, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But not much else?
Client: No, I usually just go to work and go home.
Counselor: Tell me what happens after you arrive at home, like after work?
Client: Um, well, my fiance tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep for just. I don't know. I tried, I tried reading the other day. Cause I used to like that and it's just, I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.
Counselor: What were you thinking when you put the book down?
Client: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.
Counselor: I. And before you were depressed, which is, I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading?
Client: Mm hmm. Oh, yeah, all the time.
Counselor: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?
Client: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up till like two in the morning just reading a book.
Counselor: Something you look forward to?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But not now?
Client: No, I just didn't really get any. I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like.
Counselor: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?
Client: Yeah, I used to be a runner and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I. I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.
Counselor: Alright, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running, like when you first started?
Client: Not really. I mean, it was a change to be outdoors and I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while, so. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run. I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route. And by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.
Counselor: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?
Client: Kind of a mix of, like, relief just because it was over, and then, I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.
Counselor: Sadness, maybe disappointment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I've seen you a few times now, and based on those conversations, and, of course, what you said today, it seems like you have, for a variety of reasons, given up on the activities that you used to enjoy, you're not motivated toward them anymore.
Client: Yeah, I guess you could say that.
Counselor: And that's a common symptom of depression. I think we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed. So we've been working with the cognitive piece. Right, like we did last time, we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self talk. I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. We'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle. And the technique is called behavioral activation. The theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, like with the running, that will connect to your mood. Right. Remember, we believe in cognitive therapy, that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood and what you do. Your behavior affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we talked about?
Client: It does, yeah.
Counselor: So you mentioned the reading was one thing you like to do. That's tough to do. Now you try unsuccessfully with the reading and I the running. Anything else you could think of that maybe we could plan for you to do, even if it's just a short time, even if it's a little bit uncomfortable, that we could plan to do? That would be an activity that you used to enjoy?
Client: Well, my fiance and I used to go out with two other couples, and we used to go out once or twice a week, and even if it's just each other's houses, but we haven't really seen them in a while. They've tried to schedule things, but I've kind of come up with reasons of not feeling well or to kind of just stay home.
Counselor: So they're trying to initiate meeting, going out, doing something, and you're. You're kind of pushing them off.
Client: Yeah, I just. I haven't really wanted to see anybody lately.
Counselor: All right, so that's. So we have reading, running, and then going out with these two other couples. Anything else you can think of that you used to really enjoy before that you can't quite motivate yourself to do now?
Client: I mean, I used to like going for, like, just walks and shopping with my fiance. Like, I. We used to spend a lot of time together, and lately it's just kind of. I come home, say hello, we eat dinner, and then I kind of do my own thing.
Counselor: So spending time with your fiance outside the house in some manner? Shopping was one example. Any other activities like movies or going out to eat?
Client: Yeah, I would kind of put those in with the things that we would do outside together. We would try to switch it up every now and then.
Counselor: Okay, so that's distinct from what you did with the couples because that's just you and your fiance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So let's do this. What kind of books do you like to read?
Client: I like a lot of fiction. I do a lot of reading for school, so I usually enjoy those books too. Mystery novels.
Counselor:
output: Mystery novels. Okay, let's center on mystery novels. How long would it take you to read, say, a chapter of a mystery.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Lucy. Nice to meet you.
Client: Hi.
Counselor: So I understand that you were referred here by your GP because you've been feeling quite down recently.
Client: Yeah, I thought I should. I've been feeling quite bad for quite a while, so I thought maybe it's time to see someone about it because I don't want to feel like this anymore.
Counselor: Okay. So from your notes, I saw that you saw the GP about three months ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how long have you been feeling down altogether?
Client: Quite a few months before that as well, actually. But it's gotten pretty bad these past few months, so that's kind of why I came.
Counselor: Okay. So has it got worse since you saw your GP?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so tell me, how are things at the moment?
Client: Well, it kind of started just feeling a bit low and wound up about things, but, I don't know, just recently I just can't really be bothered to do anything at all. I kind of find it hard to get motivated for things and I want to be. I really want to be better, but it's just kind of reaching the end now where I just. I want to do something about it.
Counselor: Okay, so you said that you're feeling really down, really sad?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you feel like you haven't got any motivation, but. Are you okay?
Client: Yeah, I'm fine.
Counselor: Sorry. Okay, and you haven't got any motivation, but it sounds like you've put quite a lot of pressure on yourself to try and feel a bit better.
Client: Yeah, I just. It's kind of hard as well because there's not really anyone to talk about. So I just kind of stay on my own trying to. I don't like to think about it, but I don't know.
Counselor: So you say you've been. You've been feeling quite isolated. There's not many people around.
Client: Yeah. There's no one I can talk to about it. No one would listen or understand anyway.
Counselor: Okay, so I'm just going to try and find out a little bit more about you. So I understand that you're an english student at uni.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you live away from home with some friends. Is that right?
Client: Yeah, I live here.
Counselor: Oh, okay. So you don't live far from the uni, but you say you feel like you live with your friends, but you don't feel like you can talk to them.
Client: Yeah, I mean, they're lovely. I get on really well with them, but I don't know, recently, whenever they want to go out or stuff, I just. I don't want to bring them down. I can't. They don't understand what I'm going through. They kind of. I don't know, they don't make fun of how I feel, but they don't really understand what it's like. I just. I don't want to go out with them and bring them down or stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds. Do you try and hide the way you're feeling from them?
Client: I guess. I mean, it's easier to hide it than to try and explain it all the time when no one really wants to know.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you've been feeling down, you've been feeling unmotivated, you feel like you want to be better. But actually it sounds like you feel like you can't reach out for help, you can't speak to anybody.
Client: No, I don't really talk to my parents a lot either, so that's kind of hard.
Counselor: Okay. I'm just gonna go back in time a little bit, I suppose. I'm just wondering, when did all of this start? You said it's been going on for quite a few months.
Client: Yeah, I guess it kind of started, actually, when I was revising for my exams. I guess the stress. I put a lot of stress on myself. I think I've always wanted to do well for me and I guess for my parents. So the stress of exams. And it was also kind of hard because my parents were going through a bit of a troubled time then.
Counselor: Okay, so this would be like last March, last April?
Client: Yeah, I think so.
Counselor: Around that time. So about six months ish. And it sounds like a lot was happening. So you had a lot of uni pressure on and you said that your parents were having marital problems. Okay. And it sounds like that was a real shock to you.
Client: Yeah, I guess it was hard as well because I wasn't doing well at uni. I guess I just felt a bit guilty. I know it sounds silly, but I felt like maybe if I could do better, then they would get better, but it just wasn't really happening.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you were trying to work hard and be more successful because you thought that that would make them happier and try and fix things.
Client: Yeah, I wanted to make them feel better, but it just kind of backfired a little, I guess.
Counselor: How did it backfire?
Client: Well, it just ended up with them getting worse, and I've just been feeling worse since then.
Counselor: Okay, so after the summer, after the exam period. And how did that exam period go for you in the end?
Client: Not very well.
Counselor: Okay. That's an awful lot of pressure to put on yourself that you supposed to.
Client: Think it's just annoying because I know I should have done better and I just didn't. And I guess I beat myself up a lot about it.
Counselor: So you say. I know, I know I should have done better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: I mean, I suppose hearing it from my perspective, I'm thinking it sounds like you had an awful lot going on at the time. It would be understandable, absolutely. That you wouldn't do as well as normal. I suppose I'm just wondering if you have very high standards for yourself.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Aspen. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well, thank you. How about yourself?
Counselor: I'm doing all right, thanks for asking. I had met you last time for our first session, and we talked a little bit about kind of your circumstances, what brought you here. And I was hoping today we could get into trying to really figure out how we can help you. Any thoughts on your current situation? Anything changed?
Client: Nothing's really changed. I mean, I'm amazing at my job. My boss just really is someone that I hold, you know, in higher regards than others I work with especially. We went to. We went to the same college. College, of course. And he suggested I come into counseling and he's way off. Way off. So I'm just gonna, you know, let him know.
Counselor: So, as I understand it, you came into counseling because he requested it.
Client: That was what initiated it. But now it's. I need to prove him wrong.
Counselor: Alright, so at first it was because he told you it would be a good idea, but now you kind of see it as an opportunity to prove your point.
Client: Yeah, have a little bit of fun with it. Prove my point.
Counselor: What would you. What would you like to prove through this?
Client: That I'm not the one in the wrong. You know, I. I'm extremely good at my job. I mean, I am the best employee that they have ever had. Not just currently, just. I mean, just ever. I make no errors. So how can I be wrong when it comes to these circumstances with my coworkers?
Counselor: Right. So your co workers have made some criticisms about you and that led to your boss suggesting this.
Client: I would call them criticisms because it's really hard to criticize me. So I would say they take it personally that I'm better than them, you know? So I feel that it's important for me to be able to work for this particular company. It needs to be the best company. And so I need the other employees to at least be at my level. Well, I mean, that's. That's really hard for them to come to my level, but at least be above average. At least.
Counselor: All right, so you have an expectation of them to become at least close to you in terms of your skill.
Client: I mean, it's pretty hard to not make any errors when it comes to accounting with the numbers, with the amount of numbers and the volume of accounts that we have, it's hard to be as good as I am with it, as far as no errors. But yes, I expect a higher standard from the coworkers.
Counselor: And you don't feel like they're performing at that level now?
Client: No, not at all.
Counselor: And evidently you made some different comments to them which maybe they took the wrong way.
Client: I just pointed out the facts of the situation.
Counselor: What type of facts did you, when.
Client: They make mistakes and, you know, how they should be better at certain tasks. I mean, they didn't attend the same, you know, type of college as far as, you know, Ivy League as myself. However, they do have a college education so, you know, that alone would, you know, just kind of go to speak to them having some sort of ability in that area.
Counselor: So you've kind of, in a way you've expressed your disappointment with them.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: To them?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And what are some of the observations or comments they made regarding you?
Client: Oh, they told me my ego is too big, that I'm cocky. That's one. Yeah. I'm just overall, like, I don't know how you can be too confident when your ability is at that level. I mean, I am the best employee they've ever had overall. You know, I was the best student at my college. I received numerous awards from the president of the college alone. I received numerous calls from the college and other companies as well, trying to recruit me to work for them. You know, so I don't think there's, it's impossible to be overly confident, but they, you know, they consider it cocky and arrogant. Get arrogant a lot.
Counselor: The comment arrogant. So you feel they're just really, are they misunderstanding you?
Client: I think they take it as a personal attack.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Like I'm can, like I'm that concerned with them personally. Like it affect, like I'm talking about them as a person instead of just their performance at work because I'm really not concerned with them as far as like existence outside the realm of performance at work.
Counselor: Alright. So your commentary to them has nothing to do with their value as a person, more with their performance as an employee. And you feel they're misconstruing your observations about their performance?
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: They're taking it personally.
Client: Taking it personally and trying as best they can to push it back on me as I'm the one who's wrong, but I'm obviously not.
Counselor: Alright, so you're not wrong in this and you're frustrated by their reactions.
Client: I mean, I'm okay with it, you know, I mean it's, I don't really take anything they say to heart because they're not at the level to really be able to criticize me. You know, I can take criticism, you know, from constructive criticism, from someone who would, you know, be at my level or above, however, they are not. So it's really nothing. It really doesn't affect me. It does interfere with my job as far as my employer is concerned.
Counselor: Right. That's what led to you. That's what led to him recommending you come here initially. So you don't feel that they're at a level where they can really criticize you. It doesn't really bother you if they have criticism in the first place, but you can appreciate how getting along with them would be better for you as an employee.
Client: I mean. I mean, overall, I like this company. You know, I like working for it. I've been friends with my boss. I mean, we went to the same college, you know, so we have that in common. You know, he is an extraordinary person as far as his abilities, you know, I would say as in the level realm as myself. So, you know, I hold his, you know, opinion, you know, in some sort of regards above the others, so.
Counselor: Okay, so to the extent that they communicate negative sentiment to him about you, that that affects you?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And so what do you think, if anything, what do you think needs to be fixed here?
Client: Well, I think it's on their area and, you know, on their side. They didn't take what I said the wrong way.
Counselor: Okay. So if they had accurately interpreted your comments, that would fix the problem?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Do you think that's realistic.
Client: If they worked at it, possibly.
Counselor: How long have you worked there?
Client: It's been about 15 years.
Counselor: 15 years. And how long has this been something that you've been aware of them not feeling so great about your comments to them?
Client: Well, every now and then, this is. We've hit a peak here recently because a lot of the people that I work with feel here recently more. So they've been taken in the wrong way, more prevalent than in the past. In the past, they would, you know, I'd hear, you know, certain comments, but I understood, you know, comments just directed at me, and I just understood that, you know, it was just, you know, envious because I was able to give them. I was at a level where I was able to critique their work. So it never got to a point where I had someone like my boss say anything to me. So this is really the first time that has gotten to that point.
Counselor: So you've noticed things like this in the past, but now it's become more urgent to address it.
Client: It's become more urgent to prove that I'm not wrong in this fact that it is. You know, if this were the case, then, you know, it would have been, you know, it would have been continuous, not just, oh, don't come to a head. So, I mean, that just proves my point even more, that it is their issue and not mine.
Counselor: All right, so if you could somehow prove that they're in the wrong, would that help you?
Client: I mean, it's kind of. To me, it's obvious they are in the wrong because the numbers speak for themselves. It's the fact of the matter. So if. But I guess that if there was something that could change between the relationships that I have with them, then at least would be a little bit better of a flow. So maybe we could get up to the level, you know, that this company is deserving of.
Counselor: Okay, so there's like two. There's two things operating. There's your desire for them to improve and make the company better. And then they're discontent with withdeze your comments to them. So you'd like the company to improve. And you feel that means that you need to be able to voice your opinion to them in an honest way. But everybody needs to get along too. And that's at least to some extent, and that's not happening because they're upset. So do you think there's any steps you could take that could reduce the tension in those relationships?
Client: I need to figure out a way to present the information at a level that they would understand. So drop it down to their level, but also kind of sugarcoat it so they're not, you know, taking it the wrong way.
Counselor: All right, so you need to deliver the same message in a more polite, less threatening package.
Client: I mean, you could say that, yeah.
Counselor: Do you have any ideas how that might look?
Client: I mean, I could start with not comparing their work to mine because that's just unfair. I mean, at no point in time are they ever going to reach that. That level of quality with their work. So that could be a place to start.
Counselor: Okay, so just refraining from drawing that comparison. That could help.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Do you think there could be a benefit in just taking a break from offering any comments to them, any observations, just to let things cool down a bit?
Client: I mean, I could see where you would say, you know, refer that as cool down.
Counselor: Just in an effort to restore the peace. You could still, of course, be aware of different shortcomings in their performance. It might just be helpful to not share that for a while. Just as an idea. Does that seem like an idea that might work. Yeah.
Client: Just keep to myself a little bit more. I mean, that's not very hard around.
Counselor: Them keeping to yourself.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Do you think you would be okay with the. With doing that? Because you wouldn't really be able to offer those. Those helpful comments like, about performance.
Client: If. Well, really, it would, in fact, prove my point behind it all. It would prove that I was right, that it's not me, that it is them taking it the wrong way. You know, because, in fact, if it was, you know, if it wasn't them taking it the wrong way, then I would just say that that would, you know, it would continue. As far as trying to point out, I mean, really, I think it comes down to an issue of being jealous and seeing themselves as less than, so needing to bring. To try to bring me down to make themselves feel better. So if they don't have that to do that, it would prove my point behind this whole thing.
Counselor: Yes. You feel like they're just trying to. They're just trying to tear you down to make up for their own inadequacy.
Client: Oh, definitely. Yeah.
Counselor: And by you just not kind of offering those observations, you're taking the wind out of their sails.
Client: Right. And then it's not. It's only a matter of time before someone else notices that without me pointing that out to them.
Counselor:
output: Right. So your kind of commitment to quality will still be honored because somebody else will see that.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Marcy, how you doing?
Client: I've been better.
Counselor: Been better. Yeah, I saw that you called a few times between the last session and today. You left a few messages.
Client: Yeah, I was trying to get holding you. I had something I really needed to discuss with you, but nobody called me back. I emailed you a couple times, I never got a reply, so I was just wondering what's going on with that?
Counselor: We can talk about that. I want to talk about that after getting those messages. Remember we discussed the process for when your mood deteriorates and you had a few other resources you wanted to connect with before calling me.
Client: Yeah, I kind of remember it.
Counselor: Your brother was one of those resources.
Client: Oh, yeah, that's useless anyway. Go on.
Counselor: Did you attempt to.
Client: No, he's so busy with it, like he could never help me. I don't think he even cares what I'm going through. He's got his own stuff to deal with, he's got his own family and all this stuff and. Yeah, he doesn't care.
Counselor: So you didn't contact him first because he thought he doesn't care? Yeah, and we'd also talked about a few different friends that you had that you'd reached out to, you didn't contact them or did.
Client: Well, I did call my one friend, Beth, but I. She was like, oh, can I call you back? And of course she didn't because nobody ever calls me back. You know, I'm like, they all have their own lives. No one really cares what I'm doing. You know, it's always like that. So that's why I thought I could reach out to you since you're supposed to be helping me, but apparently you never call me back or answer any of my emails, so.
Counselor: Right. We talked about how there's limitations on time and how it would be better if we could keep the therapy in here in person. Right. And not get really too excessive with the telephone calls. I realize that when you're in distress, there's that kind of feeling that it would be a good idea to call. But remember, we discussed different levels of distress. And if it's something common that you've been through before and you kind of know the outcome, connecting with one of those resources might be more helpful.
Client: Yeah, I just feel like you're the only one that can help me, you know, I mean, my boyfriend, like, things aren't going well with him. I thought he could help me, but I guess he can't. And I think he's running around on me and all that. So I was just like, well, let me reach out to doctor Grande and see if it can help me, because it seems like my last resort.
Counselor: I remember you discussing, a few weeks ago, your boyfriend, and you had a fairly high opinion of him. Like, it was. It seemed like a positive.
Client: Yeah, he was great. He was great. And then, you know, he was in the other room and he got a text message, and I was like, let me just look at that. Because I was just curious to see what's going on with him because he never talks to me about anything. And so I looked at it, and it was a girl's name and number that I don't know. And so he came back in. You know, they put it away quickly, and I didn't say anything, like, what's wrong with you? Because I was acting weird and I was like, nothing. So then he went out, so I followed him. And then he went to, like, some friend's house. And I don't know if there's girls there or not, but. So I kind of think he's running around, maybe. I don't know. And I can't trust him. I can't trust anybody, you know? So I don't know. I mean, he was so awesome before, but now I just don't know. But he was everything I ever wanted.
Counselor: Yeah, I remember. You seem very excited about where that relationship could go.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you seem like you're much more negative about.
Client: Yeah. I mean, if he's not going to be faithful to me, what am I supposed to do? Yeah, I mean, it's just like every other guy that I've ever dated, like, either leave me or cheat on me or lie to me. So, I mean, I don't know why I thought this one was going to be different. Seriously, why would this one be different?
Counselor: So you have. You had this experience with the text message and you don't know? You don't know any more than that? But it sounds like you kind of jumped to, he's cheating. So, you know, he went to a text message and went to someone's house.
Client: Yeah. I don't know if they were related. The text message and him leaving, I mean, but I just assumed. So I'm just gonna assume because it seems to be a pattern in my life. You know, everybody lets me down.
Counselor: Could it be that you're jumping to that conclusion prematurely?
Client: Probably, but I guess it's all I know that's all. I've always been treated, so I kind of feel like, why would this be different? Even though I thought it was in the beginning, but I don't know.
Counselor: So you feel like you've seen this all before, this pattern?
Client: Yeah, I guess I just always pick the wrong people or it's probably just me. I think I'm the one that's just unlovable. I've been told that growing up a lot. So I think it's me because he's great. I mean, he's great and he's good looking, he has a good job. And I always thought I'm like, why is he with me? And then now I see, like, he doesn't really want to be with me. Whoever he was texting, that's probably the person wants to be with him. She's probably, like, pretty and has, she probably has a good job and she's got everything going for her and so.
Counselor: So you really, this week at least, you don't seem to think a lot of yourself.
Client: No. I mean, when things are going bad in my relationships, they really seem to get to me, you know?
Counselor: So in a way, you feel like your mood is subject to how your current romantic relationship is going?
Client: Yeah, I guess that's pretty right on. Yeah, I would say that.
Counselor: Is there anything that you can do from your side to improve what's going on?
Client: No, I don't think so. I think it's everybody else that is treating me wrong, you know? So unless I find the right person who's going to treat me right, then I don't know what I'm going to do. So.
Counselor: So the. So the key to feeling better is finding the right person.
Client: Yeah, I think so. And like I said, I thought he was the right one in the beginning, and now I don't know anymore. But, you know, I really don't want him to leave me because, like, then when I gotta do him, now I'm gonna be alone. I want to be alone because I love him, but, you know, so I think I probably will forgive him and just stay with them because I don't want to be alone. I'm too scared to do that. I mean, I don't want to be alone without somebody. You know, I really need somebody. Yes.
Counselor: So does some of this seem like what you're describing with your mood, does some of this seem like you're out of control?
Client: Yeah, because I feel like I can't control other people's actions, and that really makes me mad. That makes me really angry, you know? That what am I supposed to do? And so I think acting out and following them and checking their text messages, and it's the only thing that makes me feel in control, I guess. I don't know.
Counselor: I know in the past, when we've talked about this, you've mentioned that you thought that that behavior could be driving them away, too.
Client: Yeah, I mean, I can see that. I mean, people want, you know, some that they can trust, too. And I'm not sure I've always been honest with them, but I'm always looking for things that they're gonna do to manipulate me or try to, like, you know, screw me over or whatever. So here's my guard down. Yeah, I'm suspicious.
Counselor: I wonder if sometimes you acting on those suspicions, that's not making things a little worse in those relationships.
Client: Yeah, probably. But, I mean, like I said before, I don't want to be alone. I don't want to move out somebody. I need somebody. I need somebody. I need somebody to be with, you know, I need someone to help me with things. I don't want to be alone. You know, that's, you know, and he has said things to me like, you can't call me all the time at work because I'm at work, and you leave me, like, 40 voice messages because I just want to know if he's actually at work. You know? He's like, you can't do those things because I'm gonna get fired, and then where are we gonna be? He's like, you know, and you can't, like, call the numbers in my phone and find out who they are and, like, hang up because my friends know it's you, and you can't, you know, have your friends come to the bar and see who I'm with and, like, report back to you. Like, that's. He's like, I don't want to be in relationship with someone that doesn't trust me like that. So now, you know, I'm really scared of losing them. Yeah.
Counselor: So you have called other boyfriends and this boyfriend many times?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: On the phone?
Client: Yeah. I just want to check up and see what they're doing. If they said they're at the place that they said they were going, you know, I just want to know that I'm not being lied to because I've always been lied to. All my life, I've been lied to.
Counselor: So is all that calling something you do to relieve anxiety?
Client: Well, when I find out they're at the place that they said they were, that I feel better for at least, you know, for a few minutes till the next time. Like, wait, maybe they left. Let me see where they are now, you know, and then it kind of builds upon itself till they just get so frustrated. And then usually it ends with, like, a screaming match when I do see them.
Counselor: Mm hmm. You know, there's a lot of screaming and yelling.
Client: A lot of screaming and yelling and accusations and finger pointing and just. Yeah, it's not good. It's not a good scene when those kinds of things go down. But like I said, I really love him. I don't want to be without him. I don't know how I live without him.
Counselor:
output: All right, so there's the. There's screaming and there's yelling and some discontentment, but there's also this love you have for him and this fear that you'll be alone. So there's a lot of emotion here driving different behaviors.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Zoe, how you doing today?
Client: I'm good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. I know that the last time we spoke, we talked about spending today's session working on units of distress. These different levels, different exercises that cause increasingly more stress around the specific phobia you have. And I know you mentioned it related to a dog, but I didn't get a lot of information last time about how that kind of all formed. So I was hoping we could start there with what happened that made you afraid of this dog.
Client: Sure, sure.
Counselor: Tell me about that.
Client: Okay, so I've had an issue that started about when I was a little bit younger. When I was about ten years old, I was really active. I was playing outside all the time. And my neighbors had large dogs that were always in their yard. They would always be outside running around, and we were separated by a fence. And if I was playing outside or like kicking a ball around or doing anything with a friend, and I had to go after the ball, it would be near the fence. And especially if I wasn't looking, I would be leaning down to grab the ball or just have my back turned. And they would come up, they would be really excited, and they would jump on the fence, and I never would be expecting it, and they would always startle me, and I would always feel this sense of fear and uneasiness around them. And so I've kind of always been a little bit more uncomfortable around dogs since all of that happened.
Counselor: And how old were you?
Client: I was about ten.
Counselor: Oh, you mentioned that. Yeah, you're around ten. And they would startle you. Would you like, jump?
Client: Yeah, yeah. It was like a whole body reaction, I guess, because I wouldn't ever be looking, I wouldn't know that they were coming, and then they would just be up against the fence, like barking and jumping, and I felt like they were gonna jump over and try to get me.
Counselor: And since that time, you haven't been a big fan of dogs?
Client: No, not really.
Counselor: And for this exercise specifically, there was one dog in particular that you wanted to kind of work through that fear?
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Cause there was an incident that happened more recently at my friend's house, and it was a really big problem. I was at a party last weekend, and they had a bunch of people outside. The dog was out loose, and it's there, and so it's never really a problem. It's always kind of around. Doesn't really come near me. I can always just kind of keep my distance from it. But we were outside, and they were playing with it, and I wasn't really paying attention. And they're throwing the frisbee for the dog between each other, and the dog was facing me, and I turned around, and it was running towards me, and I didn't realize it, and I just saw him coming up at me, just kind of like how the dogs had when I was a kid, and it really was unexpected, and it startled me, and I kind of thought, like, I did, like, when I was a kid, like, they were gonna come get me, even though he didn't. He didn't come near me. And it was a really big problem for me because I was all shaken up, and I tried to go inside and calm myself down, and I couldn't, and I had to leave. I had to leave the house, and I've been really uncomfortable ever since.
Counselor: So this is particularly stressful, this particular dog. What kind of dog is it?
Client: It was a full grown german shepherd. Yeah. His name. His name is Thor.
Counselor: His name is Thor?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you want to be able to interact specifically with Thor. You want to conquer that fear.
Client: Yeah, because I've been really hesitant to go back over there because her family, it's my good friend, so her family's super nice. And they said, like, you know, we'll lock the dog up. Like, you can. Can still come over, but I would just feel really guilty because it's their house and I'm over there. Well, I used to be over there all the time, and now if I go over there, that means that they have to keep the dog, like, away or, you know, not really where I can, like, be near it, because I'm gonna have that. That fear.
Counselor: All right, so it's important for you to get over the specific fear, and the owners of the dog you think will cooperate with the exercise that we have here?
Client: Yeah, yeah. They're so nice. So definitely, if I said, like, can you help me with this? They would totally be involved with me.
Counselor: All right, so you're getting started developing these units of distress over three days. I just want to establish the scale before we get started. Okay. One to ten. One is, like, really mild level of distress, and ten is, like, when you're in person with that dog, he's just stand there with you. So ten would be a lot of stress, the kind of anxiety and panic you described earlier. And one would be. It registers on the scale, but it's really minor. It doesn't bother you that much. So I'm going to list these different exposures, these different activities, and if you can rate them from one to ten.
Client: Okay. Okay, I understand.
Counselor: Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So we're going to build like a hierarchy of these different levels of distress.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Now, if there's any of these activities that or exposures that you just don't want to have any part of, just say that that's okay.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right. But if you think there's something that you could tolerate at some point, let's go ahead and put them on the scale and rate them. We can always take them off later.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: If you think of any others, mention them and I can add them to this list.
Client: Okay, perfect.
Counselor: So I'm going to start with what I believe is the lower levels of distress, like the activities that are associated with lower levels of distress for you and this dog, like, for you and your reaction with this dog. But I may be out of order. Really? My educated guesses. So don't feel like you have to increment the scale for each one that I read. Okay. It doesn't have to be the first one's one, the next one's two. I might have some that go backwards or that don't register at all.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right.
Client: Yep.
Counselor: All right. So how. Let's start with something I believe will be mild, which would be, if I were to, like, for example, just penniless in this paper, draw a german shepherd. So it would be a crude drawing.
Client: Okay. Yeah, that would probably be a one.
Counselor: A one?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: That wouldn't be too much.
Counselor: How about if I took a picture, like with a cell phone of a german shepherd, but it was out of focus and I showed you that picture?
Client: That would be probably a three or four.
Counselor: That would be a three or four?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What if I took a picture that was of any german shepherd that was clear.
Client: That would probably be a five. Yeah. If I could see it, that would be a five.
Counselor: Any german shepherd, clear picture. Yeah, it would be a five. How about if I took a clear picture of Thor?
Client: That would be six.
Counselor: That would be a six?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What if I took a. Now I'm going out of order here a little bit. What if I took a picture of Thor, but he was really small, like way in the distance in that picture.
Client: So he would be far away.
Counselor: He'd be far away in the picture, like. So he's like, I picture a big yard you're describing, and say, I'm way back.
Client: Okay. Okay.
Counselor:
output: It would be six if he was, like, right in the close up.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Client: Hi. How you going?
Counselor: Hi, Liz. How are you?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: I haven't seen you about in ages.
Client: Do you mind if I come in?
Counselor: Yeah, sure.
Client: Do you have a spare moment?
Counselor: Yeah, I'm just writing up some counselling notes. I had all these kids coming in with bullying issues today, so we'll talk to the staff about that tomorrow. But anyway. Yeah, so can I.
Client: Can I talk to you about something?
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I mean, I don't. I don't know. I'm really wondering if. I don't know. I don't know if this is what I'm cut out for just thinking about. Maybe I shouldn't even bother coming in tomorrow. Teaching's my thing. Maybe I need to find another job.
Counselor: What's going on? You want to tell me about what's happened to.
Client: I don't really know what to do. I really feel like I just, you know, failed sort of in everything I'm supposed to do. I don't know. You know, there's the new kid, Vince Rossi. And you heard, you know, what happened on the weekend. Well, last week on Friday, you know, the poetry assignment? He handed it in and he was just this really distressing poem. You know, he talked about his life being futile and a gun and all of this sort of thing, and it really worried me. And I did ask Nora about it. She didn't seem to think it was too much. And then I saw Chris and, you know, Chris was looking at an artwork, you know, which was. It was a really great one, but. And, yeah, and that was Vince's as well. And I. That just really distressed me. I got really worried and I thought that maybe I should have had something at the staff meeting, you know, that I was concerned for him and stuff. But, you know, Bob. I mean, he's been teaching for a long time, and he said, oh, you see, lots of kids go through stuff like that. It's just attention seeking. So I didn't bring it up at the staff meeting. And then anyway, all weekend I was really so busy with Mark, and I didn't really think about him anymore. But, you know, then I came to school on Monday morning. I was in such a hurry. I didn't really hear the news about him or anything until, like, first break, you know, I just.
Counselor: Yeah
Client: I really don't. I should have done something. I'm just feeling like I, like, you know, it's my fault if I brought it up on Friday. And then I went home.
Counselor: I couldn't.
Client: I just couldn't sleep. I just cried all the time. It was really my fault, like, said something. You know
Counselor: I can, I can see this is really. His attempted suicide really deeply affected you. And you were worried on Friday, and now you're really Tuesday afternoon, and you've been. You've been carrying this with you the last two days, if not, you know, the whole weekend. I mean, you were busy with. With your study and your marking.
Client: But think how much worse it's been for him. I mean, to try and kill yourself, you know, and I. The signs were there. I should have done something. I really should have. You know, it's really my responsibility and I just, you know, it's. It's my responsibility. And I feel so guilty that if I had said something on a Friday, we could have stopped him. You know, we could have gotten help or something, you know, reached out to him.
Counselor: But it's not your fault. It's not your fault, Liz. You know, I know you feel like you think it is at the moment, but, you know, that boy, I mean, he's only been here a few weeks. He arrived at the end of last turn and he came here deeply disturbed. Yeah. Yeah.
Client: But still, I mean, you know, especially from this poem. You know, it was. It was really obvious. And I. I just really feel that I did the wrong thing by just brushing it aside and not doing something else. You know, I just. I just think, you know, as a teacher, you know, I'm supposed to care about the kids and I've really, you know, you know, betrayed his parents trust in me and I breached my duty of care. Maybe I'm just not meant to be a teacher.
Counselor: You've just said so much there, Liz. Let's just slow down and breathe and let's think about a few things. So, you know, yes, you do care about the kids. I know. I know you do. I've known you for long enough, Liz, to know that you do put the kids first. But you have to be realistic and not so hard on yourself. You know, think back to, you know, other people in the school have discussed this sort of thing amongst themselves and not come to see me. You're the only one who's come to see me who's been very distressed about it. But I know that other people have had, you know, things to say about the situation. What happened? What happened when you came in on Monday? I mean, how did. How did that come?
Client: Oh, I didn't hear much at first. I didn't have a chance to go to the staff room or anything. And then, you know, at first break, Laura kind of said, did you hear about Vince and, oh, maybe you should have said something on Friday at the staff meeting. But, you know, in a way, it was her and Edward who told me not to. You know, they said it was, you know, nothing to worry about. And, you know, they've both been teaching longer than I have, so I guess I kind of trusted them with that. But, you know, I'm his teacher, and it's, you know, it's my responsibility. And I just feel, you know, maybe that poem was. Was him even asking for help. Maybe he wanted me to notice it and do something. I just.
Counselor: So.
Client: I don't know.
Counselor: So it's your feelings of guilt also, because you listened to Laura and Bob's comments, and then you made that decision not to. Not just say anything, and that's making you feel quite guilty.
Client: Yeah, I'm thinking that maybe, you know, my first instinct to say something was the right one, and that's my fault for making that choice when, you know, when a kid's, you know, mental health is at stake. You know, I should have. Should have just done the right thing. And now, you know, he's committed suicide. It's my fault.
Counselor: Well, he said he's okay. He's okay. All right. He's okay. Now, let's think about. Let's look at the words you're using there. You should have. You should have done this. You should have done that. I mean, where's it written that anybody should do anything? I mean, how do you know what was going to happen? You didn't know what was going to happen.
Client: I should have. I mean, in the poem, you know, he mentioned a gun and how futile life was, and I. And then seeing that artwork, you know, we're supposed to know. I mean, we're taught these things at uni. You know, we do some subjects about these sorts of things, and, you know, you're supposed to recognize you're not going to help these kids.
Counselor: You're not a mind reader. I mean, he probably didn't even know what was going to happen over the weekend. You think about all the other people who would have seen clues in some way. You know, Laura. Laura saw the poem. Laura saw the artwork. Chris and the art department, they were raving about the artwork. You know, no one was to know. And even myself, you know, I knew about. I knew about Vince's situation when he first came to this school. But under confidentiality, according to the parents, I wasn't allowed to say anything to him.
Client: Well, maybe I should have come to.
Counselor: You, but you wouldn't have known. Okay, now, I could easily be taking this on board myself as well. So could Laura, so could, so could Bob.
Client: But they've been teaching a lot longer. I guess they've seen more of this stuff. And I just don't know that I can cope with, you know, having to be responsible for kids. You know, I just. I don't know if I can do that. It's, you know, his parents trusted me to look after him and I didn't. Yeah.
Counselor: So what are you saying to yourself? Why are you feeling like running away from teaching is the answer. What sort of things are you saying to yourself?
Client: I don't know. I'm not good enough. Obviously, I can't cope. I mean, and obviously I can't choose the right thing to do, you know? Cause I didn't do the right thing.
Counselor: Hindsight's a wonderful thing, you know that it is. But, you know, you have to be realistic about the situation. There were clues evident to everybody and yourself undeniably about it. Maybe some other people did as well, but nobody did anything about it. That doesn't mean that that then led to his attempted suicide. We don't know what happened over the weekend. Okay, so there may have been some other factors come into play here that tipped him over. And there's also no guarantee, Liz, that if you had said something, that it could have prevented that attempted suicide. You just don't know. So I think you're being a bit hard on yourself, taking it along board like that.
Client: I just. I think maybe, you know, the poem was a cry for help. Maybe. Maybe if I just showed him that I cared about him, maybe that's all he needed. I don't know. You know, we have these kids, and I just feel like I'm responsible for them, you know, not just for teaching them, but for caring about them. And if I can't do that, maybe I'm in the wrong job.
Counselor: Look, I know you well enough there to know that you do care about these kids and that you do spend hours preparing for your lessons, marking as you were on the weekend. You don't put these kids second. You don't go, oh, I'll just worry about that tomorrow. I know you think hard and deep about things, you know, we've worked with each other long enough, you know, and I know you're a damn good teacher. And any kid that has you is lucky to have you as a teacher. But I think you need to be a bit easier on yourself, you know? Do you really believe that the function of a teacher is to be a whole array of different things, 100% of the time, to. To the kids. I mean, how can you possibly teach and be a little everything, but you.
Client: Still want them to know that if. If they need to talk to someone, that, you know, you're there for them.
Counselor: Sure, sure.
Client: You know, sometimes they can't talk to parents or things and I don't know, maybe I didn't make that clear enough, or.
Counselor: And maybe this is good, you know, for something for the future, you know, that will help you think. Okay, a few alarm bells are ringing here. Maybe I'm just going to go by my own instincts and have a chat with them, rather. And, okay, you talk to Laura and Bob and whoever else you spoke to, and they gave you your opinion, their opinion, you know, and ultimately it is up to you how far you want to take something. But, you know, if things don't work out as you expected, you shouldn't take it to heart and blame yourself because, you know, this world is not made for perfectionists.
Client: No, no, I suppose not. I just. I don't know, I just thought I'd have maybe more time to talk to him or. I suppose I just hoped that he would come to me. But, you know, I really hate to fail my students.
Counselor: Let's look at that one. You hate to fail your students? What does it mean to fail your students?
Client: Well, you know, to let something like this happen. You know, I want my students not just to learn English, but to grow and mature and be happy. I hate to think of them being miserable and not being able to talk to someone. I want to be that person for them.
Counselor: So let's review what you mean when you say that you had something like this happen. What do you mean that, you know, you shouldn't let something like this happen?
Client: Well, you know, to care for our students.
Counselor: Yes.
Client: To help them through difficult times. Right.
Counselor: You know, and how do you envisage doing that when you barely know a child and you don't? You see them three times a week and he's only been at the school for a few. A few weeks. So I suppose, really, how logically is it for you to take that all on board?
Client: Well, I suppose I want them to know that they can talk to me.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I mean, that's not my job. You know, you're the counsellor, but I'd like to be able to let them know that there's help for them.
Counselor: Sure.
Client: And guide them towards you. Maybe not do it all myself, but, you know, I don't like to think that I just send them on their way, not caring about them.
Counselor: But you. You know yourself that you do care about them. Yeah. And, you know, building a relationship with students does take time. So, you know, in the situation with you and Vince, you know that that wasn't going to happen when he needed it because he barely knew you. And his structures around the school where you only see him three times a week, you know, that doesn't support. That doesn't support a relationship building approach either. So how can you blame yourself for not having that opportunity to build that relationship, to let them know that you are there, to listen, you know, lots of other factors in play here, Liz.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So, you know, let's think about what you were talking about before, you know, how you led this to happen. Do you still think you. You led this to happen?
Client: Well, no. I mean, I still kind of feel like I should have done something and maybe he still would have tried to kill himself, but, you know, I just feel that, you know, what if I had taken a moment to talk to him, okay? You know, just to let one. Him know that one person noticed, and it might not have changed anything, but it might have.
Counselor:
output: And it might have. You're absolutely right. It might have. But we'll never know that. And there's your shoulds and what ifs. We can't change the past, but we can use the past to help us in the future. All right?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Client: It's like a foreign object. Like, yeah.

Client: I always do the right thing. I'm really studious, and I like to have fun.
