Counselor: Is there a particular outcome that you're afraid of? Like, when you're, well, you're in college now, right? So likely interact with males to some extent. Is there when an opportunity comes up when somebody's interested in you? Is there a particular fear that comes to mind?
Client: Yeah, like, I don't even know why you're talking to me. Like, why would you talk to me? I'm not pretty. I'm flipping awkward. Like, you know, why would you even be interested?
Counselor: So you think yourself as unattractive and awkward?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you question why they would be interested in you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So have you ever had evidence presented to the contrary, like, people who thought you were attractive and not awkward?
Client: Um, well, yeah, I mean, yeah, like, people have told me that I'm pretty and, um, you know, fun and stuff like that, so, yeah, I have.
Counselor: Yeah. But there's some, so they're telling you that? But there's something else telling you that you're not?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you think that's coming from?
Client: I guess just from my, you know, my mom and I think just her rules that I guess I just associated, you know, me not being able to date, that I wasn't presentable enough to date. And I just got this idea that that's the reason why she just didn't want me to date.
Counselor: So you think her reasoning for not allowing you to date, I wasn't the pretty daughter? Were your sisters allowed to date?
Client: They were allowed to date, but under certain circumstances, certain rules they had to follow. But just when I would, you know, even suggest it to my mom, it was just like, no, you're not.
Counselor: So you feel like you were, of you and your sisters, you were the one treated the most strictly on that. But was it much more strictly or just a little differently?
Client: I think it was much more strictly, yeah. Because it's so much so now that I can't even talk to a guy. It's just. I mean, the anxiety and the fear is so intense. I just can't explain it. It's horrible that it's not like that for my sisters because now they're married, you know, so they have kids, and it's like, what the heck happened here? And I can recognize it, but I just can't bring myself to do it, like talk to somebody or, you know.
Counselor: So the way you perceive yourself, the self image here is part of this?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, absolutely.
Counselor: So you have evidence that says that men would be interested in going out with you, dating you, but internally, these thoughts you're having say you're just not worthy.
Client: You know what I mean?
Counselor: That's kind of the theme of it, right?
Client: Yeah, absolutely. That's it.
Counselor: And maybe this is tied to a core belief. Like we talked about core beliefs before cognitive therapy. Are there any of those core beliefs in the list I gave you a few weeks ago kind of stood out that you think might be core beliefs you have?
Client: That I'm unlovable.
Counselor: Unlovable, yeah. Any others?
Client: Fear of rejection.
Counselor: So fear of being rejected?
Client: Fear of being rejected. Yeah.
Counselor: So unlovable. And a fear of being rejected. And then when you have interactions in the moment, like, say you're in class and there's a man sitting next to you in class, and they're interested in you, he's interested in you. He says something that expresses that he's interested. You're immediately suspect.
Client: Oh, yeah.
Counselor: That's what you're.
Client: Oh, yeah. That's like. It's like, what is it? Fight or flight kind of feeling like it really is. It's like, oh, you know. Yeah. Just something comes over me where, you know, it's kind of like I'm conditioned because I don't even live with my mom and my dad now, and I'm on my own, but yet I still hold their values. And not just. All I can just think of is being in high school and having. Being told I can't do that or just the rules and having to follow it. And that's really where I feel like I'm there. If someone says something to me, it.
Counselor: Takes you right back there.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. I. So how do your parents feel about now? Have they said anything like, your sisters are married and you're not? Have they pointed that out?
Client: No, they haven't. Not really. No. Because my mom really wants me. She. I guess. Well, maybe it has to do with that. Like, I'm smarter than my sisters, so she really wants me to be a doctor. And my sisters, they have, you know, they have great jobs, but, you know, they just stopped at a bachelor's degree, and I'm really working to be a doctor. And I always had straight a's in high school and my sisters didn't. So I think that my mom wants to hold on to that, you know, that hope that I'm going to be something great. So she doesn't really enforce the dating thing with me. I guess she's for fear that that's going to get in the way.
Counselor: That's different than being unlovable, right? Yeah. I mean, her reasoning, as you're describing her reasoning sounds more like she wants you to reach a higher educational goal.
Client: I mean, I guess. Yeah.
Counselor: What do you want?
Client: I want to be in a relationship with somebody because all of my friends are, and I'm always that. They're real and it's difficult. I mean, yeah, I want the education. Don't get me wrong, I want a great job, but I don't want to do that alone. I want to have somebody with me that I can confide in and just a confidante. And the time is now. I'm ready, you know? And maybe my mom was just protecting me, I guess. I don't know what she was doing, but I really don't care because I really want to try it. I just don't know how.
Counselor: There's opposing forces at work here, right? I mean, you're motivated to try it like it's a goal. You want to be able to date, you want to go out. It's important to you. Do you want to get married like your sisters?
Client: Yeah, I do.
Counselor: You do? So you have these clear goals, and that's one force. And then the supposing force is this. Well, one of them would be this anxiety that comes over you in the moment when a man's talking to you. Like in that way. Right. Like about going out or any topic like that. So a part of you. A part of you is saying, I really want to move forward and date different people and see if I can find a good match. And another part of you is saying I need to run away. Like you said, fight or flight, right? I want to run away and not have this awkwardness, this anxiety.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Because it's a. I just keep thinking of the repercussions, like now as an adult, that my mom's just. I guess that she wouldn't talk to me. But I'm not in high school anymore, so I don't know. I just. I honestly don't know what the conversation would be like if I talked to a guy that I was interested in or if a guy was interested in me. I mean, because I came to the realization, and my friends have helped me with this, that I am in college, I am an adult now. And, you know, what my mom thinks is what she thinks now. It's just me peeing in front of a male that I'm attracted to, that I want to go out with.
Counselor: And what you said is you don't know what would happen, so you don't know that it would be bad. You don't know that it would be a bad experience.
Client: Right? I don't know. I don't know if it's going to be bad, but you don't know if.
Counselor: It'S going to be good either.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a risk.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So in the situation you're in, if you can get through that anxiety and have a conversation, it could end up where things went very well or didn't. So what happens if it doesn't go well?
Client: Well, I mean, like I said, I think because my mom didn't let me date that it was sign that I was unattractive, so I could take it that way, that I was just unattractive, but that he wouldn't have initiated the date if I was unattractive.
Counselor: Good point.
Client: So for that, I was. It just didn't work. You know, there just wasn't anything in common with what I'm about. You know, that I have different hobbies and he has different hobbies, and maybe they just don't mesh well and I have to. That could be a reason why it didn't work. Not that I'm. I guess, nothing. I'm lovable. You know, I shouldn't take it that personal, but it's hard.
Counselor: It's difficult for you. This is painful for you.
Client: Yeah, it is.
Counselor: You're fighting through some strong feelings. If you try to look at the logical, right. If it's likely you just because of the way it works, you'd have to date several people to find somebody that was a match.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So some of those relationships you'll end, maybe some of the man will end, but eventually, one likely you would stumble on, or neither one of you would end it. So there's risk involved here. There's a risk of rejection. There's a risk of having to reject. That doesn't seem to be the risk you're most worried about, though. You're more worried about the risk of being rejected.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Because you're questioning their intent.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: So can you survive being rejected?
Client: I think. I think I can, you know. Yeah. I mean, because in essence, I was, you know, rejected by my mom, but I still moved forward with my life because since she didn't let me date, that's a rejection from her that I'm not worthy. So, yes, I think because my friends have helped me, so that's a step in the right direction.
Counselor: And you took that behavior from your mother as rejection. And it seems like that may not have been her reason for doing that. You don't know for sure.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But even if it was, which it seems unlikely it would have been, that's still just one person.
Client: Yeah, yeah. That is just one person.
Counselor: So if we just take it to the extreme and say for some reason.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: You know, she didn't think you were worthy. That's just one person opinion.
Client: Yeah, absolutely. Right. Because my friends think I'm worthy. Right.
Counselor: And their opinions are valid too.
Client: Right? They are.
Counselor: So if you really look at it and weigh the evidence and look at it logically, the imbalance of the evidence would say that you are worthy.
Client: Right.
Counselor: You're not unlovable. But still, in any type of relational situation, there's going to be rejection. So there's potential pain up ahead, but the reward could be you find somebody that you want to be with. And that's really your goal.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So really part of this is pushing through a good deal of uncomfortableness, discomfort, right?
Client: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. A lot of that. A lot of it, yeah, yeah. And I think that I'm willing. I'm willing to do it because I want it so bad that, you know, I have to. You don't know until you try it, and I have to try it. I have to.
Counselor: So what, kind of a behavioral experiment. Right. So let's. Let's take it one step at a time. Let's say that back to the situation I alluded to earlier. You're in class and there's somebody that's interested in you, sitting next to you or whoever they are, and they come and initiate a conversation. What's your reaction now? What do you do now?
Client: Well, I would introduce myself because I never. I have never done that before to a guy where I introduce myself. I wouldn't even make eye contact. So I think to just look up with them and just say, you know, hi, my name is, you know, Leia, and just see what that feels like because I don't know what to do.
Counselor: You've never reached that step?
Client: No. No, I haven't, because I wouldn't even, you know, I wouldn't even look them in the eye.
Counselor: Your current reaction is not look them in the eye. Not engaging in discussion.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just kind of shy away. So the. So the behavioral experiment is to nothing, do that, but instead proactively engage in another behavior, which would be to introduce yourself. So let's just make that the experiment. You seem like you're pretty comfortable and you have some confidence you could do that.
Client: Right.
Counselor:
output: And that's not a particularly long amount of time. You just have to get through that introduction. And the worst that they could do if you introduce yourself, I mean, I guess they could reject you at that point, but that seems pretty unlikely. I mean, you're just introducing yourself.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hazel, how you doing today?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: Well, last time I started to tell you a little bit about one of my friends, my best friend, actually, she had this issue. So what happened was she went to a bathroom at our local library, and she found a video camera when she was going to the bathroom.
Counselor: In the bathroom?
Client: Yeah. She actually. Yeah. And she turned it into the police, and I guess because, like, she carried it, or she had found it, her handprints were on it, and they weren't be able. They weren't able to detect who actually did it. They weren't able to catch the person.
Counselor: Oh, they didn't catch the person?
Client: No. So since then, I've been on really just high alert. Like, I'm worried that that could happen to me, to my kids, and I'm just really worried because they didn't catch the guy, that him or someone like him could be out there.
Counselor: So he's still out in the community.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So how is it affecting your. Your daily life? Can you tell me kind of what your. What you've been feeling?
Client: Um, a lot of anxiety just not knowing, maybe, you know, what if someone were to videotape me like that? I've been very aware, shall I say, of cameras.
Counselor: Okay. So anxious and aware.
Client: Right. Like, I know you have one in your office, and people on their cell phone cameras. Just all the possibilities that I could be recorded. I've just been very aware of them, which makes me not want to go anywhere. So I've been having arguments with my husband a lot because he wants to go out to restaurants, and I don't want to go because there could be cameras in the bathrooms and how I dress. Also, as you can see, I'm kind of dressed more conservatively because I remember hearing once about cameras that people use on shoes that could be used in a creepy way. And so I can't. You know, it's now almost summertime. I can't dress in skirts or be comfortable because I'm dressing like that.
Counselor: So you covered a lot of ground there. So you have the. You have the feeling of being, like, worried, nervous. Right. That's going to happen to you, but you've also had to kind of change your routine, or you feel you have to change your routine to feel safer.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Has that helped. Has changing the way you dressed or changing where you go and when you go, has that helped reduce the anxiety?
Client: Not really, no. I would say it's really starting. That's why I wanted to come in. It's really starting to affect my life.
Counselor: You mentioned specifically your husband. Like, what's been going on there?
Client: He just wants to go places with our kids, like, go out to eat. And I don't really want to go anywhere because, you know, cameras are everywhere nowadays, and I just kind of worry, like, public bathrooms, could they be there? Could someone be, you know, sometimes baby monitors are, you know, hooked up on so people can hack into that laptop, cameras. So even in my own house, I've just been really nervous, so I feel like I'm not really getting relief from that anxiety.
Counselor: Have you taken any precautions because of this persistent worry? I mean, I already mentioned, like, with the camera specifically.
Client: I mean, I've, you know, when I go into bathrooms, I've been looking for cameras to make sure they weren't there before. You know, me or my children have used the bathroom. I have tried. I read online that you can turn how to turn off the cameras on your phone and that you can close your laptop, and that way the camera will face down. And the same thing on a smart tv so it doesn't recognize your face. I've tried to turn things off. They don't need to be on as far as people being able to access my own information.
Counselor: And that seems reasonable. So you take reasonable precautions to try to avoid being video recorded against your will.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Okay. But still, you have this feeling of worry, anxiety, and your schedules being interfered with.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you'd like to cope more effectively with your feelings, reduce this anxiety. So when you enter into a public bathroom. Now, we talked about automatic thoughts before.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Those thoughts just kind of pop into our head and they connect to feelings of that can be unpleasant, like anxiety and worry. So when you walk into a public restroom, what's the first thing that goes through your mind?
Client: That there might be a video camera that I don't see. That's maybe with my friend, it was big enough, but I might not catch it. And that someone's going to use that in a vulnerable way.
Counselor: Okay, so when you walk in, you're wondering if there's a camera there.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And when that automatic thought occurs, what follows that in terms of a feeling or behavior?
Client: Usually I'll try and find the camera, but it's usually anxiety, fear. My heart rate starts going up. I start getting really anxious. And then, you know, I try and either rush to use the bathroom if I really have to go, or a lot of times if I don't, I'll just leave. Sometimes I try and use the bathroom so I don't have to go out.
Counselor: So your behavior is looking for the camera or sometimes just leaving without using restroom, and you're feeling that anxiety worry that we've been talking about. Okay, so, really, if we think about. We talked before about core beliefs, intermediate beliefs, and I'm wondering if the intermediate belief isn't I'm vulnerable, or this more specifically, maybe that's more of a core belief. More specifically, I'm vulnerable in this area, like, with this guy on the loose that committed that crime, and then that's combining with situations that you encounter, and that's where you're getting those automatic thoughts. Does that sort of make sense?
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Okay, so you remember what, in terms of cognitive therapy, we like to apply what we call the adaptive response, or self talk.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So it's that thought that you interject at that moment, you realize you're having an automatic thought that's gonna lead to, in this case, anxiety and worry and behaviors that, while looking for the camera, isn't maybe an unusual behavior, but leaving, you know, that could certainly be an unuseful behavior. So, in terms of that self talk, let's work to develop a self talk response, something you can tell yourself to that initial. I wonder if there's a camera in this bathroom. What do you think you could tell yourself that would get in between that thought and I, the feelings you're having?
Client: I could say if when I walk in the bathroom, maybe I could say, you know, while there could be a chance that there's a camera in this bathroom, the chance of it happening is not very likely. And, you know, I'm going to take steps to keep myself safe so that I won't be in a vulnerable position, such as looking for the cameras.
Counselor: Right. That's good. So you have a low probability of it happening, and you're taking useful behaviors to minimize your risk even further.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So that's a good automatic thought, I think, or good adaptive response for the automatic thought. Rather, why don't you try that one out the next time you have that automatic thought? Try out that. I think that's really logical. It's unlikely to happen. Of course there's a chance, and we acknowledge that in the self talk, there's a chance that it could happen, but there's precautions you can take, and it's a low chance sometimes as well. So keep that automatic thought. We'll review it at the end before you leave today. We'll write these down. But that's one adaptive response, rather, that I want to write down for you. I also want to talk about the worst case scenario because right now you have the anxiety and the worry about an event that while it's unlikely it could happen, it could happen. And I'm wondering how you think you would react if the worst did happen. If you used the restroom and you found out from law enforcement or by finding a camera that an offender had been watching you on a recording. I think you would react to that.
Client: I mean, I think I would be really upset. Upset. I think I would feel vulnerable probably for a while and be hesitant.
Counselor: But.
Client: I mean, I think ultimately I would be okay. My friend, this happened a while ago. She's starting to get to get over it and get back to her usual routine, although she's still hesitant. So I think I would be okay eventually, although I'd be really upset that.
Counselor:
output: It happened and it would make sense to feel upset. That would be upsetting for anybody. But as you noted, that would probably be relatively temporary, that distress, right. Well, acute. And certainly you wouldn't be happy about it and shouldn't be happy about it. It would probably go away. You'd probably learn to adapt. How long have you been in this state of anxiety and worry?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: You doing okay?
Client: I guess, yeah.
Counselor: Not sure.
Client: I don't know, just the same.
Counselor: Yeah, still a little down.
Client: Yeah, I've been sleeping a lot. Going to work is a struggle. I don't really ever want to go. Just I haven't been eating much, so I think I've lost like ten pounds since past, like four months or so.
Counselor: Past four months?
Client: Um, just the guy. I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.
Counselor: You still been working?
Client: Well, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But not much else?
Client: No, I usually just go to work and go home.
Counselor: Tell me what happens after you arrive at home, like after work?
Client: Um, well, my fiance tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep for just. I don't know. I tried, I tried reading the other day. Cause I used to like that and it's just, I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.
Counselor: What were you thinking when you put the book down?
Client: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.
Counselor: I. And before you were depressed, which is, I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading?
Client: Mm hmm. Oh, yeah, all the time.
Counselor: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?
Client: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up till like two in the morning just reading a book.
Counselor: Something you look forward to?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But not now?
Client: No, I just didn't really get any. I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like.
Counselor: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?
Client: Yeah, I used to be a runner and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I. I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.
Counselor: Alright, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running, like when you first started?
Client: Not really. I mean, it was a change to be outdoors and I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while, so. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run. I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route. And by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.
Counselor: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?
Client: Kind of a mix of, like, relief just because it was over, and then, I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.
Counselor: Sadness, maybe disappointment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I've seen you a few times now, and based on those conversations, and, of course, what you said today, it seems like you have, for a variety of reasons, given up on the activities that you used to enjoy, you're not motivated toward them anymore.
Client: Yeah, I guess you could say that.
Counselor: And that's a common symptom of depression. I think we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed. So we've been working with the cognitive piece. Right, like we did last time, we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self talk. I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. We'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle. And the technique is called behavioral activation. The theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, like with the running, that will connect to your mood. Right. Remember, we believe in cognitive therapy, that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood and what you do. Your behavior affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we talked about?
Client: It does, yeah.
Counselor: So you mentioned the reading was one thing you like to do. That's tough to do. Now you try unsuccessfully with the reading and I the running. Anything else you could think of that maybe we could plan for you to do, even if it's just a short time, even if it's a little bit uncomfortable, that we could plan to do? That would be an activity that you used to enjoy?
Client: Well, my fiance and I used to go out with two other couples, and we used to go out once or twice a week, and even if it's just each other's houses, but we haven't really seen them in a while. They've tried to schedule things, but I've kind of come up with reasons of not feeling well or to kind of just stay home.
Counselor: So they're trying to initiate meeting, going out, doing something, and you're. You're kind of pushing them off.
Client: Yeah, I just. I haven't really wanted to see anybody lately.
Counselor: All right, so that's. So we have reading, running, and then going out with these two other couples. Anything else you can think of that you used to really enjoy before that you can't quite motivate yourself to do now?
Client: I mean, I used to like going for, like, just walks and shopping with my fiance. Like, I. We used to spend a lot of time together, and lately it's just kind of. I come home, say hello, we eat dinner, and then I kind of do my own thing.
Counselor: So spending time with your fiance outside the house in some manner? Shopping was one example. Any other activities like movies or going out to eat?
Client: Yeah, I would kind of put those in with the things that we would do outside together. We would try to switch it up every now and then.
Counselor: Okay, so that's distinct from what you did with the couples because that's just you and your fiance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So let's do this. What kind of books do you like to read?
Client: I like a lot of fiction. I do a lot of reading for school, so I usually enjoy those books too. Mystery novels.
Counselor: Mystery novels. Okay, let's center on mystery novels. How long would it take you to read, say, a chapter of a mystery.
Client: Novel, roughly, depending on the size of the chapter, probably a couple minutes normally.
Counselor: So not long at all.
Client: No.
Counselor: So you could get a lot of reading done in, say, ten minutes, like something worthwhile. And how often would it. How often would you, what was the duration of a run? Like when you would go run? How long would it take?
Client: Probably, like a half hour.
Counselor: Half hour.
Client: Half hour to 45 minutes. Yeah. I used to do long distance running, so.
Counselor: Okay, and how often would you do that?
Client: Three or four times a week.
Counselor: Three or four times a week? Half hour, 40 minutes. And you mentioned you went out with the couple once or twice a week. How often would you go out with your fiance?
Client: I would say we try to do something every day, like, even if it was just going for a walk together, like around the park or walking the dog together.
Counselor: Okay. So I'd like to make collaboratively with you a schedule that involves those four activities, but I want to make it realistic. You tried a couple times, you weren't successful. So we don't want to be too ambitious, but I want to try to plan a schedule. You can get the habit of doing these activities again. So let's start with the kind of, I guess the simplest in terms of logistics, which would be probably the reading. Would it be possible, say, five nights out of seven, to read for ten or 15 minutes? Like, I know you're going to have to force your way through it a little bit, but I think it's something.
Client: I could try to do.
Counselor: So you're going to have automatic thoughts that come up, right. Like, just like you did before, and you're going to be tempted to give up. I want you to try to push through, say, this at least ten minutes. So focus on that as you go into it. It's a behavioral exercise, of course. It has a cognitive component to kind of think, you know, I just have to make this ten minutes.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And again, you might not really enjoy it the same way it did before. We kind of know that, but over time, that may change.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right, so does five nights a week seem reasonable? That's 50 minutes a week.
Client: Yeah, that seems fine.
Counselor: Okay, then let's move to the running, because you just recently tried that. You run with your dog. You said, yeah, okay, how about that? Twice a week. Would that be possible?
Client: Yeah, I can try to do that.
Counselor: What days of the week you think you could do it?
Client: Probably the weekends. So probably like Saturday or Friday night or Saturday morning.
Counselor: Okay, so Saturday morning and Friday night, would you run Friday night and then again Saturday morning?
Client: No, I guess not. So probably I'd see maybe Wednesday night and Saturday morning.
Counselor: Okay, so Wednesday night and Saturday morning run for, say, a minimum of a half hour.
Client: I can try for that, yeah.
Counselor: Again, remember, you're gonna have these automatic thoughts, likely that will be telling you that you should stop, but you have to kind of talk your way through that or do the best you can.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. The adaptive response maybe being something like, in the end, this will help me. It's tough now, but this will help me. Okay, so let's look now toward the more social aspects. Logistically, moving up the ladder here to the most complex. It sounds like going out with their fiance would be the next. At the next level.
Client: Yeah, he's. I don't know if he's kind of just been mad at me lately or if he just thinks I need to be alone, but we've kind of been getting some distance there, so I think that would, out of everything, that would be the relationship I'd want to work on the most.
Counselor: Focus on. All right, so maybe you're running Wednesdays and Saturday mornings. Could you go out and do something to fiance twice a week.
Client: Yeah, I think we could manage that.
Counselor: Cause sometimes you said you just walk around, like, the neighborhood, so it's not even. Doesn't have to be necessarily, like, a lot of time. It's just something.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: All right. What do you think you can do to motivate yourself to do that?
Client: I don't know. I guess just having, like, him maybe remind me or suggest it.
Counselor: So you could tell him that this is something that you're planning to do and you might need a little push to. To do it.
Client: Yeah, pretty much.
Counselor: Or to maintain it.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you might get outside the same thing when you run. You might want to come right back in.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. And then moving to the most complex, but also the one with the highest social engagement, going out with the two couples now, once or twice a week, you'd mentioned before. How about we shoot for. How do we shoot for now? Once every couple weeks?
Client: I think I could handle that.
Counselor: Like, maybe a Saturday night or a Friday night.
Client: Yeah, I think that could work.
Counselor: What can you see being an obstacle there? Like, what might help you be motivated to continue that?
Client: Just having to actually go to their houses or go somewhere because they don't really live close to us. They're not far. But just the fact that we would have to get in the car, drive over there, and I would actually have to, like, look relatively nice. I can't just go and pajamas.
Counselor: So for this to work, that is for you to do it, you really have to schedule at their house. You can't have them come to you.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So that's one thing we know. You have to. You have to make some time and drive over there, or maybe if your fiance drives, whichever. But you have to.
Client: We physically have to go over.
Counselor: So once you're there. So it might be tough, like, to get in the car and make the drive over once you're there, how do you think it would feel?
Client: I don't know if it's like the run, I probably just want to turn around and come back.
Counselor: Do these couples know that you're down?
Client: I think they've noticed, and I think that's probably why they've kind of started to back off with asking us to do things. So I think they've noticed it, but they don't know, like, any. They don't know what's really going on.
Counselor: Are those relationships you're worried about losing because they're backing off?
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I. I mean, they're our closest friends, so I think we've known each other for a really long time.
Counselor: And could you see this behavior being one that brings you closer together with them? Like restore some of that?
Client: Yeah, I mean, I think it would definitely just us going. They might be a little hesitant because the past couple times they've invited us, we backed out. But I think it would probably be a step in that direction of restoring the relationships of. I mean, I would like to do that.
Counselor: Okay. So I want to review the plan and just make sure that we have an agreement because we're constructing this together. So I need your buy in reading five times a week for a minimum of ten minutes. The next level up was the running. And that was, that was Wednesday night and Saturday morning.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Going out two times with their fiance and then once every couple weeks, driving to your friends, going to their houses and spending an evening with them. All that realistic?
Client: I think so, yeah. I mean, I can try to get accountability with my fiance just to let him know my plan and then see if he can help me follow through with it, I guess.
Counselor: Good. Alright, so let's set that as the plan. And I want you to be aware that as I mentioned, the automatic thoughts might come in. Right. And kind of tempt you in a direction away from that. I also want to let you know that if you are unsuccessful in any one of those things, it doesn't mean you have to stop and not try again. Just take it as a small setback. And then the next time, for example, it's time to read or go out running. Just try again. It's not unusual in this exercise that you won't be able to complete all the behaviors that you've planned for yourself. Sometimes life gets in the way things happen. Sometimes the depression gets in the way. So can you appreciate that that might be discouraging? Like, you try it and you stop. Like you told me in the beginning.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So just take that as a. You know what it is just a small setback and try to push forward the next time.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: And I want you to informally kind of keep a record of it. And when I see you next week, we'll see how it did. And specifically, I want you to keep track of what you were thinking and feeling through different stages of the behavior.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Liz. How you doing today?
Client: I'm alright. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on in the last week?
Client: It's still the same. Nothing at home is going right. It's. I'm still yelling, we're still fighting.
Counselor: Like you and your boyfriend.
Client: Yeah. He just can't get it together. He can't. He doesn't do anything right. He doesn't. And I just end up screaming every day and it takes it all out of me.
Counselor: All right, so he can't do anything right. And you're arguing, being angry every day?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So what are you taking away from this? Like, what do you think's going on?
Client: I feel like he does nothing wrong and I end up screaming at him when I come home from work, and that's a lot out of me every day, and I don't want to feel angry every single day.
Counselor: That's what's happening.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What types of things do you think are triggering your anger response?
Client: It's anything. It's. I come home, he's just sitting on the couch. I've had a long day at work. He gets homework before me, and the dishes aren't done. Nothing's, like, thawed or even started for dinner. And is that just supposed to be my, like, it's not. He could just do one thing and I just. I just lose it. I lose it and I can't. I can't control it. I just started screaming at him that he does nothing, that he could just do one thing for me. He could just have the sink clean, empty one thing, and it. Every single day. And then the next day it's something else. The trash is now, like, you name it.
Counselor: So every. Every day when you come home from work, there's something he's done or failed to do that triggers yelling?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's his response to this? Like, what's he doing when you yell at him?
Client: He gets mad back. He just starts screaming back at me. Like, I expect too much and I get too upset and why am I always yelling at him? Why can't I give him the benefit of the doubt?
Counselor: I'm.
Client: But I don't understand it. Like, you could do one thing and then. And I just. I can't help it. I scream at him.
Counselor: Are there other things he does at other times that you feel are helpful? Or is it. Or is it always, like, when you come home, is it always something that hasn't been done right or hasn't been done?
Client: I mean, on anniversaries, whole make dinner. So that's nice.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: He makes good money. So that's. He keeps that together.
Counselor: Okay, that's about it.
Client: Yeah. The rest is just. I just get angry at him.
Counselor: So if you were to pick adjectives to describe him, what adjectives might you. Might you select?
Client: Stubborn, condescending, and intelligent.
Counselor: Intelligent, stubborn, condescending, and intelligent. Do you see him as this way kind of all the time, or is this change?
Client: I don't think it's all the time. Like, there. Like sometime, like a month ago when a friend at work died. Old age, whatever. But I had a long day. He knew it beforehand. I didn't have to say anything. When I came home, everything was good. There was no trash, no dishes. So it's not all the. All the time, but just lately, it's just. I had no words.
Counselor: So lately it's all the time. Yeah, but there's been prior occasions when this hasn't been a problem. Yeah, but there's not many of those. So after you have, you yell and argue, what's it feel like to you then? Like, what's your mood?
Client: I'm still irritable. It's like the dishes don't get done. The problem didn't go away, didn't fix itself while I was yelling. So it just sucks being that angry. Just doesn't. I hate it.
Counselor: So it's not productive for you?
Client: Right, right. It's not productive.
Counselor: But there's a part of you mentioned earlier where, like you said, you just can't help yourself.
Client: Like I said, I just lose it. And I do that because that's what it feels like.
Counselor: So it's like you just. You just see, for example, like the dishes, right? So you just see the dishes aren't done, and immediately there's the.
Client: I just. I go off. Why didn't you do the dishes? You've been home an hour and a half. You could have done one thing for me. I had a longer day, and you knew it.
Counselor: All right, so let me take an example from work, right, so you work in an office with other people. Do they ever frustrate you in a way similar to what your boyfriend does?
Client: Occasionally, yeah, on occasion. Yeah.
Counselor: So there's times where you kind of have that moment with them where you just can't believe they didn't do something.
Client: Or I. Yeah, I just can't stand them sometimes.
Counselor: What's your reaction in terms of anger and yelling to those events?
Client: I get pissed, but I just. I can't. I can't yell.
Counselor: You can't yell? No. Why is that?
Client: I get fired.
Counselor: You get fired. So in those interactions with your coworkers, would be fair to say you're in that moment just as angry as you are with your boyfriend.
Client: And, oh, if not more, because I actually choose to be with my boyfriend. I don't choose to be with those people necessarily.
Counselor: You just happen to be together. And so in those instances, because there's a consequence like being fired, you're able to control the outward expression of anger, meaning you're not yelling, but inwardly, you're still angry at them.
Client: Yeah, I guess so.
Counselor: Yeah. So they don't really know you're angry.
Client: Yeah. I just walk away. I don't think they'd be able to tell.
Counselor: And they're not being yelled at, so they're not.
Client: Right. They wouldn't react. Yeah.
Counselor: No reaction. Right. So there is a thought process that occurs between the trigger and when you act, because at work, you're thinking, you have this thought that comes up, I don't want to be fired.
Client: Yeah, I get there. Must. Yeah.
Counselor: And the consequence of that thought is I'll be angry, but I'm not going to act angry.
Client: Right. I can't act angry or I'll get fired, and I don't want to get fired, I guess.
Counselor:
output: So knowing that there is a thought there when you come home and you see the dishes aren't done, maybe just stay with that example. What would that thought be like? Think back to the last time that happened. Do you remember what you were thinking at that moment as you saw those dishes sitting there not washed?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Michelle. How you doing today?
Client: Um, I'm kind of doing. I'm feeling a little bit stressed out.
Counselor: Stressed?
Client: Yeah. I feel like I have a lot on my plate. I have this test that I have to take for work.
Counselor: What kind of test?
Client: It's like an aptitude test. It has, like, math problems on it and, like, scenarios in order for me to move up to the assistant manager. Precision.
Counselor: That's a job that you've been interested in for a while?
Client: Yes, it is. Yes. So I've been just feeling a lot of anxiety about taking the test, and then they actually scheduled for me to take the test, and I went and I just got really overwhelmed, and I started, like, I felt my heart was racing. I felt like I wish my hands were shaking. And I just really couldn't concentrate on the test, even though the night before, me and my friend did practice problems and I knew all the answers with no problem, like, I didn't miss any of the questions.
Counselor: So you know the material on this test pretty well.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: But the feelings and that physiological response to heart rate and sweating, that the feelings of anxiety plus those physiological responses, they got in the way of you completing it. Like, you weren't able to complete it?
Client: No, I wasn't able to complete it. And thankfully, they gave me a chance to come back. I just told them I didn't feel well, so they rescheduled. So now I'm feeling a lot of anxiety because I'm scared the same thing's gonna happen when I go back.
Counselor: All right, so you weren't. You weren't feeling great about taking the test in the first place?
Client: The day, the night before, I felt like, I know all the answers, but the minute I walked into the room, all of a sudden, all these fears kind of took over.
Counselor: But did you know that was coming?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You did? Okay.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you had some anxiety in advance. Yes or not? You did? Okay.
Client: I had some anxiety the day before, but when I reviewed it with my friend, I'm like, oh, I know the answer. So I thought that would kind of push it down. But I think once I got there, it all came back up to the surface.
Counselor: It erupted in that moment. And that prevented you. What do you think is leading to this?
Client: Well, I've always kind of struggled with tests. Like, I can remember when I was in third grade, I had to take this test because I was really struggling in math, and I had to pass this test in order to move to the next grade. And I thought, just like this test, that I was ready for it. I had a tutor, and I felt really prepared for it. And then when I took it, I failed and I was held back. And I feel like, you know, that was so. It was. It was really embarrassing for me to be held back. And I felt like. I don't want to say, but I did feel like a failure at the time because I felt like I really did know this. So I don't know why I couldn't pass the test.
Counselor: And since that you said this was third grade?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And since that bad testing experience, have you had trouble with tests since?
Client: Yes, I always feel really anxious. I mean, I'm able to pass tests, obviously, because I graduated from grade school and went on to high school. But it's so hard for me because of this anxiety that I feel that even though I may think I know it, I may still fail the test anyway. Maybe like a repeat of what happened.
Counselor: All right, so in third grade, you had a really bad testing experience, and as you moved forward from there, you've never really been thrilled about taking tests.
Client: No.
Counselor: But you've been able to adapt. You've been able to take them and still, like, pass them.
Client: Yeah. I mean, sometimes I get an a. So that's.
Counselor: That's good, right? Yeah.
Client: I mean, yeah, it is good. Yeah, it's good.
Counselor: But with this particular test, which is not for school, which is for work.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: This one. This is more of a stomach block for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You have any ideas as to what may be making this test such a point of anxiety for you?
Client: I think it's just the fact that it's this promotion, it's almost like the same thing. Like, if I fail, I'm being held back, and I feel like it's reliving that moment of being held back. And that's like, a fear that I have, that by not being able to pass these tests, they're holding me back.
Counselor: So, really, that same feeling you had in third grade that's coming up with this test now, right?
Client: Yeah. I mean, I didn't put them together until now, but, yeah.
Counselor: And the other tests you've taken throughout the rest of grade school and high school, they didn't have that same value attached to them?
Client: No, because they didn't have all that pressure that it was either win or lose.
Counselor: Basically, you could take them again or take that course again, or I could.
Client: Take another test to raise the grade if I didn't do good on that test.
Counselor: So you maybe had more options in school.
Client: Yes. It wasn't fail, pass or fail.
Counselor: It's the pressure. It's the pressure of you need to get through this. And you don't have the safety nets that you had in school.
Client: Yeah. If I fail it, then I'm not going to be able to get the promotion. I would have to wait just like I did. I'm going to have to wait a certain amount of time, I think, an ear before I could take it again.
Counselor: So that is a lot of pressure.
Client: Yeah, it is.
Counselor: So is there any time limit to this tests for work?
Client: No, there isn't.
Counselor:
output: There's no time?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Terry. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay, I think.
Counselor: You okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know when we talked last time, you were having a rough time dealing with the passing year, Sister Sheila.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you're kind of a point where we were talking about emotional consequences, but also some of the thinking that's going on. Have you been processing that?
Client: Yeah, I've been thinking about some of that and, you know, trying to kind of work through it a little bit. So I think I'm kind of ready to kind of work through it and talk about it a little bit now.
Counselor: So, feeling a little less emotional and feeling a little more thinking about it. And, like, on the rational side, like we talked about rational and irrational beliefs.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: A little more focus there or more ability to focus there today.
Client: Yeah, I think I'm ready to think about it more.
Counselor: I know the emotional part was tough for you, and I'm sure it still.
Client: Is, but I think I've kind of got through some of that, and I'm ready to kind of get through the way I'm thinking about some things.
Counselor: Ready to look at through the thinking lens.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So to speak. All right. So what are some of the thoughts or beliefs that you've been having, you think maybe part of what's affecting your mood?
Client: Well, I've been. I've been thinking about it, and, you know, I just. I just feel like I don't. I don't have anybody that I can talk to. I mean, I just. I keep thinking about it. I don't have anybody to talk to. She was the only one I had to talk to.
Counselor: So in your relationship with her, you guys talked a lot. She was an important person in your life for a variety of reasons, but including that she was easy to talk to.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And that you could talk to her?
Client: I. Yes.
Counselor: So the thought is you have nobody to talk to.
Client: I just, you know, she was just everything to me. I talked to her about everything, and, you know, she was just always gave me good advice, and she could always work, you know, talk me through anything that I needed to talk about, and I just don't feel like I have that anymore. Since she's going, I don't have anybody like that anymore.
Counselor: That relationship is valuable to you, and you've lost that, and you feel like you've lost having anybody that you could talk to. Is that. Is that close?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right, so let's look at that thought. Let's break that down. Certainly you were able to talk to her, as you mentioned, and you have lost her.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. So you have lost someone that you could talk to that was very valuable to you, and that's understandably painful. The question would be, have you lost everybody that you could talk to? Is there anyone else in your life, for instance, currently, that you regularly speak with?
Client: Well, you know, since you said that, you know, maybe I do have some people that I can go to. They're not her. But, you know, you know, I have a couple of people that I can talk to that they're willing to talk to me about certain things. I guess if I give them the chance, you know, I'll be able to talk to them.
Counselor: So there are some people in your life that you can talk to. They certainly don't replace your sister, but you have people you can't communicate with, and that can be helpful for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So as we build kind of a rationale, self talk to replace the irrational thinking that you brought in.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Which was that you have no one to talk to. Could the replacement be something like, I had my sister to talk to, and she was really good at that, and it's painful to have lost her, but I gained something from that experience, and I do still have some people to talk to now.
Client: Yeah, that sounds about right.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Yeah, yeah. Yeah. Because nobody's gonna replace my sister. But, you know, I do think that there's other people that can. Could help me and what I need to talk. Yeah.
Counselor: And maybe one thing that you can. You can take away from this as well is that because of the way you could talk to your sister, you are a more effective communicator now, and you can make the most out of the relationships that you have now with people currently. Another rational thought kind of honors her contribution to you.
Client: Right? Yeah, because, you know, she is, like, the only one that believed in me. I mean, she just, you know, she always, you know, pushed me to go higher and, you know, on my job. She always said that, you know, that you can do it, you know, just believe in yourself. She always, you know, encouraged me to. To go back to school and, you know, I'm, you know, I have done that and, you know, continually doing that, you know, but, you know, she was a big motivator for me. And, you know, since she's gone now, you know, I don't feel like that I have anybody else that gives me that push that she did.
Counselor: So. So the thought would be, I've lost the only person that would believe in me. Yes, something like that. Okay, so she was a great positive force, great positive presence and contributor in your life, in part because she believed in you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And now that's gone, and you feel like no one else will believe in you in that way.
Client: Not like she did.
Counselor: Not like she did.
Client: No. No.
Counselor: Which could be true. Right? There may be no one else that ever believes in you that same way, but similarly, like we were doing before, can you think of some people now that believed in you, maybe in a different way that's still helpful? It doesn't replace her, but it might still be helpful to you?
Client: Well, I do have very encouraging parents. They've always, you know, been, you know, somewhat of encouraged encouragement, but, you know, they just didn't have that extra push that she did. But, you know, they are very encouraging, and I have encouraging friends. You know, some of my friends, you know, want to see me succeed, and they give me encouraging words and tell me to, you know, to keep going. So, you know, she stopped at nothing to make. Make me go, you know, she just didn't take no for an answer. And, you know, you know, if she had to go with me to do something, she would, you know, that's why, you know, I just felt like, you know, I wasn't gonna make it, you know, without her, you know, pushing me.
Counselor: Her level of belief in you was higher or different or better than what you have now? In some ways, yes. Like, she was really committed to her belief in you, it sounds like.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So some people currently do believe in you, and that's good. It doesn't replace her level of belief, her type of belief in you. I also wonder if by her believing in you, you mentioned that it helped you with all kinds of accomplishments.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I wonder if that's not a thought that you can use here as an adaptive response, that because she believed in me, I was able to do all these things. And maybe because she believed in you so much, she taught you how to believe in yourself to some extent.
Client: Well, yes, because, you know, she's been going, and I've continued to go to school, and, you know, every time I feel like I want to give up, I keep on saying, you know, I gotta keep going. You know, my sister would want me to keep going, you know, and she would want me to succeed, and I have to, you know, do, you know, keep, you know, keep my focus because she always talked about me, you know, keeping my focus. So, you know, those things that she taught me and instilled in me, I still hold on to. And it's. And it's, you know, it's kept me going.
Counselor: So she contributes to your life, even now?
Client: Well, yes. Yes.
Counselor: Because of what she did.
Client: Yeah. Because I still kind of hear her words of what she says to me. You know, what she said to me all the time, and I hold on to that, and that's what, you know.
Counselor:
output: Drives me, and I think that's a fairly useful way of looking at things. Right. Do you find that to be useful?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jesse. How you doing today?
Client: Not too good. Doctor Grande?
Counselor: Not so good.
Client: Nah. I just got into a. I got into a fight with my parents.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: Well, I. I've been doing heroin for a few months now, and I didn't think my parents knew, but I guess they. They found a needle in my room and, I mean, they knew what I was doing, and they. They told me that I have to start shaping up and I need to stop doing any kind of drugs because they said. They said the next time that they find any kind of drugs, then that's it, they're going to kick me out of the house.
Counselor: All right. So they're at the point where anything else happens and they discover it, and you're out in the street. Right. What are your feelings about being out in the street?
Client: I don't want to be out there. I don't know. I don't know who would be. I mean, it would be hard just to kind of stop cold turkey. I know a couple of buddies that did that, and it's not good when you get junk sick. And, I mean, I'm kind of stuck because. I don't know. I don't want to be out on the streets, but it's just going to be so hard, so hard to give it up.
Counselor: So there are conflicting feelings here. You don't want to be out in the street, but you don't want to give up the heroin at the same time.
SPK_3: Right. Right.
Client: I just. I mean, I don't want to give it up, but I mean, I kind of know I have to. I mean, I'm a young guy. I couldn't make it outside of my parents house, and I definitely don't want to be on the streets.
Counselor: You want to stop to avoid the consequences, what could happen, right. But to this point, you haven't been able to.
Client: I mean, I guess at this point, I really haven't had, like, something that would make me, like, I've been doing it for a while, and, I mean, it's been pretty great, but I, you know, I never really had any kind of, like, problem with it. And nothing too bad has happened. So this is kind of the first time I've been like, something's hit me where it's like, oh, man, I really gotta stop it.
Counselor: So this is the first consequence or potential consequence that's motivated you since you started using? How strong is the craving to use?
Client: I mean, when I first started, it was. I mean, it was pretty freaking great. I mean, the rush that you get from it. It's. It's just mind numbing. It's. It's just amazing. But I've. I've noticed recently that, like, the rush isn't as intense anymore, and it's even, like, it's even kind of started to backfire a little bit where, like, actually, I'll feel a little sick without using it. And that, I mean, that kind of scares me. But the crazies are definitely still there.
Counselor: All right, so when you try to cut back, have you tried to cut back?
Client: I had before, but, I mean, there was no reason to, so I didn't try very hard.
Counselor: But when you did try, did you have the feeling where you were getting sick?
Client: I did, yeah. It wasn't as bad as any of my buddies, but I definitely. I mean, I didn't feel well.
Counselor: Have your parents given you any options in terms of, like, do they understand that you're. It seems like you're a little dependent on.
Client: Yeah, I mean, they, they do. I definitely, like, I don't hold anything against my parents. Like, actually, I have a pretty good relationship with them. I know what I'm doing isn't good for me. And they said that they would completely support me. They told me that they have a place picked out where I can go and that they'd be willing to pay for it and everything. But they said if I don't meet them halfway, then it's just. That's it. They're done.

Client: I don't know if I'll go right back. Like, I think if I can get off it, if the detox actually works like they say I do, I think I can stay off it. I think, like, my. Counselor:
output: So there's kind of some, like, really, there's a physical kind of slash behavioral strategy here, which is just physically keeping you away from having to go buy his house. And it sounds like the only reason, other than to buy and use drugs, is to see your girlfriend.

Counselor:

Client: No, I don't think that I could lose my job. I don't think that. If I said something to my coworker, I hope that they wouldn't go to, like, our human resources department, but I don't know if that's something that they would do.
Counselor: So really, you're just talking about going to them and saying, hey, things feel a bit imbalanced. Is there anything maybe we could do to level out the work across us a little better?
Client: When you say it like that, that sounds really easy and non confrontational. So, yeah.
Counselor: Were you thinking of. Did you have another narrative in mind?
Client: Well, I was actually thinking about going to them and saying, hey, you remember this report? You remember this report? You remember this report? You didn't do this, this, this. And I had to pick up your slack on all of that. Can we not make that happen again in the past?
Counselor: Okay, so maybe a little more direct than what I was.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Which is, in part an expression of the way you feel.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You have feelings that match that pretty well.
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: Do you feel. I know you mentioned a lack of confidence in this area, but do you feel like you could approach it with them or they have a potential win in the end? So before you answer that, let me explain that a little. When we confront people, if we don't leave them an avenue to kind of protect their position in the relationship a bit, it's more of a trapping or cornering. But if we leave an avenue where they can make changes without really having to take full responsibility or blame, sometimes that's more productive, especially for the first introduction of a subject matter, like the first time you confront them. Clearly, if that doesn't work, there's other avenues, different types of confrontation. But I'm wondering if there's a way. So back to my original question. If there's a way that they can be confronted, that leaves them a win in the whole process?
Client: There might be one of the things for each of our projects, we have a timeline, but we don't have a set timeline within the office space to actually say, I'm going to have this done by this date. And you're going to have this done by this date. That's something that I could suggest so that we can hold each other accountable for the work that we have to do. So that might be a way that I could start to broach the subject. So that's one way, but that's the only thing that I can think off the top of my head.
Counselor: And that way may not be really consistent with the way you feel.
Client: It's definitely not consistent with the way I feel.
Counselor: What method? And I don't, you know, this isn't a question where I presume know the answer. What method do you think could lead to a better outcome? Has a better chance of leading to a better outcome?
Client: I believe if I was able to have a conversation where we didn't necessarily talk about the distribution of work, but if we had a conversation on what we're both good at and how we can actually complement each other with doing our work, I think that that would be a better conversation so that they could easily, they could take what I had to say a lot easier, so I could go to them and say, hey, I understand that you're not good at doing this type of report. However, I'm really good at doing this. However, I see that you have excellent skills when it comes to formatting and getting everything together and actually submitting it to whom it needs to get to. Can we actually start to distribute the work that way so that they can do what's. I don't want to say easy, but what's going to be productive for them? And I can do what's going to be productive for me.
Counselor: So really what you're suggesting is not even confrontational. It's just going in and saying, you have some strengths. They have some strengths. Wouldn't it be great if we could explore those strengths and the way we divide up those.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: If you went and said that, would there be a part of you that is kind of stuffing down those emotions of frustration during that talk?
Client: Yeah, but I think that if I do have that conversation that way, I think that that frustration and anger that I. That I have had, I think it would slowly disappear because then I know that they would still be doing something for the projects that we have to complete. So I think that my past feelings, they would slowly diminish because I know that we would be doing equal work moving forward.
Counselor: Okay, so you may have some feelings at that moment, but looking at the outcome, as you think about the outcome, you could think, well, this is tough right now, but I feel hopeful that it's going to work out in the future.
Client: Yes. Correct.
Counselor: And that could give you the confidence, ability to kind of push through that exercise, that discussion.
Client: Correct? Yep.
Counselor: Is there a certain time of the day where you feel less frustrated?
Client: It's probably around 03:00 generally, there's a 03:00 slump where everybody goes out and grabs coffee or something. And I think that during that time, that might be a good time to possibly bring up that conversation or at least brooch the subject. I can actually probably broach that subject with my supervisor at that time to see if they think that that might be a good idea.
Counselor:
output: Okay. To get some buy in at that level. So maybe a little bit in the afternoon. 03:00 is there a particular day of the week that's better for discussion like that? There's less stress, less going on?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Aspen. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well, thank you. How about yourself?
Counselor: I'm doing all right, thanks for asking. I had met you last time for our first session, and we talked a little bit about kind of your circumstances, what brought you here. And I was hoping today we could get into trying to really figure out how we can help you. Any thoughts on your current situation? Anything changed?
Client: Nothing's really changed. I mean, I'm amazing at my job. My boss just really is someone that I hold, you know, in higher regards than others I work with especially. We went to. We went to the same college. College, of course. And he suggested I come into counseling and he's way off. Way off. So I'm just gonna, you know, let him know.
Counselor: So, as I understand it, you came into counseling because he requested it.
Client: That was what initiated it. But now it's. I need to prove him wrong.
Counselor: Alright, so at first it was because he told you it would be a good idea, but now you kind of see it as an opportunity to prove your point.
Client: Yeah, have a little bit of fun with it. Prove my point.
Counselor: What would you. What would you like to prove through this?
Client: That I'm not the one in the wrong. You know, I. I'm extremely good at my job. I mean, I am the best employee that they have ever had. Not just currently, just. I mean, just ever. I make no errors. So how can I be wrong when it comes to these circumstances with my coworkers?
Counselor: Right. So your co workers have made some criticisms about you and that led to your boss suggesting this.
Client: I would call them criticisms because it's really hard to criticize me. So I would say they take it personally that I'm better than them, you know? So I feel that it's important for me to be able to work for this particular company. It needs to be the best company. And so I need the other employees to at least be at my level. Well, I mean, that's. That's really hard for them to come to my level, but at least be above average. At least.
Counselor: All right, so you have an expectation of them to become at least close to you in terms of your skill.
Client: I mean, it's pretty hard to not make any errors when it comes to accounting with the numbers, with the amount of numbers and the volume of accounts that we have, it's hard to be as good as I am with it, as far as no errors. But yes, I expect a higher standard from the coworkers.
Counselor: And you don't feel like they're performing at that level now?
Client: No, not at all.
Counselor: And evidently you made some different comments to them which maybe they took the wrong way.
Client: I just pointed out the facts of the situation.
Counselor: What type of facts did you, when.
Client: They make mistakes and, you know, how they should be better at certain tasks. I mean, they didn't attend the same, you know, type of college as far as, you know, Ivy League as myself. However, they do have a college education so, you know, that alone would, you know, just kind of go to speak to them having some sort of ability in that area.
Counselor: So you've kind of, in a way you've expressed your disappointment with them.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: To them?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And what are some of the observations or comments they made regarding you?
Client: Oh, they told me my ego is too big, that I'm cocky. That's one. Yeah. I'm just overall, like, I don't know how you can be too confident when your ability is at that level. I mean, I am the best employee they've ever had overall. You know, I was the best student at my college. I received numerous awards from the president of the college alone. I received numerous calls from the college and other companies as well, trying to recruit me to work for them. You know, so I don't think there's, it's impossible to be overly confident, but they, you know, they consider it cocky and arrogant. Get arrogant a lot.
Counselor: The comment arrogant. So you feel they're just really, are they misunderstanding you?
Client: I think they take it as a personal attack.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Like I'm can, like I'm that concerned with them personally. Like it affect, like I'm talking about them as a person instead of just their performance at work because I'm really not concerned with them as far as like existence outside the realm of performance at work.
Counselor: Alright. So your commentary to them has nothing to do with their value as a person, more with their performance as an employee. And you feel they're misconstruing your observations about their performance?
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: They're taking it personally.
Client: Taking it personally and trying as best they can to push it back on me as I'm the one who's wrong, but I'm obviously not.
Counselor: Alright, so you're not wrong in this and you're frustrated by their reactions.
Client: I mean, I'm okay with it, you know, I mean it's, I don't really take anything they say to heart because they're not at the level to really be able to criticize me. You know, I can take criticism, you know, from constructive criticism, from someone who would, you know, be at my level or above, however, they are not. So it's really nothing. It really doesn't affect me. It does interfere with my job as far as my employer is concerned.
Counselor: Right. That's what led to you. That's what led to him recommending you come here initially. So you don't feel that they're at a level where they can really criticize you. It doesn't really bother you if they have criticism in the first place, but you can appreciate how getting along with them would be better for you as an employee.
Client: I mean. I mean, overall, I like this company. You know, I like working for it. I've been friends with my boss. I mean, we went to the same college, you know, so we have that in common. You know, he is an extraordinary person as far as his abilities, you know, I would say as in the level realm as myself. So, you know, I hold his, you know, opinion, you know, in some sort of regards above the others, so.
Counselor: Okay, so to the extent that they communicate negative sentiment to him about you, that that affects you?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And so what do you think, if anything, what do you think needs to be fixed here?
Client: Well, I think it's on their area and, you know, on their side. They didn't take what I said the wrong way.
Counselor: Okay. So if they had accurately interpreted your comments, that would fix the problem?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Do you think that's realistic.
Client: If they worked at it, possibly.
Counselor: How long have you worked there?
Client: It's been about 15 years.
Counselor: 15 years. And how long has this been something that you've been aware of them not feeling so great about your comments to them?
Client: Well, every now and then, this is. We've hit a peak here recently because a lot of the people that I work with feel here recently more. So they've been taken in the wrong way, more prevalent than in the past. In the past, they would, you know, I'd hear, you know, certain comments, but I understood, you know, comments just directed at me, and I just understood that, you know, it was just, you know, envious because I was able to give them. I was at a level where I was able to critique their work. So it never got to a point where I had someone like my boss say anything to me. So this is really the first time that has gotten to that point.
Counselor: So you've noticed things like this in the past, but now it's become more urgent to address it.
Client: It's become more urgent to prove that I'm not wrong in this fact that it is. You know, if this were the case, then, you know, it would have been, you know, it would have been continuous, not just, oh, don't come to a head. So, I mean, that just proves my point even more, that it is their issue and not mine.
Counselor: All right, so if you could somehow prove that they're in the wrong, would that help you?
Client: I mean, it's kind of. To me, it's obvious they are in the wrong because the numbers speak for themselves. It's the fact of the matter. So if. But I guess that if there was something that could change between the relationships that I have with them, then at least would be a little bit better of a flow. So maybe we could get up to the level, you know, that this company is deserving of.
Counselor: Okay, so there's like two. There's two things operating. There's your desire for them to improve and make the company better. And then they're discontent with withdeze your comments to them. So you'd like the company to improve. And you feel that means that you need to be able to voice your opinion to them in an honest way. But everybody needs to get along too. And that's at least to some extent, and that's not happening because they're upset. So do you think there's any steps you could take that could reduce the tension in those relationships?
Client: I need to figure out a way to present the information at a level that they would understand. So drop it down to their level, but also kind of sugarcoat it so they're not, you know, taking it the wrong way.
Counselor: All right, so you need to deliver the same message in a more polite, less threatening package.
Client: I mean, you could say that, yeah.
Counselor: Do you have any ideas how that might look?
Client: I mean, I could start with not comparing their work to mine because that's just unfair. I mean, at no point in time are they ever going to reach that. That level of quality with their work. So that could be a place to start.
Counselor: Okay, so just refraining from drawing that comparison. That could help.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Do you think there could be a benefit in just taking a break from offering any comments to them, any observations, just to let things cool down a bit?
Client: I mean, I could see where you would say, you know, refer that as cool down.
Counselor: Just in an effort to restore the peace. You could still, of course, be aware of different shortcomings in their performance. It might just be helpful to not share that for a while. Just as an idea. Does that seem like an idea that might work. Yeah.
Client: Just keep to myself a little bit more. I mean, that's not very hard around.
Counselor: Them keeping to yourself.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Do you think you would be okay with the. With doing that? Because you wouldn't really be able to offer those. Those helpful comments like, about performance.
Client: If. Well, really, it would, in fact, prove my point behind it all. It would prove that I was right, that it's not me, that it is them taking it the wrong way. You know, because, in fact, if it was, you know, if it wasn't them taking it the wrong way, then I would just say that that would, you know, it would continue.
