As far as trying to point out, I mean, really, I think it comes down to an issue of being jealous and seeing themselves as less than, so needing to bring. To try to bring me down to make themselves feel better. So if they don't have that to do that, it would prove my point behind this whole thing.
Counselor: Yes. You feel like they're just trying to. They're just trying to tear you down to make up for their own inadequacy.
Client: Oh, definitely. Yeah.
Counselor:
output: And by you just not kind of offering those observations, you're taking the wind out of their sails.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Liz. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How things been going?
Client: They've been all right.
Counselor: Last time we were talking, it sounds like you're still having some difficulty with the quizzes. Is that still the case?
Client: Yeah, I still panic when I take them.
Counselor: You still panic. Can you tell me about the process of taking the quizzes? I know we've touched on this a little bit before.
Client: Okay, so I'm going to class. I'm fine. I sit down to take the test. I'm fine. The test is in front of me. Question one. I'm not going to get that answer.
Counselor: So you're looking down. So you take these quizzes in class?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Like a paper, pencil. Okay. With other students around?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. Is the. Is having other students around distracting to you?
Client: No, it's happened in previous online classes. It's the same.
Counselor: So it's. You're pretty sure it's the quiz itself and not some external. Okay. So it's paper and pencil. You're seated, you're in the room. Rooms relatively distraction free.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Everybody's quiet.
Counselor: And you're looking down at, really the first item on the.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: On the quiz. And what's happening? What's happening? Then as you look down, you read that first item. What's happening at a thought. We'll start a thought level. What's happening with your thinking?
Client: I'm thinking. I'm reading the question, and I'm thinking, oh, my God, there's. Okay, there's four. Okay. So it's got to be. It's got to be one of them. And I am not going to pick the right one. I'm going to think I picked the right one, and it's going to be the one that my second choice is, and I am not going to pick the right one.
Counselor: Okay, so your thought is that you're going to get. You're going to select the wrong response and therefore get that quiz item wrong. How about behavior? Like, do you notice anything physically going on as you're thinking about that quiz item and how you're gonna get it wrong?
Client: I'd say my palms are probably sweaty. Like, I'm probably a little tense.
Counselor: A little tense.
Client: Yeah. That's really it.
Counselor: All right. So what it could be is that this thought of I'm gonna get this item wrong is leading to these uncomfortable feelings, the physical feelings. So what happens when you answer item one like, you don't know if you have it right or wrong immediately? Right because it's a paper and pencil. So you answer item one, and you move on to item two. What happens then?
Client: It starts all over again. I'm already, like, well, I already got the first one wrong, and now I'm. My chances are higher of getting this one wrong.
Counselor: So you feel like it because you. Because you thought that you got the first one wrong, that your chances of getting the second one wrong actually increase?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Like, I get one wrong the whole test, it's all gonna be wrong.
Counselor: Have you ever had a quiz that you've taken where you were confident that you got the first item right?
Client: I'm sure I have. I can't remember any.
Counselor: But eventually you're going to come to one item that you're going to have these doubts about?
Client: Yes. Inevitably it happens.
Counselor: There's going to be one that's maybe a little more difficult or difficult for you. So it seems like what you're saying is that when you reach that item where you have that thought from that point on, the next item is. Is more difficult because you're having a similar thought. Does that pattern continue throughout the test?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So explain to me what, like, let's just go with the example of the first item, like, just to keep it more simple. So you have the first item, and that didn't work out for you, that thought? Right. The second one, your thought was, I have even a greater chance of missing a. So what happens after you respond to that second item?
Client: It just compounds. I just start. I feel worse and worse as the quiz, as I continue.
Counselor: That's awful. So it's an awful feeling for me. Right. So by the time you get to.
Client: Item five or six, I'm convinced it's over. I've gotten a zero. If it's the. Yeah, if I start at the first, I've gotten a zero. I've gotten a bad grade.
Counselor: So that's what's on your mind. And how about those physical symptoms? Are they the same, different or new symptoms?
Client: If it, like. If it's. If it, like, starts early at the beginning of the test, my heart's, like, pounding at this point, but I still have the sweaty palms. I'm still, like, tensing.
Counselor: So it really just gets mentally and physically more unpleasant for you the whole time. So when you're saying panic, the panic's really occurring a few items in after you have the first one that you thought you missed. And this has been happening for a while, as you described, right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Well, how about your grades? How have you actually been doing on the quizzes?
Client: I've been a pretty solid b student, so. And I feel. I wish I did better. I wish I got a's, but, I mean, these are fine. But when I take those quizzes, it's not. It doesn't. I don't know how it translates.
Counselor: How about your study habits? You consider yourself effective at studying?
Client: I've tried. I've taken a workshops on studying. I've. I. I think I'm pretty effective at studying. I've found what doesn't work. So I try to study by reading the chapters, taking outlines, reviewing flashcards, which has, I think, the best results, but.
Counselor: Okay, so your study habits are good, right. And your quiz scores are good, but you're still having these distressing thoughts and these uncomfortable physical sensations when you take the quizzes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is that about right?
Client: Yeah, that's absolutely right.
Counselor: So really you don't necessarily need your performance to change. You just. You just need your thoughts and feelings and behaviors to change.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: So how you. How you're reacting to the quizzes maybe?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maury. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: You doing all right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?
Client: Yeah, yeah. I mean, you know, it kind of came up again. You know, every time my wife yells at me, you know, I feel like a failure, you know, like I told you last time, I just. I just feel like I can't do anything right, you know? Like everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling, and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.
Counselor: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So it's frustrating.
Client: Yeah, it definitely is.
Counselor: How is what's going on impacted your relationship with your wife?
Client: I mean, it's rocky, you know, because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that. And then, you know, we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad, and then it just keeps going like that.
Counselor: So when you. You mentioned you feel like a failure when she. When she yells at you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Can you think back to maybe the last time, one of the last times you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We've talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts. She starts yelling at you?
Client: I mean, she'll yell at me. I mean, I feel, you know, frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And. I don't know. I mean, as I was thinking about, like we were talking about it, and as I was thinking about it more this week, kind of felt like, you know, kind of like what happened with my dad, you know? I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. You know, like, if my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way. And it feels like the same thing. Yeah. It's kind of the first. I guess kind of the first thought that comes to mind.
Counselor: The first thought is I've been through something like this before, I guess.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like, you know? Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Like, it's like just a sense that this isn't brand new.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad. Yahweh. Yeah.
Client: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So, in a sense, these arguments are taking you back to another point in time.
Client: I guess so, in a way, that's distressing.
Counselor: Yeah, it is.
Client: I mean, it feels, you know, pretty crappy.
Counselor: Now, in these arguments, she yells at you. You mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own, you know, in the midst of all that. Right. How would you rate it in terms of, like, any physical violence? Nothing like that.
Client: No, it's just words. I mean, we're just, you know, just yelling.
Counselor: And what level, like, what level of yelling would you say? How severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?
Client: Yeah, I don't know. I mean, it's like, you know, sometimes it can get up to, like, the eight or nines, you know, but just, I guess generally it's, you know, down. Closer to a seven on scale, like one to ten. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So sometimes it's seven. That would be pretty bad.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But some other times it's not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you feel like your reaction is being frustrated is disproportionate to what's really going on or you feel like it's money?
Client: I don't know what else to do. You know? I mean, it's just. It's kind of my reaction, my gut reaction to it, you know? I think I'm justified in it because, you know, she just doesn't understand how much she yells at me, you know, and how much that hurts me. You know? I do feel justified. I mean, but it just. It just keeps going, though. And I feel justified, though. I don't know.
Counselor: Let's talk for a moment about, if you're okay with it, about your father and his yelling. You've discussed this with me a little bit before. In the past few sessions. I remember you saying that most. It was in the afternoon. Most of the yelling was when you were both home.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it was. I mean, mostly when I get home from school. I mean, I wasn't, you know, I was in high school, and then after that, you know, I went to college. And so I wasn't really home much during college, but, you know, I guess it'd be after I got home from high school. You know, I'd get home and he'd get home from work and, you know, just kind of be aggravated, whatever, just start yelling and. Yeah, usually when I got back from school, yeah.
Counselor: So he would get back from work, you would get back from school. And how long would that last? How long would the period where you were kind of vulnerable to being yelled at last?
Client: I don't know. I mean, sometimes about an hour, you know, and he'd be yelling because he's, you know, frustrated from work and he's frustrated from the drive home and whatever else, you know? And at some point, he would usually start drinking, you know, so maybe about an hour or so, you know, where that was. Like, you knew you were gonna get it.
Counselor: So kind of every day you could predict that between when you. Or between when he came home after you were already home from school and when he started drinking, you were gonna. He was gonna find something to yacht you about.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And, I mean, there were some days, like, I knew when he came home, he came home the same time every day. I knew I could get out of the house, you know? Cause at some point, I had a car, my friends had cars, you know, whatever.
Counselor: You had more freedom.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. You know, at some point, I had a job, so sometimes I'd work after school and stuff, so I knew I'd be able to leave the house at times, you know, like when I knew he was gonna start yelling and stuff. But, I mean, there was a period of time probably like my senior year of high school that I just didn't, you know, I just came home and, you know, it was gonna happen, you know, that's the way it happened.
Counselor: Even though you were able to escape it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. You could have stayed out long enough for him to start drinking. Yeah.
Client: Instead you stayed in the house.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I mean, it was pretty much my whole senior year come home. I knew what was gonna happen, and I just took it. You know, I just. I knew he was gonna yell. I just took it that.
Counselor: Was there ever a period when you first got your freedom that you tried, like.
Client: Oh, yeah, yeah, I did. And. I don't know. I don't know why I didn't just keep doing that. It probably would have been easier, but. I don't know. The whole senior year, I just started. I was just back there at the house when he came home from work.
Counselor:
output: So in that period, were you. Were you. There's times when you did leave, what did he do instead of yell at you?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Marcy, how you doing?
Client: I've been better.
Counselor: Been better. Yeah, I saw that you called a few times between the last session and today. You left a few messages.
Client: Yeah, I was trying to get holding you. I had something I really needed to discuss with you, but nobody called me back. I emailed you a couple times, I never got a reply, so I was just wondering what's going on with that?
Counselor: We can talk about that. I want to talk about that after getting those messages. Remember we discussed the process for when your mood deteriorates and you had a few other resources you wanted to connect with before calling me.
Client: Yeah, I kind of remember it.
Counselor: Your brother was one of those resources.
Client: Oh, yeah, that's useless anyway. Go on.
Counselor: Did you attempt to.
Client: No, he's so busy with it, like he could never help me. I don't think he even cares what I'm going through. He's got his own stuff to deal with, he's got his own family and all this stuff and. Yeah, he doesn't care.
Counselor: So you didn't contact him first because he thought he doesn't care? Yeah, and we'd also talked about a few different friends that you had that you'd reached out to, you didn't contact them or did.
Client: Well, I did call my one friend, Beth, but I. She was like, oh, can I call you back? And of course she didn't because nobody ever calls me back. You know, I'm like, they all have their own lives. No one really cares what I'm doing. You know, it's always like that. So that's why I thought I could reach out to you since you're supposed to be helping me, but apparently you never call me back or answer any of my emails, so.
Counselor: Right. We talked about how there's limitations on time and how it would be better if we could keep the therapy in here in person. Right. And not get really too excessive with the telephone calls. I realize that when you're in distress, there's that kind of feeling that it would be a good idea to call. But remember, we discussed different levels of distress. And if it's something common that you've been through before and you kind of know the outcome, connecting with one of those resources might be more helpful.
Client: Yeah, I just feel like you're the only one that can help me, you know, I mean, my boyfriend, like, things aren't going well with him. I thought he could help me, but I guess he can't. And I think he's running around on me and all that. So I was just like, well, let me reach out to doctor Grande and see if it can help me, because it seems like my last resort.
Counselor: I remember you discussing, a few weeks ago, your boyfriend, and you had a fairly high opinion of him. Like, it was. It seemed like a positive.
Client: Yeah, he was great. He was great. And then, you know, he was in the other room and he got a text message, and I was like, let me just look at that. Because I was just curious to see what's going on with him because he never talks to me about anything. And so I looked at it, and it was a girl's name and number that I don't know. And so he came back in. You know, they put it away quickly, and I didn't say anything, like, what's wrong with you? Because I was acting weird and I was like, nothing. So then he went out, so I followed him. And then he went to, like, some friend's house. And I don't know if there's girls there or not, but. So I kind of think he's running around, maybe. I don't know. And I can't trust him. I can't trust anybody, you know? So I don't know. I mean, he was so awesome before, but now I just don't know. But he was everything I ever wanted.
Counselor: Yeah, I remember. You seem very excited about where that relationship could go.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you seem like you're much more negative about.
Client: Yeah. I mean, if he's not going to be faithful to me, what am I supposed to do? Yeah, I mean, it's just like every other guy that I've ever dated, like, either leave me or cheat on me or lie to me. So, I mean, I don't know why I thought this one was going to be different. Seriously, why would this one be different?
Counselor: So you have. You had this experience with the text message and you don't know? You don't know any more than that? But it sounds like you kind of jumped to, he's cheating. So, you know, he went to a text message and went to someone's house.
Client: Yeah. I don't know if they were related. The text message and him leaving, I mean, but I just assumed. So I'm just gonna assume because it seems to be a pattern in my life. You know, everybody lets me down.
Counselor: Could it be that you're jumping to that conclusion prematurely?
Client: Probably, but I guess it's all I know that's all. I've always been treated, so I kind of feel like, why would this be different? Even though I thought it was in the beginning, but I don't know.
Counselor: So you feel like you've seen this all before, this pattern?
Client: Yeah, I guess I just always pick the wrong people or it's probably just me. I think I'm the one that's just unlovable. I've been told that growing up a lot. So I think it's me because he's great. I mean, he's great and he's good looking, he has a good job. And I always thought I'm like, why is he with me? And then now I see, like, he doesn't really want to be with me. Whoever he was texting, that's probably the person wants to be with him. She's probably, like, pretty and has, she probably has a good job and she's got everything going for her and so.
Counselor: So you really, this week at least, you don't seem to think a lot of yourself.
Client: No. I mean, when things are going bad in my relationships, they really seem to get to me, you know?
Counselor: So in a way, you feel like your mood is subject to how your current romantic relationship is going?
Client: Yeah, I guess that's pretty right on. Yeah, I would say that.
Counselor: Is there anything that you can do from your side to improve what's going on?
Client: No, I don't think so. I think it's everybody else that is treating me wrong, you know? So unless I find the right person who's going to treat me right, then I don't know what I'm going to do. So.
Counselor: So the. So the key to feeling better is finding the right person.
Client: Yeah, I think so. And like I said, I thought he was the right one in the beginning, and now I don't know anymore. But, you know, I really don't want him to leave me because, like, then when I gotta do him, now I'm gonna be alone. I want to be alone because I love him, but, you know, so I think I probably will forgive him and just stay with them because I don't want to be alone. I'm too scared to do that. I mean, I don't want to be alone without somebody. You know, I really need somebody. Yes.
Counselor: So does some of this seem like what you're describing with your mood, does some of this seem like you're out of control?
Client: Yeah, because I feel like I can't control other people's actions, and that really makes me mad. That makes me really angry, you know? That what am I supposed to do? And so I think acting out and following them and checking their text messages, and it's the only thing that makes me feel in control, I guess. I don't know.
Counselor: I know in the past, when we've talked about this, you've mentioned that you thought that that behavior could be driving them away, too.
Client: Yeah, I mean, I can see that. I mean, people want, you know, some that they can trust, too. And I'm not sure I've always been honest with them, but I'm always looking for things that they're gonna do to manipulate me or try to, like, you know, screw me over or whatever. So here's my guard down. Yeah, I'm suspicious.
Counselor: I wonder if sometimes you acting on those suspicions, that's not making things a little worse in those relationships.
Client: Yeah, probably. But, I mean, like I said before, I don't want to be alone. I don't want to move out somebody. I need somebody. I need somebody. I need somebody to be with, you know, I need someone to help me with things. I don't want to be alone. You know, that's, you know, and he has said things to me like, you can't call me all the time at work because I'm at work, and you leave me, like, 40 voice messages because I just want to know if he's actually at work. You know? He's like, you can't do those things because I'm gonna get fired, and then where are we gonna be? He's like, you know, and you can't, like, call the numbers in my phone and find out who they are and, like, hang up because my friends know it's you, and you can't, you know, have your friends come to the bar and see who I'm with and, like, report back to you. Like, that's. He's like, I don't want to be in relationship with someone that doesn't trust me like that. So now, you know, I'm really scared of losing them. Yeah.
Counselor: So you have called other boyfriends and this boyfriend many times?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: On the phone?
Client: Yeah. I just want to check up and see what they're doing. If they said they're at the place that they said they were going, you know, I just want to know that I'm not being lied to because I've always been lied to. All my life, I've been lied to.
Counselor: So is all that calling something you do to relieve anxiety?
Client: Well, when I find out they're at the place that they said they were, that I feel better for at least, you know, for a few minutes till the next time. Like, wait, maybe they left. Let me see where they are now, you know, and then it kind of builds upon itself till they just get so frustrated. And then usually it ends with, like, a screaming match when I do see them.
Counselor: Mm hmm. You know, there's a lot of screaming and yelling.
Client: A lot of screaming and yelling and accusations and finger pointing and just. Yeah, it's not good. It's not a good scene when those kinds of things go down. But like I said, I really love him. I don't want to be without him. I don't know how I live without him.
Counselor: All right, so there's the. There's screaming and there's yelling and some discontentment, but there's also this love you have for him and this fear that you'll be alone. So there's a lot of emotion here driving different behaviors.
Client: I said I would do whatever it took for him to stay with me. You know, he doesn't really talk about it. I think he gets really mad at me for being so needy. He's like, you're needy. Why don't you do your own stuff and leave me alone? And, you know, you need to have your own life. And, you know, I don't like to be ignored. You know, I was ignored all growing up, made a big family. I just got lost in the shuffle, and now here I am.
Counselor: So with all these things going on, all these kind of negative feelings, negative self image and trouble with the boyfriend, like this week, today, what's your goal? What do you want to change?
Client: Well, I guess I would like to be able to trust people more and not feel so desperate. I mean, and I don't know what to do. I don't know how to do that.
Counselor:
output: To be able to trust people more. So maybe one place we could start is to ensure that you're accurately assessing what, for example, your boyfriend's doing. So in the past, when we've talked, you've been suspicious about different behaviors. And it turns out in many of those cases, nothing was happening. And the kind of chasing them around and making observations, that's what caused some of the problem. Does that make sense?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, Marsha, so how can I help you today?
Client: Well, I'm working full time. I'm a part time student. I've just gotten engaged, and I live at home. There's just so much stress in my life. I have everything happening all at once. Just to top it all off, I failed an exam, a really big exam, and I just feel like I can't do anything anymore. I can't do anything right. I've just got so much stress, and I feel like such a disappointment, such a failure. And I've embarrassed my family by failing. I just don't know what to do anymore. I guess I've come here today to tell you, like, I want to leave uni, and I guess that's why I've come here to you today.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a whole lot of stuff's on top of you at the moment.
Client: Yeah, just so much. Just all parting on. Yeah.
Counselor: So you're working full time, plus part time study. Part time study. And then you've got your wedding preparation.
Client: Yeah, just got engaged, and weddings just a month away now, so, yeah, so I've just got so much happening. Work is really, really demanding and. Yeah, just fail this exam. It's just. Yeah, don't know what to do all too much.
Counselor: So imagine you've been sweating on this for a while, and it's all been swirling around in your head.
Client: Just been building up and building up and so much pressure with everything. And I'm living at home, so my parents, you know, a lot of pressure, need to do everything right. And. Yeah, by failing this, I feel like I've just embarrassed and disappointed them, and I just don't feel like I'm good enough, you know, to go on studying.
Counselor: Okay. And have they said much to you about failing your exam?
Client: They haven't said much. I was really scared to tell them, actually, because I knew they'd just be so disappointed and just embarrassed by the fact that I did fail. Yeah. I've never failed anything before. And so, yeah, really hard.
Counselor: Yeah. So it's new and you don't like it at all?
Client: Not at all, no. And I think leaving uni will just be the way out, just so I don't have to go through it again.
Counselor: Right. Okay. Well, I'm glad you've come to counselling, because it's good for us to get an outsider's opinion when we've got so much on our plate and we're confused as to what to do and our emotions can get in the way. And you've just said earlier that a whole lot of stuff's on your plate at the moment. Okay. So I'm glad you've come here. Here at the clinic, we use the ABC model, which is a cognitive behavioural therapy model. So, Marsha, some counsellors have put together a list of beliefs that we often use and we don't realise that we're using those beliefs and they tend to be faulty ones. Here's the list. Here, have a look through that to see if there are any beliefs that you might be operating on at the moment.
Client: I think number two.
Counselor: Okay, read that one out for me.
Client: That it's necessary to have a high degree of order uncertainty in order to be happy and perform well.
Counselor: Yeah, yeah, you mentioned that earlier.
Client: Number four, that it's necessary to be competent and successful in all those things which are attempted.
Counselor: Yeah, that's an expectation from your family.
Client: Yeah, possibly. Number eight, that life should be entirely pleasant and enjoyable and that any frustration, discomfort or pain would be unbearable.
Counselor: Which one of those stands out the most for you at the moment?
Client: Um, probably number four.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How would you put that in your own words?
Client: That I need to be successful all the time in everything that I do. Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. And is that different from what's happening in your life at the moment?
Client: Well, failing that exam, I mean, I wasn't successful with that. So. Yeah, I mean, it just throws out, I guess, even number two because throws out all the order in my life. I need to have everything, you know? So I need to know what I'm doing, where I'm going. Yeah.
Counselor: So, okay, so if number four is an expectation that your family have and that you have of yourself, how do you measure up next to number four?
Client: I don't feel like I'm good enough.
Counselor: Okay. All right. I. Well, what I'd like to do is put some of those ideas on the board under the ABC and I'll explain as we go along.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. So what do you think the trigger point might be or the activating event for you at the moment?
Client: I mean, there are a lot of things, but I think obviously failing the exam was the main one.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. And the consequences. You thinking of leaving uni?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. And that statement you made earlier about.
Client: I'm not good enough?
Counselor: Yeah, that's. That's the b one. That's the crucial one. And I'll explain it shortly when I get up to the board.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right. Okay. I think I'll put it up there now for you so we can work through that. So, Marsha, the activating event, which is what you stated earlier.
Client: I failed my examined.
Counselor: That's right. And the kind of decision that you're thinking about is leaving uni. That's right. Yeah. Okay. So it's important that we consider the jump from here over to here. And the kind of thinking that you've been swirling around in your head affects the consequence. And you've mentioned earlier that number four seems to fit. And you put that in your own words. What were your words before?
Client: That I'm not good enough.
Counselor: Yeah. Good. That's really important for us to consider that kind of thinking. Okay, Marsha, it's good that we've got those things on the board. And what I'd like to do now is focus. Stepping out a bit from your situation and looking at it from another point of view. To me, it sounds like you're doing a whole lot of things really well. Can you list all of the things that you're doing really well?
Client: I'm working. It's a really demanding job, and I'm keeping up with it, I guess. Work things with my fiance. I mean, we're engaged, so planning the wedding, that's going really well. It's stressful, but it's going well.
Counselor:
output: And all of your other university subjects.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maury. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: You doing all right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?
Client: Yeah, yeah. I mean, you know, it kind of came up again. You know, every time my wife yells at me, you know, I feel like a failure, you know, like I told you last time, I just. I just feel like I can't do anything right, you know? Like everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling, and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.
Counselor: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So it's frustrating.
Client: Yeah, it definitely is.
Counselor: How is what's going on impacted your relationship with your wife?
Client: I mean, it's rocky, you know, because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that. And then, you know, we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad, and then it just keeps going like that.
Counselor: So when you. You mentioned you feel like a failure when she. When she yells at you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Can you think back to maybe the last time, one of the last times you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We've talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts. She starts yelling at you?
Client: I mean, she'll yell at me. I mean, I feel, you know, frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And. I don't know. I mean, as I was thinking about, like we were talking about it, and as I was thinking about it more this week, kind of felt like, you know, kind of like what happened with my dad, you know? I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. You know, like, if my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way. And it feels like the same thing. Yeah. It's kind of the first. I guess kind of the first thought that comes to mind.
Counselor: The first thought is I've been through something like this before, I guess.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like, you know? Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Like, it's like just a sense that this isn't brand new.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad. Yahweh. Yeah.
Client: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So, in a sense, these arguments are taking you back to another point in time.
Client: I guess so, in a way, that's distressing.
Counselor: Yeah, it is.
Client: I mean, it feels, you know, pretty crappy.
Counselor: Now, in these arguments, she yells at you. You mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own, you know, in the midst of all that. Right. How would you rate it in terms of, like, any physical violence? Nothing like that.
Client: No, it's just words. I mean, we're just, you know, just yelling.
Counselor: And what level, like, what level of yelling would you say? How severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?
Client: Yeah, I don't know. I mean, it's like, you know, sometimes it can get up to, like, the eight or nines, you know, but just, I guess generally it's, you know, down. Closer to a seven on scale, like one to ten. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So sometimes it's seven. That would be pretty bad.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But some other times it's not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you feel like your reaction is being frustrated is disproportionate to what's really going on or you feel like it's money?
Client: I don't know what else to do. You know? I mean, it's just. It's kind of my reaction, my gut reaction to it, you know? I think I'm justified in it because, you know, she just doesn't understand how much she yells at me, you know, and how much that hurts me. You know? I do feel justified. I mean, but it just. It just keeps going, though. And I feel justified, though. I don't know.
Counselor: Let's talk for a moment about, if you're okay with it, about your father and his yelling. You've discussed this with me a little bit before. In the past few sessions. I remember you saying that most. It was in the afternoon. Most of the yelling was when you were both home.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it was. I mean, mostly when I get home from school. I mean, I wasn't, you know, I was in high school, and then after that, you know, I went to college. And so I wasn't really home much during college, but, you know, I guess it'd be after I got home from high school. You know, I'd get home and he'd get home from work and, you know, just kind of be aggravated, whatever, just start yelling and. Yeah, usually when I got back from school, yeah.
Counselor: So he would get back from work, you would get back from school. And how long would that last? How long would the period where you were kind of vulnerable to being yelled at last?
Client: I don't know. I mean, sometimes about an hour, you know, and he'd be yelling because he's, you know, frustrated from work and he's frustrated from the drive home and whatever else, you know? And at some point, he would usually start drinking, you know, so maybe about an hour or so, you know, where that was. Like, you knew you were gonna get it.
Counselor: So kind of every day you could predict that between when you. Or between when he came home after you were already home from school and when he started drinking, you were gonna. He was gonna find something to yacht you about.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And, I mean, there were some days, like, I knew when he came home, he came home the same time every day. I knew I could get out of the house, you know? Cause at some point, I had a car, my friends had cars, you know, whatever.
Counselor: You had more freedom.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. You know, at some point, I had a job, so sometimes I'd work after school and stuff, so I knew I'd be able to leave the house at times, you know, like when I knew he was gonna start yelling and stuff. But, I mean, there was a period of time probably like my senior year of high school that I just didn't, you know, I just came home and, you know, it was gonna happen, you know, that's the way it happened.
Counselor: Even though you were able to escape it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. You could have stayed out long enough for him to start drinking. Yeah.
Client: Instead you stayed in the house.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I mean, it was pretty much my whole senior year come home. I knew what was gonna happen, and I just took it. You know, I just. I knew he was gonna yell. I just took it that.
Counselor: Was there ever a period when you first got your freedom that you tried, like.
Client: Oh, yeah, yeah, I did. And. I don't know. I don't know why I didn't just keep doing that. It probably would have been easier, but. I don't know. The whole senior year, I just started. I was just back there at the house when he came home from work.
Counselor: So in that period, were you. Were you. There's times when you did leave, what did he do instead of yell at you?
Client: I guess he had to yell at somebody else. I mean, my. My sister, my brother were home. I guess he probably yelled at them. I don't know. I mean, it felt good to not be there, but I guess he probably yelled at them, which just sucks. I mean, you know, I guess somebody had. Whoever was there was gonna take it, you know?
Counselor: Somebody was gonna get you out there.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, I guess it was them when I wasn't there. I don't know.
Counselor: And how do you think you took it. When you were there, how well did you respond?
Client: I just got used to it, you know, I knew what was gonna happen. I knew he was gonna yell. I knew that it was gonna make me upset. I knew that just those repeated times, just like now, you know, I'm gonna feel like a failure, which ultimately I did. You know, maybe I probably just became numb to it, you know, it happens so often and same thing every day. Probably just became numb to it and just kind of stopped caring and kind of stopped, I don't know, believing in myself or something, you know?
Counselor: Like you've just given up.
Client: Yeah, probably. That's probably. I don't know. Probably. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And how many years total did this experience go on? Do you endure the yelling?
Client: I mean, it would have been while I was in middle school and most of high school. I mean, I told you at some point I was able to leave, but probably all of middle school, most of high school, and I left, and then some, you know, for the rest of the senior year, I would be there. So, I don't know, quite a few years, I guess.
Counselor: A long time to suffer.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And now if we move back forward in time, you're in a relationship where you're getting yelled at a bit. Right. And that's sometimes quite a bit, and that's causing you distress.
Client: It's like the same thing. You're yelling a little bit and. Yeah.
Counselor: So you feel like you're back in the same place.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it does. Yeah. I mean, obviously, you know, she's. She's not doing anything like he was, you know, like drinking or anything like that, but it does. I mean, it's like the same thing that happened is happening again.
Counselor: So that's. In your opinion, that's the consequence of what happened to you. Like, all this yelling that you endured before in some way is significantly contributing to what you're going through now.
Client: Maybe. I mean, I guess it could, you know, because it is the same thing. So maybe it's.
Counselor: There could be some connection.
Client: Maybe. Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, maybe not 100% explain it, but it explains part of it.
Client: Yeah, it definitely could. I definitely could.
Counselor: So your functioning has been affected a bit. I mean, to the point where you're here with me now, we're talking about it, and you're frustrated, and it does sound painful. Now, I'm curious. You mentioned you had a younger sister and a younger brother, and they grew up in the same house. How are they doing?
Client: Well, my sister, she's three years younger than I am. She's doing great. I mean, she graduated from college, like, top of her class kind of thing, you know? And she's about to get married, too. That's cool. Got a really great guy, you know. She's doing great. She lives next town over for me. I get to see her a lot. Yeah, she's great, though. My brother, he's five years younger than I am. He's doing pretty good, too. He's just about to graduate from college. I think he gets really good grades, too, from what I hear, from what he tells me. I don't get to see him as much as I do her because she's in college, but I think he's doing really well, too. You know, they both. Yeah, they both do some really good stuff. They have really good goals and stuff like that.
Counselor: You seem like you have a good relationship with them. You're proud of them. Yeah, definitely.
Client: I'm definitely proud of them. I think they're doing some really good stuff, you know, really trying to make something of themselves. Yeah.
Counselor: So, you know, I wonder. They're doing pretty well. You're doing okay, but you're having a rough time right now. How would things have been if you had taken that? I know it's difficult to predict, but if you had taken that opportunity to not be there, if you had, like you said, you had a car, your friends had cars, you could have avoided. You could have avoided the situation directly between your dad and you.
Client: Yeah, I mean, yeah, I guess I could have. I don't know. I mean. I mean, I took the yelling and stuff, so, you know, it's obviously affecting me now.
Counselor: You took the brunt of the abuse.
Client: Yeah, I guess I did. I mean, you know, I bring it up to them sometimes and they're like, yeah, I mean, dad yelled sometimes, but, you know, it wasn't that bad. Definitely a different experience from what I had. You know, they don't see it like I do, you know? I don't know. Maybe things would have been worse for them.
Counselor: So, in a sense, your father verbally abused you. Nothing makes that right. But in a sense, you, because you were there and you were the target. And. Could ride it out, you shielded them from that abuse.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, you mentioned it would have been somebody else, right?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, it probably would have been them. Probably was them when I wasn't there, you know? Yeah, I don't know.
SPK_3: I guess you're probably right.
Client: I mean, they are doing pretty well, you know, I think probably they're doing better than I am, I guess.
Counselor: You know, probably no small part because of your protecting them.
Client: Right.
Counselor: I mean, you were in an impossible situation, and you made the choice to stay there.
Client: I guess I did. Right.
Counselor:
output: There was some negative consequences for you, which we'll try to work through, but some really positive consequences for your siblings.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi. Thank you for being here today. I just wanted to start off by asking how your homework was from last week and if it was helpful.
Client: Well, I think it was a little helpful. I did try the breathing exercises, but sometimes I don't think to do them right away. But I did try it a little bit and it did help. Good.
Counselor: So you said you wanted to work on the problem with your anxiety when you leave your son for therapy.
Client: Yes, that's what.
Counselor: Yeah. So we've been working on your breathing like you've been talking about, and if we work on this, then maybe we can move into other things, you know, like in addressing your anxiety elsewhere. But. So why don't you tell me about how you feel when he is in therapy or getting occupational therapy?
Client: Well, I just get very anxious. I don't want to leave him in the room without me. I want to be right there. I'm not used to leaving him alone with other people at all. And I know I get very anxious in the waiting area, and I pace and back and forth and wonder what's going on in the room and listening for anything that might be going on. So, yeah, I just have a lot of anxiety about being separated from him, even for that short time.
Counselor: So do you feel like there's anything that has caused this anxiety? Like, where is this coming from?
Client: Well, I did have a child of my own that passed away, and I think that it probably has affected me with my other children and especially now with, you know, me being older and adopting this little boy. And I'm just scared, always scared that something's going to happen to him.
Counselor: Yeah. Can you tell me more about the problem, like, what are your fears and what are your anxieties when he's in a therapy session?
Client: Well, I worry about, you know, if he's going to fall, if they're working with him on a table, if he'll fall off the table and get hurt. I don't know all the people that are in and out of the therapy bill or the building here. I have some anxiety about someone snatching him if nobody's watching him closely, which I'm sure they are, but I still have that fear that something's going to happen to him, and I'm not right there.
Counselor: So it sounds like you have a lot of anxiety just with your son in general. So does he been any time away from you?
Client: No, not really. Most of the time he's with me or I have a couple of people I trust to watch him. But other than that, he's usually with me, doctors appointments, anything like that? Of course I'm there.
Counselor: Do you trust the therapist that he sees for therapy?
Client: Well, it seems like an awfully nice guy, but I don't know him really well, and I'm hopeful that once I get to know him more, I'll be more trustful, but I still just have a lot of anxiety about him.
Counselor: So the anxiety that you feel about him being in therapy is what you want to focus on today, correct?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Pick that and work for it. And once we've addressed that, then maybe we can address some of the anxiety you feel, like you said, and you can have some time to yourself, maybe, and be able to let him go to preschool. Cause it sounds like he really needs social interaction.
Client: Yes, I'm sure. Well, I know that would be good for him. At some point, he's. I know I'm gonna have to address these issues and work through these issues. It's just very difficult.
Counselor: Do you feel this way with your other children or just with the youngest?
Client: Just with the youngest. The other children are older and they're able to verbalize and tell me if anything's going on or. But this little boy, you know, like I said, I adopted him and he has some special needs and I just worry about him, I think, more, but it sounds like.
Counselor: So your anxiety goes beyond kind of normal parent like parental worry and sounds like it's pretty extreme.
Client: Yes, it is. And I don't think it's good for him. I know I need to work on this because I don't think it's good for Jack to be in this situation with all. With my anxiety. It's not good for him.
Counselor: So what do you say your biggest fears are when he's in the therapy session, when you can't see him?
Client: My biggest fear is that he's going to get hurt, that he's going to fall off the table or he's going to. They're going to have him doing activities that he could get hurt. That's probably my biggest fear. The second one would be that somebody would not be watching him for a moment and that someone would, you know, just take off with him.
Counselor: Well, why don't we kind of, with CBT, we think about different ways, like, kind of for and against those thoughts. So if you don't mind, you have a pen and a paper, so you would just write these down. You come up, we'll come up with some evidence for and against him getting hurt or someone taking him while he's in a therapy session and you're not there. So what is some evidence for him getting hurt or taken?
Client: Well, there's a lot of different people in the building to strangers or other families, and that could possibly lead to him.
Counselor: So you write that one down.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: What else?
Client: Well, you know, he's here for occupational therapy, and he's got some motor skill issues, and I'm afraid, depending on what they have him do, that he could be hurt, that he could hurt, get hurt or fall because he's not always real steady on his feet at times.
Counselor: Can you think of any other evidence that support these thoughts?
Client: Not really.
Counselor: So what is some evidence against these thoughts?
Client: Well, evidence against would be, obviously, the therapist, as a trained professional who knows, you know, what they're doing, and obviously, I'm sure safety is number one concern. So that would be something, you know, against. And I am pretty sure he would never be left alone at three years old, you know, where someone would be able to take him.
Counselor: Right.
Client: So in my mind, I know that, but I just can't get past that and feeling anxious about these things that might happen. Right.
Counselor: Well, it sounds to you, like, do you think any other children have ever been kidnapped or hurt at the center?
Client: I've never heard of anyone, but every day you see stuff on the news and about children in a lot of daycare centers and that kind of thing being hurt, abused, or, you know, abducted.
Counselor: Right. But with all the therapists and the adults in the building, it sounds like. And with the way things are set up, it sounds like him being kidnapped from the center is probably not very likely.
Client: No. Right. Like I say, in my mind, I understand that it's probably not very likely at all that that would happen.
Counselor: Right. So you can add that that's just not a very good, not a very high chance of anything happening. So let me ask you, why is he or why do you have to stay in the lobby? Kids don't. Typically, parents go back in the session with their kids.
Client: Well, I have been in, sat in with a few sessions with him, but he actually does much better if I'm not there, he participates more, and if I'm in there, he wants me to hold him, he wants to cling to me, and he doesn't seem to want to participate with the therapy, and I really want him to get the benefit out of the therapy. So, you know, that's why they suggested that I stay out in the lobby during the session. Right.
Counselor: So it sounds like you care about your son and you want him to do well in therapy. So that's why you're addressing this, but.
Client: Right.
Counselor: It's not good for either of you if you're having this kind of anxiety while he's in. While he's in therapy sessions, right.
Client: Yeah, because I think he picks up on it also.
Counselor:
output: So what are some other kind of issues that you feel like you deal with? Like anxiety? Do you feel. Are you, do you feel the same kind of anxiety like when you go to the grocery store or when you're out or if you leave him with the sitter?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Terry. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay, I think.
Counselor: You okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know when we talked last time, you were having a rough time dealing with the passing year, Sister Sheila.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you're kind of a point where we were talking about emotional consequences, but also some of the thinking that's going on. Have you been processing that?
Client: Yeah, I've been thinking about some of that and, you know, trying to kind of work through it a little bit. So I think I'm kind of ready to kind of work through it and talk about it a little bit now.
Counselor: So, feeling a little less emotional and feeling a little more thinking about it. And, like, on the rational side, like we talked about rational and irrational beliefs.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: A little more focus there or more ability to focus there today.
Client: Yeah, I think I'm ready to think about it more.
Counselor: I know the emotional part was tough for you, and I'm sure it still.
Client: Is, but I think I've kind of got through some of that, and I'm ready to kind of get through the way I'm thinking about some things.
Counselor: Ready to look at through the thinking lens.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So to speak. All right. So what are some of the thoughts or beliefs that you've been having, you think maybe part of what's affecting your mood?
Client: Well, I've been. I've been thinking about it, and, you know, I just. I just feel like I don't. I don't have anybody that I can talk to. I mean, I just. I keep thinking about it. I don't have anybody to talk to. She was the only one I had to talk to.
Counselor: So in your relationship with her, you guys talked a lot. She was an important person in your life for a variety of reasons, but including that she was easy to talk to.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And that you could talk to her?
Client: I. Yes.
Counselor: So the thought is you have nobody to talk to.
Client: I just, you know, she was just everything to me. I talked to her about everything, and, you know, she was just always gave me good advice, and she could always work, you know, talk me through anything that I needed to talk about, and I just don't feel like I have that anymore. Since she's going, I don't have anybody like that anymore.
Counselor: That relationship is valuable to you, and you've lost that, and you feel like you've lost having anybody that you could talk to. Is that. Is that close?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right, so let's look at that thought. Let's break that down. Certainly you were able to talk to her, as you mentioned, and you have lost her.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. So you have lost someone that you could talk to that was very valuable to you, and that's understandably painful. The question would be, have you lost everybody that you could talk to? Is there anyone else in your life, for instance, currently, that you regularly speak with?
Client: Well, you know, since you said that, you know, maybe I do have some people that I can go to. They're not her. But, you know, you know, I have a couple of people that I can talk to that they're willing to talk to me about certain things. I guess if I give them the chance, you know, I'll be able to talk to them.
Counselor: So there are some people in your life that you can talk to. They certainly don't replace your sister, but you have people you can't communicate with, and that can be helpful for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So as we build kind of a rationale, self talk to replace the irrational thinking that you brought in.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Which was that you have no one to talk to. Could the replacement be something like, I had my sister to talk to, and she was really good at that, and it's painful to have lost her, but I gained something from that experience, and I do still have some people to talk to now.
Client: Yeah, that sounds about right.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Yeah, yeah. Yeah. Because nobody's gonna replace my sister. But, you know, I do think that there's other people that can. Could help me and what I need to talk. Yeah.
Counselor: And maybe one thing that you can. You can take away from this as well is that because of the way you could talk to your sister, you are a more effective communicator now, and you can make the most out of the relationships that you have now with people currently. Another rational thought kind of honors her contribution to you.
Client: Right? Yeah, because, you know, she is, like, the only one that believed in me. I mean, she just, you know, she always, you know, pushed me to go higher and, you know, on my job. She always said that, you know, that you can do it, you know, just believe in yourself. She always, you know, encouraged me to. To go back to school and, you know, I'm, you know, I have done that and, you know, continually doing that, you know, but, you know, she was a big motivator for me. And, you know, since she's gone now, you know, I don't feel like that I have anybody else that gives me that push that she did.
Counselor: So. So the thought would be, I've lost the only person that would believe in me. Yes, something like that. Okay, so she was a great positive force, great positive presence and contributor in your life, in part because she believed in you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And now that's gone, and you feel like no one else will believe in you in that way.
Client: Not like she did.
Counselor: Not like she did.
Client: No. No.
Counselor: Which could be true. Right? There may be no one else that ever believes in you that same way, but similarly, like we were doing before, can you think of some people now that believed in you, maybe in a different way that's still helpful? It doesn't replace her, but it might still be helpful to you?
Client: Well, I do have very encouraging parents. They've always, you know, been, you know, somewhat of encouraged encouragement, but, you know, they just didn't have that extra push that she did. But, you know, they are very encouraging, and I have encouraging friends. You know, some of my friends, you know, want to see me succeed, and they give me encouraging words and tell me to, you know, to keep going. So, you know, she stopped at nothing to make. Make me go, you know, she just didn't take no for an answer. And, you know, you know, if she had to go with me to do something, she would, you know, that's why, you know, I just felt like, you know, I wasn't gonna make it, you know, without her, you know, pushing me.
Counselor: Her level of belief in you was higher or different or better than what you have now? In some ways, yes. Like, she was really committed to her belief in you, it sounds like.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So some people currently do believe in you, and that's good. It doesn't replace her level of belief, her type of belief in you. I also wonder if by her believing in you, you mentioned that it helped you with all kinds of accomplishments.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I wonder if that's not a thought that you can use here as an adaptive response, that because she believed in me, I was able to do all these things. And maybe because she believed in you so much, she taught you how to believe in yourself to some extent.
Client: Well, yes, because, you know, she's been going, and I've continued to go to school, and, you know, every time I feel like I want to give up, I keep on saying, you know, I gotta keep going. You know, my sister would want me to keep going, you know, and she would want me to succeed, and I have to, you know, do, you know, keep, you know, keep my focus because she always talked about me, you know, keeping my focus. So, you know, those things that she taught me and instilled in me, I still hold on to. And it's. And it's, you know, it's kept me going.
Counselor: So she contributes to your life, even now?
Client: Well, yes. Yes.
Counselor: Because of what she did.
Client: Yeah. Because I still kind of hear her words of what she says to me. You know, what she said to me all the time, and I hold on to that, and that's what, you know.
Counselor: Drives me, and I think that's a fairly useful way of looking at things. Right. Do you find that to be useful?
Client: I find it to be very useful.
Counselor:
output: Very useful.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maria. How are you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How things been going?
Client: Um, okay. I've been having some trouble with some friends and stuff. I just. I think just people just don't get me. I just don't think people get me.
Counselor: They don't understand it. Your friends don't understand you?
Client: No, they just don't. And right now, I just, you know, I just don't want to be friends with anybody right now because they just don't understand me. And I don't know. I think I'm just not gonna have friends for a while.
Counselor: That seems like a fairly large shift from kind of your position before on having friends, you seem to really like spending time with them. Has something happened that led to this?
Client: Well, you know, I just said some things, and now it's just gotten out of hand, and I just think I need to break from this friendship group for a little bit.
Counselor: You seem upset about this.
Client: Yeah, I mean, we were just talking about some things, and, you know, I was just telling them that, you know, I play tennis and I enjoy tennis, and I was just maybe went on a little bit about how I play tennis.
Counselor: Tell me about that.
Client: Well, it's a little embarrassing. I just. I was exaggerating about how I play tennis, and they were telling me how they had wanted to go to the US Open, and they want to go every year because they love it. And I've never been really. But I wanted to. I wanted to be part of the conversation a little bit. So I told them that I had studied under a famous tennis player and that they were really impressed with that. And so I just kept talking about that and all the stuff that I learned and told them that I was really good at tennis.
Counselor: And in reality.
Client: I maybe played a couple of times, so. And I've never met that person, let alone studied under them. And I really don't know how I got to the point where I was elaborating the story. And so they want to have some lessons. They want to learn what I learned under this person. And, you know, they started talking back, getting together, and at that moment, I kind of got caught up and I said, sure. And, yeah, we'll schedule it, like, Saturday mornings. We'll get together and we'll just kind of hit together and play some sets. And I don't know. I don't know what to do. It's just really embarrassing now because they're gonna know that I really don't know how to play tennis. You know, I could maybe have faked it a little bit, but now they think I had professional training, so.
Counselor: So it's gonna be very obvious to them that you weren't being completely honest if you have to play tennis with them.
Client: Right. And they're just gonna know and then they might question some other things.
Counselor: I've said things that are not tennis related.
Client: Yeah. So.
Counselor: Do you feel that in your relationship with these friends that you have not been honest? Frequently? A few times. Like, how would you categorize this is.
Client: Really hard to admit. It's just stupid. I just. It's stupid. It's just something I do. Sometimes I get kind of caught up or I'm feeling left out of a situation and they're all talking about a topic and I want to fit in. So I might say a couple of things that make it sound like I know what I'm talking about or that I can relate to the topic when I can't.
Counselor: Alright, so in social situations, when you're feeling isolated from the conversation or maybe detached from the people, you create a story that helps reintegrate you back into that conversation.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. You know, it's hard. I feel stupid just standing there, like, having no idea. Like, when they talk about traveling and seeing different cities and stuff, I haven't really been outside of my small town, you know, gone to Florida, went to Disney World and went to Epcot. So, you know, when they're talking about going to Paris and, you know, seeing the Eiffel Tower and seeing Notre Dame, or they're talking about going to Rome and, you know, I just. I can't. I can't really. I don't really have anything to say. I don't really have that kind of a life, and it's not very exciting. So sometimes I might say stuff about that and it's a lot of little things, you know, that I just. I find myself saying things that aren't true and trying to just go along with what they're talking about when I don't even know what they're saying, you know, and they talk about fashion or they talk about just different things, and I don't know what to do in that situation. And I'm just finding myself just making things up and saying things that I think that they want to hear and I don't even know if they believe it. You know, I kind of got the feeling this time that they were kind of calling me out because they were. They were getting an idea of what I had been doing, and it was really embarrassing. I feel like I just want to run away from the situation, and I don't want to talk to anybody, and I just want to break off friendships.
Counselor: So a possible solution to what you consider the inevitable embarrassment if you have to play tennis with them is to just not see them, just not return their calls.
Client: Right. I just. I don't want them to know what, you know, that I have a really boring life and that I don't. I'm not as smart as they are, and I'm not as successful, and I just. I don't want them to know and that I'm kind of like a loser compared to all of their exciting things that they do and say. I just don't match up.
Counselor: You feel you can't keep up with them on really so many levels. You talked about travel and fashion and, of course, now the athletics area with the tennis. So is a sense of being inadequate when you're with them or.
Client: Oh, yeah, yeah, definitely.
Counselor: So your options here are somewhat restrictive, right? Just let them go as friends or go and play tennis, and they'll figure out that you might have been making up that story, or I suppose telling them the truth would be an option as well. Have you thought about the different options available?
Client: I mean, I have, and I don't want to lose my friends. You know, I enjoy being with them, but it's like I'm gonna be mortified if I go out there and try to teach them things. I don't know. I mean, I guess, like, maybe I can watch some YouTube videos, but, you know, they're gonna realize that I don't. I've never played, and they're gonna realize that they're better than I am, you know? And. I don't know. I wonder if they'll still accept me if I tell them the truth.
Counselor: So you fear you might have lost them either way at this point?
Client: Yeah, but maybe there's a chance, if I tell them the truth, that they might have, you know, some understanding of what I've been doing because I don't even understand it myself.
Counselor: But how long has this been. Been going on? Like, the exaggeration or less than complete honesty in these social situations, it's really.
Client: When I get really nervous about being around a group or, you know, get around people that I really admire, and I feel like I can't match up to them. So, I don't know. It's probably. I probably did it here and there in high school when I was a kid, but it's just lately it's been more as I started, you know, I got a new job with this really big company, and I have more responsibility, and I got promoted. So I'm kind of in circles with people that really intelligent and successful and, you know, financially secure. And so it's probably when I get into situations socially with people that I really feel are above me, you know, whether it be socially or just intellectually.
Counselor: So your circle of friends is one group that you've been less than honest with? Any other individuals or groups you've been less than honest with?
Client: No, not really. It's just really been in these friendship groups. Like, I think with my family, they know me and they know who I am, so I feel comfortable. I take a lot of pride in my job, so I don't do anything there. You know, I'm pretty honest with my, with anyone who's under me and above me, obviously. So it's nothing like that. It's just this really strange, pressured social situation. I just kind of, I lose all confidence at that point when I'm hearing what other people are doing and how successful they are.
Counselor: So I wonder, has there ever been a situation where you're with your friends and they're kind of doing what you described, where they're talking about their accomplishments, and you have chosen to not be less than honest? Like, either you made no contribution to the conversation or you made the contribution that was within. That was truthful? Has that ever occurred?
Client: Have I ever been truthful? Only if it's an area that I feel confident in.
Counselor: Okay, but you. But you have been a few times. Yeah, but only if you start out confident.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How is. How's that worked out?
Client: It's been great. I mean, it's fine. I guess it works. Like it's fine. Like, they. We have good conversation and we get along. We laughed, and it's. I feel. I feel comfortable. I get really anxious when I start telling lies. Like, it doesn't feel comfortable. And I know I'm telling lies and I'm getting caught up in it, and then it's just building and building and building, and then I don't even know. I don't even know what I've said anymore. People say things to me sometimes. I'm like, oh, yeah, yeah, that's true.
Counselor: You can't remember what she told me?
Client: I don't remember.
Counselor: So, really? I mean, from what you're describing, there's two. There's two outcomes to the social situations that occur. One is that you're less than honest and you don't feel good about yourself. When you do that, or if it happens to be an area where you are confident, you can participate in that discussion, but it seems like what you haven't tried is when you're not confident, kind of still being honest.
Client: Right. Right.
Counselor: Because that's when that sense of inadequacy is really strong for you.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you suppose would happen if you weren't as impressive as they were and you relayed that, like, you know, in the particular area that they're discussing?
Client: I don't know. You know, I think they would think I was. I didn't belong there. I didn't belong with them, you know, that I wasn't really good enough to be their friend. You know, kind of as I'm saying it out loud, it seems kind of weird to say it out loud, but I guess that's what I'm thinking. I'm thinking that if people see who I really am, you know, they're not gonna like it.
Counselor: But you've not really tested that theory.
Client: No.
Counselor: And you know what the outcome is from being less than honest because you're stuck in that situation now with some difficult choices. Right.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And, you know, no one's good at everything, so you can't always count on having that feeling of confidence that would allow you to be honest with them and fully engage in the conversation. You'll have to decide what to do there. But it seems like it might be worth trying that. Right. Trying the honesty route and seeing if that. Seeing what feelings come out of that.
Client: Well, I feel like I just. Like, even with just this situation, I just don't want to be here again. I know that I took this way too far. And at times when people are coming up to me and I don't even remember what I said, I was starting to get that sense. This is the first time that I'm really caught red handed. And so I'm almost forced at this point to make a decision, and, you know, I don't want to hit the nuke button. I don't want to just decide to just disappear from my friendships. So. And maybe it'll help if I just say, this is. This is what I do sometimes, and it's not okay, but I did it this time, and I'm sorry. You know, I don't know if I'll end up with any friendships anyway, but.
Counselor: Well, there's no doubt you have hard choices, and I think you can see you've kind of constructed that the less than honesty policy has led to the situation, and you don't want to repeat?
Client: No, definitely not.
Counselor: But only you can really decide this. We can continue to talk this through. When do you have the tennis thing scheduled?
Client: It's supposed to be Saturday. So.
Counselor: So that's coming up quickly.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: I want to touch on the automatic thoughts. Right. We talked about this before. These are the thoughts that come up in the moment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. When a stressful situation is introduced, and it sounds like the stressful situation in this case is your friends talking about successes or I. Interesting things.
Client: Right.
Counselor: What. What's the thought that pops into your mind in that moment? Try to. Try to take yourself to that moment where your friends are talking and you talk about feeling isolated. What was the thought you were thinking?
Client: I'm just not that interesting. I'm not that smart. I. I'm not that successful. I mean, it's almost like a mantra.
Counselor: I'm not that successful. I'm not that interesting. I'm not that smart. So really all automatic thoughts that are putting you down.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Are those automatic thoughts defensible? Is that realistic?
Client: I guess it's a matter of perspective. You know, I just got a promotion, so, you know, in terms of success, like, I have some. That was something that I just did, but I don't know, like, interesting is kind of relative, you know, I don't know what makes somebody interesting over another.
Counselor: Person, but that automatic thought is telling you you're not interesting.
Client: Yeah.
