instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Liz. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How things been going?
Client: They've been all right.
Counselor: Last time we were talking, it sounds like you're still having some difficulty with the quizzes. Is that still the case?
Client: Yeah, I still panic when I take them.
Counselor: You still panic. Can you tell me about the process of taking the quizzes? I know we've touched on this a little bit before.
Client: Okay, so I'm going to class. I'm fine. I sit down to take the test. I'm fine. The test is in front of me. Question one. I'm not going to get that answer.
Counselor: So you're looking down. So you take these quizzes in class?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Like a paper, pencil. Okay. With other students around?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. Is the. Is having other students around distracting to you?
Client: No, it's happened in previous online classes. It's the same.
Counselor: So it's. You're pretty sure it's the quiz itself and not some external. Okay. So it's paper and pencil. You're seated, you're in the room. Rooms relatively distraction free.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Everybody's quiet.
Counselor: And you're looking down at, really the first item on the.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: On the quiz. And what's happening? What's happening? Then as you look down, you read that first item. What's happening at a thought. We'll start a thought level. What's happening with your thinking?
Client: I'm thinking. I'm reading the question, and I'm thinking, oh, my God, there's. Okay, there's four. Okay. So it's got to be. It's got to be one of them. And I am not going to pick the right one. I'm going to think I picked the right one, and it's going to be the one that my second choice is, and I am not going to pick the right one.
Counselor: Okay, so your thought is that you're going to get. You're going to select the wrong response and therefore get that quiz item wrong. How about behavior? Like, do you notice anything physically going on as you're thinking about that quiz item and how you're gonna get it wrong?
Client: I'd say my palms are probably sweaty. Like, I'm probably a little tense.
Counselor: A little tense.
Client: Yeah. That's really it.
Counselor: All right. So what it could be is that this thought of I'm gonna get this item wrong is leading to these uncomfortable feelings, the physical feelings. So what happens when you answer item one like, you don't know if you have it right or wrong immediately? Right because it's a paper and pencil. So you answer item one, and you move on to item two. What happens then?
Client: It starts all over again. I'm already, like, well, I already got the first one wrong, and now I'm. My chances are higher of getting this one wrong.
Counselor: So you feel like it because you. Because you thought that you got the first one wrong, that your chances of getting the second one wrong actually increase?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Like, I get one wrong the whole test, it's all gonna be wrong.
Counselor: Have you ever had a quiz that you've taken where you were confident that you got the first item right?
Client: I'm sure I have. I can't remember any.
Counselor: But eventually you're going to come to one item that you're going to have these doubts about?
Client: Yes. Inevitably it happens.
Counselor: There's going to be one that's maybe a little more difficult or difficult for you. So it seems like what you're saying is that when you reach that item where you have that thought from that point on, the next item is. Is more difficult because you're having a similar thought. Does that pattern continue throughout the test?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So explain to me what, like, let's just go with the example of the first item, like, just to keep it more simple. So you have the first item, and that didn't work out for you, that thought? Right. The second one, your thought was, I have even a greater chance of missing a. So what happens after you respond to that second item?
Client: It just compounds. I just start. I feel worse and worse as the quiz, as I continue.
Counselor: That's awful. So it's an awful feeling for me. Right. So by the time you get to.
Client: Item five or six, I'm convinced it's over. I've gotten a zero. If it's the. Yeah, if I start at the first, I've gotten a zero. I've gotten a bad grade.
Counselor: So that's what's on your mind. And how about those physical symptoms? Are they the same, different or new symptoms?
Client: If it, like. If it's. If it, like, starts early at the beginning of the test, my heart's, like, pounding at this point, but I still have the sweaty palms. I'm still, like, tensing.
Counselor: So it really just gets mentally and physically more unpleasant for you the whole time. So when you're saying panic, the panic's really occurring a few items in after you have the first one that you thought you missed. And this has been happening for a while, as you described, right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Well, how about your grades? How have you actually been doing on the quizzes?
Client: I've been a pretty solid b student, so. And I feel. I wish I did better. I wish I got a's, but, I mean, these are fine. But when I take those quizzes, it's not. It doesn't. I don't know how it translates.
Counselor: How about your study habits? You consider yourself effective at studying?
Client: I've tried. I've taken a workshops on studying. I've. I. I think I'm pretty effective at studying. I've found what doesn't work. So I try to study by reading the chapters, taking outlines, reviewing flashcards, which has, I think, the best results, but.
Counselor: Okay, so your study habits are good, right. And your quiz scores are good, but you're still having these distressing thoughts and these uncomfortable physical sensations when you take the quizzes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is that about right?
Client: Yeah, that's absolutely right.
Counselor: So really you don't necessarily need your performance to change. You just. You just need your thoughts and feelings and behaviors to change.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how you. How you're reacting to the quizzes maybe?
Client: Yeah, because I get b is, like I said, so, yeah.
Counselor: And b is good.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So. All right, so I want to take you back to the moment when you're looking at the first item. Let's go back to that for a second. Okay. So you're taking a quiz and you're having those thoughts surrounding that first item, which I'm not mistaken, the automatic thought. We talked about this, right? With the cognitive behavioral therapy. The automatic thought is that I'm not going to get this one right or something to that effect. What does that mean to you?
Client: It means once I don't get that right, I'm not going to get anything else right.
Counselor: All right. So what that thought means to you is that you're going to miss that item and then you're going to miss all the rest of the items. So you're going to fail the whole quiz.
Client: The whole thing, yeah.
Counselor: So looking at that, let's call that an intermediate belief, right. It's more of a rule or an expectation. Right. What does that mean to you?
Client: It just gets worse. If I fail the quiz, then I'm like, oh, my God, I'm gonna fail the final, I'm gonna fail the course and that's going to affect my GPA.
Counselor: So it just keeps stacking. So other beliefs. So you're going to fail the course and we're going to fail the final rather than you can fail the course. So if you failed the course, what would that mean to you then?
Client: I'm not going to graduate.
Counselor: You're not going to graduate. So we move from fail in the quiz if we just look at the meaning, right. To fail in the final, to fail in the course, and now to not graduating. So if you didn't graduate, what would that mean to you?
Client: I can't. I can't be a teacher. I can't do what I want to do.
Counselor: So your chosen vocation to be a teacher would be not possible.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Right. So we go a step further and say, what would it mean to you if you couldn't be a teacher?
Client: I don't know who I'd be at that point. That's what I always saw as my career. So I don't know what my future would look like at that point without that.
Counselor: So if you were to phrase it and kind of think back as we to the CBT techniques and I kind of conceptualization we've covered, if you're to phrase that as an I am statement, right. What would you. What would you be if you couldn't be a teacher? What would that make you?
Client: I am a person who didn't make it. I'm a person that failed.
Counselor: Like we said earlier, I'm a person that didn't make it. I'm a person who failed. So in a way you're saying I'm a failure, right? Is that close?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So remember we talked before about core beliefs and how these core beliefs drive these intermediate beliefs which combine with situations like, in your case, taking a quiz to form these automatic thoughts. So one of your core beliefs may be that you're a failure. You may believe that. Does that seem like something that you've said to yourself before or thought before.
Client: About it like that? Until we did the step up to it now. But I can relate to that because a lot of times I do feel like, oh, I'm not going to be able to do this because it's me. I won't be able to do it.
Counselor: Not because it's challenging or difficult, but something to do with you. So that's where kind of you're personalizing.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you're saying to yourself at a variety of levels, I'm going to be unsuccessful, I'm going to fail. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you think that's what's happening?
Client: It must be because, like I said, I study, I get good grades. I've been tested years ago. I don't have ADHD. Anything intrinsic that would prohibit me.
Counselor: So you're able to focus and concentrate.
Client: Well, yes, I can do all of that, but when it comes to it, I'm like, I can't do it.
Counselor: So somewhere. Somewhere is this discord belief, and it's possible that it has something to do with you believing that you are a failure. Unsuccessful.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How do you think your, say, friends or family would interpret that? Like, if. I'm not suggesting, telling them that, but if they were to somehow know that, that you believed you were a failure, how would they react?
Client: I don't think they would see the connection. I think they would be like, well, you do well in school. I don't understand.
Counselor: So they wouldn't believe that you're a failure?
Client: No.
Counselor: You may believe it.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And similarly, if you had a classmate that was in the same situation and, you know, struggled with these disturbing thoughts and feelings and behaviors during quizzes, how would you evaluate them?
Client: I guess I'd say the same thing that my family would say. Like, you're look at the evidence, you're not a failure.
Counselor: You'd say, look at the evidence and you'd evaluate that they weren't a failure.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But with yourself, you're being a little more harsh.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Which isn't uncommon. So there's a few levels in which I think we can go after this, what I'll call a problem. But really it's a series of thoughts and beliefs. Okay. The first is that the kind at the ground level, and that's when you are taking the quiz and you have that automatic thought that says, I'm going to miss this item.
Client: I'm not going to get it right.
Counselor: I'm not going to get it right. That's your thought. I'm not going to get it right. In these situations, I like to encourage clients to apply what's called an adaptive response or self talk. If you're in a quiz in a quiet classroom, it wouldn't literally be self talking.
Client: Right? Right.
Counselor: But it's a thought that you're consciously applying. So the other thought, that's automatic.
Client: Right.
Counselor: That just pops in your head. Right.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: This one would be one that you deliberately think and make myself. So what could you think to yourself that would be a counter to that automatic thought that you're having, that you're gonna get that item wrong?
Client: I guess that in my past quizzes, like, chances are I have a good chance of getting it right.
Counselor: Okay. So just looking at the probabilities based on your past performance, even though I'm thinking I'm going to get it wrong, chances are I'm going to get it right.
Client: Right. Somehow I still have a b. So.
Counselor: So you are getting most of them right.
Client: Right. So I have a good chance.
Counselor: So I like that adaptive response. Right. Do you think that makes sense for you? Yeah, I think you did well there. So the next time you're taking a quiz, I want you to apply that adaptive response. Now, this takes work, right. So this automatic thought is going to come upon you, and before you know it, you're gonna have that feeling. Right. The physical symptoms you discussed. The sweaty palms. Right. And the feeling of, I think you mentioned.
Client: Intense. Yeah.
Counselor: So don't let it discourage you. Those symptoms come on so quickly.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Right. There is an intervening thought, and you've identified it. So you will have an opportunity most likely to apply that automatic thought at some point. But the first few times, it might be a little rough.
Client: Yeah. Touch and go.
Counselor: I guess the nice thing about a quiz is, I mean, how many items are on these quizzes?
Client: Yeah. 1515.
Counselor: So you have a few different chances to apply that adapter. Right.
Client: Right. It's more than one.
Counselor: Yeah. So, you know, you would like to get on the first time where you have that mag thought, where you identify the automatic thought, but if you don't, it's not a big deal. So later on, maybe it takes item two or three, and then you might remember, hey, I have this.
Client: Yeah. Oh, wait. I'm supposed to be thinking this.
Counselor: Yeah. And my hope is that as you apply this adaptive response more and more, you can reduce the probability that that automatic thought is going to come in.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So that's one level that I want you to go after. It. Does that make sense?
Client: It does. I think I can do that.
Counselor: That's something you feel like you could.
Client: It is.
Counselor: You could do. At the other level. I guess you'd call this a deeper level, but it's all really, you know, in your brain. Right. It's just this core belief.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Okay. And why I use the word deeper is because we think of core beliefs as more stubborn. They don't change as easily as automatic thoughts might. I'd like you to. And this is really just more reflection. Reflect on the evidence or evaluate the evidence that supports and refutes this idea that you are unsuccessful, that you're a failure. I think cognitively, you kind of understand that you're not right, but in other sense, you feel like you are right. So, in a way, cognitively, you're.
Client: There's that discrepancy.
Counselor: Right. There's a little bit of both. You know, you can tell me that your family would say that's not the case, but you still.
Client: Right on paper, technically, I would. I'm not, but I still, I guess, feel that way.
Counselor:
output: There's a part of you that still feels that way, part of you that still believes that cognitively, there's also a part of you that thinks through that and says that's not accurate. So I want you to weigh the validity of that core belief. And actually, I think with this, it's helpful to write down evidence that would support it, and that's certainly something to note. But also, and this is really more important, evidence that refutes it, evidence that runs counter.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: You doing okay?
Client: I guess, yeah.
Counselor: Not sure.
Client: I don't know, just the same.
Counselor: Yeah, still a little down.
Client: Yeah, I've been sleeping a lot. Going to work is a struggle. I don't really ever want to go. Just I haven't been eating much, so I think I've lost like ten pounds since past, like four months or so.
Counselor: Past four months?
Client: Um, just the guy. I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.
Counselor: You still been working?
Client: Well, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But not much else?
Client: No, I usually just go to work and go home.
Counselor: Tell me what happens after you arrive at home, like after work?
Client: Um, well, my fiance tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep for just. I don't know. I tried, I tried reading the other day. Cause I used to like that and it's just, I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.
Counselor: What were you thinking when you put the book down?
Client: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.
Counselor: I. And before you were depressed, which is, I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading?
Client: Mm hmm. Oh, yeah, all the time.
Counselor: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?
Client: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up till like two in the morning just reading a book.
Counselor: Something you look forward to?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But not now?
Client: No, I just didn't really get any. I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like.
Counselor: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?
Client: Yeah, I used to be a runner and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I. I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.
Counselor: Alright, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running, like when you first started?
Client: Not really. I mean, it was a change to be outdoors and I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while, so. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run. I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route. And by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.
Counselor: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?
Client: Kind of a mix of, like, relief just because it was over, and then, I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.
Counselor: Sadness, maybe disappointment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I've seen you a few times now, and based on those conversations, and, of course, what you said today, it seems like you have, for a variety of reasons, given up on the activities that you used to enjoy, you're not motivated toward them anymore.
Client: Yeah, I guess you could say that.
Counselor: And that's a common symptom of depression. I think we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed. So we've been working with the cognitive piece. Right, like we did last time, we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self talk. I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. We'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle. And the technique is called behavioral activation. The theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, like with the running, that will connect to your mood. Right. Remember, we believe in cognitive therapy, that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood and what you do. Your behavior affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we talked about?
Client: It does, yeah.
Counselor: So you mentioned the reading was one thing you like to do. That's tough to do. Now you try unsuccessfully with the reading and I the running. Anything else you could think of that maybe we could plan for you to do, even if it's just a short time, even if it's a little bit uncomfortable, that we could plan to do? That would be an activity that you used to enjoy?
Client: Well, my fiance and I used to go out with two other couples, and we used to go out once or twice a week, and even if it's just each other's houses, but we haven't really seen them in a while. They've tried to schedule things, but I've kind of come up with reasons of not feeling well or to kind of just stay home.
Counselor: So they're trying to initiate meeting, going out, doing something, and you're. You're kind of pushing them off.
Client: Yeah, I just. I haven't really wanted to see anybody lately.
Counselor: All right, so that's. So we have reading, running, and then going out with these two other couples. Anything else you can think of that you used to really enjoy before that you can't quite motivate yourself to do now?
Client: I mean, I used to like going for, like, just walks and shopping with my fiance. Like, I. We used to spend a lot of time together, and lately it's just kind of. I come home, say hello, we eat dinner, and then I kind of do my own thing.
Counselor: So spending time with your fiance outside the house in some manner? Shopping was one example. Any other activities like movies or going out to eat?
Client: Yeah, I would kind of put those in with the things that we would do outside together. We would try to switch it up every now and then.
Counselor: Okay, so that's distinct from what you did with the couples because that's just you and your fiance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So let's do this. What kind of books do you like to read?
Client: I like a lot of fiction. I do a lot of reading for school, so I usually enjoy those books too. Mystery novels.
Counselor: Mystery novels. Okay, let's center on mystery novels. How long would it take you to read, say, a chapter of a mystery.
Client: Novel, roughly, depending on the size of the chapter, probably a couple minutes normally.
Counselor: So not long at all.
Client: No.
Counselor: So you could get a lot of reading done in, say, ten minutes, like something worthwhile. And how often would it. How often would you, what was the duration of a run? Like when you would go run? How long would it take?
Client: Probably, like a half hour.
Counselor: Half hour.
Client: Half hour to 45 minutes. Yeah. I used to do long distance running, so.
Counselor: Okay, and how often would you do that?
Client: Three or four times a week.
Counselor: Three or four times a week? Half hour, 40 minutes. And you mentioned you went out with the couple once or twice a week. How often would you go out with your fiance?
Client: I would say we try to do something every day, like, even if it was just going for a walk together, like around the park or walking the dog together.
Counselor:
output: Okay. So I'd like to make collaboratively with you a schedule that involves those four activities, but I want to make it realistic. You tried a couple times, you weren't successful. So we don't want to be too ambitious, but I want to try to plan a schedule. You can get the habit of doing these activities again. So let's start with the kind of, I guess the simplest in terms of logistics, which would be probably the reading. Would it be possible, say, five nights out of seven, to read for ten or 15 minutes? Like, I know you're going to have to force your way through it a little bit, but I think it's something.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Client: Hey, Doug. Nice to see you.
Counselor: Nice to see you. It's been about a week since I seen you last. I know you're having some different difficulties, particularly at work.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Any changes there?
Client: Not really. I mean, it's pretty much the same pace. I'm very frustrated with the whole system. I'm working with inner city kids, african american kids, males in particular. And, you know, I sit and talk with these kids and I realize that there's not much I can do for them. You know, for the most part, we're talking about, you know, criminal arrest, drug abuse, you know, no education. And, you know, I don't know what I can really do for them anymore. I mean, you know, I sit and talk to them, but really, in terms of their statistics, it's looking pretty bad for them. So, you know, I get pretty frustrated and it's kind of depressing to do this every day.
Counselor: All right, so as you're working with these use, you're looking at their circumstances and you're saying the odds just don't look good for major improvement. That's leading you to lose hope in your ability to help them into different circumstances.
Client: Absolutely, yeah. I mean, it's just their reality. A kid comes in and mom is either dad's incarcerated, rotted, a picture. Mom is either on drugs or not fully engaged. And this kid has absolutely no life skills. None. He's self medicating or smoking marijuana. At the very least, it's marijuana. And he is just totally convinced that, you know, this is who he is the rest of his life. And he's sitting in front of me looking for answers, and I don't know if I have him.
Counselor: What kind of questions do they ask you?
Client: It's not even questions as more as it is just statements of, you know, this is my life, you know, the struggle is real. This is what I do, this is where I am. And, you know, anything other than this is not even, you know, I didn't fathom. So I'm sitting here, just kidding, I'm trying to draw him out of that whole mindset. But we're talking about years of social conditioning, years and years and years of it. And I just don't know if, you know, I have the skills and the tools to really break through that way of thinking.
Counselor: All right, so can you think of a particular case, particular youth that you're working with that, where you're finding the struggle. I just think of one particular individual where you're frustrated, you're making these statements that kind of. This is the way it is. They don't seem like they have much hope. You don't seem like they have much hope for them. Right. So you have one in mind.
Client: Yes, they do.
Counselor: Okay, so what's his self statement? What's he saying to you that you think is getting a reaction from you?
Client: That he's a drug dealer. He's going to continue to be a drug dealer. He's not going to stop. And that he's involved with gang activity, and that's his family. It's the only family he's ever known, and he's loyal to them. And that loyalty is deep. And he has absolutely no. Even the thought of going back to prison doesn't shape this kid.
Counselor: Not afraid of that.
Client: Not afraid of it for them. Gerald is like going to the school courtyard. There's all his boys in jail. So I'm sitting here like, what in the hell am I doing here with this kid? You know, what kind of options do I give him when I don't even believe he has any at this point?
Counselor: So that's really your automatic thought, is I don't believe he has any options. That's what's going through your mind when he says things like he's involved in gang activity and wants to continue dealing drugs? That's your thought?
Client: That's my thought, yeah.
Counselor: There's no way out for him.
Client: I don't see it. I just don't. I really don't see it for him. You know, he's self medicating. He's giving dirty urine to the probation office. He doesn't care. The judge has given them pass after pass after pass. But the kid just seems intent to, you know, to live this life.
Counselor: So in a sense, your mood, the sadness, the frustration is linked to, for example, this use statements and his philosophy. So he's saying that success is not an option, as you would think of success.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And you're reacting to that, and your mood is moving because of that.
Client: Yes. Yes. And I mean, to a certain degree, I understand where he's coming from. I mean, I was raised with the understanding that you were born black. That's one strike. You were born male. That's two strikes. A criminal arrest record, that's it. Life is over. So to a certain degree, his perception is reality. So I can't disagree with him. But at the same time, this is my job. And I'm having a very difficult time trying to give this kidde any glimpse of hope, which I don't even think he really wants.
Counselor: So it's hard for you to give the hope, and I'm sure he's looking for the hope. And you can understand his situation in terms of being african american, being male and having the criminal record and how that seems to stack the deck severely against him.
Client: Severely, yeah. And that's nothing. I mean, there's some truth to that. I don't know. That criminal arrest record, a conviction in this country pretty much relegates you to a certain level of society, in my.
Counselor: Opinion, in terms of employment opportunities.
Client: In terms of employment opportunity and things like that. So to a certain degree, I understand where he's coming from. It's just an absolute sense of hopelessness that comes from this kid. He'll sit in front of me and he'll just laugh. He'll laugh about it like, Mister D, this is my life. Why are you tripping? Why do you care so much? So I'm just starting not to carry.
Counselor: So you're starting to mirror that approach, the approach he's using.
Client: Yes, I am.
Counselor: So what's bothering you in all this? Not only the circumstances, the racism, the discrimination, the circumstances in with the criminal record, that all bothers you, but also you're bothered because you're losing hope for him.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And for others like him.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: Have you expressed that thought? Sentiment?
Client: No, I haven't. Not in so many words. Not, you know, because to do that, I think, gives the kid credibility. I don't want to increase to his way of thinking if I, you know, agree with him on doing that, giving him a license to be an asshole, so to speak.
Counselor: You don't want to let on that his loss of hope is really. You kind of share that, in a way. You get it. You understand that.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: His lack of hope is grounded in a lot of reality.
Client: Yes, exactly.
Counselor: At the same time, you do this work every day. Do you believe there's hope at some level?
Client: Absolutely. I do believe at my core, I do believe there is hope at some level. I believe in resilience. I think once you tap into it, you can pretty much achieve anything. But it's just hard to peel back so many different layers with this particular generation of kids. It really takes a lot out of you.
Counselor: It's hard to get through.
Client: Hard to get through. Hard to penetrate that shell. So I leave work someday saying, I'm not coming back. We've had enough, you know, and it's depressing after all.
Counselor: So let's go back to that automatic thought. When a youth like the one that you were talking about makes a statement like, you know, their life is essentially defined in this and these narrow parameters, drug dealing and maybe other criminality or other behaviors that aren't productive, and you're kind of thinking there's some truth to that and you're kind of thinking there may not be hope. That's kind of the automatic thoughts or something close to the automatic thoughts. You're having much?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Your reaction to that is to not help them or to not say what you feel to them. What's going on?
Client: I don't want to say what I feel because I think they don't possess the filter to be able to understand it, to understand it. So I think for them it's going to be a license to continue the behavior. So I just hit them bullshit for half an hour, 45 minutes. Because what I really want to say, I don't think it would be beneficial to him.
Counselor: Partially because of the message, but partially because of how they would interpret the message.
Client: Very good.
Counselor: There's two levels to that.
Client: Right? That's how they would interpret the message. I think the message is, you know, for the right person with the right kind of filter would be receivable. But I think how they interpret it is going to be the issue.
Counselor: Right. So what is the message? Tell me what you would want to say to them.
Client: That all this, that what you said is real, that, you know, with a criminal arrest record, you know, your circumstances growing up in the city, broken homes, racism. It's real. But at the same time, somebody else made it before you, someone else went through this and someone else made it out. So if that was the case, I wouldn't be sitting in course with you. I came from the inner city, broken homes, the same scenario. So if that were the case for all of us, then how in the hell am I sitting in? Course, I'm no different. There's nothing special about me. I wasn't an a student to get scholarships. So there has to be some quality that we tap into to really sort of center us, you know, as we go, as we go along. That's what I would like to say to them, but I'm just not too sure how it would be this evening.
Counselor: So your concern seems to be that they would hear the first part but not really the second part. So they hear that their concerns are understandable and they've had circumstances stacked against them. They would hear that, yes, but not so much. There's a way to make it out, or there's hope.
Client: Exactly. Exactly. And I would be devastated by that. Mister Don said that I'm right. I didn't get the job because I'm black. I'm right because I didn't. You know, my situation is what it is. Cause of racism. Mister Don. Mister Don said I wouldn't want that. It would taunt the reputation, probably hurt my employment here. So, you know, I bite my tongue.
Counselor:
output: Is there a way to deliver your message, kind of with the same realism and heart, without including a piece that you feel like they could latch onto? It would be negative.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how you doing today?
Client: Good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How has the anxiety been going since last session?
Client: It seems to be in check. Nothing really major has been going on with it. So I think I'm getting to a point where it's under control.
Counselor: It subsided a bit. That's good. That's good. How's things been going at work lately?
Client: So work's a little bit of a different story. We have our daily meetings, and. I. Actually had to pull, like, one of my coworkers aside because I feel like they undermine me all the time, and they, like, they don't give me the respect, basically, that I deserve. So I took her outside after the meeting and leaned into her about it. And afterwards, I mean, the next day, because we have these meetings every day, she, like, she came back and came at me again, but it was worse even after talking to her.
Counselor: So talking to her, that didn't improve your situation?
Client: No.
Counselor: So you have these. Someone understands. You have these daily meetings, and you mentioned that she's not showing you respect and that you deserve respect, something to that effect. So tell me about that belief. Remember we talked about ABC before, activating events and beliefs and consequences in rabt. Tell me about that belief.
Client: Well, I just feel that I do a good job and I deserve to be respected by my coworkers. Yeah, it just.
Counselor: Are there levels of respect? Is there a certain level of respect that you demand or need?
Client: I don't know if there's a certain level, but I feel just like I deserve it. Mm hmm.
Counselor: You know, and what did she do that kind of convinced you that she wasn't meeting that level of respect?
Client: Well, she was, like, shooting down my ideas and just kind of made me feel like a fool, basically. So I just. I didn't understand.
Counselor: All right, so she had criticisms of your ideas, right? A few of them, it sounds like. So that would upset anybody. But were those criticisms unusual, given the tone of these meetings? Like, is this a type of meeting where people criticize each other or attempt to in a constructive way?
Client: I mean, I guess.
Counselor: Have you criticized other coworkers?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you think that her criticism was within normal limits, like, within the. What you've kind of seen there regularly?
Client: I mean, now that you pointed out? I mean, I guess I can view it in that way that it wasn't.
Counselor: It wasn't too far out of line the first time. Right. But then after you talked to her, you said that it got worse.
Client: Yeah. So it just felt like she was purposely trying to nitpick, if you will.
Counselor: Trying to get at you a little bit.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So maybe the second time around, correct me if I'm wrong, maybe she was actively showing you disrespect just because of what you had done, because you came after her. Or was that with the normal limits, too? I don't know.
Client: I mean, I. I guess I may have gone at her a little harshly, but I felt at the time that.
Counselor: It was reasonable at the time when you were.
Client: When I was talking to her outside of the meeting.
Counselor: All right, so you felt that she was a bit harsh. You talk to her about it, but then she's become more harsh. So where do you stand with her now, like, with the meetings?
Client: Well, I've just been trying not to talk to her, and obviously in a work situation, doesn't really help.
Counselor: That's not convenient. Yeah, it might not help. All right, so let's work this through. Using the ABC model, like we used for the anxiety that you had before that was troublesome to you before. What would the activating event be here in this situation?
Client: So I guess the confrontation I had with her.
Counselor: Well, you could look at that as an activating event. Another way to look at it is her criticism of you could have been the activating event, and your conversation with her could have been the consequence. But these things are cyclical, so it's sometimes hard to know where to cut in and put the a and the b and the c. But let's just work it through with the activating event being what she said. Let's just try that, okay, and see how that works out. Would that be reasonable? That could have been kind of what started it was this criticism.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: All right. So then what would the belief. So all activating events, right, are filtered through our belief system. So what would your beliefs be in that scenario?
Client: So she criticized me, and I felt disrespected.
Counselor: That's a feeling.
Client: And I feel, or my belief is that I deserve respect.
Counselor: Right. And that came first. Right. So you have the activating event, which is her criticism, processed through your belief, which is that you. You must have respect. You deserve respect. You mentioned the feeling. So tell me what the feelings.
Client: So that being upset and disrespected and aggravation.
Counselor: It was aggravation. Frustration.
Client: Frustration.
Counselor: So that would be one of the consequences of how you processed her behavior. Does that make sense? The feeling. The frustration feeling would be one of the consequences. Like an ABC.
Client: Gotcha.
Counselor: So you have the activating event. She criticizes you. Your belief is that you deserve respect. And that clearly she violated that belief. Right. She didn't show you the respect that you deserved according to your belief system. And then one of the consequences, therefore, was this feeling of frustration. Were there any other consequences?
Client: Well, if we, like, go forward, it's the kind of disarray or the tension, I guess, now in the office.
Counselor:
output: So you get. That's definitely a consequence. I'm thinking there's an intermediate consequence, though. So you had that feeling of frustration, and what's the next thing you did after that meeting was over?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Sarah. How are you doing today?
Client: Good.
Counselor: Doing well.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Yeah. A little better than last time. Worse?
Client: Kind of. No change.
Counselor: No change?
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: So you're still having sadness?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. And frustrated.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So tell me what's been going on this last week.
Client: Well, Mary's been crying a lot and I'm really tired, so I've needed extra help, you know, with her because I'm so tired and I just can't get out of bed.
Counselor: How much have you been sleeping each night? Like, on average?
Client: I don't know. Maybe 810, maybe more.
Counselor: Maybe more? Yeah. And how long did you sleep each night before you had Mary?
Client: I don't know. Maybe six, eight at the most.
Counselor: So your sleep habits have changed a bit?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you talked last time about feeling sad. What else has changed?
Client: I'm kind of feeling, you know, like I'm not doing good with Mary, that maybe I should think about getting a job again.
Counselor: And when you say not doing good with Mary, what specifically is going on that's contributing to that thought?
Client: I just remember with George, you know, he would cry in the middle of the night and I would hop right up. And with Mary, when she cries, I just want to roll over.
Counselor: So you're less enthusiastic about caring for her than were as compared to George?
Client: That's a good way of putting it, yeah.
Counselor: You still do care for her though.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Anything else has changed?
Client: I can't think of anything, but I'm sure there is.
Counselor: Well, tell me more about the sadness. Where do you think that's coming from?
Client: Um, I'm not really sure. Maybe just because she's crying all the time and I don't feel like I did with George. You know, everyone said I did such a good job with him and I was a fantastic mother and I was doing such a great job. And, you know, and I just. People are saying it, but I just don't feel like I'm doing as good a job as I did with him.
Counselor: All right, so people are giving the same input. They're saying that you're. You're a great mother in regard to Mary, like you were with George, but you're feeling differently about it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So their piece really hasn't changed. Like, they're still giving you the same feedback, but your feelings definitely have changed.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: To the point where you feel like you should just get a full time job. And I guess Mary go to daycare.
Client: Yeah. Because she's, you know, little. She's only six weeks now, so, yeah, she would go to daycare.
Counselor: So what comes to mind when you consider doing that, like, working full time.
Client: Um, kind of mixed feelings. Like, I was home with George until he went to school, so I feel like Mary wouldn't be getting the same thing that George got, but I feel like she's not getting the same thing right now.
Counselor: Like, you're just, you're just not doing the same quality job.
Client: Right.
Counselor: What kind of things did you do with George that you look forward to? Like, when he was that age, I.
Client: Would sing to him a lot and we would read books. You know, I started reading to him when he was still in my belly. And then when he came out, everyone's like, oh, it's too soon. But we would read all the time. I would take him to the playground quite often.
Counselor: Like, most days, pretty much, yeah. And that was something you really look forward to.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Have you done those same things with Mary?
Client: I try to, but maybe it's because she's a little fussier. You know, I try singing to her, and with George, it would be like one or two songs, maybe even just one song, and he'd calm down. And Mary's just not the same. It takes longer. Or she just doesn't respond to singing or reading books like he did.
Counselor: All right, so each infant or baby is going to be a little different.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But that feedback is still important to you. You'd prefer if her temperament was more in line with how George's was?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: If it were, do you think that would make enough of a difference to kind of break you out of this, these feelings of sadness?
Client: I would like to hope so.
Counselor: Mm hmm. So part of this could be just adapting to her personality?
Client: Maybe.
Counselor: Maybe. What else could be a part of it?
Client: Um, I don't know. I mean, you know, some of my girlfriends have kids the same age, or I babies the same age, and they're going back to work now, or they have been working for a while. And I kind of feel like now that they're working and have two kids, they kind of look down on me.
Counselor: So they look upon you negatively because you don't work.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Now you say you get that feeling. Is there evidence that you talked about cognitive behavioral therapy and evaluating evidence? Do you have evidence that that's the way they feel?
Client: It's kind of just a feeling. And I forget exactly what she said, but one of my friends was like, oh, you have so much time to do all this? And I'm always working. And it just, the way she worded it kind of made it feel like, you know, I have so much to do. What are you doing?
Counselor:
output: Kind of minimized your place. Well, I can see how that would hurt. And there's always going to be people that say things that we prefer they not say or feel a way that we perceive negatively as a negative effect. But this sadness, I mean, as we've been talking about it in weeks prior, is really markedly worse than what you've experienced ever before.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Leigh. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good.
Counselor: You're doing good?
Client: Yeah. Okay. I guess you guessed. Yeah. Um. Well, I guess I'll tell you, but I, I'm kind of embarrassed to tell you, but, so, like, I'm in college, and all my friends are dating, and I'm just really, like, nervous to just tell you, but, like, I really haven't dated before, and I'm really nervous and scared to date, and I just I just don't know how to do it, and I don't know. I'm just nervous.
Counselor: So, nervousness and some anxiety around dating. You said you'd never really dated before.
Client: No, not really. I mean, I just was never, you know, that was never enforced in my family. I was never allowed to really do that. So just the thought of it is, like, like, scary, scary for you? Yeah. So, you know, I mean, I tend to talk to guys, but it was just like, like, you know, real short and bye, like hi bye kind of thing. Because, like I said, that just was never enforced in my family. And just never, I was never, that's never applaud. That was never applauded in when I was growing up, so I never did it, and I was scared to do it for the repercussions, getting in trouble. So.
Counselor: All right, so no dating in high school. And what type of interactions did you have in high school? You said, you said hi a few times.
Client: Yeah, just like in my science class, you know, particularly this one time, I actually sat next to this boy who was super cute, but, you know, we would say hi, and that was it. He would try to ask me stuff about classwork or the assignment, and I would not even look at him and just tell him and look at my schoolwork. And that was the extent of it, you know?
Counselor: So let's talk about your anxiety. You have anxiety and earlier, like, reaction just to thinking about it. Right. You think about dating. It's just, it's a lot for you. Do you think this anxiety comes from a fear of what might happen, or is this something more how you'll be perceived? Like, what do you think is leading to?
Client: I think it's a little bit of both. I definitely always compare myself to my sisters, and they're super pretty, and I just don't feel attractive enough to have somebody be interested in me. And if they were to be interested in me, I'm not allowed to date, you know, so the repercussion would just be, you know, I'd kind of be shunned for doing so. So it kind of just stayed with me, you know, now I'm 24 and I'm in school, and it's just so overwhelming. And I'm kind of envious of my girlfriends because they're able to do it, and I'm like, damn. Like, how did they do that? So.
Counselor: So that process is far from removed from you. You look at that and think, I don't even know how to approach it.
Client: It's like a foreign object. Like, yeah.
Counselor: So how would you say, how would you describe yourself? Like, how do you feel about yourself?
Client: I always do the right thing. I'm really studious, and I like to have fun. When I'm with my girlfriends, we have a great time, and I'm personable with them and my family, but it's just when it comes to interacting with male, it's just super difficult for me. And I can tell you why, but I can't tell you why. You know, it's kind of that, like, it's like a seesaw every time I'm with a male, you know, in a dating aspect anyway, so it's just difficult for me.
Counselor: Is there a particular outcome that you're afraid of? Like, when you're, well, you're in college now, right? So likely interact with males to some extent. Is there when an opportunity comes up when somebody's interested in you? Is there a particular fear that comes to mind?
Client: Yeah, like, I don't even know why you're talking to me. Like, why would you talk to me? I'm not pretty. I'm flipping awkward. Like, you know, why would you even be interested?
Counselor: So you think yourself as unattractive and awkward?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you question why they would be interested in you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So have you ever had evidence presented to the contrary, like, people who thought you were attractive and not awkward?
Client: Um, well, yeah, I mean, yeah, like, people have told me that I'm pretty and, um, you know, fun and stuff like that, so, yeah, I have.
Counselor: Yeah. But there's some, so they're telling you that? But there's something else telling you that you're not?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you think that's coming from?
Client: I guess just from my, you know, my mom and I think just her rules that I guess I just associated, you know, me not being able to date, that I wasn't presentable enough to date. And I just got this idea that that's the reason why she just didn't want me to date.
Counselor: So you think her reasoning for not allowing you to date, I wasn't the pretty daughter? Were your sisters allowed to date?
Client: They were allowed to date, but under certain circumstances, certain rules they had to follow. But just when I would, you know, even suggest it to my mom, it was just like, no, you're not.
Counselor: So you feel like you were, of you and your sisters, you were the one treated the most strictly on that. But was it much more strictly or just a little differently?
Client: I think it was much more strictly, yeah. Because it's so much so now that I can't even talk to a guy. It's just. I mean, the anxiety and the fear is so intense. I just can't explain it. It's horrible that it's not like that for my sisters because now they're married, you know, so they have kids, and it's like, what the heck happened here? And I can recognize it, but I just can't bring myself to do it, like talk to somebody or, you know.
Counselor: So the way you perceive yourself, the self image here is part of this?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, absolutely.
Counselor: So you have evidence that says that men would be interested in going out with you, dating you, but internally, these thoughts you're having say you're just not worthy.
Client: You know what I mean?
Counselor: That's kind of the theme of it, right?
Client: Yeah, absolutely. That's it.
Counselor: And maybe this is tied to a core belief. Like we talked about core beliefs before cognitive therapy. Are there any of those core beliefs in the list I gave you a few weeks ago kind of stood out that you think might be core beliefs you have?
Client: That I'm unlovable.
Counselor: Unlovable, yeah. Any others?
Client: Fear of rejection.
Counselor: So fear of being rejected?
Client: Fear of being rejected. Yeah.
Counselor: So unlovable. And a fear of being rejected. And then when you have interactions in the moment, like, say you're in class and there's a man sitting next to you in class, and they're interested in you, he's interested in you. He says something that expresses that he's interested. You're immediately suspect.
Client: Oh, yeah.
Counselor: That's what you're.
Client: Oh, yeah. That's like. It's like, what is it? Fight or flight kind of feeling like it really is. It's like, oh, you know. Yeah. Just something comes over me where, you know, it's kind of like I'm conditioned because I don't even live with my mom and my dad now, and I'm on my own, but yet I still hold their values. And not just. All I can just think of is being in high school and having. Being told I can't do that or just the rules and having to follow it. And that's really where I feel like I'm there. If someone says something to me, it.
Counselor: Takes you right back there.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. I. So how do your parents feel about now? Have they said anything like, your sisters are married and you're not? Have they pointed that out?
Client: No, they haven't. Not really. No. Because my mom really wants me. She. I guess. Well, maybe it has to do with that. Like, I'm smarter than my sisters, so she really wants me to be a doctor. And my sisters, they have, you know, they have great jobs, but, you know, they just stopped at a bachelor's degree, and I'm really working to be a doctor. And I always had straight a's in high school and my sisters didn't. So I think that my mom wants to hold on to that, you know, that hope that I'm going to be something great. So she doesn't really enforce the dating thing with me. I guess she's for fear that that's going to get in the way.
Counselor: That's different than being unlovable, right? Yeah. I mean, her reasoning, as you're describing her reasoning sounds more like she wants you to reach a higher educational goal.
Client: I mean, I guess. Yeah.
Counselor: What do you want?
Client: I want to be in a relationship with somebody because all of my friends are, and I'm always that. They're real and it's difficult. I mean, yeah, I want the education. Don't get me wrong, I want a great job, but I don't want to do that alone. I want to have somebody with me that I can confide in and just a confidante. And the time is now. I'm ready, you know? And maybe my mom was just protecting me, I guess. I don't know what she was doing, but I really don't care because I really want to try it. I just don't know how.
Counselor: There's opposing forces at work here, right? I mean, you're motivated to try it like it's a goal. You want to be able to date, you want to go out. It's important to you. Do you want to get married like your sisters?
Client: Yeah, I do.
Counselor: You do? So you have these clear goals, and that's one force. And then the supposing force is this. Well, one of them would be this anxiety that comes over you in the moment when a man's talking to you. Like in that way. Right. Like about going out or any topic like that. So a part of you. A part of you is saying, I really want to move forward and date different people and see if I can find a good match. And another part of you is saying I need to run away. Like you said, fight or flight, right? I want to run away and not have this awkwardness, this anxiety.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Because it's a. I just keep thinking of the repercussions, like now as an adult, that my mom's just. I guess that she wouldn't talk to me. But I'm not in high school anymore, so I don't know. I just. I honestly don't know what the conversation would be like if I talked to a guy that I was interested in or if a guy was interested in me. Counselor: But when you did try, did you have the feeling where you were getting sick?
Client: I did, yeah. It wasn't as bad as any of my buddies, but I definitely. I mean, I didn't feel well.

Client: Yeah, yeah.

Client: It is. Yeah. It's. Yeah. I mean, my. My definite plan is to go in the detox. Client: Right.
