Counselor: Because they couldn't take care of it because their parents said, you know, we're not going to support you financially because they didn't want to because there wasn't a partner in the picture, because they want to go to college, because they.
Client: Wanted to stay young.
Counselor: Isn't it better life? Yeah. Yeah. So, I mean, I think this woman, we don't know her name, right? No, she gave you up. And then let's talk about Ruth and Abe. So they wanted a baby real bad.
Client: That's what they told me. Yeah.
Counselor: And so they chose you. I mean, they went and they had to, you know, to adopt a baby. It's a lot of work. It's a lot of money. So they chose you.
Client: Well, why do I feel so bad?
Counselor: Well, I think you're telling yourself. I think you're telling yourself some things, Ed. You're telling yourself you're different because you're adopted.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, let's look at that. Can I backtrack for a second? Before you found out on your 13th birthday that you were adopted, your relationship with your parents, on a scale one to 1010, being fantastic. Great, wonderful relationship.
Client: One being, oh, it was good. 910. I mean, it was my friends envy. Yeah.
Counselor: So before. We'll make a line here, before 13, your relationship with your parents was a nine or a ten, the envy of your friends.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Why was it a nine or a ten? Because you knew that your parents.
Client: I got along with them. They supported me. My dad helped me with sports. My mother helped me with sports. Both of them were good athletes.
Counselor: So they were loving.
Client: They took care of you, they took.
Counselor: You to sports, they paid for the sports. Did you all have fun together?
Client: Oh, yeah. A lot of fun.
Counselor: Okay. Did a lot of fun things. Are you're an only child.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So was the reason that you loved your mom and dad because your mother had pushed you out of her body? Is that why you loved your mom?
Client: Which mom?
Counselor: Your biology? Your adoptive mother, Ruth? Is that why I love Ruth?
Client: Because, one, I thought she was my mother, and two, she was nice, kind. Yeah.
Counselor: So, Ruthenhouse, let's just stick with that, okay? Ruth, aka mom, the only mother you've ever known was kind, you said. And she loved you and she took care of you and she did stuff with you, and she did all the things that a mom does. So the only difference between Ruth and or your mom, the mom that you know and now this, now calling her Ruth, is the fact that you found out you didn't come out of her body. I mean, that's how I see it, kind of. You see what I'm saying there? What makes a mom, Ed?
Client: Probably those things.
Counselor: So when you say, these are not my parents. They've done all the things that parents do, but you've got this voice inside your head, this little voice that's saying, well, they're not my parents. I'm angry because I didn't know what's the matter with me. You're telling yourself kind of junky thoughts, right? Here's a crazy thing, right? Something in here. This is. You know what this is?
Client: Looks like a plastic brain.
Counselor: It's a plastic brain. It's actually a jello mold, but, yeah, it's a brain. And our brain is. Our brain is so cool, because if you tell yourself stuff, your brain will believe it. So even though your brain's in charge of the thinking, if you tell your brain stuff, your brain will believe it. So for 12.9 years, you told yourself, I love these people. They're my parents. They're great parents. Their parents at a nine or a ten, right? And from my perspective, those are true thoughts. That's true feelings. You see this water? It's clear. I could. I could even see you through it, kind of. Those are true beliefs. Those are true thoughts. They took. These people took care of me. They loved me. They were there for me. That's true. That's. That's what was in your brain. True thoughts.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: You with me? Then you found this out, and you started having some kind of untrue thoughts or cloudy thoughts, murky thoughts, right? Look at this. Hold that up in front of me. Can you see that through me? Can you see me through that?
Client: No.
Counselor: Yeah. So imagine.
Client: No.
Counselor: Your brain, it sits in water. So your brain is actually, you know, almost 70, 75% water, right? So, true thoughts, all good water. Good. If you put coke in your brain, if you put bad thoughts, right, that'd be bad. It's. It would be bad. It would hurt you. It'd be junk. It would make you feel bad. Right? These thoughts. It's almost like poison, bad stuff in your brain. What's wrong with me? My parents aren't my parents. They're Ruth and Abe. You're telling yourself junk thoughts, and it doesn't feel good. What do you think when I say that?
Client: Are you saying I can feel the way I felt before I found this out? How is that possible?
Counselor:
output: Well, let me show you this a little more clearly. You got it? It's your job to remember these words, not my parents. What's wrong? We tell ourselves things that are true. We mostly feel. Okay, sometimes true things are sad, right? Or disappointing. Hurtful. Right? So. So these are true things. And these are things that are not true. What's true is that you tell me true.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Kathy. How you doing today? You okay? I know when you spoke last time, you had some goals that you want to talk about this time. Are you ready to do that?
Client: I need to. Yeah?
Counselor: Yeah. What do you have in mind?
Client: I just keep thinking about, you know, losing this weight, and I just. I really want to do it, and I just. I just can't get there, and I don't know why I.
Counselor: So you're frustrated.
Client: So ridiculous.
Counselor: Yeah, frustrated trying to lose the weight. Now, you'd said before that you had a specific number of pounds in mind, a specific amount of weight to lose. Do you still have that in mind?
Client: I would like 20 pounds.
Counselor: 20 pounds.
Client: I mean, I would like more, but I've tried to do more in the past, and I don't even get past a couple of days, so if I can do 20, that would be great.
Counselor: All right. And you tried before, and what do you think got in the way?
Client: I don't know. I guess it wasn't convenient. You know, I want to do it, and it means a lot, you know, for me and my family. I think I'd be a lot healthier.
Counselor: It's important to you. Yeah.
Client: But just, like, something always gets in the way, you know? And then I lose focus. I'm not very good at staying focused on stuff like that anyway, so.
Counselor: All right, so loss of focus. So you start trying to lose the weight, and your focus gets disrupted, and I forget.
Client: And then I make, you know, spaghetti casserole for six people, and then I eat a lot of it, and that's carbs and cheese and fat. And then I will eat what my kids don't eat. And then it's just like, I forget that I'm supposed to be making healthy choices.
Counselor: All right, so you know how to lose weight, and you know, you can lose weight, but your focus is a little off when you're, when you're trying, and that's. That's causing the problem.
Client: I think so, yeah.
Counselor: Could we break that goal of losing 20 pounds down into smaller units, like, say, five pounds, do you think?
Client: Well, maybe, yeah. Cause I've never. I always just keep, like, the chunk of weight, you know, ahead of me. I don't break it into smaller increments. That might work. I mean, I don't know how. I'd have to stay on top of it, though. Weigh myself every day.
Counselor: Is that something you can do.
Client: I'm so busy. I don't know.
Counselor: Or once a week.
Client: I probably do once a week. Put a sticky note somewhere or something, you know, maybe. Yeah. I mean, I want to try. I'm going to say yes because I want to try it, you know?
Counselor: So you mentioned the loss of focus is one problem. How about motivation? Do you feel motivated to move through all those steps, like five pounds and five pounds and so on.
Client: Right now? Yes. I think I would need a. Something to keep me going, you know.
Counselor: Week to week, a little bit of that. Something extra to help you stay motivated.
Client: Yeah. Like when you're. Sometimes when, you know, your kid does your homework early or does their homework early, and you can give them a special treat for dessert that helps, you know, keep it going.
Counselor: Okay. So some sort of activity or item that you enjoy that you could reserve for when you reach that goal of, say, the first five pounds.
Client: Right, right. I would love. I mean, I'm just. I've been so embarrassed, you know, lately. So I feel like I just. If I can find something that keeps me bone at me, keeps you motivated, that would be great.
Counselor: All right. Do you have an activity or item in mind that we could put in place as something you could reward yourself.
Client: With, like, after the first five pounds?
Counselor: Well, there's a few ways we could do it. We could do that. So you reach five pounds, and then you can give yourself that reward. Or it could be for something you do every day. If that day you're successful in eating the way you want to eat, what do you think would benefit you more?
Client: Maybe something every day. So I remember, you know, I just get so distracted by other stuff. So there was something every day that maybe I put out, almost like a goal at the end of the day or something.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: You know, if I made the right choices.
Counselor: Yes. So, you know, each and every day, as you're trying to lose weight, you're aware when that day comes to a close, if you had a successful day or a less than successful day.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And if you have a successful day, then you could engage in an activity or receive an item that we work out in advance that, you know, would motivate you.
Client: Right. And that could be, you know, maybe watching, like, a favorite tv show.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: You know, because I don't watch tv at night because I'm so busy, you know, cleaning up and everything. And maybe I could just take some time for myself because I did something good, you know, and just watch a tv show.
Counselor: All right, so let's do that on a day you know, towards the evening when, you know, you have had a successful day. By what time would you know in the evening?
Client: Probably as I'm preparing dinner. If I prepare a good dinner, or if I prepare fun food for my kids, but I don't eat it, like, chicken nuggets and french fries and stuff, I would know, you know, maybe by, like, six or seven. Okay.
Counselor: Say seven.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So by 07:00 p.m. at that point, in terms of the day being successful or less than successful, you know.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Right. By 07:00 p.m. you're aware. And at that point, if you have met your goal, then you have a tv show that you maybe have recorded on the DVR or something you would watch if you were not as successful. You wouldn't.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So that would be, like, something to keep you motivated throughout the day because you really want to watch that show.
Client: Right. It'd be a lot of fun.
Counselor: Do you think that structure, that kind of behavioral strategy, would give you enough motivation to have successful days through this process?
Client: I don't know, honestly, but it would probably beat the way I feel right now. Anything's kind of better than carrying this frustration around. So I'm willing to try anything, and I'll try to remember. Like I said, I'll write it down. I'll have it in the kitchen. Have it on a note. 07:00 p.m. how did I do today?
Counselor:
output: Yeah. This is something you could also track. You could write down days that were successful, days that were less than successful, and we could look at if there's any patterns. Maybe weekends are harder, weekends are easier, or something where we can identify days that have maybe more triggers or where you're less motivated.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Hannah. Nice to meet you.
Client: Hi.
Counselor: So I understand that you were referred to me by your GP because you've been experiencing some anxiety difficulties.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, I guess it kind of started, like, five, six years ago.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: It kind of escalated a bit. I've just recently moved out from living with my parents, so it's made it a bit worse, I think.
Counselor: Is this the first time that you've left home?
Client: Yeah, it's the first time, actually. I was going to a few years ago, thought it would be easier to stay home.
Counselor: Okay. So it's been quite a big step and a big change. And it sounds like that that was what led you to go to your GP.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how has that changed things for you?
Client: It's kind of. I haven't really told anyone, so, I mean, it's made it better in the sense I feel hopefully this is. This is it. Like, it'll help, but I don't know. I don't like thinking that I've had, like, how to do this. I never thought I'd be the kind of person who'd have to actually go and, like, get help, if that makes sense.
Counselor: Okay, so how do you feel about being here today?
Client: Bit like scared? I don't know. Hopefully it will help.
Counselor: Okay, so you've been feeling a little bit anxious about today?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So I guess just going back to why you went to the GP and how you've ended up kind of coming here today. So it sounds like you've been experiencing anxiety for quite a few years, but just recently you moved out of home for the first time, and that was what kind of led you to go to the GP. So how did that change things? How were things after you moved out?
Client: I thought that they'd be better because I thought I'd have to kind of be independent. And it's actually a lot worse. I'm just kind of staying in the house a lot. I don't really have any friends or anything. I mean, my family come and visit a bit, but it's nothing. I don't know. It's kind of scary because I've just been kind of literally just in the flat by myself, which I always thought I'd like, but I don't actually like it.
Counselor: Okay, so what are the kind of difficulties that you have been experiencing?
Client: I mean, I'm a photographer, so I kind of. It's been stopping me a bit, my anxiety from being able to get work, and because every time there's an opportunity that is kind of involving me having to interact with people, I just tend to just turn it down. So I was kind of making things hard in that respect and just kind of friends wise and everything, I feel like I'm just kind of increasingly more alone. So it's kind of stopping me from making friends and, you know, like, relationships and stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so you said that your difficulties are getting in the way of you doing certain things, so they're stopping you from taking up kind of certain types of work. And as a freelance photographer, I guess that can be kind of a problem. And they're also stopping you, or you feel like it's stunting you socially. You're not kind of able to make new friends and get to meet new people.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. It was kind of easier when I was at home because I was obviously. I mean, my parents and stuff, that's fine. But, you know, they would. I'd go to places with them or I'd kind of have people there. But more and more, I'm just finding myself just staying in a lot. I mean, I went, like, two weeks to get coffee with my friends, and the whole time I was just kind of wanting to go home again. So I just don't want to. I don't want that to happen. I don't want to lose everyone.
Counselor: So you're kind of worried about where this is going to lead to.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you said that you first noticed the anxiety kicking in about five or six years ago, so you would have been about 19?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And what was happening around that time?
Client: I guess I'd finished school about a year before that. And, I mean, I've always been a bit shy at school, but it was never, ever like. It didn't really affect things as much as. Not at all, as much as it has been doing the last few years. I guess it just started when my friends went to university, and, I don't know, I felt like I was expected to kind of move out or just do something, and then it just kind of escalated from there. I'd just stop going to parties, or I'd just say no to invitations or. I thought my job would help because, I mean, I love it. I really like doing photography, but I'm just kind of getting less and less work as it goes on, which is my fault. I keep saying no, but what kind.
Counselor: Of work is the most difficult for.
Client: You in your job? I guess when I have to kind of be working with other people, I don't like that. It's like when I'm trying to kind of do an event or something where there's a lot of people there, not just photographers, but actual, you know, if I'm, like, taking photos of people that I don't know, I just kind of find myself saying no. I mean, I want to do them, but it's scary, so I just don't do it.
Counselor: So, I guess, tell me a bit more about what happens then. So let's focus on maybe an invitation to do a job with. You know, it's going to involve photography with a group of people, and you're going to have to have social interaction. What kind of thoughts go through your head?
Client: I mean, I get really hot and sweaty, and I feel like everyone's kind of looking at me and thinking that I'm just, like, really stupid. And I feel like they're all going to be staring and thinking, I just can't do my job and I'm just an idiot. And, I mean, they'll think that I just look like a weirdo. And I just try. And, I mean, I just kind of just try and get out of the situation or just focus on something else. So that's why I like doing shots where it's just me and the camera, because then I can just put all my attention on that instead of having to, you know, be with other people.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you have quite a lot of thoughts rushing through your head. Then at the point where you get that invitation, you think people look, people will stare, people will think I'm a weirdo. There's quite a lot about what you think other people will think. Yeah. And how does that make you feel?
Client: It just makes me feel like an idiot. Makes me feel like I just shouldn't even bother trying to do it anymore. I should just go home. And I just. I think I just don't want to be in that situation. I just feel like everyone else is fine and they're normal, and I'm just the freak who can't, like, do normal things.
Counselor: Okay, can you give me an example of a recent situation? Maybe we can focus on that, like.
Client: A work situation or just. Yeah.
Counselor: A time when you were maybe doing a job with some people and you felt the social anxiety, you know, that you're describing. You felt that kick in.
Client: Yeah. I was doing a job where it was kind of like a nature shoot, and I was having to work with a lot of different people. And when they told me about the job, I thought it would be fine. I thought it was just going to be a few other photographers, but there were actually people in, you know, I was taking photos of people kind of ingest the trees and stuff like that. And I get. They asked me to.
Counselor: That sounds quite interesting. Was that a fashion shoot or something?
Client: Yeah, yeah, it was a fashion thing. I think it was for some kind of. I'm not sure if it was a campaign or something, but.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah, it was really cool. But I found it really hard to try and focus on that because I was so. I was kind of feeling really anxious. And.
Counselor: So it wasn't what you expected?
Client: No, it was. No.
Counselor: So how long ago was that?
Client: That was two weeks ago.
Counselor: Okay, so it's quite recent.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So on that particular day, what were the thoughts that you had in your head when you were in that situation?
Client: I just felt really. Just really kind of hot. I couldn't really breathe and just felt like I wanted to just get out. And I was kind of trying really, really hard to just focus and just, you know, like, kind of hold the camera and just not think about anything. But I just felt like everyone was looking at me and, like, when they'd say action, and they try and get me to start, and I was just felt like everyone was just thinking I was really stupid and I shouldn't have been there.
Counselor: And I can tell you're getting kind of anxious, even just thinking about that day.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so you're describing quite a lot there to me. So you're saying that you kind of got hot and sweaty. You said that you held the camera.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What was do you mean? You were kind of trying to hide behind it or.
Client: I was just trying to focus on it, just thinking if I could just hold it really tightly, it would just. I don't know, I'd kind of just be able to just get through it and just focus.
Counselor: So you're holding the camera very tightly?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And why was that helpful?
Client: Because I felt like I was getting really, like, hot and flushed. And I just thought, at least if I can just. I don't know, it sounds weird, but I was just trying to keep my hands still on it because my hands were kind of sweaty and, like, shaking, like, loads, like. And I could just tell everyone Washington looking and they could see, and I just thought if I just managed to hold onto it, it wouldn't be as noticeable, but.
Counselor: Okay, so, okay, so it sounds like you had a lot of thoughts going through your head. You said that you worried that everyone's looking at you. What other thoughts were there that were in your mind?
Client: Just. I was just stupid. And it just really just felt really like a. Kind of like everyone was just going to be staring and just thinking that I just felt like everyone was looking at me and just. They could tell and just thinking, what's she doing? And they could tell what? I was just really, like, sweaty and.
Counselor: Just that they could see that that was okay.
Client: Yeah. So I always try and wear black. So this kind of tries to cover it up and just, like, a lot of layers so they can't tell. But, I mean, my hands, like, they were so shaking. I was really red and just wishing that I just wasn't there.
Counselor: So, I mean, you've already described it to me a little bit, but if you think about how you looked that day, how do you say, how do you think you looked?
Client: I think just really stupid. And, like, I think my face was really red. I could feel it flushing, and I knew that I was probably sweating and shaking. Like, my hands were definitely, really, really shaking, and it was, like, definitely, really noticeable. Everyone could definitely see.
Counselor: Okay, and what did you do about how did you try and conceal that or hide that?
Client: Well, again, I was trying to grip the camera, just look down, just trying not to do anything weird or. Because, I mean, they could probably tell I was being weird anyway, but hopefully I just tried really hard to just focus and look down, not try, like, not look at anyone else, and just. Yeah, just kind of try and get on with it as best as I could.
Counselor: So you avoided looking at people. It sounds like you wore black as well in kind of preparation anyway.
Client: Yeah, no, I always do that, even if it's really hot or I wear just loads of layers and just because otherwise I'll just be really sweaty and, like, people would definitely be able to see, so.
Counselor:
output: Okay, and how did it end?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Samantha. How you doing today?
Client: Good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm doing all right. How have things been since last week?
Client: Things? You know, I've been really sort of preoccupied and anxious a lot this weekend. My daughter got sick, so I had to take three days off of work to take care of her. And I'm starting to worry. She's been sick a lot since I've gone back to work, and she's in daycare, and I've had to take a lot of time off work, and I'm getting close to going over my allotted amount of days. And so I'm finding myself being very anxious about that and then feeling guilty because when I'm trying to take care of her, I'm always worrying about work. So.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a couple things may be going on. Child. Child's been sick, so you're taking off days. So you're a little worried about your relationship with your employer. At the same time, you want to make sure you're taking good care of your child, so you're having trouble reconciling those two.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. What was the last time it happened? Can you describe what happened the last.
Client: Time I had to take off work? It was just this week. She woke up one morning with a really high fever, so I had to call out that day, and then she still had a fever the next day, and then I had to take a third day because she has to be fever free before she can go back to daycare. So the first day was, I was okay with that. But then, like, the second. And then when I started realizing that I was going to have to take a third day, then I really start to get kind of panicky and worried about it.
Counselor: All right, so let me see. Let's go through each day. So the first day when you discovered that she was sick, right. What were you thinking then when you had to call out of work?
Client: Well, because she's been sort of sick a lot lately, I was a little bit worried, and I was sort of, you know, I have this number, ten, because I only have ten days for the whole year. So I have this number in my head, and I just thought, well, there's one more day I gotta take away from that ten that I have. And. But I was able to sort of think about. I was a little worried about any work that I would miss, you know, keeping up with my caseload and stuff at work, so. But I was able to kind of figure out that I would be okay for a day. And I can kind of make up for that when I get back.
Counselor: Okay, so your thinking was, this isn't ideal, but I can live with it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just one day, right? How about on day two when you realize that you're going to have to take a second day?
Client: Then I got a little bit more worried. And then I did start to also, you know, add the worry of I was going to start to get behind at work. Not only was I missing more time, but I was also going to be behind on my work. So then I started thinking, when I go back, it's going to be a mad scramble to kind of catch up and keep up with everything and, you know, so then it became worrying about my workload and worrying about taking more time.
Counselor: Okay, so a little more stressful version of what happened on day one. And then how about when you discovered that you had to take a third day off?
Client: I was. Then it was just more amplified, you know, amplified worry. And it was a lot harder for me to let it go. I just kept thinking. I kept going back to it. And then I started feeling guilty because I was so preoccupied, worried about that. And I was trying to answer emails and do some stuff and send out some emails to people that I work with to try to help me out with things at work since I wasn't there. And then I felt guilty because I wasn't really caring for my child as best as I felt I should have been. You know, I started feeling kind of like a bad mom.
Counselor: So, so guilty and a bad mom. And that was mostly on the third day? That was the worst of it, yes. Now, did this go up against the weekend? It was the third day, Friday. So then you kind of knew that by Monday things would be able to return to work. So tell me what happened when you returned to work on Monday.
Client: Well, I checked in with the main office and, you know, I just said, I'm really, you know, I'm starting to worry. I'm getting. I know I had to take a lot of time, but you. I've done the best I can to try to make other arrangements, but just starting back in, starting in daycare, she's just been sick a lot and I can't control it. I'm doing the best I can. I asked them if there was anything I needed to do as far as providing doctor's notes and stuff, and they said, no, they don't need a doctor's note since it was my daughter that was sick. They said there's nothing, nothing that I really can do and just try to not have it happen much more if I can just do what I can to not miss more.
Counselor: So they said that to you?
Client: Yeah, but. Yeah.
Counselor: How did they frame that?
Client: They kind of just said, you know, do what you can to not have it happen, but if it, you know, if it has to happen, you know, what can I do about it? It's kind of. They were saying.
Counselor: So they were understanding.
Client: I didn't feel like they were that understanding, but I also didn't feel like they were gonna take any punitive action against me. Right. Right then and there or anything.
Counselor: Did you anticipate a worse reaction than you experienced?
Client: Yeah, I did. And I also anticipated that they would maybe have more of a procedure for how to handle it, and they didn't have a procedure, which also made me feel a little worried. I can't imagine I'm the first mom that has had to deal with this. And they kind of talked like it's never happened before, so I kind of felt anxious because I thought, am I really the first mom that's had to take a lot of time off because their child's sick? They didn't give me the impression that they had sort of a protocol or like they had dealt with this before.
Counselor: Right. So sort of like it took them by surprise.
Client: Yeah. Or they just didn't have a plan for what to do about it.
Counselor: They weren't investing a lot of energy in thinking about that?
Client: No. No, I guess nothing.
Counselor: And when was this again? How long ago?
Client: Just this past week.
Counselor: So how has this week been? Bag of work?
Client: Oh, it's been very busy because I'm trying to catch up and get everything handled, but that's the way it always is. So nobody has said anything to me or anything about the absences other than that first, yeah.
Counselor: And there have been no more absences. Okay. Earlier you mentioned being a good mom. What does a good mom look like?
Client: Somebody who takes care of their child and puts them. Makes them a priority, like their first priority, and, you know, does the things that they need to do to make sure they're child is taken care of.
Counselor: And you're a little worried through this last experience you were telling me about that you didn't rise to the level of good mom.
Client: Yeah, I felt like I wasn't being a good mom because I was preoccupied and making work a bit of a bigger priority than taking care of my kidney.
Counselor: Okay. So good mom's more about. More than just rather your behavior, what you're doing. It's about what you're also thinking. So you took care of your child.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But your mind, your thoughts were somewhere else some of the time, and that's where you feel like you've wandered out of the good mom area. Okay, how about on the other side? How about a good employee? Did you mention that you want to be a good employee?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. What's that look like?
Client: Well, somebody that, you know, takes care of all of their workload and handles all of the tasks that they have each day, and someone that's consistent and reliable and, you know, puts effort into what they're doing and gets their job done, really, you know, reliably.
Counselor: And that's where you feel like with this. So the last eight work days you missed. You missed three. Okay, how about in the last year, how many days have you missed?
Client: Well, I missed a lot for maternity leave, certainly.
Counselor: Understandable.
Client: But excluding that I've missed since the school year started, I've missed. If you include the three, I've missed nine days. But some of those were half days. They add up to nine days.
Counselor: Okay, total nine days?
Client: Yeah. And you're allowed ten per school year? For school year, it's only January and I'm already at nine.
Counselor: I can see where that would cause worry. What happens if you go over the.
Client: I don't know. I mean, I think that they would dock my pay for those. If I was there a day and I didn't have any more sick days left, they would just dock my pay for that day. But outside of that, I don't know what else would happen.
Counselor: Is there anybody that you work with that you could ask that question to, like an HR department?
Client: Yeah, I guess I could contact the HR department.
Counselor: I'm just thinking. Cause you're just one day away from being at that number, might be prudent just to talk with them and see. So you know what to expect.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So this is this whole thing, though, the missing days cause you anxiety, frustration?
Client: Yeah, a little bit, yeah.
Counselor: How about any type of feeling down at all?
Client: A little bit. Sometimes when I start feeling like I'm a bad mom.
Counselor: Okay, so as far as your child is concerned, your relationship with your child, you have some anxiety, relationship at work, some anxiety. But the sadness mostly surrounds how you feel you're treating your child. Of all the emotions, frustration, anxiety, what I'll refer to as depression, let's just say sadness. What's bothering you the most? What emotional response does bother you most?
Client: Probably sort of the guilt and the feelings of not being able to be the best mom.
Counselor: How would you rate yourself right now as a mother if, say, ten was the best mother you could imagine. Right. And one was the absolute worst.
Client: Probably like, I don't know, an eight.
Counselor: An eight? Okay. That's pretty good, right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What would be the cutoff to where. What's the cutoff score in that little scale I just gave you for good mother and not good mother?
Client: I guess, like halfway, like.
Counselor: So five is good enough?
Client: Yeah, I don't feel like it's good enough for me.
Counselor: Okay. Okay.
Client: I wouldn't be okay with that.
Counselor: So if you looked at somebody else, another person in a similar situation, a five would be acceptable, right?
Client: Probably, yeah.
Counselor: But how about for you specifically?
Client: Yeah, that's not.
Counselor: That's not gonna cut it. What would cut it?
Client: Um. I don't know. At least a seven.
Counselor: At least a seven, yeah. And you're an eight?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Sure.
Client: No, not sure.
Counselor:
output: Okay. So you're close to the border. I feel like you're close to the border and you're.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Gabriella. I understand that you're here today because you've been experiencing some low mood.
Client: Yeah, I just. Recently, I'm just feeling down a lot and I can't really, like, snap out of it. Like, sometimes if it's happened before, I can just, like, get myself back on track, but recently I just find it really difficult to do.
Counselor: Hey, so it sounds like you've been experiencing some low mood and you're kind of struggling to get going a bit.
Client: Yeah, yeah, definitely.
Counselor: You've had low mood in the past, but it's kind of. You've been able to pull yourself out of it before, but more recently you found that harder. Okay, so I understand that you first went to your GP. He referred you here about two months ago. Can I ask what led you to go to the GP in the first place?
Client: My long term boyfriend broke up with me and it was such a shock. Like, I really wasn't expecting it and it just got me really down and I just felt really lonely and I didn't really want to see people and just wanted to be in my own space. And my mum told me I should probably go to the doctors. Oh. And he's referred me to you.
Counselor: Okay. So it sounds then like you had that breakup and you weren't expecting it, so it kind of came out of the blue a bit and that you've been on your own quite a lot, so you've not been seeing people as much. And it sounds like your mum noticed that there's been a bit of a change in you. Okay. And how have things been then, since then, since that happened and since you went to the GP?
Client: I just. Nothing's really changed. Nothing's really improved. I just feel down, like everything's an effort and just feel distant from things. And like I said, I can't snap out of it.
Counselor: Okay. And how did you feel about coming here today?
Client: I was kind of disappointed in myself because I feel like nobody else my age is doing this. Like, I should have been able to snap out of it. Like, it's just another thing that I've not really. It's another thing that's making me stand out for the wrong reasons.
Counselor: Okay. So you feel like it's kind of odd or unusual to be coming to see a clinical psychologist? I suppose I just want to reassure you that it's absolutely normal to have feelings of depression and anxiety. It's really very common and it certainly isn't odd or strange at all. So it sounds like it was actually quite hard for you to come here today?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So what, I guess led you to do that? Because it sounds like maybe there was a lot pushing you against coming here today, but you've managed to come anyway.
Client: I'm just hoping that it's gonna help, I think. I didn't really want to admit it because it's just another failure, but my mum was talking to me and I know she's not really happy with the way I'm behaving. I didn't really want to disappoint her again and so I thought there's no harm in it, so she thought it'd come.
Counselor: So it sounds like partly you're doing it then, for your mum because you're a bit worried that she isn't pleased with you at the moment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Well, I think it's great that you've come here and definitely there's a lot of evidence to suggest that psychological therapy can help depression and particularly the type of therapy that we're going to be doing, which is called cognitive behaviour therapy. And I'll tell you a bit more about that as we go on, but I'm just trying to find out a bit more about you today. So I saw from your notes that you're a medic student.
Client: Yeah, I'm not currently in uni at the moment, but, yeah, last year as a medic student.
Counselor: Okay. So I guess what's the reason that you're not in uni this year?
Client: It was pretty tough first year, so they then suggested that I took a year out. This is the break.
Counselor: Okay. So just thinking. So that would be about six months ago, was it that your year out started? Yeah. And it sounds then maybe like your first year was also quite tough.
Client: Yeah, it was. I thought it's tough for everyone, but obviously we all take it in different ways, don't we?
Counselor: And you're planning on. Are you planning on returning and.
Client: Yeah, I'm gonna have to. Really? So. Yeah.
Counselor: Don't sound too sure about that, though.
Client: I think returning is probably that's what's gonna make everyone happy. And I think, you know, at least I'll be able to finally achieve something and get something right, so. Yeah, like, next year I'm gonna. I'll get through it. Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So it doesn't. It doesn't sound like you want to go back.
Client: I do. I do enjoy it. I just don't feel like me at the moment and I just. It's a lot of work and it's a lot of pressure, but that's what comes of it. And, you know, it'll work out for the best if I go.
Counselor: Okay. So I guess then there's quite a lot of thoughts and feelings about going back at the moment. I'm just wondering, in the meantime, what are you up to? What have you been doing?
Client: Well, I've not really had much on the horizon. My mum, her friend, owns a restaurant and she suggested that I did a bit of waitressing there just for a bit of money and stuff, because obviously I'm not in uni, so I've done that.
Counselor: Okay. How many shifts have you done there?
Client: I've only done one so far. Yeah. I don't know whether it's something that I'd probably go back to, but.
Counselor: Okay. When was that shift?
Client: It was last week, actually. Okay.
Counselor: And how was it? I suppose I'm intrigued. Can you tell me a bit more about that?
Client: It was different, you know, because it was like, I could. I did enjoy it because there was like. It's just different aspect and I had to, like, speak to people and, like, try to get their orders and try to remember it and stuff. Like, I wasn't very good, but I suppose, like, it was handy to have some money and, like, get out the house.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you quite enjoyed that, then.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What makes you think you weren't very good?
Client: I just. I was just a bit slow and people sometimes didn't understand what I was saying, so I'd have to talk louder or quieter or slower. And I got a bit confused sometimes with the orders and I just don't really think that I'm not really, like, a friendly. Like, people don't really think that I'm a friendly person, so they didn't really want to talk to me and stuff. I felt like I was, like, inconveniencing them by, like, asking them things and getting things wrong. But, yeah, they said that apparently most people get, like, a few mistakes on their first shift. But then again, she's my mum's friend, so it's probably why she's saying it.
Counselor: So the person who owns a restaurant is your mum's friend?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So it says you're saying that you think you weren't very good and that's because you're a bit slow and you got confused with some orders.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is it? But you said it's common for people to do that on their first shift.
Client: That's what she said to us. But it's probably just. She's just trying to make me feel better. She probably felt sorry for me because I'm obviously not very good at it. Like, I'm not very good at any things. Recently, I think she just felt sorry for me.
Counselor: Okay. So I've just been noting down some of those thoughts that you've been having. You kind of say that you feel like you're not very good. You're slow, you're confused with the orders, and you feel like you're inconveniencing her and she feels. So for you. I suppose I'm wondering, I mean, what makes you think that she feels sorry for you?
Client: Well, like, like I said, she's my mum's friend, and she's obviously feeling sorry for my mum as well because she's got a daughter that's not like anyone else of her age, and she's just, like, all alone and she's not getting involved. So I think she just feels sorry for me and she doesn't want to say anything to upset me.
Counselor: But, yeah, when you're having these kind of thoughts, because that's quite a lot of negative thoughts you're describing, how do you feel?
Client: Empty? I don't. I'm just calling as it is. I'm just calling it as reality. And I feel like I'm being honest with myself by just voicing it and not trying to get around hiding it, because I know, like, I can say in myself.
Counselor: So it sounds like you feel like those thoughts are very true, then. I mean, if you were going to rate them, say, I'm going to pick out some of those thoughts you described. So you said I'm not very good and I'm inconveniencing them. How much would you say you believe those on a scale out of a hundred, where a hundred is like, I absolutely believe it and zero is like, I don't believe it at all.
Client: I'm about 80. Yeah.
Counselor: So you feel quite sure that you definitely believe those? Okay. And you said that when you're thinking those thoughts, you start to feel quite empty.
Client: I just feel distant. And like I said, I'm not really myself. I just. It's like I'm not really there, but when I am, I can't even do a good job.
Counselor: Are there any other emotions that you experience?
Client: I feel drained. I don't feel like I'm in touch with anything. Just. It's like everything's going on around me, but I'm just not there. I'm just. It's like I'm just watching.
Counselor: Okay, so you feel empty, distant. You feel drained. And how when you're feeling these emotions, how do you feel in your body? Kind of what sensations do you notice?
Client: I don't know how to describe it. I get, like, I have a bit of, like, you know when you kind of get, like, butterflies when you're nervous and stuff? Kind of get a bit of that.
Counselor: Do you feel some butterflies?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Did you have butterflies that night when you were at the restaurant?
Client: Yeah, I was pretty nervous then, but when I got into it, they went away and, like, it distracted me for a bit until, obviously, I realized that I wasn't doing a very good job.
Counselor: Okay. And when you have those emotions, how does it affect your energy levels? Do you feel more energetic, less energetic or about the same?
Client: When I'm feeling down, yeah.
Counselor: When you're having those emotions that you were describing, I just feel drained.
Client: Like, I didn't even have, like, the energy to wake up in the morning sometimes. Like, oh, I just feel pointless and, like, my body's heavy and I don't want to. Yeah.
Counselor: So it sounds like you feel very tired, you're struggling to wake up. You said it's pointless. And what do you do then when you feel like that? So I guess you just talked about when you wake up in the morning and you feel heavy, and I suppose you've been maybe having some of these thoughts and those emotions potentially the night before. What do you then do? How do you respond to that?
Client: I just have to get up. I suppose I don't really have a choice because my mum. I live with my mum, and I know it's hard for her, so I don't want her to be too worried. So I just. I just try to carry on as normal. I get up. It takes longer and I don't want to, but I do, and I'll get on with my routine.
Counselor: So you're a bit slower in getting up.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: But you are still getting up anyway. And what about your kind of. What do you think about when you're doing that?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: You doing okay?
Client: I guess, yeah.
Counselor: Not sure.
Client: I don't know, just the same.
Counselor: Yeah, still a little down.
Client: Yeah, I've been sleeping a lot. Going to work is a struggle. I don't really ever want to go. Just I haven't been eating much, so I think I've lost like ten pounds since past, like four months or so.
Counselor: Past four months?
Client: Um, just the guy. I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.
Counselor: You still been working?
Client: Well, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But not much else?
Client: No, I usually just go to work and go home.
Counselor: Tell me what happens after you arrive at home, like after work?
Client: Um, well, my fiance tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep for just. I don't know. I tried, I tried reading the other day. Cause I used to like that and it's just, I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.
Counselor: What were you thinking when you put the book down?
Client: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.
Counselor: I. And before you were depressed, which is, I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading?
Client: Mm hmm. Oh, yeah, all the time.
Counselor: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?
Client: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up till like two in the morning just reading a book.
Counselor: Something you look forward to?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But not now?
Client: No, I just didn't really get any. I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like.
Counselor: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?
Client: Yeah, I used to be a runner and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I. I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.
Counselor: Alright, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running, like when you first started?
Client: Not really. I mean, it was a change to be outdoors and I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while, so. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run. I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route. And by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.
Counselor: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?
Client: Kind of a mix of, like, relief just because it was over, and then, I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.
Counselor: Sadness, maybe disappointment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I've seen you a few times now, and based on those conversations, and, of course, what you said today, it seems like you have, for a variety of reasons, given up on the activities that you used to enjoy, you're not motivated toward them anymore.
Client: Yeah, I guess you could say that.
Counselor: And that's a common symptom of depression. I think we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed. So we've been working with the cognitive piece. Right, like we did last time, we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self talk. I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. We'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle. And the technique is called behavioral activation. The theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, like with the running, that will connect to your mood. Right. Remember, we believe in cognitive therapy, that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood and what you do. Your behavior affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we talked about?
Client: It does, yeah.
Counselor: So you mentioned the reading was one thing you like to do. That's tough to do. Now you try unsuccessfully with the reading and I the running. Anything else you could think of that maybe we could plan for you to do, even if it's just a short time, even if it's a little bit uncomfortable, that we could plan to do? That would be an activity that you used to enjoy?
Client: Well, my fiance and I used to go out with two other couples, and we used to go out once or twice a week, and even if it's just each other's houses, but we haven't really seen them in a while. They've tried to schedule things, but I've kind of come up with reasons of not feeling well or to kind of just stay home.
Counselor: So they're trying to initiate meeting, going out, doing something, and you're. You're kind of pushing them off.
Client: Yeah, I just. I haven't really wanted to see anybody lately.
Counselor: All right, so that's. So we have reading, running, and then going out with these two other couples. Anything else you can think of that you used to really enjoy before that you can't quite motivate yourself to do now?
Client: I mean, I used to like going for, like, just walks and shopping with my fiance. Like, I. We used to spend a lot of time together, and lately it's just kind of. I come home, say hello, we eat dinner, and then I kind of do my own thing.
Counselor: So spending time with your fiance outside the house in some manner? Shopping was one example. Any other activities like movies or going out to eat?
Client: Yeah, I would kind of put those in with the things that we would do outside together. We would try to switch it up every now and then.
Counselor: Okay, so that's distinct from what you did with the couples because that's just you and your fiance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So let's do this. What kind of books do you like to read?
Client: I like a lot of fiction. I do a lot of reading for school, so I usually enjoy those books too. Mystery novels.
Counselor: Mystery novels. Okay, let's center on mystery novels. How long would it take you to read, say, a chapter of a mystery.
Client: Novel, roughly, depending on the size of the chapter, probably a couple minutes normally.
Counselor: So not long at all.
Client: No.
Counselor: So you could get a lot of reading done in, say, ten minutes, like something worthwhile. And how often would it. How often would you, what was the duration of a run? Like when you would go run? How long would it take?
Client: Probably, like a half hour.
Counselor: Half hour.
Client: Half hour to 45 minutes. Yeah. I used to do long distance running, so.
Counselor: Okay, and how often would you do that?
Client: Three or four times a week.
Counselor: Three or four times a week? Half hour, 40 minutes. And you mentioned you went out with the couple once or twice a week. How often would you go out with your fiance?
Client: I would say we try to do something every day, like, even if it was just going for a walk together, like around the park or walking the dog together.
Counselor: Okay. So I'd like to make collaboratively with you a schedule that involves those four activities, but I want to make it realistic. You tried a couple times, you weren't successful. So we don't want to be too ambitious, but I want to try to plan a schedule. You can get the habit of doing these activities again. So let's start with the kind of, I guess the simplest in terms of logistics, which would be probably the reading. Would it be possible, say, five nights out of seven, to read for ten or 15 minutes? Like, I know you're going to have to force your way through it a little bit, but I think it's something.
Client: I could try to do.
Counselor: So you're going to have automatic thoughts that come up, right. Like, just like you did before, and you're going to be tempted to give up. I want you to try to push through, say, this at least ten minutes. So focus on that as you go into it. It's a behavioral exercise, of course. It has a cognitive component to kind of think, you know, I just have to make this ten minutes.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And again, you might not really enjoy it the same way it did before. We kind of know that, but over time, that may change.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right, so does five nights a week seem reasonable? That's 50 minutes a week.
Client: Yeah, that seems fine.
Counselor: Okay, then let's move to the running, because you just recently tried that. You run with your dog. You said, yeah, okay, how about that? Twice a week. Would that be possible?
Client: Yeah, I can try to do that.
Counselor: What days of the week you think you could do it?
Client: Probably the weekends. So probably like Saturday or Friday night or Saturday morning.
Counselor: Okay, so Saturday morning and Friday night, would you run Friday night and then again Saturday morning?
Client: No, I guess not. So probably I'd see maybe Wednesday night and Saturday morning.
Counselor: Okay, so Wednesday night and Saturday morning run for, say, a minimum of a half hour.
Client: I can try for that, yeah.
Counselor: Again, remember, you're gonna have these automatic thoughts, likely that will be telling you that you should stop, but you have to kind of talk your way through that or do the best you can.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. The adaptive response maybe being something like, in the end, this will help me. It's tough now, but this will help me. Okay, so let's look now toward the more social aspects. Logistically, moving up the ladder here to the most complex. It sounds like going out with their fiance would be the next. At the next level.
Client: Yeah, he's. I don't know if he's kind of just been mad at me lately or if he just thinks I need to be alone, but we've kind of been getting some distance there, so I think that would, out of everything, that would be the relationship I'd want to work on the most.
Counselor: Focus on. All right, so maybe you're running Wednesdays and Saturday mornings. Could you go out and do something to fiance twice a week.
Client: Yeah, I think we could manage that.
Counselor: Cause sometimes you said you just walk around, like, the neighborhood, so it's not even. Doesn't have to be necessarily, like, a lot of time. It's just something.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: All right. What do you think you can do to motivate yourself to do that?
Client: I don't know. I guess just having, like, him maybe remind me or suggest it.
Counselor: So you could tell him that this is something that you're planning to do and you might need a little push to. To do it.
Client: Yeah, pretty much.
Counselor: Or to maintain it.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you might get outside the same thing when you run. You might want to come right back in.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. And then moving to the most complex, but also the one with the highest social engagement, going out with the two couples now, once or twice a week, you'd mentioned before. How about we shoot for. How do we shoot for now? Once every couple weeks?
Client: I think I could handle that.
Counselor: Like, maybe a Saturday night or a Friday night.
Client: Yeah, I think that could work.
Counselor: What can you see being an obstacle there? Like, what might help you be motivated to continue that?
Client: Just having to actually go to their houses or go somewhere because they don't really live close to us. They're not far. But just the fact that we would have to get in the car, drive over there, and I would actually have to, like, look relatively nice. I can't just go and pajamas.
Counselor: So for this to work, that is for you to do it, you really have to schedule at their house. You can't have them come to you.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So that's one thing we know. You have to. You have to make some time and drive over there, or maybe if your fiance drives, whichever. But you have to.
Client: We physically have to go over.
Counselor: So once you're there. So it might be tough, like, to get in the car and make the drive over once you're there, how do you think it would feel?
Client: I don't know if it's like the run, I probably just want to turn around and come back.
Counselor: Do these couples know that you're down?
Client: I think they've noticed, and I think that's probably why they've kind of started to back off with asking us to do things. So I think they've noticed it, but they don't know, like, any. They don't know what's really going on.
Counselor: Are those relationships you're worried about losing because they're backing off?
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I. I mean, they're our closest friends, so I think we've known each other for a really long time.
Counselor: And could you see this behavior being one that brings you closer together with them? Like restore some of that?
Client: Yeah, I mean, I think it would definitely just us going. They might be a little hesitant because the past couple times they've invited us, we backed out. But I think it would probably be a step in that direction of restoring the relationships of. I mean, I would like to do that.
Counselor: Okay. So I want to review the plan and just make sure that we have an agreement because we're constructing this together. So I need your buy in reading five times a week for a minimum of ten minutes. The next level up was the running. And that was, that was Wednesday night and Saturday morning.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Going out two times with their fiance and then once every couple weeks, driving to your friends, going to their houses and spending an evening with them. All that realistic?
Client: I think so, yeah. I mean, I can try to get accountability with my fiance just to let him know my plan and then see if he can help me follow through with it, I guess.
Counselor:
output: Good. Alright, so let's set that as the plan. And I want you to be aware that as I mentioned, the automatic thoughts might come in. Right. And kind of tempt you in a direction away from that. I also want to let you know that if you are unsuccessful in any one of those things, it doesn't mean you have to stop and not try again. Just take it as a small setback. And then the next time, for example, it's time to read or go out running. Just try again. It's not unusual in this exercise that you won't be able to complete all the behaviors that you've planned for yourself. Sometimes life gets in the way things happen. Sometimes the depression gets in the way. So can you appreciate that that might be discouraging? Like, you try it and you stop. Like you told me in the beginning.

Client: Yes.
Counselor: Your thoughts were, I won't be able to make the presentation well, I am not qualified, and these people will not like it. These were the thoughts that were going through your head. Is that correct?
Client: Yes.

Client: Yes.

Client: Well, I don't know. Maybe not.
Counselor: How were you doing before you lost those two matches?
Client: We've only had four matches so far, but I won my first two matches.

Client: Yeah.

Counselor: In the bathroom?
Client: Yeah. She actually. Yeah. And she turned it into the police, and I guess because, like, she carried it, or she had found it, her handprints were on it, and they weren't be able. They weren't able to detect who actually did it. They weren't able to catch the person.
Counselor: Oh, they didn't catch the person?
Client: No. So since then, I've been on really just high alert. Like, I'm worried that that could happen to me, to my kids, and I'm just really worried because they didn't catch the guy, that him or someone like him could be out there.
Counselor: So he's still out in the community.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So how is it affecting your. Your daily life? Can you tell me kind of what your. What you've been feeling?
Client: Um, a lot of anxiety just not knowing, maybe, you know, what if someone were to videotape me like that? I've been very aware, shall I say, of cameras.
Counselor: Okay. So anxious and aware.
Client: Right. Like, I know you have one in your office, and people on their cell phone cameras. Just all the possibilities that I could be recorded. I've just been very aware of them, which makes me not want to go anywhere. So I've been having arguments with my husband a lot because he wants to go out to restaurants, and I don't want to go because there could be cameras in the bathrooms and how I dress. Also, as you can see, I'm kind of dressed more conservatively because I remember hearing once about cameras that people use on shoes that could be used in a creepy way. And so I can't. You know, it's now almost summertime. I can't dress in skirts or be comfortable because I'm dressing like that.
Counselor: So you covered a lot of ground there. So you have the. You have the feeling of being, like, worried, nervous. Right. That's going to happen to you, but you've also had to kind of change your routine, or you feel you have to change your routine to feel safer.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Has that helped. Has changing the way you dressed or changing where you go and when you go, has that helped reduce the anxiety?
Client: Not really, no. I would say it's really starting. That's why I wanted to come in. It's really starting to affect my life.
Counselor: You mentioned specifically your husband. Like, what's been going on there?
Client: He just wants to go places with our kids, like, go out to eat. And I don't really want to go anywhere because, you know, cameras are everywhere nowadays, and I just kind of worry, like, public bathrooms, could they be there? Could someone be, you know, sometimes baby monitors are, you know, hooked up on so people can hack into that laptop, cameras. So even in my own house, I've just been really nervous, so I feel like I'm not really getting relief from that anxiety.
Counselor: Have you taken any precautions because of this persistent worry? I mean, I already mentioned, like, with the camera specifically.
Client: I mean, I've, you know, when I go into bathrooms, I've been looking for cameras to make sure they weren't there before. You know, me or my children have used the bathroom. I have tried. I read online that you can turn how to turn off the cameras on your phone and that you can close your laptop, and that way the camera will face down. And the same thing on a smart tv so it doesn't recognize your face. I've tried to turn things off. They don't need to be on as far as people being able to access my own information.
Counselor: And that seems reasonable. So you take reasonable precautions to try to avoid being video recorded against your will.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Okay. But still, you have this feeling of worry, anxiety, and your schedules being interfered with.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you'd like to cope more effectively with your feelings, reduce this anxiety. So when you enter into a public bathroom. Now, we talked about automatic thoughts before.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Those thoughts just kind of pop into our head and they connect to feelings of that can be unpleasant, like anxiety and worry. So when you walk into a public restroom, what's the first thing that goes through your mind?
Client: That there might be a video camera that I don't see. That's maybe with my friend, it was big enough, but I might not catch it. And that someone's going to use that in a vulnerable way.
Counselor: Okay, so when you walk in, you're wondering if there's a camera there.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And when that automatic thought occurs, what follows that in terms of a feeling or behavior?
Client: Usually I'll try and find the camera, but it's usually anxiety, fear. My heart rate starts going up. I start getting really anxious. And then, you know, I try and either rush to use the bathroom if I really have to go, or a lot of times if I don't, I'll just leave. Sometimes I try and use the bathroom so I don't have to go out.
Counselor: So your behavior is looking for the camera or sometimes just leaving without using restroom, and you're feeling that anxiety worry that we've been talking about. Okay, so, really, if we think about. We talked before about core beliefs, intermediate beliefs, and I'm wondering if the intermediate belief isn't I'm vulnerable, or this more specifically, maybe that's more of a core belief. More specifically, I'm vulnerable in this area, like, with this guy on the loose that committed that crime, and then that's combining with situations that you encounter, and that's where you're getting those automatic thoughts. Does that sort of make sense?
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Okay, so you remember what, in terms of cognitive therapy, we like to apply what we call the adaptive response, or self talk.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So it's that thought that you interject at that moment, you realize you're having an automatic thought that's gonna lead to, in this case, anxiety and worry and behaviors that, while looking for the camera, isn't maybe an unusual behavior, but leaving, you know, that could certainly be an unuseful behavior. So, in terms of that self talk, let's work to develop a self talk response, something you can tell yourself to that initial. I wonder if there's a camera in this bathroom. What do you think you could tell yourself that would get in between that thought and I, the feelings you're having?
Client: I could say if when I walk in the bathroom, maybe I could say, you know, while there could be a chance that there's a camera in this bathroom, the chance of it happening is not very likely. And, you know, I'm going to take steps to keep myself safe so that I won't be in a vulnerable position, such as looking for the cameras.
Counselor: Right. That's good. So you have a low probability of it happening, and you're taking useful behaviors to minimize your risk even further.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So that's a good automatic thought, I think, or good adaptive response for the automatic thought. Rather, why don't you try that one out the next time you have that automatic thought? Try out that. I think that's really logical. It's unlikely to happen. Of course there's a chance, and we acknowledge that in the self talk, there's a chance that it could happen, but there's precautions you can take, and it's a low chance sometimes as well. So keep that automatic thought. We'll review it at the end before you leave today. We'll write these down. But that's one adaptive response, rather, that I want to write down for you. I also want to talk about the worst case scenario because right now you have the anxiety and the worry about an event that while it's unlikely it could happen, it could happen. And I'm wondering how you think you would react if the worst did happen. If you used the restroom and you found out from law enforcement or by finding a camera that an offender had been watching you on a recording. I think you would react to that.
Client: I mean, I think I would be really upset. Upset. I think I would feel vulnerable probably for a while and be hesitant.
Counselor: But.
Client: I mean, I think ultimately I would be okay. My friend, this happened a while ago. She's starting to get to get over it and get back to her usual routine, although she's still hesitant. So I think I would be okay eventually, although I'd be really upset that.
Counselor: It happened and it would make sense to feel upset. That would be upsetting for anybody. But as you noted, that would probably be relatively temporary, that distress, right. Well, acute. And certainly you wouldn't be happy about it and shouldn't be happy about it. It would probably go away. You'd probably learn to adapt. How long have you been in this state of anxiety and worry?
Client: Probably it happened, like, two months ago.
Counselor: Two months. And how many days in the average week are you affected by these feelings?
Client: Usually every day.
Counselor: Every day. So if we can compare it, right, we have the chances of being recorded. Right. Illegally. That's a low probability event. It can happen. Probably not likely. The anxiety and the worry that you're having, that's a high probability event because you're suffering from it every day.
Client: Yeah, that's true. I never thought about it that way.
Counselor: So there's a point at which maybe you reach and you say, I'd rather take. I'd rather take the risk. I'd rather deal with the potential consequence of an unlikely event of being recorded and face that if it happens, than be in the state of anxiety and worry.
Client: Right. Because right now I'm suffering every day.
Counselor: Right now you're suffering, right. If you could adaptively respond effectively, you're still going to have that risk of being recorded, but, you know, you could survive that event if it happened, right?
Client: Yeah, I think I could have.
Counselor: And you're taking reasonable cautions and, you know, all the things we talked about. So as you think about this in a more general sense, is there an adaptive response you could apply to that, to that automatic thought of, I need to be worried about this, or whatever that thought looks like. Sometimes the thought's an image, right? Maybe an image of being recorded, but whatever that kind of general series of automatic thoughts are that are getting you anxious and worried before you even get out of the house. What adaptive response could you apply there?
Client: Maybe, like I said, I'm worried about all the cameras. Maybe I could say, I understand there's some cameras that, you know, used for good purposes, like security.
Counselor: Probably most are right.
Client: And the chances of being recorded illegally are not likely. And I'm taking precautions to, you know, go to the right places, the good area, good areas. So it's not likely to happen overall. And me going outside the house is worth the risk, you know, the minimal risk that it would happen. And if it did happen, I could survive.
Counselor: That's great. That's a great adaptive response. Yeah. And actually, that's kind of a few adaptive responses, but that's good. And you can apply them, and we'll kind of break them down. Like I said before you leave today, we'll break those down so you can hammer it down as you go out. And I think it's important because the automatic thoughts tend to spring on us quickly. It's important to rehearse these adaptive responses so we're ready to go and kind of, we're preparing ourselves to apply that adaptive response. And in order to be prepared, you have to know what it is. So it's good to have it written down and kind of more or less commit to memory.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Does that kind of make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so before you leave today, I'll take care of that, and I want you to use those adaptive responses for this week. I'll see you next week and record what the outcome was every time you're able to apply the adaptive response. And that includes what you felt and what you actually did.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And, of course, as you mentioned, any physiological reactions like your heart racing or anything like that. So that's really. That's a behavior. But note both physiological behaviors and other behaviors. Once you're consciously controlling. And then any feelings. And we'll go through them. We'll go through each time you use it one by one, depending how many there are. I and kind of see if we need to adjust the adaptive response and see how well it's working.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: Does that sound like the plan?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Leigh. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good.
Counselor: You're doing good?
Client: Yeah. Okay. I guess you guessed. Yeah. Um. Well, I guess I'll tell you, but I, I'm kind of embarrassed to tell you, but, so, like, I'm in college, and all my friends are dating, and I'm just really, like, nervous to just tell you, but, like, I really haven't dated before, and I'm really nervous and scared to date, and I just I just don't know how to do it, and I don't know. I'm just nervous.
Counselor: So, nervousness and some anxiety around dating. You said you'd never really dated before.
Client: No, not really. I mean, I just was never, you know, that was never enforced in my family. I was never allowed to really do that. So just the thought of it is, like, like, scary, scary for you? Yeah. So, you know, I mean, I tend to talk to guys, but it was just like, like, you know, real short and bye, like hi bye kind of thing. Because, like I said, that just was never enforced in my family. And just never, I was never, that's never applaud. That was never applauded in when I was growing up, so I never did it, and I was scared to do it for the repercussions, getting in trouble. So.
Counselor: All right, so no dating in high school. And what type of interactions did you have in high school? You said, you said hi a few times.
Client: Yeah, just like in my science class, you know, particularly this one time, I actually sat next to this boy who was super cute, but, you know, we would say hi, and that was it. He would try to ask me stuff about classwork or the assignment, and I would not even look at him and just tell him and look at my schoolwork. And that was the extent of it, you know?
Counselor: So let's talk about your anxiety. You have anxiety and earlier, like, reaction just to thinking about it. Right. You think about dating. It's just, it's a lot for you. Do you think this anxiety comes from a fear of what might happen, or is this something more how you'll be perceived? Like, what do you think is leading to?
Client: I think it's a little bit of both. I definitely always compare myself to my sisters, and they're super pretty, and I just don't feel attractive enough to have somebody be interested in me. And if they were to be interested in me, I'm not allowed to date, you know, so the repercussion would just be, you know, I'd kind of be shunned for doing so. So it kind of just stayed with me, you know, now I'm 24 and I'm in school, and it's just so overwhelming. And I'm kind of envious of my girlfriends because they're able to do it, and I'm like, damn. Like, how did they do that? So.
Counselor: So that process is far from removed from you. You look at that and think, I don't even know how to approach it.
Client: It's like a foreign object. Like, yeah.
Counselor: So how would you say, how would you describe yourself? Like, how do you feel about yourself?
Client: I always do the right thing. I'm really studious, and I like to have fun. When I'm with my girlfriends, we have a great time, and I'm personable with them and my family, but it's just when it comes to interacting with male, it's just super difficult for me. And I can tell you why, but I can't tell you why. You know, it's kind of that, like, it's like a seesaw every time I'm with a male, you know, in a dating aspect anyway, so it's just difficult for me.
Counselor: Is there a particular outcome that you're afraid of? Like, when you're, well, you're in college now, right? So likely interact with males to some extent. Is there when an opportunity comes up when somebody's interested in you? Is there a particular fear that comes to mind?
Client: Yeah, like, I don't even know why you're talking to me. Like, why would you talk to me? I'm not pretty. I'm flipping awkward. Like, you know, why would you even be interested?
Counselor: So you think yourself as unattractive and awkward?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you question why they would be interested in you?
Client: Yeah.
