Counselor: So have you ever had evidence presented to the contrary, like, people who thought you were attractive and not awkward?
Client: Um, well, yeah, I mean, yeah, like, people have told me that I'm pretty and, um, you know, fun and stuff like that, so, yeah, I have.
Counselor: Yeah. But there's some, so they're telling you that? But there's something else telling you that you're not?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you think that's coming from?
Client: I guess just from my, you know, my mom and I think just her rules that I guess I just associated, you know, me not being able to date, that I wasn't presentable enough to date. And I just got this idea that that's the reason why she just didn't want me to date.
Counselor: So you think her reasoning for not allowing you to date, I wasn't the pretty daughter? Were your sisters allowed to date?
Client: They were allowed to date, but under certain circumstances, certain rules they had to follow. But just when I would, you know, even suggest it to my mom, it was just like, no, you're not.
Counselor: So you feel like you were, of you and your sisters, you were the one treated the most strictly on that. But was it much more strictly or just a little differently?
Client: I think it was much more strictly, yeah. Because it's so much so now that I can't even talk to a guy. It's just. I mean, the anxiety and the fear is so intense. I just can't explain it. It's horrible that it's not like that for my sisters because now they're married, you know, so they have kids, and it's like, what the heck happened here? And I can recognize it, but I just can't bring myself to do it, like talk to somebody or, you know.
Counselor: So the way you perceive yourself, the self image here is part of this?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, absolutely.
Counselor: So you have evidence that says that men would be interested in going out with you, dating you, but internally, these thoughts you're having say you're just not worthy.
Client: You know what I mean?
Counselor: That's kind of the theme of it, right?
Client: Yeah, absolutely. That's it.
Counselor: And maybe this is tied to a core belief. Like we talked about core beliefs before cognitive therapy. Are there any of those core beliefs in the list I gave you a few weeks ago kind of stood out that you think might be core beliefs you have?
Client: That I'm unlovable.
Counselor: Unlovable, yeah. Any others?
Client: Fear of rejection.
Counselor: So fear of being rejected?
Client: Fear of being rejected. Yeah.
Counselor: So unlovable. And a fear of being rejected. And then when you have interactions in the moment, like, say you're in class and there's a man sitting next to you in class, and they're interested in you, he's interested in you. He says something that expresses that he's interested. You're immediately suspect.
Client: Oh, yeah.
Counselor: That's what you're.
Client: Oh, yeah. That's like. It's like, what is it? Fight or flight kind of feeling like it really is. It's like, oh, you know. Yeah. Just something comes over me where, you know, it's kind of like I'm conditioned because I don't even live with my mom and my dad now, and I'm on my own, but yet I still hold their values. And not just. All I can just think of is being in high school and having. Being told I can't do that or just the rules and having to follow it. And that's really where I feel like I'm there. If someone says something to me, it.
Counselor: Takes you right back there.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. I. So how do your parents feel about now? Have they said anything like, your sisters are married and you're not? Have they pointed that out?
Client: No, they haven't. Not really. No. Because my mom really wants me. She. I guess. Well, maybe it has to do with that. Like, I'm smarter than my sisters, so she really wants me to be a doctor. And my sisters, they have, you know, they have great jobs, but, you know, they just stopped at a bachelor's degree, and I'm really working to be a doctor. And I always had straight a's in high school and my sisters didn't. So I think that my mom wants to hold on to that, you know, that hope that I'm going to be something great. So she doesn't really enforce the dating thing with me. I guess she's for fear that that's going to get in the way.
Counselor: That's different than being unlovable, right? Yeah. I mean, her reasoning, as you're describing her reasoning sounds more like she wants you to reach a higher educational goal.
Client: I mean, I guess. Yeah.
Counselor: What do you want?
Client: I want to be in a relationship with somebody because all of my friends are, and I'm always that. They're real and it's difficult. I mean, yeah, I want the education. Don't get me wrong, I want a great job, but I don't want to do that alone. I want to have somebody with me that I can confide in and just a confidante. And the time is now. I'm ready, you know? And maybe my mom was just protecting me, I guess. I don't know what she was doing, but I really don't care because I really want to try it. I just don't know how.
Counselor: There's opposing forces at work here, right? I mean, you're motivated to try it like it's a goal. You want to be able to date, you want to go out. It's important to you. Do you want to get married like your sisters?
Client: Yeah, I do.
Counselor: You do? So you have these clear goals, and that's one force. And then the supposing force is this. Well, one of them would be this anxiety that comes over you in the moment when a man's talking to you. Like in that way. Right. Like about going out or any topic like that. So a part of you. A part of you is saying, I really want to move forward and date different people and see if I can find a good match. And another part of you is saying I need to run away. Like you said, fight or flight, right? I want to run away and not have this awkwardness, this anxiety.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Because it's a. I just keep thinking of the repercussions, like now as an adult, that my mom's just. I guess that she wouldn't talk to me. But I'm not in high school anymore, so I don't know. I just. I honestly don't know what the conversation would be like if I talked to a guy that I was interested in or if a guy was interested in me. I mean, because I came to the realization, and my friends have helped me with this, that I am in college, I am an adult now. And, you know, what my mom thinks is what she thinks now. It's just me peeing in front of a male that I'm attracted to, that I want to go out with.
Counselor:
output: And what you said is you don't know what would happen, so you don't know that it would be bad. You don't know that it would be a bad experience.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: You doing okay?
Client: I guess, yeah.
Counselor: Not sure.
Client: I don't know, just the same.
Counselor: Yeah, still a little down.
Client: Yeah, I've been sleeping a lot. Going to work is a struggle. I don't really ever want to go. Just I haven't been eating much, so I think I've lost like ten pounds since past, like four months or so.
Counselor: Past four months?
Client: Um, just the guy. I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.
Counselor: You still been working?
Client: Well, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But not much else?
Client: No, I usually just go to work and go home.
Counselor: Tell me what happens after you arrive at home, like after work?
Client: Um, well, my fiance tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep for just. I don't know. I tried, I tried reading the other day. Cause I used to like that and it's just, I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.
Counselor: What were you thinking when you put the book down?
Client: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.
Counselor: I. And before you were depressed, which is, I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading?
Client: Mm hmm. Oh, yeah, all the time.
Counselor: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?
Client: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up till like two in the morning just reading a book.
Counselor: Something you look forward to?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But not now?
Client: No, I just didn't really get any. I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like.
Counselor: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?
Client: Yeah, I used to be a runner and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I. I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.
Counselor: Alright, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running, like when you first started?
Client: Not really. I mean, it was a change to be outdoors and I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while, so. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run. I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route. And by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.
Counselor: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?
Client: Kind of a mix of, like, relief just because it was over, and then, I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.
Counselor: Sadness, maybe disappointment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I've seen you a few times now, and based on those conversations, and, of course, what you said today, it seems like you have, for a variety of reasons, given up on the activities that you used to enjoy, you're not motivated toward them anymore.
Client: Yeah, I guess you could say that.
Counselor: And that's a common symptom of depression. I think we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed. So we've been working with the cognitive piece. Right, like we did last time, we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self talk. I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. We'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle. And the technique is called behavioral activation. The theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, like with the running, that will connect to your mood. Right. Remember, we believe in cognitive therapy, that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood and what you do. Your behavior affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we talked about?
Client: It does, yeah.
Counselor: So you mentioned the reading was one thing you like to do. That's tough to do. Now you try unsuccessfully with the reading and I the running. Anything else you could think of that maybe we could plan for you to do, even if it's just a short time, even if it's a little bit uncomfortable, that we could plan to do? That would be an activity that you used to enjoy?
Client: Well, my fiance and I used to go out with two other couples, and we used to go out once or twice a week, and even if it's just each other's houses, but we haven't really seen them in a while. They've tried to schedule things, but I've kind of come up with reasons of not feeling well or to kind of just stay home.
Counselor: So they're trying to initiate meeting, going out, doing something, and you're. You're kind of pushing them off.
Client: Yeah, I just. I haven't really wanted to see anybody lately.
Counselor: All right, so that's. So we have reading, running, and then going out with these two other couples. Anything else you can think of that you used to really enjoy before that you can't quite motivate yourself to do now?
Client: I mean, I used to like going for, like, just walks and shopping with my fiance. Like, I. We used to spend a lot of time together, and lately it's just kind of. I come home, say hello, we eat dinner, and then I kind of do my own thing.
Counselor: So spending time with your fiance outside the house in some manner? Shopping was one example. Any other activities like movies or going out to eat?
Client: Yeah, I would kind of put those in with the things that we would do outside together. We would try to switch it up every now and then.
Counselor: Okay, so that's distinct from what you did with the couples because that's just you and your fiance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So let's do this. What kind of books do you like to read?
Client: I like a lot of fiction. I do a lot of reading for school, so I usually enjoy those books too. Mystery novels.
Counselor: Mystery novels. Okay, let's center on mystery novels. How long would it take you to read, say, a chapter of a mystery.
Client: Novel, roughly, depending on the size of the chapter, probably a couple minutes normally.
Counselor: So not long at all.
Client: No.
Counselor: So you could get a lot of reading done in, say, ten minutes, like something worthwhile. And how often would it. How often would you, what was the duration of a run? Like when you would go run? How long would it take?
Client: Probably, like a half hour.
Counselor: Half hour.
Client: Half hour to 45 minutes. Yeah. I used to do long distance running, so.
Counselor: Okay, and how often would you do that?
Client: Three or four times a week.
Counselor: Three or four times a week? Half hour, 40 minutes. And you mentioned you went out with the couple once or twice a week. How often would you go out with your fiance?
Client: I would say we try to do something every day, like, even if it was just going for a walk together, like around the park or walking the dog together.
Counselor: Okay. So I'd like to make collaboratively with you a schedule that involves those four activities, but I want to make it realistic. You tried a couple times, you weren't successful. So we don't want to be too ambitious, but I want to try to plan a schedule. You can get the habit of doing these activities again. So let's start with the kind of, I guess the simplest in terms of logistics, which would be probably the reading. Would it be possible, say, five nights out of seven, to read for ten or 15 minutes? Like, I know you're going to have to force your way through it a little bit, but I think it's something.
Client: I could try to do.
Counselor: So you're going to have automatic thoughts that come up, right. Like, just like you did before, and you're going to be tempted to give up. I want you to try to push through, say, this at least ten minutes. So focus on that as you go into it. It's a behavioral exercise, of course. It has a cognitive component to kind of think, you know, I just have to make this ten minutes.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And again, you might not really enjoy it the same way it did before. We kind of know that, but over time, that may change.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right, so does five nights a week seem reasonable? That's 50 minutes a week.
Client: Yeah, that seems fine.
Counselor: Okay, then let's move to the running, because you just recently tried that. You run with your dog. You said, yeah, okay, how about that? Twice a week. Would that be possible?
Client: Yeah, I can try to do that.
Counselor: What days of the week you think you could do it?
Client: Probably the weekends. So probably like Saturday or Friday night or Saturday morning.
Counselor: Okay, so Saturday morning and Friday night, would you run Friday night and then again Saturday morning?
Client: No, I guess not. So probably I'd see maybe Wednesday night and Saturday morning.
Counselor: Okay, so Wednesday night and Saturday morning run for, say, a minimum of a half hour.
Client: I can try for that, yeah.
Counselor: Again, remember, you're gonna have these automatic thoughts, likely that will be telling you that you should stop, but you have to kind of talk your way through that or do the best you can.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. The adaptive response maybe being something like, in the end, this will help me. It's tough now, but this will help me. Okay, so let's look now toward the more social aspects. Logistically, moving up the ladder here to the most complex. It sounds like going out with their fiance would be the next. At the next level.
Client: Yeah, he's. I don't know if he's kind of just been mad at me lately or if he just thinks I need to be alone, but we've kind of been getting some distance there, so I think that would, out of everything, that would be the relationship I'd want to work on the most.
Counselor: Focus on. All right, so maybe you're running Wednesdays and Saturday mornings. Could you go out and do something to fiance twice a week.
Client: Yeah, I think we could manage that.
Counselor:
output: Cause sometimes you said you just walk around, like, the neighborhood, so it's not even. Doesn't have to be necessarily, like, a lot of time. It's just something.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, so you said that when you're at work, you really worry that you're gonna say something stupid?
Client: Yeah, that's something that's always on my mind.
Counselor: What would be so bad about that if you did say something stupid at work?
Client: Because people would think I was weird.
Counselor: Then what would be so bad if people. People at work thought you were weird?
Client: They wouldn't want to be friends with me.
Counselor: And what would be so bad about that if people at work didn't want to be friends with you?
Client: Well, I just have no one to talk to at work.
Counselor: Then what would be so bad about having no one to talk to at work?
Client: I mean, the shoots can go on the whole day, so I'd just be by myself the whole time.
Counselor: And what would be so bad about being by yourself, you know, for a whole day?
Client: I don't know. I guess I should be used to it now. I spend a lot of my time by myself.
Counselor: Oh, that must be tough. What does that mean to you? That you spend a lot of time on your own?
Client: Dunno. I guess it's just like I spend so much time by myself that it's kind of like I'm nothing even worth being friends with.
Counselor: So it sounds like deep down that you think that you're not worth being friends with. That's quite a negative belief. I mean, how much would you say that you believe that out of a hundred? If 100 is where you believe it totally. And zero is where you don't believe it at all?
Client: I guess like 9500.
Counselor: When did you start believing that?
Client: I think it was probably at school. Yeah, I think at school.
Counselor: And what was it about school that made you start to believe that you weren't worth being friends with?
Client: Just like quite a lot of things. Like I wouldn't have anyone sit at lunch or people's birthdays and stuff. I wasn't invited and you know, like I was the last one picked for teams and stuff like that.
Counselor: And what is it now that makes you think that that's still true?
Client: I mean, it's kind of similar at work, obviously. Difference is that it's work, not school. But you know, people go for drinks and stuff after work or after a shoot, and I just kind of excluded a lot of the time.
Counselor: That sounds tough. Is there anything that makes you think that it's not true that you are worth being friends with?
Client: I guess my friends and family would say that I am. Like, I try to make a lot of time for my friends and stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like deep down you have this thought that you're not worth being friends with. And that started at school when you had trouble making friends at school and that you weren't always picked for teams and that now at work it feels like the same thing is happening, that you're not always invited out for drinks with people and that sometimes you feel that you're excluded from their social groups. But then that's not the whole story. That on the other hand, you are close to family and you do have friends who would say that it's not true that you are worth being friends with. In CBT, we do a thing called thought challenging where when we have these negative thoughts, sometimes we actually put them up to scrutiny. We weigh up the evidence for and against them. I like to think of it as putting the thought on trial. Could we do that now where we just actually try and weigh up the evidence for and against that thought a bit more?
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. So if I just put two columns here, so for and against. And it sounds like the evidence for this thought that makes you think that it is true is difficulty at school, making friends, being picked for teams, and difficulty at work, feeling excluded sometimes from groups.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But actually in this other column we have that you are close with your family and that you have some close friends. Okay. Now moving back to this first column, is there anything else that makes you think it's true that you're not worth being friends with?
Client: Just like, I kind of don't go to a lot of stuff. People have, like gatherings and things and a lot of the time I just. I don't go and rather just stay at home.
Counselor: Don't go to parties. What kind of parties are we talking? Like big parties, small parties, mainly big ones.
Client: If there's a lot of people there, I just find it really. It kind of makes me really anxious. So a lot of the time I just prefer not even to be in that situation in the first place.
Counselor: Okay. So you don't go to larger parties and events. Okay. Is there anything else that maybe thinks that it's makes you think that it's not true that actually you are worth being friends with?
Client: I mean, I guess my friends would say that I was. I do have close friends and, you know, when it's like their stuff that's important to them, I always make sure that I think about that. And even if I find it stressful, I'll always make sure that I can kind of put them first.
Counselor: Okay. So your friends would say that you are worth being friends with and it sounds like you put your friends first.
Client: Yeah, I do. Make sure I try and do that.
Counselor: In what kind of ways do you put your friends first?
Client: I guess when it's birthdays or, you know, something important to them, I'll always make sure that I'm there and that I put a lot of thought into presence and stuff like that.
Counselor: Can you give me an example of a time that you've done that?
Client: It was my friend's birthday a few weeks ago and we did like a big surprise at hers and I made a cake and stuff like that.
Counselor: So you actually helped to organize events for your friends?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is there anything that you do that you wouldn't do if you weren't a good friend?
Client: I guess I kind of always put myself in a situation, even if I find it kind of. It makes me anxious. If it's for my close friends and I know that it's something that's important to them, then I'll always put them first and make sure I'm there.
Counselor: So you'll tolerate your anxiety if it means something to a friend of yours?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So at the moment in the four category we've got that you had difficulty making friends at school, that you're having difficulty now at work making friends, and that you don't go to larger parties or events. But actually there's a lot of evidence in the against column, evidence that would suggest that actually you are worth being friends with and you're a good friend, that you're close with your family, you're close with your friends, your friends would say that you're a good friend of you put your friends first. Even when you're anxious, you tolerate that anxiety if you know it will mean something to them. That when things are important to your friends, like birthdays, you'll make a real effort. You'll even actually go to the effort of organising events and baking cakes and doing things like that for other people. Is there anything else that you do that makes you think that maybe you are a good friend, you are worth being friends with?
Client: I mean, I still have my friends, so I guess if I wasn't worth being friends with, I wouldn't have these friends I've had for quite, quite a long time.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you've got long term friendships as well, so you might have trouble making friends, but when you make them, you stick with them.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, I'm just going to give you this list now to have a look at.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: How do you feel now that you're looking at that list?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Leigh. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good.
Counselor: You're doing good?
Client: Yeah. Okay. I guess you guessed. Yeah. Um. Well, I guess I'll tell you, but I, I'm kind of embarrassed to tell you, but, so, like, I'm in college, and all my friends are dating, and I'm just really, like, nervous to just tell you, but, like, I really haven't dated before, and I'm really nervous and scared to date, and I just I just don't know how to do it, and I don't know. I'm just nervous.
Counselor: So, nervousness and some anxiety around dating. You said you'd never really dated before.
Client: No, not really. I mean, I just was never, you know, that was never enforced in my family. I was never allowed to really do that. So just the thought of it is, like, like, scary, scary for you? Yeah. So, you know, I mean, I tend to talk to guys, but it was just like, like, you know, real short and bye, like hi bye kind of thing. Because, like I said, that just was never enforced in my family. And just never, I was never, that's never applaud. That was never applauded in when I was growing up, so I never did it, and I was scared to do it for the repercussions, getting in trouble. So.
Counselor: All right, so no dating in high school. And what type of interactions did you have in high school? You said, you said hi a few times.
Client: Yeah, just like in my science class, you know, particularly this one time, I actually sat next to this boy who was super cute, but, you know, we would say hi, and that was it. He would try to ask me stuff about classwork or the assignment, and I would not even look at him and just tell him and look at my schoolwork. And that was the extent of it, you know?
Counselor: So let's talk about your anxiety. You have anxiety and earlier, like, reaction just to thinking about it. Right. You think about dating. It's just, it's a lot for you. Do you think this anxiety comes from a fear of what might happen, or is this something more how you'll be perceived? Like, what do you think is leading to?
Client: I think it's a little bit of both. I definitely always compare myself to my sisters, and they're super pretty, and I just don't feel attractive enough to have somebody be interested in me. And if they were to be interested in me, I'm not allowed to date, you know, so the repercussion would just be, you know, I'd kind of be shunned for doing so. So it kind of just stayed with me, you know, now I'm 24 and I'm in school, and it's just so overwhelming. And I'm kind of envious of my girlfriends because they're able to do it, and I'm like, damn. Like, how did they do that? So.
Counselor: So that process is far from removed from you. You look at that and think, I don't even know how to approach it.
Client: It's like a foreign object. Like, yeah.
Counselor: So how would you say, how would you describe yourself? Like, how do you feel about yourself?
Client: I always do the right thing. I'm really studious, and I like to have fun. When I'm with my girlfriends, we have a great time, and I'm personable with them and my family, but it's just when it comes to interacting with male, it's just super difficult for me. And I can tell you why, but I can't tell you why. You know, it's kind of that, like, it's like a seesaw every time I'm with a male, you know, in a dating aspect anyway, so it's just difficult for me.
Counselor: Is there a particular outcome that you're afraid of? Like, when you're, well, you're in college now, right? So likely interact with males to some extent. Is there when an opportunity comes up when somebody's interested in you? Is there a particular fear that comes to mind?
Client: Yeah, like, I don't even know why you're talking to me. Like, why would you talk to me? I'm not pretty. I'm flipping awkward. Like, you know, why would you even be interested?
Counselor: So you think yourself as unattractive and awkward?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you question why they would be interested in you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So have you ever had evidence presented to the contrary, like, people who thought you were attractive and not awkward?
Client: Um, well, yeah, I mean, yeah, like, people have told me that I'm pretty and, um, you know, fun and stuff like that, so, yeah, I have.
Counselor: Yeah. But there's some, so they're telling you that? But there's something else telling you that you're not?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you think that's coming from?
Client: I guess just from my, you know, my mom and I think just her rules that I guess I just associated, you know, me not being able to date, that I wasn't presentable enough to date. And I just got this idea that that's the reason why she just didn't want me to date.
Counselor: So you think her reasoning for not allowing you to date, I wasn't the pretty daughter? Were your sisters allowed to date?
Client: They were allowed to date, but under certain circumstances, certain rules they had to follow. But just when I would, you know, even suggest it to my mom, it was just like, no, you're not.
Counselor: So you feel like you were, of you and your sisters, you were the one treated the most strictly on that. But was it much more strictly or just a little differently?
Client: I think it was much more strictly, yeah. Because it's so much so now that I can't even talk to a guy. It's just. I mean, the anxiety and the fear is so intense. I just can't explain it. It's horrible that it's not like that for my sisters because now they're married, you know, so they have kids, and it's like, what the heck happened here? And I can recognize it, but I just can't bring myself to do it, like talk to somebody or, you know.
Counselor: So the way you perceive yourself, the self image here is part of this?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, absolutely.
Counselor: So you have evidence that says that men would be interested in going out with you, dating you, but internally, these thoughts you're having say you're just not worthy.
Client: You know what I mean?
Counselor: That's kind of the theme of it, right?
Client: Yeah, absolutely. That's it.
Counselor: And maybe this is tied to a core belief. Like we talked about core beliefs before cognitive therapy. Are there any of those core beliefs in the list I gave you a few weeks ago kind of stood out that you think might be core beliefs you have?
Client: That I'm unlovable.
Counselor: Unlovable, yeah. Any others?
Client: Fear of rejection.
Counselor: So fear of being rejected?
Client: Fear of being rejected. Yeah.
Counselor: So unlovable. And a fear of being rejected. And then when you have interactions in the moment, like, say you're in class and there's a man sitting next to you in class, and they're interested in you, he's interested in you. He says something that expresses that he's interested. You're immediately suspect.
Client: Oh, yeah.
Counselor: That's what you're.
Client: Oh, yeah. That's like. It's like, what is it? Fight or flight kind of feeling like it really is. It's like, oh, you know. Yeah. Just something comes over me where, you know, it's kind of like I'm conditioned because I don't even live with my mom and my dad now, and I'm on my own, but yet I still hold their values. And not just. All I can just think of is being in high school and having. Being told I can't do that or just the rules and having to follow it. And that's really where I feel like I'm there. If someone says something to me, it.
Counselor: Takes you right back there.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. I. So how do your parents feel about now? Have they said anything like, your sisters are married and you're not? Have they pointed that out?
Client: No, they haven't. Not really. No. Because my mom really wants me. She. I guess. Well, maybe it has to do with that. Like, I'm smarter than my sisters, so she really wants me to be a doctor. And my sisters, they have, you know, they have great jobs, but, you know, they just stopped at a bachelor's degree, and I'm really working to be a doctor. And I always had straight a's in high school and my sisters didn't. So I think that my mom wants to hold on to that, you know, that hope that I'm going to be something great. So she doesn't really enforce the dating thing with me. I guess she's for fear that that's going to get in the way.
Counselor: That's different than being unlovable, right? Yeah. I mean, her reasoning, as you're describing her reasoning sounds more like she wants you to reach a higher educational goal.
Client: I mean, I guess. Yeah.
Counselor: What do you want?
Client: I want to be in a relationship with somebody because all of my friends are, and I'm always that. They're real and it's difficult. I mean, yeah, I want the education. Don't get me wrong, I want a great job, but I don't want to do that alone. I want to have somebody with me that I can confide in and just a confidante. And the time is now. I'm ready, you know? And maybe my mom was just protecting me, I guess. I don't know what she was doing, but I really don't care because I really want to try it. I just don't know how.
Counselor: There's opposing forces at work here, right? I mean, you're motivated to try it like it's a goal. You want to be able to date, you want to go out. It's important to you. Do you want to get married like your sisters?
Client: Yeah, I do.
Counselor: You do? So you have these clear goals, and that's one force. And then the supposing force is this. Well, one of them would be this anxiety that comes over you in the moment when a man's talking to you. Like in that way. Right. Like about going out or any topic like that. So a part of you. A part of you is saying, I really want to move forward and date different people and see if I can find a good match. And another part of you is saying I need to run away. Like you said, fight or flight, right? I want to run away and not have this awkwardness, this anxiety.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Because it's a. I just keep thinking of the repercussions, like now as an adult, that my mom's just. I guess that she wouldn't talk to me. But I'm not in high school anymore, so I don't know. I just. I honestly don't know what the conversation would be like if I talked to a guy that I was interested in or if a guy was interested in me. I mean, because I came to the realization, and my friends have helped me with this, that I am in college, I am an adult now. And, you know, what my mom thinks is what she thinks now. It's just me peeing in front of a male that I'm attracted to, that I want to go out with.
Counselor: And what you said is you don't know what would happen, so you don't know that it would be bad. You don't know that it would be a bad experience.
Client: Right? I don't know. I don't know if it's going to be bad, but you don't know if.
Counselor: It'S going to be good either.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a risk.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So in the situation you're in, if you can get through that anxiety and have a conversation, it could end up where things went very well or didn't. So what happens if it doesn't go well?
Client: Well, I mean, like I said, I think because my mom didn't let me date that it was sign that I was unattractive, so I could take it that way, that I was just unattractive, but that he wouldn't have initiated the date if I was unattractive.
Counselor: Good point.
Client: So for that, I was. It just didn't work. You know, there just wasn't anything in common with what I'm about. You know, that I have different hobbies and he has different hobbies, and maybe they just don't mesh well and I have to. That could be a reason why it didn't work. Not that I'm. I guess, nothing. I'm lovable. You know, I shouldn't take it that personal, but it's hard.
Counselor: It's difficult for you. This is painful for you.
Client: Yeah, it is.
Counselor: You're fighting through some strong feelings. If you try to look at the logical, right. If it's likely you just because of the way it works, you'd have to date several people to find somebody that was a match.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So some of those relationships you'll end, maybe some of the man will end, but eventually, one likely you would stumble on, or neither one of you would end it. So there's risk involved here. There's a risk of rejection. There's a risk of having to reject. That doesn't seem to be the risk you're most worried about, though. You're more worried about the risk of being rejected.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Because you're questioning their intent.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: So can you survive being rejected?
Client: I think. I think I can, you know. Yeah. I mean, because in essence, I was, you know, rejected by my mom, but I still moved forward with my life because since she didn't let me date, that's a rejection from her that I'm not worthy. So, yes, I think because my friends have helped me, so that's a step in the right direction.
Counselor: And you took that behavior from your mother as rejection. And it seems like that may not have been her reason for doing that. You don't know for sure.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But even if it was, which it seems unlikely it would have been, that's still just one person.
Client: Yeah, yeah. That is just one person.
Counselor: So if we just take it to the extreme and say for some reason.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: You know, she didn't think you were worthy. That's just one person opinion.
Client: Yeah, absolutely. Right. Because my friends think I'm worthy. Right.
Counselor: And their opinions are valid too.
Client: Right? They are.
Counselor: So if you really look at it and weigh the evidence and look at it logically, the imbalance of the evidence would say that you are worthy.
Client: Right.
Counselor: You're not unlovable. But still, in any type of relational situation, there's going to be rejection. So there's potential pain up ahead, but the reward could be you find somebody that you want to be with. And that's really your goal.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So really part of this is pushing through a good deal of uncomfortableness, discomfort, right?
Client: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. A lot of that. A lot of it, yeah, yeah. And I think that I'm willing. I'm willing to do it because I want it so bad that, you know, I have to. You don't know until you try it, and I have to try it. I have to.
Counselor: So what, kind of a behavioral experiment. Right. So let's. Let's take it one step at a time. Let's say that back to the situation I alluded to earlier. You're in class and there's somebody that's interested in you, sitting next to you or whoever they are, and they come and initiate a conversation. What's your reaction now? What do you do now?
Client: Well, I would introduce myself because I never. I have never done that before to a guy where I introduce myself. I wouldn't even make eye contact. So I think to just look up with them and just say, you know, hi, my name is, you know, Leia, and just see what that feels like because I don't know what to do.
Counselor: You've never reached that step?
Client: No. No, I haven't, because I wouldn't even, you know, I wouldn't even look them in the eye.
Counselor: Your current reaction is not look them in the eye. Not engaging in discussion.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just kind of shy away. So the. So the behavioral experiment is to nothing, do that, but instead proactively engage in another behavior, which would be to introduce yourself. So let's just make that the experiment. You seem like you're pretty comfortable and you have some confidence you could do that.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And that's not a particularly long amount of time. You just have to get through that introduction. And the worst that they could do if you introduce yourself, I mean, I guess they could reject you at that point, but that seems pretty unlikely. I mean, you're just introducing yourself.
Client: Right. Right. I mean, I guess that would be really shallow if they did that. So.
Counselor: Yeah. That's not a great indicator that there would be a suitable mate. Right.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you introduce yourself and you're open. I guess the second part would be you're open to whatever conversation comes next.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you're not committing to anything. Right. You're not committing to an engaged, long engaged social interaction. You're just saying, here's my name, what's your name? Or whatever, and just see where the conversation goes. So this is really all new?
Client: Oh, yeah, it's all new. And it's like. It's embarrassing, but I feel. I feel, like, safe with you, so I feel okay that I'm able to talk about it. And, like, my friends know, you know, like, 24 and never really introducing yourself to a guy is. It's embarrassing. It's embarrassing. Yeah.
Counselor: So not doing. That's embarrassing.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So by doing that, you can overcome that embarrassment, but you'll have some anxiety.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a trade off.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So my guess is the more you introduce yourself, the less that anxiety will be.
Client: Yeah, I think so. Absolutely. Yeah.
Counselor: So let's just start with that.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Right. Let's start with that. And when's the next time you'll be in a class?
Client: Actually, next week.
Counselor: Okay, next week. So you'll have the opportunity in that class to introduce yourself to who's there.
Client: Yeah. And I'm always early.
Counselor: You're always early.
Client: Always early. Because, you know, I have to make sure that I'm getting grades, but, yeah, I'm always up.
Counselor: It's good to be early.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you're always early. And this way, you know, people come in.
Client: Right.
Counselor: One at a time, whatever. And you can introduce yourself.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And that's really for this first experiment. That and just being open to whatever conversation comes next.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just talking.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: So try not to borrow any worry into the future, past that. Okay. Like, in terms of will they like me? What will they think of me? Where will this go? Just focus on the introduction and the conversation and just try to enjoy that. I know there's some anxiety with it, certainly a lot, but try to enjoy that experience and try to look at it as a victory. It's an important step for you to overcome this initial contact fear. So if you can get through that, the possibilities are wide open.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: Been doing okay. It's been a while now. You've been practicing with the waiting after you wash your hands? Mm hmm. How's that been going for you?
Client: Well, I think it's been going pretty well. I've been able to, you know, wait pretty good. I'm gonna start it out slow like you suggested, with three minutes. Then I would wash my hands for five minutes. I would wash my hands, and I got up to about 15 minutes.
Counselor: That's great.
Client: And there were some times that I was really proud of myself that I actually forgot.
Counselor: You forgot to wash your hands entirely?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So when was the next time you washed them?
Client: When I would go to, like, eat. Dinner,
Counselor: which is when you normally wash your hands. So really, you touched something that had germs, and you had some anxiety as you had to get to that waiting period. But then the anxiety subsided to a point where I forgot about it just wasn't a priority. You just completely forgot and went on with your day?
Client: Yeah. I was really proud of myself, but I got really concerned because I got sick. I got sick recently, and I'm afraid it's from one of those times that I didn't wash my hands.
Counselor: Well, tell me about the sickness.
Client: Well, my throat started to get hurt real bad, and I was just really congested. And all I could think about was, it's because I didn't wash my hands when I went to the store or when I went to my car when I touched a jacket. That's, you know, been everywhere.
Counselor: How many times do you normally get it? Sounds like a cold.
Client: I mean, it was kind of a light cold.
Counselor: Light cold.
Client: I mean, we wouldn't wait in a.
Counselor: Few days, a couple days. So how long or how many times a year would you get something like that normally?
Client: I mean, I get sick. I mean, quite often because of my job. I'm around a lot of people, and hand sanitizer can only work so much. I do get sick.
Counselor: So it's been six weeks since you started waiting? Right. I think it was around session three where we talked about putting a gap between when you touch something, when you wash your hands, like a time gap, and you got a cold once. Would that be out of the ordinary to get a cold one time in six weeks this time of year?
Client: I suppose not. I mean, the rational part of me knows that I get sick, but just because I'm trying something new with the, you know, and then the waiting and then the not washing, I'm just afraid that there was, you know, you're afraid.
Counselor: They were linked at one cause the other that waiting to wash your hands got you sick. And that could have happened. I don't know. But let's talk about the cold. You said it was a couple days.
Client: It wasn't severe. I mean, I took some, you know, over the counter medicine, slept it off.
Counselor: So wasn't a catastrophe.
Client: No, I've definitely been sicker in my life. And I mean, it did seem like one of those ones that I get every now and then.
Counselor: So when we spoke, I remember before you had said that the kind of worst case scenario, the reason that you're thinking so much about the germs on your hands is that it could make you sick. But you did get sick and you were able to tolerated.
Client: Yeah, I was. Which I found kind of odd because I was. I was panicked at the beginning when I started to feel those first, you know, the itchy throat, the headaches.
Counselor: Sure, it's miserable, right? Nobody wants to get sick.
Client: And I got concerned, you know, that it was because of that. Then it just kind of subsided. I guess I felt a little better, you know, as the days went on, I felt better about it happening, about.
Counselor: The whole getting sick and you started to recover. So kind of the worst case scenario occurred and you survived. And again, we don't know if the, the amount of hand washing you were doing before the ERP exposure and response prevention, we don't know if that would have prevented the cold or not. Yeah, because you do get sick several times, several times a year, in a year. So there's a lot we don't know. But we do know that you survived it and it wasn't as bad looking back at it.
Client: I mean, in my head, not washing my hands and the sick that I would get is a lot worse. It's like hospital worthy. And this was, you know, like I said over the counter, you know, relax a little bit.
Counselor: So not pleasant, but survivable.
Client: It definitely wasn't pleasant, but it wasn't as bad as it could have gone in my mind.
Counselor: So presume for a moment that it was a consequence of not immediately rushing over and washing your hands. What would you rather have? The occasional cold like that or the excessive hand washing and anxiety?
Client: I mean, I definitely don't like the excessive hand washing. I don't. I mean, it ruins my skin and I. It's expensive and it makes me feel bad about myself. And I mean, I guess the trade off is if I get a little sick and that would be okay.
Counselor: Again, that's presuming that it did cause you to get sick, which it may not have.
Client: I suppose that's true.
Counselor: So I wanted to point out, too, that I remember when we, we first started the exposure response prevention exercise, we did it right here in session by touching the arms of the chair. And I can see now your arms are.
Client: Oh, I didn't even notice I was doing that. Oh, I don't, you know, even noticing it, I don't feel like I need to go, you know, wash my elbows or anything.
Counselor: You don't feel that compulsion?
Client: No, I don't. I mean, I know that it's dirty. I know that people sit here and people can be dirty, but I don't feel that need to go wash my hands right now.
Counselor: So your anxiety increased a little when I told you, I pointed out that you were touching it, but not as much as it did before.
Client: I mean, on that scale, I think it'd be about a two.
Counselor: Well, with one being the lowest anxiety and ten being the highest, you're about two.
Client: Well, when you pointed it out, I didn't notice before.
Counselor: So you were a one in anxiety before that. So now you're aware of it a little bit. Right. So your elbows. Your elbows have to touch the chair.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you're aware of it a little bit and you're a little anxious.
Client: I mean, not so much anymore. I mean, it's kind of. You mentioned it. I got anxious for a moment, and then it's just kind of like, oh, well, you're already doing it and nothing bad's happening right now.
Counselor: Well, good. You made a lot of progress.
Client: Thank you.
Counselor: A lot of progress. So you're still going to have, as we move forward, you're still going to have some anxiety, like when I mentioned that your arms are touching the chair. You're still going to have some anxiety from time to time. Anxiety is part of life.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: It's going to happen from time to time. So one of the things I hope that you've gained from this is that just like you tolerated being sick for those few days, right. Is to tolerate that anxiety. Right. To be able to be okay with having some anxiety in your life.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: In a sense, the fear of being anxious kind of causes a vicious cycle. Right. You have fear of being anxious. You'll do not anything, but you'll do many things to get rid of that.
Client: Anxiety because it gets really bad. It starts consuming me.
Counselor: It's uncomfortable. I remember when you touched the chair before, right? Like many weeks ago, that you had the urge to go wash your hands right away, you were anxious.
Client: Yeah, I remember that.
Counselor: So you become less anxious by waiting and kind of getting used to it. And with that remaining anxiety, what I'm getting at is that at some point you have to learn to tolerate that. And it sounds like that's kind of the direction you're moving that you're able to tolerate. Like, the anxiety is still unpleasant for you, but you're able to survive to.
Client: Kind of live through it. Yeah, yeah, I would really say that.
Counselor: So tolerating that degree of anxiety, is that better than the frequent hand Washington?
Client: I mean, the little bit of unpleasantness versus, you know, the depression and the anxiety that comes with washing my hands? I would really rather take the little unpleasantness, I guess, in the grand scheme of things. Yeah.
Counselor: So where are you now in terms of how many minutes do you wait after you touch something.
Client: On average? Because I write them down, on average, I wait a good seven minutes.
Counselor: So you've been averaging around seven minutes. So I want to continue ramping that up. So if you had no awareness of germs, how many times would you normally wash your hands in a day?
Client: You know, wash them after eating or before eating, touching anything, you know, like a toilet or stuff like that. I mean, so definitely a fraction of what I do.
Counselor: So maybe in a day, ten times, a dozen times maybe would be normal.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: For you. And you were way beyond that before.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So we'll keep working those minutes up. Right. That's using that same schedule and trying to get to the point where you're only washing your hands when you really want to, when you normally would, rather than. Because you're being pushed to by the compulsion. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah, you know, choosing to wash my hands instead of needing to wash my hands.
Counselor: Yeah. Because sometimes you're going to touch unpleasant objects and you won't be in a place where you can wash your hands.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: Even though it'd be a good idea too. If you're good, you have to be able to tolerate, tolerate that anxiety and be okay with your hands being dirty until you get to a place where you can wash them. So let's go if you're at seven now, let's move up to, let's go to ten minutes between now and I see you next week.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Right. And you're timing this, right?
Client: Yeah, I am timing it.
Counselor: You mentioned. Okay, good. So let's move from seven to ten and we'll just keep getting further away and hope that we can get you onto a kind of a schedule. Washing your hands. That's normal for you.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: That sound good?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Liz. How you doing today?
Client: I'm alright. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on in the last week?
Client: It's still the same. Nothing at home is going right. It's. I'm still yelling, we're still fighting.
Counselor: Like you and your boyfriend.
Client: Yeah. He just can't get it together. He can't. He doesn't do anything right. He doesn't. And I just end up screaming every day and it takes it all out of me.
Counselor: All right, so he can't do anything right. And you're arguing, being angry every day?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So what are you taking away from this? Like, what do you think's going on?
Client: I feel like he does nothing wrong and I end up screaming at him when I come home from work, and that's a lot out of me every day, and I don't want to feel angry every single day.
Counselor: That's what's happening.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What types of things do you think are triggering your anger response?
Client: It's anything. It's. I come home, he's just sitting on the couch. I've had a long day at work. He gets homework before me, and the dishes aren't done. Nothing's, like, thawed or even started for dinner. And is that just supposed to be my, like, it's not. He could just do one thing and I just. I just lose it. I lose it and I can't. I can't control it. I just started screaming at him that he does nothing, that he could just do one thing for me. He could just have the sink clean, empty one thing, and it. Every single day. And then the next day it's something else. The trash is now, like, you name it.
Counselor: So every. Every day when you come home from work, there's something he's done or failed to do that triggers yelling?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's his response to this? Like, what's he doing when you yell at him?
Client: He gets mad back. He just starts screaming back at me. Like, I expect too much and I get too upset and why am I always yelling at him? Why can't I give him the benefit of the doubt?
Counselor: I'm.
Client: But I don't understand it. Like, you could do one thing and then. And I just. I can't help it. I scream at him.
Counselor: Are there other things he does at other times that you feel are helpful? Or is it. Or is it always, like, when you come home, is it always something that hasn't been done right or hasn't been done?
Client: I mean, on anniversaries, whole make dinner. So that's nice.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: He makes good money. So that's. He keeps that together.
Counselor: Okay, that's about it.
Client: Yeah. The rest is just. I just get angry at him.
Counselor: So if you were to pick adjectives to describe him, what adjectives might you. Might you select?
Client: Stubborn, condescending, and intelligent.
Counselor: Intelligent, stubborn, condescending, and intelligent. Do you see him as this way kind of all the time, or is this change?
Client: I don't think it's all the time. Like, there. Like sometime, like a month ago when a friend at work died. Old age, whatever. But I had a long day. He knew it beforehand. I didn't have to say anything. When I came home, everything was good. There was no trash, no dishes. So it's not all the. All the time, but just lately, it's just. I had no words.
Counselor: So lately it's all the time. Yeah, but there's been prior occasions when this hasn't been a problem. Yeah, but there's not many of those. So after you have, you yell and argue, what's it feel like to you then? Like, what's your mood?
Client: I'm still irritable. It's like the dishes don't get done. The problem didn't go away, didn't fix itself while I was yelling. So it just sucks being that angry. Just doesn't. I hate it.
Counselor: So it's not productive for you?
Client: Right, right. It's not productive.
Counselor: But there's a part of you mentioned earlier where, like you said, you just can't help yourself.
Client: Like I said, I just lose it. And I do that because that's what it feels like.
Counselor: So it's like you just. You just see, for example, like the dishes, right? So you just see the dishes aren't done, and immediately there's the.
Client: I just. I go off. Why didn't you do the dishes? You've been home an hour and a half. You could have done one thing for me. I had a longer day, and you knew it.
Counselor: All right, so let me take an example from work, right, so you work in an office with other people. Do they ever frustrate you in a way similar to what your boyfriend does?
Client: Occasionally, yeah, on occasion. Yeah.
Counselor: So there's times where you kind of have that moment with them where you just can't believe they didn't do something.
Client: Or I. Yeah, I just can't stand them sometimes.
Counselor: What's your reaction in terms of anger and yelling to those events?
Client: I get pissed, but I just. I can't. I can't yell.
Counselor: You can't yell? No. Why is that?
Client: I get fired.
Counselor: You get fired. So in those interactions with your coworkers, would be fair to say you're in that moment just as angry as you are with your boyfriend.
Client: And, oh, if not more, because I actually choose to be with my boyfriend. I don't choose to be with those people necessarily.
Counselor: You just happen to be together. And so in those instances, because there's a consequence like being fired, you're able to control the outward expression of anger, meaning you're not yelling, but inwardly, you're still angry at them.
Client: Yeah, I guess so.
Counselor: Yeah. So they don't really know you're angry.
Client: Yeah. I just walk away. I don't think they'd be able to tell.
Counselor: And they're not being yelled at, so they're not.
Client: Right. They wouldn't react. Yeah.
Counselor: No reaction. Right. So there is a thought process that occurs between the trigger and when you act, because at work, you're thinking, you have this thought that comes up, I don't want to be fired.
Client: Yeah, I get there. Must. Yeah.
Counselor: And the consequence of that thought is I'll be angry, but I'm not going to act angry.
Client: Right. I can't act angry or I'll get fired, and I don't want to get fired, I guess.
Counselor: So knowing that there is a thought there when you come home and you see the dishes aren't done, maybe just stay with that example. What would that thought be like? Think back to the last time that happened. Do you remember what you were thinking at that moment as you saw those dishes sitting there not washed?
Client: I mean, just that he never does anything. Right.
Counselor: He never does anything. Right. So you see. So you see the dishes not washed. He never does anything. Right. That's the thought, yeah. And then the reaction, the behavior is finding him. Right. And yelling at him.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so you see how there is an intervening thought between the trigger, which in this case, the dishes, and the behavior, which is the yelling.
Client: Yeah. I guess there's a thought where I'm sitting there and I'm looking at him, thinking about it, saying, you never do anything. Right.
Counselor: So remember we talked a few weeks ago about cognitive distortions? We talked about, like, the errors, like, consistent. There are consistent errors in thinking. Right. And I'm wondering if that thought, he never does anything right. If that's similar to or matches up with any of the cognitive distortions we talked about. And I'm wondering if it's not. If it's not kind of blocking off your path in terms of thinking. Right. So you're saying he never does anything right.
Client: Right.
Counselor: It's kind of like maybe a kind of all or nothing thinking that we talked about that.
Client: Oh, it's absolute tunnel vision at that point.
Counselor: Tunnel vision, yeah. Okay. So a few different distortions at work. But you mentioned earlier there are times when he does do things right.
Client: Yeah. There are occasions where he must have thought about me.
Counselor: He was more thoughtful than more considerate. Okay. More considerate. So the statement he never does the thought, he never does anything right that could be challenged.
Client: Yeah, I guess technically it could.
Counselor: And what might be as an alternative to the behavior? Right. To the yelling. Instead of doing that, what might be a thought that you could kind of insert right after that he never does anything right. Thought that might change the outcome for you. That might disrupt that connection between that thought and your yelling.
Client: Maybe that he has done something right in the past.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So it's bound to happen again. It is possible.
Counselor: All right. So an adapted response, as we call him or his self talk, that says he's not. He's not altogether bad because he has done things right in the past.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. Which is a little more flexible in thinking than thinking. He. Then your automatic thought.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Yeah. That's your automatic thought. Never does anything right. So a little bit more flexibility in the thinking might get you to a place where you're not yelling. And then on the other side of it, too, I'm wondering if we can't challenge the usefulness of yelling. You mentioned that you've done it quite a bit, but you're not really getting a different result.
Client: It doesn't. The dishes don't get done after that. And the next day, I might still find the dishes there. It doesn't.
Counselor: It's not working.
Client: It hasn't worked. Yeah.
Counselor: So when you're yelling, there's an expression of emotion, but there's also this hope that the yelling will change his behavior.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Something, but it's not.
Client: Yep.
Counselor: And when was the first time in terms of, like, how long ago this was a problem?
Client: I've had previous boyfriends where this was a problem, and that relationship has long gone because of it.
Counselor: So due to the yelling?
Client: Due to the yelling. So I don't. I really do like this guy who's not all bad, and I don't want my yelling to be a problem, my anger.
Counselor: But it's hard to control for you. You're struggling with the anger.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Yelling.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Rationally, you understand it doesn't work. Like, it's not getting what you want, but somehow it feels like a release it feels like justice. It feels good to be able to.
Client: It feels like that's what I'm supposed to be doing, and that's what I do.
Counselor:
output: That's what you're supposed to be doing. Okay. So it feels like it's what you're supposed to be doing. Do you have an idea of what might be a more productive path for you as an alternative to the yelling?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Kathy. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay. How are you?
Counselor: I'm good. Thanks for asking.
Client: Sure.
Counselor: So I know last time we talked you had just touched on this relationship you're in and how it has led to some concerns and some people's feedback has led to concerns. You want to talk about that today?
Client: Yeah. Stu and I were talking about it before I came in, and I can't really figure out why I'm so bothered. We have such a great relationship. I mean, I feel lucky as a woman in the 21st century to have a man who cares about her and takes her out and makes her feel appreciative. I've never had that before. And I go home happy. I go home excited to see him. I can't name a single friend or even my sisters who have that. And still all I hear is there are criticisms, there are words, how weird it is, and why would a 58 year old man want to be with you? You're not even 30 yet, you know? And I just don't see that. I don't see age being an issue. But again, like, I'm just, I'm waking up with those thoughts.
Counselor: The criticisms come from a few of your family members, and you'd mentioned some people at work, too.
Client: Yeah, my mom and my sister. They haven't gotten any better since you and I spoke last. They text me all the time and I just try to not play into it. I just, you know, play civil because it's not their life. I don't live there anymore. But the co workers, that's gotten worse, I think, in that more people are talking about it. It's almost like it's gossip. And that's just not my thing. I don't like being in anyone's business. No one should be in mine. And, you know, love is love. Why should it be a topic for discussion at work? I don't know.
Counselor: So their area of focus is really just the age difference.
Client: They think it's bizarre for sure.
Counselor: They feel it's over some socially accepted limit.
Client: I think so. I don't even know what that limit would be. I mean, I'm 29, you know, I've been living on my own. I can make my own decisions. I've had a job for who knows how long. I'm a capable woman. Like, it's not, I don't, I don't think that should be a measure of me being weird or he being weird just because we're together.
Counselor: Just. Just that age difference. That shouldn't be a factor.
Client: It should not be a factor.
Counselor: And they're not. They're not criticizing any other elements of the relationship.
Client: I mean, maybe they make fun of him because they think he's too old to, you know, come to the bar with us. And I play tennis, as you know, so they think he's gonna, like, fall and break his leg or something if he plays with me.
Counselor: Right. So they're still kind of on the age subject.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So that really seems to be their primary concern, is their giving you advice or criticizing all the things they're doing. So we've talked before, and there's been other issues where you've received criticism from family members and even co workers and even conscientious, and you've examined it and just kind of accepted it and moved on. This is a little different for you, though.
Client: It is. I don't know. And this is why at the beginning, I don't know why these things are infiltrating so deeply. I mean, it's been a great year with him, and, you know, I'm still, like I said, I'm still really happy, but I just don't. I don't get it. I mean, I want their acceptance, but I want this relationship, too. And I'm thinking, I don't know if I can have both because I just feel pushed further away. And he's great. He's great, but he's not my family, you know?
Counselor: All right, so there's kind of a part where you feel like you're being forced to choose.
Client: I definitely feel like I'm being forced to choose right now.
Counselor: So that's one of the problems. Do you have any concerns whether they were generated from outside advice or criticism? Do you have any concerns about the age difference yourself?
Client: I mean, honestly, I think about it, you know, because I think what we have, Stu and I, is great, but, you know, are we gonna get married? Is he gonna wanna have kids? Like, do I wanna have kids? I don't even know if I want to be a wife. I mean, he's been married before. Maybe he doesn't want to do that, but what if he doesn't want to do that? But I do. I don't know. I haven't figured these things out yet. And I think that's part of why I'm listening to these criticisms more, because maybe they're right. Maybe I don't have my head on right. About this.
Counselor: They're definitive. Right. So they have a clear direction, whereas you're still a bit confused.
Client: Yeah. And it's great to hide behind a strong relationship when you don't necessarily have those things figured out because you just go out and you have fun. But thinking about it right now, I have. Yeah. I don't know. I don't have any definitive priorities, really, aside from keeping my job, I guess.
Counselor: So maybe. Maybe part of the solution is talking with him and figuring out how your goals might align with his goals. And that seems to be a concern of yours.
Client: Yeah. We haven't necessarily talked too deeply about that. We joke about things like that, but.
Counselor: So there maybe hasn't been a serious discussion yet where you've really talked about the age difference and how it could.
Client: Play out in a serious manner. Yeah, we have it.
Counselor: I mean, you may not know this, but has he received criticism in a similar way? So this is maybe something he could understand because he's gone through it, too.
Client: Very much.
Counselor: So. Ultimately, I suppose you have to make a decision. Not right now, but eventually you have to make a decision about what to do with this relationship. I know, and there's many factors that weigh into this. Right. So you have your values, what you want for your future, your coworker's relationship with you, your family's relationship with you, his relationship with you. All these things come together.
Client: That's a lot. That's a lot. Yeah. I don't know.
Counselor: There's a lot of factors to it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Sometimes when a relationship is new, there's like a. There's like a period it goes through wherever kind of love is in the air, so to speak. Right. And sometimes facts don't get weighed as heavily. You familiar with what I'm talking about there?
Client: I know the feeling. Absolutely. Yeah.
Counselor: Where do you feel that you are in terms of that?
Client: I think the veil has been taken off, I think, you know, we've said I love you to each other, but that rosy kind of honeymoon phase, it's definitely going away. It's showing itself to be a messier situation, I think.
Counselor: So you feel like you're able to look at it realistically now as your way, the pros and cons.
Client: I don't know how, but I know I have to. I think. I mean, that's why, like, I just wanted to talk to you about this because I have to figure out, you know, a system to write it down and just make sense of it, you know?
Counselor: Yes. Some process that allows you to come to the conclusion that works best for you, which may mean staying with them and may mean not staying with them or somewhere in between where you have a relationship that is not a full commitment to be with one another, but you still see them. I mean, I guess there's a lot of shades of grey here available, but you're kind of being pressed to figure that out. And you're feeling that pressure to figure that out.
Client: Definitely. The pressure is much more now as I'm starting to realize. There are lots of layers to this that maybe didn't exist when it was all fun and games at the beginning.
Counselor: So how do you make a calculation like this?
Client: I have no idea. I don't know. You know, I've talked with one of my best friends about it, but really, it's just such a weird thing in society that people just don't understand it. And I've got close friends that have stuck by me. I've had so many friends leave because they think what I'm doing is just totally inappropriate. And I don't know who to talk to about it, really, because aside from you, anyone I talk to, just, like, instantly they have a judgment and they know better. So I've tried that. I've. You know, I keep a diary, so I talk about that and I talk to Stu about it, but it just seems like it gets bigger the more I think and try to work on it. And then I just walk away and kind of give up.
Counselor: Give up for a while.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So, yeah, this age difference issue is certainly one where you would expect to get strong reactions one way or the other, right? So somebody is really okay with it and others are very strongly against it. Maybe somewhere in the middle. But it's a polarizing issue. So I'm curious. So if there was. If the larger kind of attitude, society, toward these age differences was that it was fine, how would that affect your decision making process?
Client: If it was okay, I think I would just be asking the normal questions, like, do we have a future together? You know, should we buy a place together? You know, the stuff that I think most girlfriends and boyfriends ask. But this just becomes so much murkier because I don't know if I'm making a decision because he's older than me or, you know, because people see him as maybe not being good for me or his friends seeing me not being good for him. Like, I'm just taking into account everyone's judgments. So I think if that was off the table, it would just be easier. I'd have decisions to make, but it would just be so much easier.
Counselor: You'd still have to work through it, but you could manage that process.
Client: Yeah, like I have. I mean, I've come to you about so many things and we just work through it and I accept it and I kind of use it as a building block. But this is just, like I said, just. It's messy.
Counselor: Yeah. Certainly a lot of moving parts.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So maybe we start here, and you mentioned this earlier about writing things down.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Again, how one makes these calculations is really, it's just up to the individual. But what you could do is maybe write down some of the areas that are definitively positive, like things you like about the relationship and where it's going and where it could go at the same time, definitively negative. Some of the areas that are going to be challenges and maybe a column for challenges or opportunities. You just, you don't know how to categorize neutral or maybe slightly negative or slightly positive, but you're just unsure about. Right. And maybe some of those areas are the ones more influenced by people's criticisms because those judgments have made this harder. If you were to go home and just use that system, like just three columns, that which you have really figured out is good, that which you know is going to be tough. No getting around it. And those areas where you just really would like to work harder to try to figure out if they should be categorized as good or bad, or maybe they just stay as just neutral items. Maybe that can help inform the next session. We can kind of talk through your list.
Client: Sure. And go over it piece by piece and make sense of it.
Counselor: Yeah. I would hope, too. As you write these things down, it's not just a matter of recording information. It's also a process where it might get you thinking about different aspects. And you may look at that list, maybe you do that tonight or tomorrow night, and you may look at that list a few days from now and say, well, I'm going to move this item over to a different column because you're. It's made you think about it more.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. This is something. I agree. This is something you really have to sit with.
Client: Yeah. I'll start it tonight.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I think. And just visit it throughout the day for the next week. You know what I mean? Each day, just kind of keep it. Maybe even travel with it in my bag or something. Yeah. Right. Because even, like, even every day is different. Like if he and I get in a fight, you know how we fight. And that might be a pro or a con, you know? So, yeah, I can. I can definitely do that.
Counselor: Yes. It's going to be, you know, rather than a static recording, it's going to be kind of a living document you work on. And probably after you meet the next time, you work on some more and we'll continue that.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: It might make. I hope it would make this decision a little more clear. But I can see that you. You're struggling with this. I appreciate how tough it is and that you really brought this in to talk about. I know this can't be fun to talk about. It's really weigh on your mind.
Client: Yeah. It's just. I know we could be having fun, I think, if I didn't have to worry about this as much, you know? And maybe this will help me make a decision that's actually better for everybody, that doesn't include us being together in this capacity. So we'll see. And I think I just have to grow to accept that.
Counselor: Great. So we'll start with that homework assignment and it might change throughout the week. And then next session week, we'll look over it and we'll kind of see where you are after you've considered all those different items.
Client: I can do that.
Counselor:
output: That sounds good.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
