Counselor: Okay, so you said that when you're at work, you really worry that you're gonna say something stupid?
Client: Yeah, that's something that's always on my mind.
Counselor: What would be so bad about that if you did say something stupid at work?
Client: Because people would think I was weird.
Counselor: Then what would be so bad if people. People at work thought you were weird?
Client: They wouldn't want to be friends with me.
Counselor: And what would be so bad about that if people at work didn't want to be friends with you?
Client: Well, I just have no one to talk to at work.
Counselor: Then what would be so bad about having no one to talk to at work?
Client: I mean, the shoots can go on the whole day, so I'd just be by myself the whole time.
Counselor: And what would be so bad about being by yourself, you know, for a whole day?
Client: I don't know. I guess I should be used to it now. I spend a lot of my time by myself.
Counselor: Oh, that must be tough. What does that mean to you? That you spend a lot of time on your own?
Client: Dunno. I guess it's just like I spend so much time by myself that it's kind of like I'm nothing even worth being friends with.
Counselor: So it sounds like deep down that you think that you're not worth being friends with. That's quite a negative belief. I mean, how much would you say that you believe that out of a hundred? If 100 is where you believe it totally. And zero is where you don't believe it at all?
Client: I guess like 9500.
Counselor: When did you start believing that?
Client: I think it was probably at school. Yeah, I think at school.
Counselor: And what was it about school that made you start to believe that you weren't worth being friends with?
Client: Just like quite a lot of things. Like I wouldn't have anyone sit at lunch or people's birthdays and stuff. I wasn't invited and you know, like I was the last one picked for teams and stuff like that.
Counselor: And what is it now that makes you think that that's still true?
Client: I mean, it's kind of similar at work, obviously. Difference is that it's work, not school. But you know, people go for drinks and stuff after work or after a shoot, and I just kind of excluded a lot of the time.
Counselor: That sounds tough. Is there anything that makes you think that it's not true that you are worth being friends with?
Client: I guess my friends and family would say that I am. Like, I try to make a lot of time for my friends and stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like deep down you have this thought that you're not worth being friends with. And that started at school when you had trouble making friends at school and that you weren't always picked for teams and that now at work it feels like the same thing is happening, that you're not always invited out for drinks with people and that sometimes you feel that you're excluded from their social groups. But then that's not the whole story. That on the other hand, you are close to family and you do have friends who would say that it's not true that you are worth being friends with. In CBT, we do a thing called thought challenging where when we have these negative thoughts, sometimes we actually put them up to scrutiny. We weigh up the evidence for and against them. I like to think of it as putting the thought on trial. Could we do that now where we just actually try and weigh up the evidence for and against that thought a bit more?
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. So if I just put two columns here, so for and against. And it sounds like the evidence for this thought that makes you think that it is true is difficulty at school, making friends, being picked for teams, and difficulty at work, feeling excluded sometimes from groups.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But actually in this other column we have that you are close with your family and that you have some close friends. Okay. Now moving back to this first column, is there anything else that makes you think it's true that you're not worth being friends with?
Client: Just like, I kind of don't go to a lot of stuff. People have, like gatherings and things and a lot of the time I just. I don't go and rather just stay at home.
Counselor: Don't go to parties. What kind of parties are we talking? Like big parties, small parties, mainly big ones.
Client: If there's a lot of people there, I just find it really. It kind of makes me really anxious. So a lot of the time I just prefer not even to be in that situation in the first place.
Counselor: Okay. So you don't go to larger parties and events. Okay. Is there anything else that maybe thinks that it's makes you think that it's not true that actually you are worth being friends with?
Client: I mean, I guess my friends would say that I was. I do have close friends and, you know, when it's like their stuff that's important to them, I always make sure that I think about that. And even if I find it stressful, I'll always make sure that I can kind of put them first.
Counselor: Okay. So your friends would say that you are worth being friends with and it sounds like you put your friends first.
Client: Yeah, I do. Make sure I try and do that.
Counselor: In what kind of ways do you put your friends first?
Client: I guess when it's birthdays or, you know, something important to them, I'll always make sure that I'm there and that I put a lot of thought into presence and stuff like that.
Counselor: Can you give me an example of a time that you've done that?
Client: It was my friend's birthday a few weeks ago and we did like a big surprise at hers and I made a cake and stuff like that.
Counselor: So you actually helped to organize events for your friends?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is there anything that you do that you wouldn't do if you weren't a good friend?
Client: I guess I kind of always put myself in a situation, even if I find it kind of. It makes me anxious. If it's for my close friends and I know that it's something that's important to them, then I'll always put them first and make sure I'm there.
Counselor: So you'll tolerate your anxiety if it means something to a friend of yours?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So at the moment in the four category we've got that you had difficulty making friends at school, that you're having difficulty now at work making friends, and that you don't go to larger parties or events. But actually there's a lot of evidence in the against column, evidence that would suggest that actually you are worth being friends with and you're a good friend, that you're close with your family, you're close with your friends, your friends would say that you're a good friend of you put your friends first. Even when you're anxious, you tolerate that anxiety if you know it will mean something to them. That when things are important to your friends, like birthdays, you'll make a real effort. You'll even actually go to the effort of organising events and baking cakes and doing things like that for other people. Is there anything else that you do that makes you think that maybe you are a good friend, you are worth being friends with?
Client: I mean, I still have my friends, so I guess if I wasn't worth being friends with, I wouldn't have these friends I've had for quite, quite a long time.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you've got long term friendships as well, so you might have trouble making friends, but when you make them, you stick with them.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Okay, I'm just going to give you this list now to have a look at.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Janice. How are you doing today?
Client: Good. I'm good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm good. I'm really impressed that you came back for a second session.
Client: Oh, no, I'm really glad to, I'm really glad to come back because meeting with you last week really helped me to really think about why I want to do this. So I'm really happy to be back. Yeah.
Counselor: Good. Good. So as we met last week, we talked about a few things. And to recap, we talked about alcohol dependency, anxiety, feelings of hopelessness and failure and the impact that alcoholism has had on you and your ability to perform your schoolwork.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I really want to work on my addiction and I feel like it's really effective, my schoolwork.
Counselor: So how has the last week been there for you?
Client: Um, last week, I think, um, I was thinking about what we talked about last week and I try to, you know, think about some things I want to work on and so it was better than before, but I still had a difficult time managing my work and my time and. Yeah.
Counselor: So have you, did you have any drinks last week?
Client: I had a couple of drinks, yeah, I went out with my friend a couple of times and even at home, you know, I felt kind of anxious because deadlines are coming up and my assignments are coming up, so I feel really anxious. So, yeah, I had a couple of drinks at home by myself.
Counselor: Good. So one of the things that we talked about was meeting with your professor or sending out an email to tell them how you, you need some assistance in completing your work because you have missed a lot of days from school.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, yeah. So I actually talked to my professor and asked him if I could get any extra help and he suggested to kind of reach out to the tutoring center that they, they have on campus. So I email them and I'm in the process of setting up some time where I could get extra help. And I'm also talking with my tas to meet for office hours.
Counselor: That's great. That's awesome. And I think that's part of your goals that you've already achieved.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. So I'm really glad that we were able to talk last week because that really helped me to kind of plan ahead.
Counselor: Yeah, that's good. That's good. So let's talk about a little bit more of the schoolwork and the anxiety that you experienced during that time. So you said that whenever those schoolwork accumulates, you find yourself getting anxious and resolving to drinking. And you mentioned that you've been out a few times last week. Yeah. So in terms of anxiety, one of the things I've used with my clients when they experience anxiety, it's kind of a relaxation tool that will help them to stop and relax and get their focus back and come back and be able to complete whatever activity that they working on. So what stop is it really? It's a point for you to reflect.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So from the time you start experiencing the anxiety, you stop. You put everything down, put all the papers, push them aside, and you just take a deep breath, breath in, and you breathe out. You could do it a few times and really reflect on what you want to achieve and how your feelings are impacting the way that you accomplish those goals. So you need to complete your assignment, but being anxious, you get worked up, and you cannot finish those assignments. So what this activity does is help you to relax. You can practice breathing techniques. You could put your arms on the, like, put your arms under your legs, or you could practice just stretching. Whenever you feel worked out, you could do it to the back, and that really helps to calm the nerves in the body and help you to relax a little bit. And then you can really gain your focus and come back to look at whatever you were doing, whatever assignment that you were trying to complete. So you could do this exercise as often as you feel any type of anxiety coming on. And I think that would really help to, like, relax.
Client: Yeah, I think it's gonna help.
Counselor: Breathing exercise, especially the stretching, will get you, when you get worked up to, you know, like, take out all the tension in your body.
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: So another thing we could touch on now that we've talked about an activity or something you can do to relieve anxiety, another thing I see that's been affecting you is the expectations from your family.
Client: Yeah. I mean, they really want me to do well, but whenever I feel like I'm, like, I don't pass my classes, I just fail one of the tests, and I just feel like I'm a failure. And I don't want to be a failure. I don't want to do that to my parents.
Counselor: I know that's a big expectation for you, to have that placed on you and knowing that if you fail that you will bring disappointment to your family.
Client: And, like, if I fail the school, that I'm just gonna fail for my life. I don't know what to do.
Counselor: So do you think that's positive thinking? Do you think that is true?
Client: I mean, I'm not going to fail my life, but I just feel like, you know, I'm a failure because I cannot even finish school.
Counselor: So let's try to restructure that thinking because I think probably that thinking is 40, so probably to think of it in another way. Okay, how about you try thinking about times that you've been successful?
Client: Hmm? Yeah, actually I, well, until last semester I did pretty well in my classes. And so far it's just this last semester I just have a lot of things to do. But so far I did pretty well and I'm pretty involved in school and I am involved in student council, so I do a lot of activities and you know, I work too, so. And people, people like me, I think so, yeah.
Counselor: So that's good. You have a lot of things here that you should be positive about, especially being part of an organization, being part of student council. It shows that you're responsible and you're capable of handling your task. So what really is taking the best of you is like the last semester and I being overwhelmed with the papers that are coming to you. So I think thinking positive about being capable and using positive self talk and telling yourself that you're able to complete your assignments, you have done this before and you've been reliable and responsible. So using those things, at least try using them throughout the day to motivate you to keep up the good work and believe in yourself that you can complete your assignments. And you know, just take the focus of the negative thinking and think positive about yourself and think positive that you will complete your assignments because you've done it before and you're capable of doing it again. So I think that would work for you. Probably using that as a tool.
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: And we also mentioned about quitting. I think that's one of your top goals you already discussed.
Client: Yeah, I wanted to stop thinking.
Counselor: Yeah. So I think stopping can be dangerous sometimes. I'll more likely influence you to think of it as minimizing your drinking and dealing with all the soft goals. And then I think that would really help you. And another way to do that is I found this agency that started a clinic that I have researched as we talked about the last time, and they're starting a session next Saturday at twelve.
Client: How does that look for you to schedule next Saturday? I think, I think at twelve I think I can make it. Yeah.
Counselor: So we have the intake form, so what we could do, we could fill that out and I could call and make the appointments for you. And it is a, it is a five session, it's within a group. So you have other people who also struggle in dependency. So you get to meet with others and talk about your feelings and probably that would help you to cope with it and find ways to deal with that. How is that?
Client: Yeah, I like that.
Counselor: So good. I glad that we're making some steps. So what we've discussed overall, just to do a recap, we talked about the, the school, like reaching out to your professors and you said that worked for you. We talked about the techniques, the coping skills. You could do some breathing techniques or exercise and stretching and also the clinic dependency clinic that's setting up. So I think we on a good start.
Client: Yeah, I'm excited to start the therapy and I'll definitely try the stop method that you're telling me about.
Counselor: That's good. All right.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Nice meeting you again.
Client: See you next week. Okay, bye. Hi, Janice. Hi. Welcome back.
Counselor: Thank you.
Client: It's really good to see you again. I'm really glad that you're able to come back this time.
Counselor: Yeah, I really want to do this and I thought about it and I think that in order to reach my goals I need to participate and do something about it. And I'm glad that you going to help me.
Client: Okay. I'm here to help you. I'm really glad that you're able to really make your time and come.
Counselor: Thank you.
Client: So today what we're going to do is you shared with me last time how you are feeling anxious about not being able to finish school because of your alcohol dependency. Am I correct?
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Okay. So how was that for the last, last week after we met? Yeah.
Counselor: I've been drinking a lot because I've accumulated a lot of papers. I work full time and I really don't have the time to do my assignment. So whenever I feel overwhelmed I just want to feel better and relax. So I have a few drinks, probably too many, and try to resume assignments. And then I find myself not going to class because I just can't make it and my assignments are not complete. So I just feel like hopeless and I drink some more in the mornings and that's just my days.
Client: So it sounds like you're not able to finish a lot of work because of the stress, but at the same time, whenever you try to cope with that stress and drink, that also makes you not be able to go to class and that just cycle, just repeats.
Counselor:
output: Yeah, that's exactly my problem.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: You doing okay?
Client: I guess, yeah.
Counselor: Not sure.
Client: I don't know, just the same.
Counselor: Yeah, still a little down.
Client: Yeah, I've been sleeping a lot. Going to work is a struggle. I don't really ever want to go. Just I haven't been eating much, so I think I've lost like ten pounds since past, like four months or so.
Counselor: Past four months?
Client: Um, just the guy. I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.
Counselor: You still been working?
Client: Well, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But not much else?
Client: No, I usually just go to work and go home.
Counselor: Tell me what happens after you arrive at home, like after work?
Client: Um, well, my fiance tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep for just. I don't know. I tried, I tried reading the other day. Cause I used to like that and it's just, I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.
Counselor: What were you thinking when you put the book down?
Client: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.
Counselor: I. And before you were depressed, which is, I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading?
Client: Mm hmm. Oh, yeah, all the time.
Counselor: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?
Client: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up till like two in the morning just reading a book.
Counselor: Something you look forward to?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But not now?
Client: No, I just didn't really get any. I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like.
Counselor: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?
Client: Yeah, I used to be a runner and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I. I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.
Counselor: Alright, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running, like when you first started?
Client: Not really. I mean, it was a change to be outdoors and I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while, so. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run. I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route. And by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.
Counselor: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?
Client: Kind of a mix of, like, relief just because it was over, and then, I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.
Counselor: Sadness, maybe disappointment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I've seen you a few times now, and based on those conversations, and, of course, what you said today, it seems like you have, for a variety of reasons, given up on the activities that you used to enjoy, you're not motivated toward them anymore.
Client: Yeah, I guess you could say that.
Counselor: And that's a common symptom of depression. I think we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed. So we've been working with the cognitive piece. Right, like we did last time, we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self talk. I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. We'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle. And the technique is called behavioral activation. The theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, like with the running, that will connect to your mood. Right. Remember, we believe in cognitive therapy, that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood and what you do. Your behavior affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we talked about?
Client: It does, yeah.
Counselor: So you mentioned the reading was one thing you like to do. That's tough to do. Now you try unsuccessfully with the reading and I the running. Anything else you could think of that maybe we could plan for you to do, even if it's just a short time, even if it's a little bit uncomfortable, that we could plan to do? That would be an activity that you used to enjoy?
Client: Well, my fiance and I used to go out with two other couples, and we used to go out once or twice a week, and even if it's just each other's houses, but we haven't really seen them in a while. They've tried to schedule things, but I've kind of come up with reasons of not feeling well or to kind of just stay home.
Counselor: So they're trying to initiate meeting, going out, doing something, and you're. You're kind of pushing them off.
Client: Yeah, I just. I haven't really wanted to see anybody lately.
Counselor: All right, so that's. So we have reading, running, and then going out with these two other couples. Anything else you can think of that you used to really enjoy before that you can't quite motivate yourself to do now?
Client: I mean, I used to like going for, like, just walks and shopping with my fiance. Like, I. We used to spend a lot of time together, and lately it's just kind of. I come home, say hello, we eat dinner, and then I kind of do my own thing.
Counselor: So spending time with your fiance outside the house in some manner? Shopping was one example. Any other activities like movies or going out to eat?
Client: Yeah, I would kind of put those in with the things that we would do outside together. We would try to switch it up every now and then.
Counselor: Okay, so that's distinct from what you did with the couples because that's just you and your fiance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So let's do this. What kind of books do you like to read?
Client: I like a lot of fiction. I do a lot of reading for school, so I usually enjoy those books too. Mystery novels.
Counselor: Mystery novels. Okay, let's center on mystery novels. How long would it take you to read, say, a chapter of a mystery.
Client: Novel, roughly, depending on the size of the chapter, probably a couple minutes normally.
Counselor: So not long at all.
Client: No.
Counselor: So you could get a lot of reading done in, say, ten minutes, like something worthwhile. And how often would it. How often would you, what was the duration of a run? Like when you would go run? How long would it take?
Client: Probably, like a half hour.
Counselor: Half hour.
Client: Half hour to 45 minutes. Yeah. I used to do long distance running, so.
Counselor: Okay, and how often would you do that?
Client: Three or four times a week.
Counselor: Three or four times a week? Half hour, 40 minutes. And you mentioned you went out with the couple once or twice a week. How often would you go out with your fiance?
Client: I would say we try to do something every day, like, even if it was just going for a walk together, like around the park or walking the dog together.
Counselor: Okay. So I'd like to make collaboratively with you a schedule that involves those four activities, but I want to make it realistic. You tried a couple times, you weren't successful. So we don't want to be too ambitious, but I want to try to plan a schedule. You can get the habit of doing these activities again. So let's start with the kind of, I guess the simplest in terms of logistics, which would be probably the reading. Would it be possible, say, five nights out of seven, to read for ten or 15 minutes? Like, I know you're going to have to force your way through it a little bit, but I think it's something.
Client: I could try to do.
Counselor: So you're going to have automatic thoughts that come up, right. Like, just like you did before, and you're going to be tempted to give up. I want you to try to push through, say, this at least ten minutes. So focus on that as you go into it. It's a behavioral exercise, of course. It has a cognitive component to kind of think, you know, I just have to make this ten minutes.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And again, you might not really enjoy it the same way it did before. We kind of know that, but over time, that may change.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right, so does five nights a week seem reasonable? That's 50 minutes a week.
Client: Yeah, that seems fine.
Counselor: Okay, then let's move to the running, because you just recently tried that. You run with your dog. You said, yeah, okay, how about that? Twice a week. Would that be possible?
Client: Yeah, I can try to do that.
Counselor:
output: What days of the week you think you could do it?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Susan. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: You? Okay? I know that when you saw me last time, you were going through a bit of a struggle. How things go in with that, it's still a struggle. Yeah.
Client: I'm planning a surprise party for my husband.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And his mother doesn't talk to me.
Counselor: So you're planning a surprise party for your husband? His mom doesn't. Doesn't talk to you?
Client: No.
Counselor: That must make things tense.
Client: Really tense.
Counselor: Really tense, yeah.
Client: So she doesn't really try to interact with her grandkids or me. And the way I was raised is the matriarch is going to, you know, make all attempts to, you know, keep the family connected. So I try to call her and let the kids talk to her, but she won't answer her phone. And now with the party coming up, I would like her to be there, but she's not responding.
Counselor: And just so I can get a little bit of background, understand. Is this relationship new or this dynamic new or. You've been part of this family for a while?
Client: Yeah, we've been married for five years and dated for about eleven, but we dated in the past and, you know, lost, parted ways and then came back together later.
Counselor: And this dynamic with his mother not talking to you, that's been the whole time?
Client: Yeah, she. So during, when I got pregnant with my first daughter, before we got married and he was away at school, so she felt that I was trying to interrupt his studies and trap him. So she's been. She disapproved of the relationship from the beginning for the wedding. She had insight and she kind of like, just took over my wedding, like.
Counselor: In terms of organizing it.
Client: Yeah. So.
Counselor: So she dis. You're saying that she disapproves and that she felt as though you were trying to trap her son. How do you. How did you come by this information?
Client: Well, when I was pregnant, she told me.
Counselor: She told you? Okay, so it's not something that you're the. You were reading into it or guessing. It was fairly direct.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And in kind of those words?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, she. She. Well, I guess not. Maybe she. She kind of said that he's in school, he's not ready for a kid and suggested that I have an abortion.
Counselor: So she made that suggestion to you and made it clear that she disapproved of the whole. The whole relationship or just the timing?
Client: I think it's the. My feelings is the whole relationship. Because she just. Because now he graduated, he has a great job, we have three kids. He's able to do whatever he wants to do, and she still behave in the same way. So I would think it's the whole relationship.
Counselor: So you feel as though your relationship with him has been productive for you, for him, for the children? Like it's been a success?
Client: No.
Counselor: No. You don't feel that way? You feel it's been failure?
Client: Some aspects, I guess. I really believe in family. My family's not here, so I think it's really important that the family I'm a part of is together. So if I'm the cause that this family is not together is really her fault.
Counselor: So you're really hurt by all this, and you feel like all these relationships, none of them have been productive and successful. This has been anxiety provoking, frustrating, sad. How long have you been in this, with these emotions, with the anxiety inside this?
Client: Um, I'll say, like, maybe the last, like, maybe three years.
Counselor: Three years you've been suffering this?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: This way?
Client: Yeah. Because we, we tend to end up in, like, the same, the same mix of active, like, people and activities. And she treats us well. She treats me like I'm. I'm not even there. And then there's the kids. That's just. I don't know what to say to them.
Counselor: So she treats you poorly, like you're not there. She doesn't interact much with the kids or at all.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And how about with your husband? With her son?
Client: I guess they still need him for stuff. So he can talk to them. They'll talk to him. He still pays for her daughter, his little sister, Bondale, and she's an adult, and she lives with her mom, so they still depend on how to serve things.
Counselor: And you feel as though that's why there's still communication.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Otherwise, what would happen?
Client: I don't, like, I think. I think he's also kind of dependent on them.
Counselor: It goes both ways.
Client: Yeah. Because I. I kind of feel like there's no way he doesn't see how she behaves and knows how she behaves. And I don't feel that he is receptive to my pain.
Counselor: So you've conveyed to him that you have pain. This is. You haven't. So he doesn't know what's going on.
Client: No. So she, at one point in time, I think, said something to him about the. When I was pregnant the first time, which was kind of like insight into her feelings about what was going on, and I think he kind of just, like, brushed it off, like she was just being a mom kind of situation. But he has to be aware of his kids. Don't go over there. She doesn't call them. I had an incident where it was grandparents day, so I suggested to him that he, you know, take the kids over there and, like, call her and just kind of like, you know, celebrate grandparents day, you know? And so he came back in this, like his mom said, oh, this must have been Susan's idea. Like, what does that mean?
Counselor: She was sensing a lot of hostility, but there haven't been lately, anyway, a lot of direct conversations.
Client: Well, I tried to call her regarding the party, and I called, like, I guess, like, every day for, like, maybe a week. And when she finally answered the phone, she just said, susan stopped calling me and hung up the phone.
Counselor: So that's fairly direct.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there has. There has been that. Do you have any evidence. Is there any evidence that suggests that her behavior is going to change?
Client: I mean, I would want to. I think, you know, if I was to hang in there and be the best parent I can be, maybe eventually she'll want to have a relationship with her grandkids. I'm not really worried about her liking me as much.
Counselor: You're not worried about that?
Client: Not as much.
Counselor: Not as much.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But the children.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So even with that, you hang in there, and it's your hope that she'll come around, her attitude will change.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But so far, it doesn't sound like she's giving you a lot of evidence that represent a lot of evidence that that's a likely outcome. But you can be hopeful. Of course. How about your emotions, the sadness, the anxiety? Is there something. Is that something you want to work on to resolve those absent of a change in her?
Client: Yeah, because I think. I think it's important to have family, and right now, all I want to do is, I think it would be best if I moved away, like, to another state, maybe.
Counselor: Do you think it would be better to move away?
Client: Yeah. So I'm wondering if that's just because I'm sad, you know? So maybe if I was to work on my sadness, then maybe I'll feel more okay with being here.
Counselor: Do you. With all this, you know, with all her disapproval and all these stressors, which sound really tough. I mean, what you've described sounds like a tough scenario where it would be understandable to be sad and frustrated. Do you feel as though you can move through all this if nothing in her changes? So let's just assume for a second that her behavior will never change. It may, but we don't know that. So let's just run an assumption that it is the way it is. Like, this is what you're facing. Can you at some level, be okay with all this in terms of frustration, sadness?
Client: I think so, yeah, I can try.
Counselor: I mean, is that. Is that a goal?
Client: Yeah, because I really can't control her.
Counselor: So.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: It's not ideal, though. So the idea would be if she would warm up to you and engage in the family, kind of, as you. As you mentioned before, a more inviting role and friendlier and accepting. That's what you'd like, kind of in a perfect scenario. There hasn't been much in our discussion here in the way of evidence that seems to lead to that as a conclusion. Like, some change is going to occur. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Like, again, it could happen. I have no way of knowing. It just doesn't seem likely based on what you've introduced. So that leaves you not on your own, but that leaves you without her as a support to work through all these emotions. What do you think about when I say that?
Client: I think that it's going to be.
Counselor: Hard.
Client: Because I do consider how her behavior affects my kids, but I know I probably would have to, like, let go of one of her approval in order to be a better, like, more involved parent instead of just, like, kind of allowing myself to stress over that relationship. So if she. The invite has always been there, she can always engage with the kids, she has contact with her son. So it's not like, you know, I'm stopping her from being involved.
Counselor: So what you're saying is that. That. That desire for approval, that's what's causing these symptoms. That's what's maintaining them, and that's what you want to be able to let go of, is that desire. So you have a belief at some level that she must give you approval. There's a belief in there somewhere that reads something like that, yeah. She should give me approval.
Client: Yeah. I think I'm a pretty likable person.
Counselor:
output: Okay. You're a likable person. Right. And I would agree. You're a likable person, and it would make sense. She should give you approval. That's kind of the belief, yes. And the consequence of that belief, when it meets the reality that she doesn't seem to be giving you approval, is that sadness and frustration and anxiety, does that make sense?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Lucy. Nice to meet you.
Client: Hi.
Counselor: So I understand that you were referred here by your GP because you've been feeling quite down recently.
Client: Yeah, I thought I should. I've been feeling quite bad for quite a while, so I thought maybe it's time to see someone about it because I don't want to feel like this anymore.
Counselor: Okay. So from your notes, I saw that you saw the GP about three months ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how long have you been feeling down altogether?
Client: Quite a few months before that as well, actually. But it's gotten pretty bad these past few months, so that's kind of why I came.
Counselor: Okay. So has it got worse since you saw your GP?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so tell me, how are things at the moment?
Client: Well, it kind of started just feeling a bit low and wound up about things, but, I don't know, just recently I just can't really be bothered to do anything at all. I kind of find it hard to get motivated for things and I want to be. I really want to be better, but it's just kind of reaching the end now where I just. I want to do something about it.
Counselor: Okay, so you said that you're feeling really down, really sad?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you feel like you haven't got any motivation, but. Are you okay?
Client: Yeah, I'm fine.
Counselor: Sorry. Okay, and you haven't got any motivation, but it sounds like you've put quite a lot of pressure on yourself to try and feel a bit better.
Client: Yeah, I just. It's kind of hard as well because there's not really anyone to talk about. So I just kind of stay on my own trying to. I don't like to think about it, but I don't know.
Counselor: So you say you've been. You've been feeling quite isolated. There's not many people around.
Client: Yeah. There's no one I can talk to about it. No one would listen or understand anyway.
Counselor: Okay, so I'm just going to try and find out a little bit more about you. So I understand that you're an english student at uni.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you live away from home with some friends. Is that right?
Client: Yeah, I live here.
Counselor: Oh, okay. So you don't live far from the uni, but you say you feel like you live with your friends, but you don't feel like you can talk to them.
Client: Yeah, I mean, they're lovely. I get on really well with them, but I don't know, recently, whenever they want to go out or stuff, I just. I don't want to bring them down. I can't. They don't understand what I'm going through. They kind of. I don't know, they don't make fun of how I feel, but they don't really understand what it's like. I just. I don't want to go out with them and bring them down or stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds. Do you try and hide the way you're feeling from them?
Client: I guess. I mean, it's easier to hide it than to try and explain it all the time when no one really wants to know.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you've been feeling down, you've been feeling unmotivated, you feel like you want to be better. But actually it sounds like you feel like you can't reach out for help, you can't speak to anybody.
Client: No, I don't really talk to my parents a lot either, so that's kind of hard.
Counselor: Okay. I'm just gonna go back in time a little bit, I suppose. I'm just wondering, when did all of this start? You said it's been going on for quite a few months.
Client: Yeah, I guess it kind of started, actually, when I was revising for my exams. I guess the stress. I put a lot of stress on myself. I think I've always wanted to do well for me and I guess for my parents. So the stress of exams. And it was also kind of hard because my parents were going through a bit of a troubled time then.
Counselor: Okay, so this would be like last March, last April?
Client: Yeah, I think so.
Counselor: Around that time. So about six months ish. And it sounds like a lot was happening. So you had a lot of uni pressure on and you said that your parents were having marital problems. Okay. And it sounds like that was a real shock to you.
Client: Yeah, I guess it was hard as well because I wasn't doing well at uni. I guess I just felt a bit guilty. I know it sounds silly, but I felt like maybe if I could do better, then they would get better, but it just wasn't really happening.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you were trying to work hard and be more successful because you thought that that would make them happier and try and fix things.
Client: Yeah, I wanted to make them feel better, but it just kind of backfired a little, I guess.
Counselor: How did it backfire?
Client: Well, it just ended up with them getting worse, and I've just been feeling worse since then.
Counselor: Okay, so after the summer, after the exam period. And how did that exam period go for you in the end?
Client: Not very well.
Counselor: Okay. That's an awful lot of pressure to put on yourself that you supposed to.
Client: Think it's just annoying because I know I should have done better and I just didn't. And I guess I beat myself up a lot about it.
Counselor: So you say. I know, I know I should have done better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, I suppose hearing it from my perspective, I'm thinking it sounds like you had an awful lot going on at the time. It would be understandable, absolutely. That you wouldn't do as well as normal. I suppose I'm just wondering if you have very high standards for yourself.
Client: Probably maybe more than other people. My parents have always kind of taught me. Not in a loving way, I guess, but that you should do your best, but also get the best. And I agree with that. I think that's the right thing to think. But when I don't do that, I don't know, it annoys me a lot and I worry that it annoys them.
Counselor: So it sounds like you feel you should always do your best. Is that the word you used? Yeah. And that there isn't any kind of exceptions for that, but no. Okay. So I can see then that was a really difficult time for you and that was when your mood started to get lower. And things are still quite bad now. I mean, what's the situation with your parents at the moment?
Client: I think it doesn't sound good. I don't really talk to them a lot, but I don't think they're going through very good. I don't like to talk to them about it because it just makes me feel worse. But I don't think it's getting any better.
Counselor: Were you home over the summer?
Client: For a little bit, yeah.
Counselor: And how was that?
Client: Not very fun? No, it was quite tense all the time. Stress me out more than relaxed me over the summer, I guess.
Counselor:
output: Okay. Okay. So it sounds then like quite a lot has been happening. You've been feeling very low, you've had uni pressure on, and you've had problems with your parents marriage. And sounds like you feel like you can't really reach out to anyone. Like you can't understand, but you can't really reach out to your parents right now. You can't really confide in your friends. So I suppose I'm just wondering if you can tell me a bit more about how you've been feeling. I mean, say this past week.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Liz. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How things been going?
Client: They've been all right.
Counselor: Last time we were talking, it sounds like you're still having some difficulty with the quizzes. Is that still the case?
Client: Yeah, I still panic when I take them.
Counselor: You still panic. Can you tell me about the process of taking the quizzes? I know we've touched on this a little bit before.
Client: Okay, so I'm going to class. I'm fine. I sit down to take the test. I'm fine. The test is in front of me. Question one. I'm not going to get that answer.
Counselor: So you're looking down. So you take these quizzes in class?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Like a paper, pencil. Okay. With other students around?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. Is the. Is having other students around distracting to you?
Client: No, it's happened in previous online classes. It's the same.
Counselor: So it's. You're pretty sure it's the quiz itself and not some external. Okay. So it's paper and pencil. You're seated, you're in the room. Rooms relatively distraction free.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Everybody's quiet.
Counselor: And you're looking down at, really the first item on the.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: On the quiz. And what's happening? What's happening? Then as you look down, you read that first item. What's happening at a thought. We'll start a thought level. What's happening with your thinking?
Client: I'm thinking. I'm reading the question, and I'm thinking, oh, my God, there's. Okay, there's four. Okay. So it's got to be. It's got to be one of them. And I am not going to pick the right one. I'm going to think I picked the right one, and it's going to be the one that my second choice is, and I am not going to pick the right one.
Counselor: Okay, so your thought is that you're going to get. You're going to select the wrong response and therefore get that quiz item wrong. How about behavior? Like, do you notice anything physically going on as you're thinking about that quiz item and how you're gonna get it wrong?
Client: I'd say my palms are probably sweaty. Like, I'm probably a little tense.
Counselor: A little tense.
Client: Yeah. That's really it.
Counselor: All right. So what it could be is that this thought of I'm gonna get this item wrong is leading to these uncomfortable feelings, the physical feelings. So what happens when you answer item one like, you don't know if you have it right or wrong immediately? Right because it's a paper and pencil. So you answer item one, and you move on to item two. What happens then?
Client: It starts all over again. I'm already, like, well, I already got the first one wrong, and now I'm. My chances are higher of getting this one wrong.
Counselor: So you feel like it because you. Because you thought that you got the first one wrong, that your chances of getting the second one wrong actually increase?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Like, I get one wrong the whole test, it's all gonna be wrong.
Counselor: Have you ever had a quiz that you've taken where you were confident that you got the first item right?
Client: I'm sure I have. I can't remember any.
Counselor: But eventually you're going to come to one item that you're going to have these doubts about?
Client: Yes. Inevitably it happens.
Counselor: There's going to be one that's maybe a little more difficult or difficult for you. So it seems like what you're saying is that when you reach that item where you have that thought from that point on, the next item is. Is more difficult because you're having a similar thought. Does that pattern continue throughout the test?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So explain to me what, like, let's just go with the example of the first item, like, just to keep it more simple. So you have the first item, and that didn't work out for you, that thought? Right. The second one, your thought was, I have even a greater chance of missing a. So what happens after you respond to that second item?
Client: It just compounds. I just start. I feel worse and worse as the quiz, as I continue.
Counselor: That's awful. So it's an awful feeling for me. Right. So by the time you get to.
Client: Item five or six, I'm convinced it's over. I've gotten a zero. If it's the. Yeah, if I start at the first, I've gotten a zero. I've gotten a bad grade.
Counselor: So that's what's on your mind. And how about those physical symptoms? Are they the same, different or new symptoms?
Client: If it, like. If it's. If it, like, starts early at the beginning of the test, my heart's, like, pounding at this point, but I still have the sweaty palms. I'm still, like, tensing.
Counselor: So it really just gets mentally and physically more unpleasant for you the whole time. So when you're saying panic, the panic's really occurring a few items in after you have the first one that you thought you missed. And this has been happening for a while, as you described, right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Well, how about your grades? How have you actually been doing on the quizzes?
Client: I've been a pretty solid b student, so. And I feel. I wish I did better. I wish I got a's, but, I mean, these are fine. But when I take those quizzes, it's not. It doesn't. I don't know how it translates.
Counselor: How about your study habits? You consider yourself effective at studying?
Client: I've tried. I've taken a workshops on studying. I've. I. I think I'm pretty effective at studying. I've found what doesn't work. So I try to study by reading the chapters, taking outlines, reviewing flashcards, which has, I think, the best results, but.
Counselor: Okay, so your study habits are good, right. And your quiz scores are good, but you're still having these distressing thoughts and these uncomfortable physical sensations when you take the quizzes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is that about right?
Client: Yeah, that's absolutely right.
Counselor: So really you don't necessarily need your performance to change. You just. You just need your thoughts and feelings and behaviors to change.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how you. How you're reacting to the quizzes maybe?
Client: Yeah, because I get b is, like I said, so, yeah.
Counselor: And b is good.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So. All right, so I want to take you back to the moment when you're looking at the first item. Let's go back to that for a second. Okay. So you're taking a quiz and you're having those thoughts surrounding that first item, which I'm not mistaken, the automatic thought. We talked about this, right? With the cognitive behavioral therapy. The automatic thought is that I'm not going to get this one right or something to that effect. What does that mean to you?
Client: It means once I don't get that right, I'm not going to get anything else right.
Counselor: All right. So what that thought means to you is that you're going to miss that item and then you're going to miss all the rest of the items. So you're going to fail the whole quiz.
Client: The whole thing, yeah.
Counselor: So looking at that, let's call that an intermediate belief, right. It's more of a rule or an expectation. Right. What does that mean to you?
Client: It just gets worse. If I fail the quiz, then I'm like, oh, my God, I'm gonna fail the final, I'm gonna fail the course and that's going to affect my GPA.
Counselor: So it just keeps stacking. So other beliefs. So you're going to fail the course and we're going to fail the final rather than you can fail the course. So if you failed the course, what would that mean to you then?
Client: I'm not going to graduate.
Counselor: You're not going to graduate. So we move from fail in the quiz if we just look at the meaning, right. To fail in the final, to fail in the course, and now to not graduating. So if you didn't graduate, what would that mean to you?
Client: I can't. I can't be a teacher. I can't do what I want to do.
Counselor: So your chosen vocation to be a teacher would be not possible.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Right. So we go a step further and say, what would it mean to you if you couldn't be a teacher?
Client: I don't know who I'd be at that point. That's what I always saw as my career. So I don't know what my future would look like at that point without that.
Counselor: So if you were to phrase it and kind of think back as we to the CBT techniques and I kind of conceptualization we've covered, if you're to phrase that as an I am statement, right. What would you. What would you be if you couldn't be a teacher? What would that make you?
Client: I am a person who didn't make it. I'm a person that failed.
Counselor: Like we said earlier, I'm a person that didn't make it. I'm a person who failed. So in a way you're saying I'm a failure, right? Is that close?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So remember we talked before about core beliefs and how these core beliefs drive these intermediate beliefs which combine with situations like, in your case, taking a quiz to form these automatic thoughts. So one of your core beliefs may be that you're a failure. You may believe that. Does that seem like something that you've said to yourself before or thought before.
Client: About it like that? Until we did the step up to it now. But I can relate to that because a lot of times I do feel like, oh, I'm not going to be able to do this because it's me. I won't be able to do it.
Counselor: Not because it's challenging or difficult, but something to do with you. So that's where kind of you're personalizing.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you're saying to yourself at a variety of levels, I'm going to be unsuccessful, I'm going to fail. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you think that's what's happening?
Client: It must be because, like I said, I study, I get good grades. I've been tested years ago. I don't have ADHD. Anything intrinsic that would prohibit me.
Counselor: So you're able to focus and concentrate.
Client: Well, yes, I can do all of that, but when it comes to it, I'm like, I can't do it.
Counselor: So somewhere. Somewhere is this discord belief, and it's possible that it has something to do with you believing that you are a failure. Unsuccessful.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How do you think your, say, friends or family would interpret that? Like, if. I'm not suggesting, telling them that, but if they were to somehow know that, that you believed you were a failure, how would they react?
Client: I don't think they would see the connection. I think they would be like, well, you do well in school. I don't understand.
Counselor: So they wouldn't believe that you're a failure?
Client: No.
Counselor: You may believe it.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And similarly, if you had a classmate that was in the same situation and, you know, struggled with these disturbing thoughts and feelings and behaviors during quizzes, how would you evaluate them?
Client: I guess I'd say the same thing that my family would say. Like, you're look at the evidence, you're not a failure.
Counselor: You'd say, look at the evidence and you'd evaluate that they weren't a failure.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But with yourself, you're being a little more harsh.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Which isn't uncommon. So there's a few levels in which I think we can go after this, what I'll call a problem. But really it's a series of thoughts and beliefs. Okay. The first is that the kind at the ground level, and that's when you are taking the quiz and you have that automatic thought that says, I'm going to miss this item.
Client: I'm not going to get it right.
Counselor: I'm not going to get it right. That's your thought. I'm not going to get it right. In these situations, I like to encourage clients to apply what's called an adaptive response or self talk. If you're in a quiz in a quiet classroom, it wouldn't literally be self talking.
Client: Right? Right.
Counselor: But it's a thought that you're consciously applying. So the other thought, that's automatic.
Client: Right.
Counselor: That just pops in your head. Right.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: This one would be one that you deliberately think and make myself. So what could you think to yourself that would be a counter to that automatic thought that you're having, that you're gonna get that item wrong?
Client: I guess that in my past quizzes, like, chances are I have a good chance of getting it right.
Counselor: Okay. So just looking at the probabilities based on your past performance, even though I'm thinking I'm going to get it wrong, chances are I'm going to get it right.
Client: Right. Somehow I still have a b. So.
Counselor: So you are getting most of them right.
Client: Right. So I have a good chance.
Counselor: So I like that adaptive response. Right. Do you think that makes sense for you? Yeah, I think you did well there. So the next time you're taking a quiz, I want you to apply that adaptive response. Now, this takes work, right. So this automatic thought is going to come upon you, and before you know it, you're gonna have that feeling. Right. The physical symptoms you discussed. The sweaty palms. Right. And the feeling of, I think you mentioned.
Client: Intense. Yeah.
Counselor: So don't let it discourage you. Those symptoms come on so quickly.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Right. There is an intervening thought, and you've identified it. So you will have an opportunity most likely to apply that automatic thought at some point. But the first few times, it might be a little rough.
Client: Yeah. Touch and go.
Counselor: I guess the nice thing about a quiz is, I mean, how many items are on these quizzes?
Client: Yeah. 1515.
Counselor: So you have a few different chances to apply that adapter. Right.
Client: Right. It's more than one.
Counselor: Yeah. So, you know, you would like to get on the first time where you have that mag thought, where you identify the automatic thought, but if you don't, it's not a big deal. So later on, maybe it takes item two or three, and then you might remember, hey, I have this.
Client: Yeah. Oh, wait. I'm supposed to be thinking this.
Counselor: Yeah. And my hope is that as you apply this adaptive response more and more, you can reduce the probability that that automatic thought is going to come in.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So that's one level that I want you to go after. It. Does that make sense?
Client: It does. I think I can do that.
Counselor: That's something you feel like you could.
Client: It is.
Counselor: You could do. At the other level. I guess you'd call this a deeper level, but it's all really, you know, in your brain. Right. It's just this core belief.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Okay. And why I use the word deeper is because we think of core beliefs as more stubborn. They don't change as easily as automatic thoughts might. I'd like you to. And this is really just more reflection. Reflect on the evidence or evaluate the evidence that supports and refutes this idea that you are unsuccessful, that you're a failure. I think cognitively, you kind of understand that you're not right, but in other sense, you feel like you are right. So, in a way, cognitively, you're.
Client: There's that discrepancy.
Counselor: Right. There's a little bit of both. You know, you can tell me that your family would say that's not the case, but you still.
Client: Right on paper, technically, I would. I'm not, but I still, I guess, feel that way.
Counselor: There's a part of you that still feels that way, part of you that still believes that cognitively, there's also a part of you that thinks through that and says that's not accurate. So I want you to weigh the validity of that core belief. And actually, I think with this, it's helpful to write down evidence that would support it, and that's certainly something to note. But also, and this is really more important, evidence that refutes it, evidence that runs counter.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But record both, and we'll meet next time, and we'll look at the evidence, and we'll evaluate it.
Client: Yeah, I can do that.
Counselor: So those two steps you feel like you're comfortable with, and they make sense to you?
Client: Yeah, they do. I do. I definitely think I can do those.
Counselor: When's the next time you'll be taking a quiz?
Client: I think next week.
Counselor: Next week. Okay. You have these quizzes often?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So we'll set up a session for next week. Let's try to get to where it's after your next quiz. So we'll have that to talk about, because I think that's the next area to make. It sounds like the next area would be good to try to make progress. Yeah, I mean, seems like that's what you want to work on.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: So we'll go from there. So I'll set you up with an appointment for just after that quiz. Try the adaptive response and try evaluating evidence with the core belief. That sounds good.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Jordan. How you doing today?
Client: Could have been better.
Counselor: Could be better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: Um, well, you know, I have two jobs.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: And I lost one of them.
Counselor: You lost your job? Yes. Which one did you lose?
Client: I lost one at the grocery store.
Counselor: That was your part time?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I'm sorry to hear that.
Client: Me too. And I'm just. It's all I think about now.
Counselor: And when did this happen?
Client: It happened about two, three days ago.
Counselor: Two, three days ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if I remember right, you took that job not too long ago to kind of supplement your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So certainly that would be upsetting, but I know that's not a major part of your income.
Client: It's not, but, I mean, I'm still very worried about it.
Counselor: Tell me about the worry.
Client: I mean, I worry that, you know, I'm. Now I only had so much money, and now I have less than that. I mean, without my money, you know, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: So before you had the job, you were paying all your bills. You want some extra income, you've lost that extra income. And I can certainly understand how that would be disturbing. But as I understand that you were doing okay before with your full time job.
Client: I was doing okay, but, I mean, I got comfortable with that extra income, and so now my fear is that I've gotten too comfortable with it, and now that it's not there anymore, it's going to affect the fact I'm not going to be able to pay for food or my rent.
Counselor: Okay, so you adjusted to the new income level with the full time and the part time job together, and you're worried you can't adjust back?
Client: I'm worried that, I mean, things are just gonna get worse from here. I mean, it's a big deal, losing your job. Even if it was part time, I've gotten comfortable from having so much money, from the money I had to. Now that's, you know, been divided and, I mean, God knows how many things, like I said, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: Well, what. What can happen? So you have that income, your income is reduced now to just your full time job. What can happen from this point on?
Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. So, I mean, if I can't, if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not gonna have insurance on my cardinal. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work, and then I'll get fired there too.
Counselor: All right, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something the police officer could see, don't have insurance, give you a ticket, which is just money. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?
Client: Because I wouldn't be able to get to work.
Counselor: So it'd be. So the ticket would be so expensive, you would lose your.
Client: Well, the ticket would be expensive, so I wouldn't be able to try to pay the next month's insurance. So I just wouldn't have insurance on my car. So I.
Counselor: So you'd lose your insurance?
Client: I'd lose my insurance.
Counselor: And then by losing your insurance, you lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive that insurance. And then you lose your job.
Client: Mm hmm. I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car, and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times.
Counselor: No, that's serious. Yeah. You wouldn't want to do that.
Client: I wouldn't go to jail.
Counselor: So there's two. You have two kind of causal change. One is losing your job. And now even just the idea you can end up incarcerated.
Client: Yes. I mean, which I definitely lose my.
Counselor: Job if I'm in jail, I would imagine.
Client: And so that would have. So then I wouldn't even have, like, any money to help me through jail. Like, to. For the commissary and stuff.
Counselor: Because you would have no income.
Client: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm. No one's gonna hire me.
Counselor: Because you have a criminal record.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances. So what's happened is kind of in your mind, and we've talked about how thoughts work and beliefs work, is you, in reality, you've lost this part time job. And as I said, that's certainly. That's understandable that you'd be upset about that. I doubt many people would be happy about losing additional income, but you move from there, from losing additional income, which is what has actually happened to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this. So I remember maybe last week. Week before, you're talking about the. The letter that you received from. It was like a late notice. It wasn't. Turned out wasn't.
Client: Yeah, it was sent to me, but it was somebody else's credit card mistake. Yeah.
Counselor: Do you remember the conclusions you drew from when you believe that was actually for you, that late notice, that my.
Client: Credit score was gonna go down, that I would. I'd be stuck in that apartment, and then I'd go into depression. I wouldn't be able to do anything.
Counselor: Yeah. So you ended up in that scenario. You end up in a situation where you just couldn't function at all. And you moved there from a letter that you believe was addressed to you, saying you were one month or six days late or something on a credit card, which, of course, you don't want to be late on a credit card, but you move from there to being so depressed you couldn't work, couldn't function, I think, is how you put it. Couldn't function. Do you see, kind of, given how we've talked about cognitive behavioral strategies and concepts, do you see a pattern that's emerged over the last few times I've seen you?
Client: I mean, I've seen that, you know, sometimes I can. I can think the worst, and then. And I know it didn't happen last time, but that was, you know, a stroke of good luck.
Counselor: That it wasn't you.
Client: Yeah. That it was, you know, it wasn't me. And, you know, that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part time job anymore.
Counselor: You've lost real income.
Client: I mean, this isn't a mistake. This isn't a. We fired the wrong person. You know, this is real. So there's real concerns here.
Counselor: I.
Client: Unlike last time, where I was lucky.
Counselor: So this. This situation, you see, is different than the first situation because the first situation was more. You were perceiving something was wrong that wasn't wrong because you weren't the intended recipient of the letter.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But in this situation, it's different because it's real. You really lost your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: And, of course, keeping in mind that this job, again, only a few months old, and you survived well before that, is it reason to believe you could survive well again, that you could adapt to this lost income?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hey, Carly. How are you doing today?
Client: I'm good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on this last week?
Client: I've just been feeling kind of in a rut. I mean, I've been looking for a job and haven't really gotten anywhere. And then I had a drink the other night, and I just felt like me not having a job and me going out and having that drink, it wasn't deserved. And I just felt like such a loser because that was the time that I should have been at work if I had a job, and instead I was at the bar drinking. So I had one drink, and then it led to another. Cause then I just felt worse and I figured I had one, so.
Counselor: All right, so how much did you drink in total?
Client: I think I lost track after four or five.
Counselor: How long had it been since you had a drink before that?
Client: I did really well. It was, I think, like three weeks.
Counselor: Three weeks?
Client: Three weeks or so.
Counselor: Oh, so you did really well and then you had one drink and that just made you feel like you weren't successful?
Client: I felt like a loser.
Counselor: Felt like a loser. And you feel that kind of led to drinking some more? So you had a rough time with things?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. How about now?
Client: I mean, now I just kind of. I don't know, I'm afraid to go back. Like, I'm afraid to go out with, like, some friends. They invite me out to dinner, but I know there's alcohol and.
Counselor: Is that where you were when you had that first drink? Was that with friends?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so there's a few things going on. We've talked in the past, right, about separating the behavior from the person. Right. So behavior is what we do, not who we are. You remember those discussions? And correct me if I'm wrong, but it sounds like I'm going to use some different words than you used. But it sounds like when you had that first drink, you're kind of ashamed that you had a drink and you had it during the time when you would have been working.
Client: Yeah, that's pretty accurate.
Counselor: That's pretty accurate. So, taking yourself back to that moment, right. We had that first. That first drink, like, you finished that first drink. What was your thought at that moment?
Client: Just, like, shameful. Like, I did really, really well, and then here I was, and I had just finished a drink, and I knew I wanted another one.
Counselor: Okay, so shameful is kind of like the feeling, but the thought is I did really, really well. Right. So that's what you're thinking was, I did really, really well. And what was that the end of the thought? Or was that. Was there more before you had that next drink?
Client: I guess just I was doing well, and then I had a drink, and I just felt like an awful person. So figured what was the. The hurt and having more.
Counselor: So the sequence would have been you had the drink, you felt shameful. At the same time, you're thinking that you were doing really well, and then just really, as you said before, you just felt like a loser. And then you decided, might as well just have the second drink. So another thought might be that, like, I might as well, just might as well just have a second drink.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So you can see how there's some thoughts and some feelings at work. Right. As you finished that first drink, was it fairly quick? Were those thoughts and feelings fairly occur fairly quickly after the drink?
Client: Yeah, I would say as I was finishing and then finished.
Counselor: Right away, you regretted it. And in that regret, as you thought about it, thought, might as well just continue drinking now because you kind of blew it.
Client: Yeah, I already messed up. I might as well keep going.
Counselor: Okay. And that's a common cycle to fall into. And you had three weeks where you hadn't had a drink prior to that. So let's look at this. Let's try to separate the behavior from the self a little bit. If you had a friend who was in the same predicament, who had a history of using alcohol and then had three weeks without any alcohol use, and then their behavior was to have a drink, what would you think of them?
Client: I would think that they had a rough day or something must have happened where? I mean, it's just one drink.
Counselor: Okay. They had a rough day. One drink. And what would you think of their behavior? How would you categorize that behavior?
Client: I guess just they made a mistake.
Counselor: So not ideal, depending on their point of view. Maybe a little irresponsible.
Client: Yeah, I think irresponsible would be irresponsible.
Counselor: But you wouldn't necessarily characterize them as a bad person. No, but their behavior was a bit irresponsible, you know, in terms of, like, the recovery plan, which would be to not drink. But when you apply that same examination to your own situation, how do you characterize yourself after you had that first drink?
Client: It was my mistake. It was in it. It makes me a worse person for doing it.
Counselor: So you see how you're being a little. Well, it'd be quite a bit rougher on yourself. Like, your evaluation of yourself is. Is fairly harsh. You mentioned loser earlier and ashamed. Whereas you wouldn't necessarily evaluate someone else that way. How would you evaluate your behavior? How would you judge your behavior of taking that first drink?
Client: Shameful. I mean, irresponsible, bad overall.
Counselor: So bad, irresponsible, shameful. Is there a way to separate that behavior in terms of your thinking, in terms of the way you evaluate it from yourself? Like, are you into behavior together, enmeshed, or can you be separated?
Client: Um, I think we could be separated, but it. It feels like we're, like I am.
Counselor: That behavior in that moment, it's very congruent for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. The shame matches the behavior. The behavior matches shame like it's there one at that moment. But really, logically, rationally, you're you. Right? Your identity and values and your behavior is something you do, but in the moment, it's hard for you to see that. Looking back on it now, are you able to see the distinction between what people do and what they are?
Client: Yeah. I mean, just because you have one drink doesn't make you a horrible person, I don't think. Right.
Counselor: No, certainly not. No. And you were clean for three weeks, and you had one drink. So really, your behavior was a slip, right? It was. And irresponsible in relationship to your goals, I suppose, but still a slip. And you could have stopped, but that shame got ahold of you, right? That thought, well, now I've done it.
Client: I blew it.
Counselor: Yeah. So with that mentality, you kind of set yourself up for drinking more. So I think this is important because we've seen this cycle, like, where you have weeks of sobriety, and then you'll drink a bit and then have weeks of sobriety. And I'm wondering if part of the difficulty you're facing is you're not coping with the slips as just slips.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: You're allowing them to be gateways into a lot more drinking than a slip. Does that make sense?
Client: That sounds pretty accurate.
Counselor: And you see how the shameful feelings kind of just interfere with the behavior that you really. That's really consistent with your goals, which would be to not continue drinking. Another piece of this, too, is the associating with friends who drink. You're putting yourself in a treacherous situation. And again, that's a behavior, right? That doesn't make you one way or the other. It's a behavior. How would you judge that behavior, going out with friends?
Client: I don't know. I mean, difficult, because I like being around those people, but I guess it would be. It's risky.
Counselor: Risky? Okay. It's a risky behavior. And what does it make you? Who are you? Because you do that behavior. Like, how do you feel about yourself when you take that risky behavior?
Client: Guilty.
Counselor: Okay. So you have guilt when you go out with your friends, and then you have shame if you drink. And both, in this case, both emotions that kind of point you in the direction of more drinking. So part of this behavioral strategy here is to avoid those circumstances. Like, to recognize that's a risky behavior, which you have. And the other part would be to deal more effectively if you do slip.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Right. Does that separation of what we do and who we are make sense to you rationally? Kind of feels a little unnatural, though.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So maybe as you're confronting similar situations in the course of the next week, you could be aware of behaviors that might put you at risk and try to try to separate your identity from that behavior. So just judge the behavior and don't pass any judgment on yourself. Does that make sense?
Client: Kind of, yeah.
Counselor: It might help you to, since it's a little tough to. Because right now the feeling and the judgment are intertwined. Right. It might help to write it down when these things happen and kind of write down, like, one row for this is how I judge this behavior that I'm thinking about doing, and this is how I judge myself. So if you see a lot of self judgment, that might be a clue that you're falling into that cycle a little bit where you're making decisions based on that emotion instead of a rational judgment of the behavior.
Client: Okay.
