Counselor: Would that help a little bit?
Client: Yeah, I think that would probably be beneficial.
Counselor: Right. So that will be our plan going forward until next week is note, document your judgment about your behavior and any judgment you may have about yourself. And there's some insight that can be gained there. You kind of distinguish the two and make a note of those and try to use that evidence before making a decision that might put you in a risky spot.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: Sound like a plan?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maury. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: You doing all right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?
Client: Yeah, yeah. I mean, you know, it kind of came up again. You know, every time my wife yells at me, you know, I feel like a failure, you know, like I told you last time, I just. I just feel like I can't do anything right, you know? Like everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling, and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.
Counselor: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So it's frustrating.
Client: Yeah, it definitely is.
Counselor: How is what's going on impacted your relationship with your wife?
Client: I mean, it's rocky, you know, because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that. And then, you know, we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad, and then it just keeps going like that.
Counselor: So when you. You mentioned you feel like a failure when she. When she yells at you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Can you think back to maybe the last time, one of the last times you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We've talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts. She starts yelling at you?
Client: I mean, she'll yell at me. I mean, I feel, you know, frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And. I don't know. I mean, as I was thinking about, like we were talking about it, and as I was thinking about it more this week, kind of felt like, you know, kind of like what happened with my dad, you know? I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. You know, like, if my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way. And it feels like the same thing. Yeah. It's kind of the first. I guess kind of the first thought that comes to mind.
Counselor: The first thought is I've been through something like this before, I guess.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like, you know? Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Like, it's like just a sense that this isn't brand new.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad. Yahweh. Yeah.
Client: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So, in a sense, these arguments are taking you back to another point in time.
Client: I guess so, in a way, that's distressing.
Counselor: Yeah, it is.
Client: I mean, it feels, you know, pretty crappy.
Counselor: Now, in these arguments, she yells at you. You mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own, you know, in the midst of all that. Right. How would you rate it in terms of, like, any physical violence? Nothing like that.
Client: No, it's just words. I mean, we're just, you know, just yelling.
Counselor: And what level, like, what level of yelling would you say? How severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?
Client: Yeah, I don't know. I mean, it's like, you know, sometimes it can get up to, like, the eight or nines, you know, but just, I guess generally it's, you know, down. Closer to a seven on scale, like one to ten. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So sometimes it's seven. That would be pretty bad.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But some other times it's not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you feel like your reaction is being frustrated is disproportionate to what's really going on or you feel like it's money?
Client: I don't know what else to do. You know? I mean, it's just. It's kind of my reaction, my gut reaction to it, you know? I think I'm justified in it because, you know, she just doesn't understand how much she yells at me, you know, and how much that hurts me. You know? I do feel justified. I mean, but it just. It just keeps going, though. And I feel justified, though. I don't know.
Counselor: Let's talk for a moment about, if you're okay with it, about your father and his yelling. You've discussed this with me a little bit before. In the past few sessions. I remember you saying that most. It was in the afternoon. Most of the yelling was when you were both home.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it was. I mean, mostly when I get home from school. I mean, I wasn't, you know, I was in high school, and then after that, you know, I went to college. And so I wasn't really home much during college, but, you know, I guess it'd be after I got home from high school. You know, I'd get home and he'd get home from work and, you know, just kind of be aggravated, whatever, just start yelling and. Yeah, usually when I got back from school, yeah.
Counselor: So he would get back from work, you would get back from school. And how long would that last? How long would the period where you were kind of vulnerable to being yelled at last?
Client: I don't know. I mean, sometimes about an hour, you know, and he'd be yelling because he's, you know, frustrated from work and he's frustrated from the drive home and whatever else, you know? And at some point, he would usually start drinking, you know, so maybe about an hour or so, you know, where that was. Like, you knew you were gonna get it.
Counselor: So kind of every day you could predict that between when you. Or between when he came home after you were already home from school and when he started drinking, you were gonna. He was gonna find something to yacht you about.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And, I mean, there were some days, like, I knew when he came home, he came home the same time every day. I knew I could get out of the house, you know? Cause at some point, I had a car, my friends had cars, you know, whatever.
Counselor: You had more freedom.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. You know, at some point, I had a job, so sometimes I'd work after school and stuff, so I knew I'd be able to leave the house at times, you know, like when I knew he was gonna start yelling and stuff. But, I mean, there was a period of time probably like my senior year of high school that I just didn't, you know, I just came home and, you know, it was gonna happen, you know, that's the way it happened.
Counselor: Even though you were able to escape it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. You could have stayed out long enough for him to start drinking. Yeah.
Client: Instead you stayed in the house.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I mean, it was pretty much my whole senior year come home. I knew what was gonna happen, and I just took it. You know, I just. I knew he was gonna yell. I just took it that.
Counselor: Was there ever a period when you first got your freedom that you tried, like.
Client: Oh, yeah, yeah, I did. And. I don't know. I don't know why I didn't just keep doing that. It probably would have been easier, but. I don't know. The whole senior year, I just started. I was just back there at the house when he came home from work.
Counselor: So in that period, were you. Were you. There's times when you did leave, what did he do instead of yell at you?
Client: I guess he had to yell at somebody else. I mean, my. My sister, my brother were home. I guess he probably yelled at them. I don't know. I mean, it felt good to not be there, but I guess he probably yelled at them, which just sucks. I mean, you know, I guess somebody had. Whoever was there was gonna take it, you know?
Counselor: Somebody was gonna get you out there.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, I guess it was them when I wasn't there. I don't know.
Counselor: And how do you think you took it. When you were there, how well did you respond?
Client: I just got used to it, you know, I knew what was gonna happen. I knew he was gonna yell. I knew that it was gonna make me upset. I knew that just those repeated times, just like now, you know, I'm gonna feel like a failure, which ultimately I did. You know, maybe I probably just became numb to it, you know, it happens so often and same thing every day. Probably just became numb to it and just kind of stopped caring and kind of stopped, I don't know, believing in myself or something, you know?
Counselor: Like you've just given up.
Client: Yeah, probably. That's probably. I don't know. Probably. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And how many years total did this experience go on? Do you endure the yelling?
Client: I mean, it would have been while I was in middle school and most of high school. I mean, I told you at some point I was able to leave, but probably all of middle school, most of high school, and I left, and then some, you know, for the rest of the senior year, I would be there. So, I don't know, quite a few years, I guess.
Counselor: A long time to suffer.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And now if we move back forward in time, you're in a relationship where you're getting yelled at a bit. Right. And that's sometimes quite a bit, and that's causing you distress.
Client: It's like the same thing. You're yelling a little bit and. Yeah.
Counselor: So you feel like you're back in the same place.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it does. Yeah. I mean, obviously, you know, she's. She's not doing anything like he was, you know, like drinking or anything like that, but it does. I mean, it's like the same thing that happened is happening again.
Counselor: So that's. In your opinion, that's the consequence of what happened to you. Like, all this yelling that you endured before in some way is significantly contributing to what you're going through now.
Client: Maybe. I mean, I guess it could, you know, because it is the same thing. So maybe it's.
Counselor: There could be some connection.
Client: Maybe. Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, maybe not 100% explain it, but it explains part of it.
Client: Yeah, it definitely could. I definitely could.
Counselor: So your functioning has been affected a bit. I mean, to the point where you're here with me now, we're talking about it, and you're frustrated, and it does sound painful. Now, I'm curious. You mentioned you had a younger sister and a younger brother, and they grew up in the same house. How are they doing?
Client: Well, my sister, she's three years younger than I am. She's doing great. I mean, she graduated from college, like, top of her class kind of thing, you know? And she's about to get married, too. That's cool. Got a really great guy, you know. She's doing great. She lives next town over for me. I get to see her a lot. Yeah, she's great, though. My brother, he's five years younger than I am. He's doing pretty good, too. He's just about to graduate from college. I think he gets really good grades, too, from what I hear, from what he tells me. I don't get to see him as much as I do her because she's in college, but I think he's doing really well, too. You know, they both. Yeah, they both do some really good stuff. They have really good goals and stuff like that.
Counselor:
output: You seem like you have a good relationship with them. You're proud of them. Yeah, definitely.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Miss Payne. My name is Rebecca, and I will be your therapist today. And I see on your notes that you prefer to be called Kelly. Is that correct?
Client: Yes, ma'am. My name is Kelly, but a lot of people call me Kelly Joe. They do? Yeah. My papa in particular. He likes to call me Joe. Kelly Joe. I was named after my great grandfathers.
Counselor: Okay, well, would you prefer that I call you Kelly or Kelly Joe?
Client: No, just call me Kelly. I think Kelly Joe is really country. Okay, we'll just go with Kelly.
Counselor: All right, Kelly. The first thing I want to do is I'm going to explain our roles that we have today in our session. And of course, you know, as I said, I'm your therapist, but you're also actively participating in this session. And anytime you have a question, if you have any comments, if you don't understand something, I want you to tell me so that I can make sure that you understand everything that we're doing, that we're talking about, and it will be actively. Yeah. Between both of us will be a team, if you want.
Client: Oh, I definitely ask questions. Trust me. I like to ask a lot of questions. I like to talk.
Counselor: Well, that's good. And then the other thing, we have an agenda that I'm going to try to stick by. We want to start off with a mood check. I'll just kind of see how you're feeling today. We'll talk about your presenting problems, and we'll go into making some goals, and I'll explain a little bit of the theory that I use for our sessions. Kind of do a little educational piece to make sure you understand what's going on, and we'll give a summary. And also, I may have some homework that we can talk about.
Client: Okay. Because I sure do have lots of problems. I can tell you about tons of problems.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: So I'm going to be talking your ears off.
Counselor: Well, we have approximately about 15 to 20 minutes today, and I'll let you know when the time starts to run short so you're not taken by surprise.
Client: Okay, that will be fine. But if I need more time, I'll just have to buy it, I guess.
Counselor: Well, we can work something out, I'm sure.
Client: Well, I'll try to keep it short.
Counselor: Okay. Well, the first thing I do want to do is check on your mood and just kind of see how you're feeling today.
Client: Well, today, I just tell you, that teenager of mine, I could just hang him up by his toes. That right there. If I could just get that settled for a while. I think I might have get some common ground with him. I think I might be okay.
Counselor: Okay. So you would say you're kind of feeling frustrated.
Client: I'm frustrated and stressed and can't sleep. Just, you know, really just snappy. I just snap at him all the time.
Counselor: Okay. And I guess the biggest thing would be your frustration. On a scale of one to ten with your frustration, how would you rate that?
Client: Why? Twelve, of course. Yeah. Frustration with a teenage boy. Have you ever said girls are hard to raise? Boys, they're hard to raise.
Counselor: Okay. So you're really having some frustration issues. And I noticed you mentioned your sleep that you're not sleeping very well.
Client: No, not sleeping well. I think I'm just stressed with him all the time and just, you know, just the day to day life stuff. And I'm just stressed. Just stressed. Not sleeping really good at all.
Counselor: And it seems like maybe not sleeping, you know, a lot of times that can also add to you're being more prone to de stressed. So that's something we need to kind of get balanced out. So you're getting the sleep that you need, but you're also able to, you know, deal with your teenager, deal with your child and kind of get to where you need to be.
Client: That would be great. That would be great. I've got to get some sleep.
Counselor: So you said that you're very frustrated or stressed out. And that kind of leads me right into, you know, the main reason that you're here today to presenting problems. And I know you didn't mention it has to do with your teenager, but can you clarify a little bit about what's going on with him?
Client: I think it's racing hormones.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: He just can't. Anything that I say, he just disagrees. You know, he's right, I'm wrong. We can't come to common ground on anything. Curfew. He's just, you know, I feel I give him everything and he feels that we're too strict, you know? You know, and he wants to do things that I don't feel that is appropriate. But who knows? Just, who knows? What is he, what is he really wanting? But we've got. We've got to come to some type of common ground to figure out what we can do. Just make our life just a little bit easier and not fight all the time.
Counselor: So it sounds to me y'all have a lot of little things that y'all disagree on, but it's all added up to be a very big stressor.
Client: Oh, yes. I could just hang him up by his toenails okay.
Counselor: Okay. Well, let me remind you that I am a mandated reporter. So anything that you say, if it is something that would leave me of concern, I do have to make a report.
Client: Well, hate him, but by his toenails. I'll just tell you what.
Counselor: Okay, so I know you said you have some communication problems. I believe I heard you say that.
Client: We do.
Counselor: Okay. And do you feel that maybe it's just he's not listening or that y'all just.
Client: We just can't agree.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: We just can't agree.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: We can't because he thinks that we're just so strict.
Counselor: Okay. Okay, well, and, you know, how old is he?
Client: He's 15.
Counselor: And that is very common for 15 year olds, for teenagers. They're going through the changes in the school and the peer pressure and friends. So that is something very common. But it can also be very frustrating. And I see where you're having some struggles with that, and that's perfectly understandable.
Client: We've got sexting going on. We have things that are going on on the computer, so we're having to watch that and leave at that. We're having to put curfews on his phone, things like that, but things that we're trying not to be unreasonable about. But sex seems a little bit. Some things that he shouldn't be doing.
Counselor: Yes, and that's true. That's very true.
Client: He's going to keep on to get himself in trouble, lying, not letting us know what he's going try and do things behind our back, which, I mean, he's not that he's a bad kid, but I think we've got some peer pressure going on. Things that he wants to be out doing, the grown up stuff, and he's just not ready for.
Counselor: Well, and I can see, I'm glad that you just mentioned that, that, you know, that he's not a bad kid, because that kind of does let me know that your perspective on your child, that you do still, you know, feel like he has a good child. You're just having some issues right now dealing with, and that's. That's a positive thing.
Client: Yeah, I told him, you know, he can start considering doing these things when he's pretty white and 21.
Counselor: Yeah. Okay.
Client: Well, one thing that I would like.
Counselor: For you to think about is some goals that we can set.
Client: Set.
Counselor: I know your big goal, like you said, your overall goal would be to have better communication with your son, but I think it would need to take little steps and little goals to get to your big goal. Is that something that you would agree?
Client: I can agree on that. Okay.
Counselor: So I want to get your feedback and kind of know what you think the first goal that you would like for us to work on would be.
Client: Me just trying to understand.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: What I, you know, I feel that I understand what it's like being a teenager, but, you know, today's time is so much different from, you know, how long, you know, when we were teenagers. So, you know, it's just understanding the peer pressures and things that he's going through and. But still also be. Be a parent and understand what he's going through. I mean, that's my main goal. And like I said, for us to be able to come to common ground, and I just don't see it at this point being able to do it by ourselves at some point that we're going to have to work to something with someone to be that person, to mediate between us.
Counselor: Well, and I, you know, I admire you for the fact that you have realized that you do need some mediation, that you need some outside help, and that also gives you kind of an unbiased position between you and your son, somebody who's looking in from the outside and can see, you know, kind of what the situation is and what might. Might need to be done to help the situation. And one thing that I think we could do is to work on maybe have some sessions with you and your son together after we've done some individual sessions.
Client: That would be so great. That would be great. Just got to help me remember to keep an open mind.
Counselor: Yes, ma'am. And really, that's the theory that I use. The therapy that I use is called cognitive behavioral therapy or cognitive based therapy. Therapy. Have you heard of that? Are you familiar with that term at all?
Client: A little bit, but not much. So if you could just help me.
Counselor:
output: With that a little bit. Part of what that is, your emotions are linked with your feelings and your actions and your presenting circumstances also control your actions, your thoughts, control your emotions. And basically an example of that would be, you know, your son gets in late for curfew one night, and, you know, your thoughts, you're thinking, he's going to do this every time. I can't trust him anymore. And so you start having just different emotions. Different whether it's anger or frustration or whatever your emotions may be. But in turn, it could just have been a one time thing. You know, say he could have gotten, you know, there could have been a wreck and he could have got caught in some traffic. But your thoughts at the time were he's come in, he's always going to be late. And so your emotions lead towards the distrust, the anger, the frustration. And that's one example. Does that make sense?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Lisa. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good, but there has been an issue, you know, we've been working on, like, my motivation.
Counselor: Sure.
Client: Well, kind of. It's kind of related to that. So I'm in school, and every few weeks we have, like, papers to write, and I know, I know it. I know I can do it. It's just actually sitting down and doing it.
Counselor: All right, well, tell me about the papers.
Client: Well, they're usually about five pages long. And I just look at it, and I'm like, it's five pages. But I'm like, okay. So I go sit down, you know, at my computer. I'm like, all right, I'm gonna start on references. Mm hmm. So I get, you know, I start off good. I do the references, but then it's like I get sidetracked so easily, and then I end up killing, like, 2 hours checking the news. Checking. And then it goes to my phone, and then just looking up recipes. I mean, it gets really off topic. And then I realize, you know, I haven't done anything.
Counselor: All right, so you. You have a five page paper. You sit down to work on it. You have the references. You get that part taken care of, but then it sounds like you kind of wander off a little bit.
Client: Oh, big time.
Counselor: Yeah. Okay, and then what happens after you are done wandering a little bit?
Client: Well, I get kind of annoyed with it, and then I'm like, well, you know, I've already, you know, it's already night time. I'll try and try to do it tomorrow. And then, you know, either tomorrow doesn't happen or the same thing happens, and it's just. And then I end up, you know, rushing right at the end of, you know, due tomorrow, and I'm getting all these five pages done. It's really hard for me.
Counselor: So you are, you are finishing the assignment on time? So the problem isn't lateness?
Client: No. I mean, I get it done.
Counselor: You get it done.
Client: It's just all at the last minute.
Counselor: So it's really the, how the time breaks out isn't working out well for you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: You'd rather not be doing it at the last moment?
Client: No. I mean, I try not to. I mean, I set time aside to go sit down. I'm like, all right, you know, we're going to start on this paper, then sidetracked. I'm watching tv. I'm on my phone. I'm on some other website.
Counselor: So these, so these activities that you're engaging in between when you start the work and before you start writing. So, gathering the references before you start writing, you said check an email. Yeah, and other kind of. It sounds like unplanned, small activities.
Client: Yeah. I mean, there's small things that keep my attention, but that's not where my attention needs to go.
Counselor: These aren't particularly engaging activities, like something you need to do at that moment.
Client: No. I mean, I look up, you know. Right. I start on one reference, and then, oh, this article looks cool. Ooh, this article. You know, next thing I know, I'm researching octopuses or something.
Counselor: So, like, distracted.
Client: Yeah, distracted is a good word.
Counselor: And then there's a moment when you kind of catch yourself and realize you haven't really started writing.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But it's like 2 hours later, it's too late. Yeah. So you're consuming time there. All right. So you have a few different levels of activity here. You have the paper, which it sounds like you're okay writing, but you're maybe not highly motivated to write. Okay. But you seem to be getting the references done. Okay.
Client: Yeah, I mean, I get the references done. Okay.
Counselor: You collect the material, and then the writing part, that's the difficult part. And then you have these behaviors in the middle, which you enjoy doing a little, but they're not something that, I.
Client: Mean, they're not something that, like, you know, I'm jumping for joy about. It's just something to procrastinate. So I don't have to do my paper. And I don't think that, you know, I'm not like, oh, I need to check my emails, but I don't have to do my paper. It's just, oh, I should check my email. Oh, I should check my phone. Oh, I haven't done this. Oh, I haven't seen this in a while.
Counselor: But these behaviors still fulfill purpose. They do delay the writing of the paper.
Client: Yeah, that's true.
Counselor: You may not be fully aware of that in the moment, but then you kind of become aware of that later. That that's the purpose that those behaviors accomplished.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Was that they kept you distracted from the.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: From writing. All right, so the. The writing of papers and activity, that's a behavior that's something you're not really looking forward to. What's a behavior that. What's an activity that you really do look forward to, that you think about and some level of engagement? Is there.
Client: Well, there is this new tv show out that they just started a new season, and I have it all recorded, like, 24 episodes, but I can't find time to watch it. But I'm really, you know, I've seen the first season. I'm so interested in it, you know, I can't wait to see the next one. You know, I guess that that would, that's, I guess what makes me really happy right now.
Counselor: So. So you're excited about this television show and you have, you have the episodes already recorded.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: And maybe one of the reasons you can't find the time is because the time you're using between the two parts writing this paper.
Client: Yeah. I mean, this paper's taking me a lot longer than it should.
Counselor: So let's try this. When you do write the paper, you're really writing it. The writing part, not the preparing part, but the writing part kind of all at the end. Right. Getting it done is the night before it's due. Alright. So I want to try a couple different behavioral strategies here.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And these might be similar to what we tried before working with motivation. One is I think that it might be helpful and I want you to let me know if I'm right here to break, if it's a five page paper to break it up into more than one night because right now, functionally, at least a lot of it you're doing on the last night.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What would be a more comfortable pace? Like, for example, how long does it take you to write one page?
Client: About an hour, hour and a half.
Counselor: So around an hour to an hour and a half you can complete one page edited, proofread?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So it would take about five days for you to complete the whole paper. Yes. If you did an hour and a half each day? An hour to an hour and a half each day. Okay. And how much time do you have from when the papers are signed to when it's due?
Client: They give us about a week and a half to do it. Okay.
Counselor: So around ten days.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if you could maintain the pace of an hour to an hour and a half a day, you would be done in plenty of time. Is there a good time to write? Like to start writing?
Client: I guess around 06:00 because then I'm already done eating, I'm home from work and I've kind of de stressed already. 06:00 pretty good time.
Counselor: So if you could work without distraction, you would be done by around 730 at the latest. With just one page?
Client: Yeah, with the one page.
Counselor: Okay. So no distractions and just one page.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so let's talk about the episodes, the tv episodes that you want to watch.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: How long are they?
Client: They're an hour.
Counselor: They're an hour. Okay. And what's a time that you could watch those that you get the maximum enjoyment out of watching them? Like, no distractions, I guess around 08:00.
Client: Because that's when I'm, you know, starting to get ready for bed and starting to, like, really relax. And, you know, my husband's home by that time and we can watch it together. He loves the show, too.
Counselor: Okay. So eight o'clock's a really good time for you to maximize what you'll get out of the show, the enjoyment you'll get out of the show. So what I want to do is try to pair these behaviors together. The behavior of writing, which is not something that you're necessarily thrilled about all the time, but you are getting it done, just not in the time sketch you like, and the behavior of watching a show, which you are, I mean.
Client: I'm very interested in that.
Counselor: That's a great, you know, that's a great motivator for you. And I want to try to use it as a motivator, kind of like a reward.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So I'd like you to try to do is when you start, like, when you get one of these papers assigned from the five page papers, pick the five nights that you want to work on it.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Could be Monday through Friday or whatever works for you.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right. Clearly within the ten day window, though.
Client: All right.
Counselor: So five days within the ten day window that you have to turn in and then set that time at 06:00 is when you're going to start because that's a good time for you to work. And when you try to work straight through to seven or 730, I know that's a challenge, right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And when that period of distraction might encroach, we know that might happen. Focus on. I really want to watch that show.
Client: At 08:00 so just keep thinking about that when I feel like I'm getting off track.
Counselor: Yeah. That's your. In a way, that's your reward. That's your motivation. That's kind of what you're looking forward to, to get through something that you don't necessarily enjoy a lot. You're going to be using what you do enjoy a lot to help push you through that.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: In the process, I hope that the writing becomes more enjoyable. You know, we'll see. But whether it does or it doesn't, you still want to be able to complete it.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jeff. How you doing today?
Client: I'm alright. Thanks for actually seeing me today. Sure.
Counselor: How have you been? I know last time I spoke with you, you were having some difficulties at work.
Client: I'm still having difficulties at work and that's why I'm glad I have a session today because it hasn't stopped. The frustration and anger is just, it's there ten times more than normal.
Counselor: You're really frustrated. Way more than normal, way more angry.
Client: Yes, it's, there seems to be a lot that's going on and I continually don't get the help that I need, not only not from my coworker, but also my supervisor. So it just feels so that everything is my responsibility and I have to make it happen. And if I don't make it happen, it's not going to happen. And then it's just, it's all on me and I don't feel as though that it's fair. But I also don't want us to not succeed. So I don't know how to navigate those two field.
Counselor: So the weight of the work assignments is really on you. You're feeling that pressure. You want to do right by your employer and there's an emotional toll this is taken on you. Has it reached a point where you've talked to your, it's a coworker supervisor you mentioned?
Client: Yes. So I talked to my supervisor about my coworker actually assisting me with some of the projects that we have going on. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, they're helping out and they're doing what they're supposed to do, but they're not doing what they're supposed to do because I end up doing their work. Because, say, for example, last week we actually had to turn in this huge report that we were working on for over a month. Literally, my coworker came to me on Monday and said I didn't do my portion of the report. And I was just like, we had a month to work on a lot of time. And so I spent the next three days doing everything for their part of the report. Luckily, I had already finished my part of the report and then combined it and actually turned it into my supervisor. Of course we get the, oh, this is a wonderful, great job that you guys did. And I'm just like you guys, as.
Counselor: If you both contributed equally.
Client: Correct? Correct.
Counselor: So in three days, you made up for a month's worth of work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I could see how that could be. It's very stressful.
Client: Very, very taxing. Very, very taxing.
Counselor: And this wasn't an isolated incident?
Client: Oh, no. This has been going on for probably three or four months now.
Counselor: So this is almost the expectation when you get to work.
Client: Correct? Correct. I think that you hit the nail on the head. It's expected of me and nobody actually sees it as an expectation anymore.
Counselor: It's just what you do. It's just what I do. So you can know that going into work the next day, you go in, whenever that is, that there's always this probability, this chance that you could have work just thrown on you that wasn't budgeted for, you weren't planning on.
Client: Correct. And sometimes that work actually comes out from my supervisor, but it's mostly coming from my coworker. Like, I know they're not going to do their portion, so I just automatically start doing it anyway because, you know.
Counselor: You kind of have to.
Client: I know it's going to fall on my lap either today, tomorrow, next week. So I would rather be preemptive and actually start it then so that I'm not rushing like I was, like last week to finish a month's worth of work and three days worth of time. So I'm not as stressed.
Counselor: So you've tried to address this in the framework, in the context of your work. You've talked to the supervisor, to the co worker?
Client: I talked to the supervisor, I'm afraid. Well, I can't really talk to the coworker because I don't feel as though that's my position. However, I have expressed my frustration, my anger, my disappointment with my supervisor. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, I'll fix it, or, oh, it doesn't seem as though that they haven't done their piece of the work because I do all of it and it's turned in. So I have. But there doesn't seem to be anything happening outside of that.
Counselor: What kind of options, in terms of your job do you feel like you have now?
Client: I don't feel as though that I have any options. That's the thing. I think that either if I can, if I don't do the work and we fail, we're going to lose some of these big projects that we're working with, which then is going to impact our entire office. And if it impacts our entire office, like somebody might be let go. And because I am the newest person in our office, I feel as though that's going to be me. So I need to protect my job by doing not only my work, but my coworkers work and sometimes my supervisors work.
Counselor: So you're really figuratively fighting for survival?
Client: Correct.
Counselor: Do you think your coworker is aware that if there is a failure with getting projects done, that you would be the one that would be let go?
Client: I think, yes. I think that they understand that since they are the senior member on team, it would be most likely that the junior member myself would possibly be let go if a budget cut were to happen.
Counselor: So you're really largely stuck.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: With having to do the work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: How about the emotions involved? You mentioned before, the frustration? Anger. Anger directed at.
Client: I think most of my anger is directed at my supervisor for not doing something because they can clearly see that something's wrong or that I'm handling a lot more, but they're not willing to step in. And I think a little bit of that anger is also at myself, because I haven't just said to my coworker, like, you need to step up and you need to do this. So I'm a little disappointed and angry at myself as well.
Counselor: You're angry at yourself, so you feel like you don't have the ability or courage to make that confrontation?
Client: I don't have the confidence to. The confidence to actually confront my coworker.
Counselor: All right, so before we dig into that too much, is it a good idea to confront the coworker?
Client: I think it would be good for them to understand how their lack of participation in our projects is impacting me and could also possibly impact our entire department. However, I don't know exactly how to say that and not come off as I'm. I know more than you, even though that you've been here longer than me.
Counselor: So you're searching for a friendly, understanding way to convey a tough subject matter.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: To someone who may or may not be receptive.
Client: Correct.
Counselor: But you may presume that they're more likely to not be receptive.
Client: I can 100%. I don't want to say 100%. I will say 99.9% say that they will not probably be receptive if I said that.
Counselor: So you're in for a bit of a battle.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And that was started.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So one option is to avoid it and continue do the work. And that's unpleasant, but you survived. Another option is to, in the gentlest way possible, introduce that confrontation to the relationship and then deal with the fallout of that.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Any potential benefit?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So let's look at that. What's the worst that can happen from making that, confronting that cohort.
Client: It could make things in the office be a little bit more tense. It could possibly put an additional spotlight on what I am doing, or rather not doing, which I'm doing everything. So what I'm doing, it could cause friction between my coworker and my supervisor. It could just cause this unwarranted or unnecessary stress for me to actually just go and say something to them.
Counselor: Could you lose your job or anything like that?
Client: No, I don't think that I could lose my job. I don't think that. If I said something to my coworker, I hope that they wouldn't go to, like, our human resources department, but I don't know if that's something that they would do.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:

Client: Good.
Counselor: Doing well?
Client: Yeah, I guess so. I've been working still on the fear of leaving the home for extended periods of time, like vacation, and it's been a little harder recently because I have this planned trip with a friend of mine coming up in a few months, and that's kind of been weighing on my mind.

Client: She wants to go, like, six days, but, yeah, I'm not sure. With work and school and everything, I can make the full six days, and plus, I'm a little nervous to go that long.

Counselor: All right, so you had two kind of conflicting thoughts, right. So one. One is, I could never go that long. Six days, way too long. And the other one is, that would be enjoyable. You enjoy that?
Client: Absolutely, yeah.
Counselor: So which way are you leaning right now?
Client: I want to go to go, but maybe not for six days. Maybe just like a long weekend.
Counselor: Three, four days.
Client: Two would be ideal, but two would probably be idea, but two or three days. Yeah.
Counselor: So what do you think is causing this worry about being gone more than two days?
Client: I don't know. I mean, I've always, as a late teenager in my twenties, I've always had just nervous to leave home. As much as I love being home, I love to travel, too, and do different things. It's just, I guess I'm just afraid something to happen when I'm not around.
Counselor: So you're afraid something will happen to your house or.
Client: Well, I have pets, so I worry about them. My parents are getting older, so I worry about them mainly, like, my immediate family, mainly, I guess, my dad, because he's had a history of heart attacks, and then my pets, that's just worry something will happen. I won't be there.
Counselor: And how about when you were younger, you said this problem's been out for a while.
Client: It's the same thing.
Counselor: The same thing. So mostly family and now some pets.
Client: Well, I had pets then, too.
Counselor: You had pets then, too? Okay, so that's really what's bothering you here, is that you'll be away, and that's when something will happen and it'll be something bad. What about coming back? Like, you can come back?
Client: Yeah, like, I'm ready to come back, but then I'm missing home. Like, I want to go back to my family and everything's okay, but I miss, you know, where I just left because it's away from home. I know it sounds really conflicting and weird, but, you know, I like to get away. I enjoy being away from this small town.
Counselor: So, yes, you have feelings that are fighting one another.
Client: Absolutely.
Counselor: And right now, the feeling, the thought, anyway, of, you know, I would like to go on a trip is winning, but the fear thought is kind of dragging you down. So what's the sensation? Anxiety.
Client: Yeah. I get anxious. Yeah. My heart gets. Feels like it's heavy. My chest heavy. And I just. All these thoughts go through my mind, like, you know, I know my parents. Somebody can watch my pets, but they may not take care of them like I would. I don't know, it's just. I mean, you know, they've always. They'll take care of them. I know, but they'll miss me and they might tear my house up. I don't know. All these thoughts go through my mind that seem crazy to me.
Counselor: So it seems like an endless stream of worries.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Surrounding family and the pets and what might happen. So really, that's. That's it. Right. It's what might happen. It's the uncertainty.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So has anything ever happened?
Client: No. No.
Counselor: So, so far, all this worrying, anxiety really hasn't paid any dividends.
Client: No.
Counselor: Do you end up going on the trips anyway?
Client: Yes. And now that I'm older, when I was younger, I probably wouldn't like an overnight, but now that I'm older. Yes, I do. I just say I got to live my life and it'll be okay. I just try to tell myself they're in good hands. If something happens, somebody will call me. But then I feel like, oh, but I'm going to be hours away. I'm a plane ride away. And then I get thinking about that, but I do go.
Counselor: But you didn't in the past.
Client: No.
Counselor: So something changed. What changed?
Client: I don't know. I really I don't know. I don't know what what made a difference. Maybe I just feel more and, I don't know, say in control. But now that I'm living on my own, so that's what I wouldn't go is when I lived at home with my parents still, which seems weird because somebody was always there to look after my animals and. But now that I'm living on my own, maybe I just feel yden more responsible that I have to go do these things. I really don't know what changed.
Counselor: All right. So you're not sure what changed. But you used to not go. Now you do go. So when you're down there or wherever you're going, the trip, you're feeling better, like you're enjoying yourself, but you're also worried at the same time.
Client: Not too. Once I get there, I'm usually okay. Maybe the first night I get a little worried. And then maybe when I'm getting ready to come home, I'm, like, a little anxious. I'm ready to get home to make sure everything's okay.
Counselor: And the rest of the time I'm usually okay.
Client: I want to get some alcohol involved, so it kind of limits my anxiety. But once I get into, like, playing the golf and all that, I really do allow myself to enjoy it. It's just. It seems like it's going and coming. That's all.
Counselor: Right. So the problem really isn't when you're there leading up to the problem is now leading up to. Right.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: And maybe just the first half day or day when you're there. Maybe the last half day or day.
Client: You'Re there, it's like a plane. Like, I don't have a problem riding, like, flying out, but it's the thinking, like, while I'm waiting for the plane, like, what if a terrorist is on there? What if we crash? I'll think about all that before. But once I'm there and on the plane, it's like, right. Take off. I'm fine. I'm completely fine. I'm not anxious. It's leading up to the actual event that makes me anxious.
Counselor: It's just anticipation. So that's the worst part. So the period between now and when you leave is going to be the worst part?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: But you'll probably still go.
Client: Probably. But I'll have changed my mind probably a dozen times before I actually say, yes, I'm going.
Counselor: And when you do go, you have a good time. And the probability of something happening that you're worried about based on the history seems low.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Something could happen, certainly, but it hasn't so far. All right, so there's a few angles here. So what happens if you go down there and a bad scenario or worst case scenario does happen?
Client: I don't know. I try not to think that far. If I get thinking about it, I try to, like, shut it out. I don't want to think about the worst. I guess the worst. I'll get on the plane and come home and I'll deal with it then.
Counselor: All right, so you'll return and the best case scenario would be you enjoy yourself, which is the more likely. Historically, that's the more likely scenario.
Client: Yeah. But it still doesn't stop me from worrying when I get these trips planned.
Counselor: Yeah. So the probabilities of it really doesn't. That doesn't alleviate the worry. The worry is still there, even though, you know, the worry is probably going to transition to enjoyment and looking forward to that. That doesn't.
Client: No, not at all.
Counselor: That doesn't relieve anything.
Client: Not at all.
Counselor: So what are you thinking when you're thinking about the trip now, if you were to think about getting ready to go on this trip, what would go through your mind? What specific thoughts?
Client: I gotta get my house cleaned up and make sure my animals are every. They have enough food and, like, preparing to leave.
Counselor: Preparing is productive, right? Yeah. That makes sense.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How about the thoughts that you feel more connected to? The worrying.
Client: Probably. Like, I want to. I want to say. I don't know. I really. It's kind of hard. Like, I want to. Like, I can't say bye enough to my parents or I can't, you know, say bye enough to my pets. Like, I feel like I don't. I don't know. I don't. I really. That's, I guess, part of the problem. I don't know what I'm connecting it to. I just get really anxious.
Counselor: So if you don't tell them goodbye enough times.
Client: Yeah. I don't know. Maybe. I know it sounds so.
Counselor: Well, it sounds like maybe if you don't say. If you don't say goodbye enough times and settle that. That you'll feel guilty if something happens, maybe like you regret it.
Client: Maybe. I don't know. I just know that's when I. That's what I think about when. That's one thing that first comes to my mind when you ask me to connect the thoughts to the worry. And I think about telling everybody by.
Counselor: So that. So that's a focal point of this anxiety in some way. Right.
Client: Like, let him go for a few days.
Counselor: And the way you start to let go is when you tell them. Tell them goodbye. So what do you find yourself doing? You say goodbye and then leave and then come back or call them up?
Client: No, I just finally say bye. I'll talk to you later. Love you. You know, I'll check in when I land or whatever. And then that's it. Then it's like. Like I just have to try to breathe and just put those thoughts behind me. Because once I say it, it's like, okay, that's it, I'm gone.
Counselor: But your. But your thoughts are still coming. Thoughts are still coming. And say, you should have said goodbye one more time.
Client: No, it's not. I don't know. I just. No, that doesn't come to my mind.
Counselor: That you didn't say goodbye well enough.
Client: I don't know.
Counselor: I'm trying to. What's the property of. What's the property of saying goodbye that you feel like you're not doing?
Client: Maybe it's just the fact that I'm leaving and I shouldn't leave. Maybe that way you say that. Yeah, maybe I feel like I. Maybe it's just a guilt of leaving.
Counselor: So the act of leaving itself leaves you guilty. And what are you guilty of?
Client: Not being there if something happens.
Counselor: So abandoning them, maybe for a short time. Neglecting them for a short time. Is that what it felt like when you were younger? When you weren't able to travel? When it did stop you, anxiety did stop you?
Client: Probably. Maybe I did feel guilty.
Counselor: And now you're in, would you say, more of a caregiver role than you were then?
Client: Maybe a little bit. I mean, I've always been. I'm the youngest of me and my sister, but my parents have always looked up to me to be the responsible one and make sure everything's taken care of. So I probably kind of allowed myself to take on that role of the caregiver more so. Or be the more responsible one of the two.
Counselor: So to be the responsible one, there needs to be guilt when you leave.
Client: I guess maybe I should stay home and be responsible. And they don't make me feel guilty. They say, go have a good time. Your babies will be okay. We'll take care of them. I mean, I know they're in good hands. That's what makes it so difficult. I know they'll be okay, but I just feel like I probably shouldn't go.
Counselor: So there's not another person driving this guilt towards you. That's me that's coming in from inside.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if I. If I leave, well, I'm responsible. And if I leave, something bad will happen and that'll be on me.
Client: Yeah. I wasn't there to fix it or take care of it or make it better. Like, I put it on somebody else that have to do with that? Yeah.
Counselor: So fear of being caught is irresponsible?
Client: Maybe, yeah. If something happened to my pets, then my parents, I know they'll take care of them, but they would have to be the one doing that. I wouldn't be there for them and I'd want to be there if something happened to my dad, it'd be on my mom and I'd want to be there to help and support and, you know, do what I can.
Counselor: And you could be. If you left, it would just take you a day's travel or whatever, however far away. Yeah, but that's. That's still doesn't help relieve anxiety. No one even come back. Doesn't help?
Client: No. Really? No. Because it's like I want immediate access. Like I want to be able to be right there within minutes if they need me.
Counselor: Have you ever taken a trip that was like within less than 4 hours driving distance or something? That's overnight. Does that cause the same anxiety? It does, but you can get back fairly quickly?
Client: I mean, not. It's not as bad, but yeah, there's. If I go stay with a friend for like an overnight, there's. On the way up. Sometimes I'm thinking I should just stay home or I could be right in the same town. Sometimes that if I'm. I wake up at five in the morning, I just get up and go home because I just start feeling really anxious and I want to be home.

Client: Probably usually like six, 7 hours into. It just depends. Like now it's getting dark, so when it kind of gets dark, if I don't leave the light on or something, I get a little anxious. I feel like I need to go home and leave the light on. And I would just let my pets know I'm coming back. It's weird, but I know they miss me. But if I'm busy, then I don't really think about it. So if I'm busy at work doing something, I don't really think about it until I stop what I'm doing or I slow down and I'm thinking, wow, I got ten more hours or eight more hours. Sometimes I go home, sometimes I don't. Sometimes it's worse than others.
Counselor: All right, so if you're busy at work, the same reality exists, meaning your pets are alone. But the way you're responding to it is different.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: You're less anxious.
Client: Because I know I'm close. I can get there. I know I'm in control. To be able to go there, to a degree.
Counselor: Well, but let's say not at work. Let's say when you're on the vacations, in those days in the middle, when you're enjoying yourself, is that a distraction? Like, the more you enjoy yourself, the less you're. Yeah, but the same reality exists. They're alone. So really it's your way of. It's your way of viewing things that's leading to your anxiety. It's not necessarily what's actually happening.
Client: That's my perception.
Counselor: Perception of what's happening or could happen. I guess in this case, not so much what is happening as what you worry could happen.
Client: Yeah, definitely.
Counselor: Because nothing's happened yet.
Client: No, not yet.
Counselor:
output: So how many? Well, I guess there's a few different. There's a few different issues here. Right. How many vacations do you take a year?

Client: Well, I. Sadness that maybe I'm not having or not going to have a good relationship with my father. Yeah. I'm a little wary of that.
Counselor: And I'm wondering what's changed this week compared to last week in regards to your thinking about this issue.
Client: Well, some of it is just that I've been thinking more about it because you called. And then also as this deadline approaches, I was thinking about the deadline for declaring my major as I'm taking this chemistry class, and since it's hard, then it's making me think twice about the mood, about the.
Counselor: Okay, well, it definitely sounds like this has been something that's been on your mind. Really? These thoughts you've been having impacted the way you're feeling. And you also mentioned that you've been a shut in. Yeah. I'm wondering if mystery is my master. So you not doing the things you enjoy may also be impacting how you feel. Do you think that that's possible?
Client: Yeah, I mean, I think it's. I'm sure, you know, it sucks.
Counselor: Yeah. So, for the last few weeks, we've been working a little bit on restructuring the way you are thinking. That's with the goal of that making you feel different, and that's what we'll continue to do. And I'm thinking that just from what I'm hearing, it might be a good idea to add the relationship with your father and feeling like you're a failure in size to the agenda. Something we might want to work on.

Counselor: Sure, sure. And then we'll do a little bit more agenda setting, actually. Next. So I'm wondering, what problems are you most interested in working on in this session today?
Client: Yeah, I mean, I'm definitely. You know, the thing with my dad is, like, a big thing. So I was hoping that this therapy, these sessions, might make some headway with that.
Counselor: Absolutely. I know that he's that relationship, something that we have been talking about in session, so I think it would be a good idea to include that today also. So, as we've been doing, I think it's a good idea that we both write that down. You have a list in your notebook. And then I also have a list of what we talked about. Okay. So I'm wondering, is there anything else you mentioned some other things that may have impacted your mood this last week?
Client: Well, I've been thinking about. I mean, like I said, I've been thinking about the deadline to declare my major, and.
Counselor: I.
Client: So it's kind of an involved process to.
Counselor: Okay, so maybe. I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I'm wondering if maybe you could just write that down as approaching deadline for your major.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, basically.
Counselor: Is that a fair way to sum that up? Is there anything else that you want to work on together today?

Counselor: The band practice is something that's important to you, and you're not. You haven't been able to do it as regularly as you'd like.
Client: You want to talk about.
Counselor: I think I'll write that down as well. We can just write down finding time for. Fantastic. Does that sound good, or do you think. All right, is there anything else you'd like to add to our agenda today.

Counselor: That's the one. And I think what we had talked about. I'm looking at notes from last week right now. instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Elizabeth. How you doing today?
Client: I'm all right.
Counselor: How things been going since the last time I met?
Client: It's about the same. I'm still feeling pretty down. I mean, I just. I feel really stuck and not happy, and I just don't know why.
Counselor: Okay, so there's a few things going on there. You said you're feeling stuck, not happy, and sound like you're a little confused as to what's going on, what's causing it. Do you have any suspicions about what might be causing it?
Client: I mean, I've been feeling, like, really isolated lately, you know, because I'm a stay at home mom. It's hard. There's not a lot of people, you know, right at my fingertips to spend my time with, you know, obviously my family, but. So I guess, you know, I kind of. I had some friends in the neighborhood, but, like, our friendships just kind of fizzled out, and I. Ever since then, it's just like, I don't really feel like doing much. I just kind of feel like, what's the point? And let my husband take care of a lot of stuff. You know, I used to, you know, shop for the groceries all the time and make sure the house is always stocked and make dinner every night and get the kids ready for school in the morning. And I still do that stuff. But a lot of times, you know, I let it slide. Sometimes I won't make dinner or whatever. And when I do do it, I just feel like I'm forcing myself to do it. The passion is gone.
Counselor: And how long have you been. You say housewife, right? How long have you been housewife?
Client: For a long time. I have two boys. They're eight and ten. And I've been staying home since my first one was born, so ten years. And, you know, it's been really rewarding for me. I'm not really interested in going back to work or anything like that because I know people always say you're feeling unfulfilled, like you should go back to work, but it's not, you know, I felt happy with it for so long. I don't think that it's being home. I think it's something inside of me.
Counselor: Something's changed. So for a long time, you were satisfied being a housewife. You enjoyed that life or found satisfaction in that life. And somewhere along the line, something changed in you and now you're not happy with it. So what it represents in terms of activities like caring for your children and shopping, now, that's what changed.
Client: Yeah, exactly. Well, I guess, you know, my youngest is eight, so he's only been in school for a couple of years. So I guess, like, it's not super recent, but recently I finally have no children in the home, so it's more. It's more time to myself, and I kind of filled that gap a little bit with other things. Like, I did Cub scouts with the boys for a while, and like I said, I had some friends around the neighborhood, so that kind of, like, filled that time. But now that stuff, it's just not really happening anymore. So now I kind of feel like it's not boredom. You know, it's not like I don't have enough to do. It's like I don't want to do anything, but then at the same time, I feel frustrated because there's nothing to do.
Counselor: All right, so you're frustrated with your situation, maybe with yourself a little bit?
Client: Yeah, I think a lot more with myself because I know that I would feel better if I had, you know, maybe found more friends or found something to do with my time, but I don't want to at the same time. So I'm frustrated with myself because I kind of know what would help, but then I don't really have the, like, the volition to do it.
Counselor: You're not motivated?
Client: Yeah, I'm not motivated.
Counselor: Have you received any feedback from other people about this meeting? Has anyone else noticed that you're down?
Client: Yeah, I mean, obviously my husband has noticed because he has to get the boys ready in the morning. He's really supportive. I know he can tell that I'm not feeling the same, but, you know, he works, and then he has to come home and pick up my slack. So he is getting frustrated, which I understand. And, you know, my mom has said to me that, you know, she thinks I'm not doing as much, and so it kind of hurts. It feels like everybody's trying to tell me I'm lazy and that I'm not doing enough. And it's always that, like, feeling, you know, like nobody really understands how much work goes into being a mother. But then, at the same time, now that I'm doing less and less, I feel like they're all right, you know? I am lazy. I'm not doing anything.
Counselor: They use the word lazy?
Client: No, not that I can remember. You know, I think my mom said, like, you're not doing as much as you used to. And I kind of took offense to that, even though it's kind of true. It's like. I don't know. It hurt.
Counselor: Okay. That was painful for you what about what your husband said? What's he been saying?
Client: You know, I think at first we didn't really acknowledge it. It was like, you know, I took a break here. He picked up the slack, and it was fine. But now that it's been more and more, he's kind of getting frustrated. And, you know, he's been asking me about how I feel and why I'm not doing as much. But at the same time, like, even though he knows that, not motivated, it's still frustrating because it's my responsibility. So I think he's. You know, he's been saying, like, I need you to do more around the house, pretty much is what he said. I need you to do more.
Counselor: What was your response to that? When he said, I need you to.
Client: Do more, I started crying because I know he's right. And that's what I tell myself every day. I need to do more, but I don't have the motivation to do it. And so I'm so frustrated with myself, and, you know, I know that he needs that from me, and I don't know why I'm not motivated to do it.
Counselor: Okay, so you're frustrated for feeling down.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you're frustrated for lacking motivation, and just as little as a few years ago, you didn't feel it this way at all.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I actually think, you know, I've been feeling this way more, like, in the past, like, six months or something like that. Like, I. It was hard for me when my youngest son went to school, but more in, like, the natural way that it is hard, but this is something else. This is more consuming. It's, you know, like, the difficulty of him going away to school almost was motivating. Like, it was hard, but at the same time, it was freeing because I had other opportunities to do stuff. This is just, like, stunting.
Counselor: Okay, so let me shift gears a little bit. Can you tell me about your. Well, a recent day. It's kind of typical of what you're telling me now. Meaning not motivated. Down.
Client: Sure. On Wednesday, I was having a really hard time getting out of bed, so my husband just got the kids ready in the morning, and I felt really bad about that. So I just stayed in bed for a couple more hours, probably until, like, 1030, and I got up, you know, and made myself something to eat. And then I thought, you know, I should probably go to the store because we're almost out of milk and, you know, and I think the boys need shampoo. But I just. I just sat down and I just sat there, and I think I sat for. I don't even know how long the boys came home from school. It was like, you know, 330, and I hadn't even gotten up. And so then I said, okay, the boys are home. I should probably get started on dinner soon because my husband will be home soon. And I. I found something in the fridge to make, and I made dinner. And, you know, after that, everybody, you know, just sat down. We just watched tv, and I just sat there until it was time to go to bed.
Counselor: You said this was recently, right? What would the ideal day have looked like? Take that same day and do what you wish you could have done.
Client: I wish that I would wake up and, you know, I would want to wake up when it was time for the kids to get ready to go to school. You know, I could make sure that everything that they had, everything they needed, I could pack their lunches and get the boys dressed and, you know, check if they needed any permission slip sign, that kind of thing, send them out the door, and then I would see if we needed anything from the store. I probably do a little bit of cleaning around the house. I used to, like, have a list of chores that I would do different things on different days and different days of the month and stuff. So bedding would get washed one day of the week and that kind of thing. Probably, like, follow that list. Nowadays, I just, you know, if it gets done, it gets done. And usually my husband helps me with some of the stuff. And, you know, I would do the bathrooms one day a week. That probably gets done, like, once a month now, but I would do that. So do the cleaning. If we. If I needed to go to the store, I would do that. I'd get ready for the boys to come home. I'd probably make them a snack and figure out what was going to be for dinner. I would go ahead and do that, and then probably, you know, sometimes we would watch tv after my husband got home after dinner, or I would figure out something for us to do. We could play a board game, or I'll watch a movie as a family or something like that. But that would be after the kids did their homework and everything like that. And then after we spent some time together, I'd put them to bed.
Counselor: All right, so there's a fairly wide discrepancy between where you are in terms of behavior and where you want to be. So let me ask you a very specific question about one of the first things in the day. You had mentioned that when it was time to get up you didn't. So you were awake and aware of it, but you went back to sleep, I presume. And of course, your husband got up and he took care of things. How did you feel allowing that to happen? Because clearly that's not what you wanted to happen. How did you feel about that? Oversleeping?
Client: It's just like, you know, the alarm goes off and I know it's time to get up, and my husband's getting out of bed, and I just look at the clock and I think, what's the point? And, you know, it's just this instant feeling of. I can't even describe it, like pointlessness of getting up. And so I go back to sleep, but I feel worse for doing it, you know, like it's a catch 22. Like, I don't want to wake up. I just don't want to. But then when I go back to sleep, I feel bad. I feel guilty.
Counselor: Okay, so by not getting up in the time you wanted, you feel guilty. But you also mentioned something that you thought, which was, if I'm not mistaken, you said, what's the point? Can you expand on that?
Client: It just. It's just like, you know, when I'm sleeping, I don't realize how sad I am, and I don't realize how hard it is to function when I'm sleeping. I'm not aware of that. And as soon as I wake up, I am. And so I just have this feeling of, like, what's the point of getting up and experiencing these feelings when I could go back to sleep and not have to?
Counselor: What's the point of getting up when sleeping will keep the pain at bay?
Client: Yes. Yeah.
Counselor: But then when you do get up, you feel sad and guilty about having overslept.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, definitely. Definitely.
Counselor: So really, functionally, what you're doing is you're delaying experiencing the pain. And then in terms of how it affects your relationships and your family, you're not getting your kids off to school, your husband's getting real frustrated, and all you've really bought yourself is a couple extra hours of sleep and presumably without pain because you're sleeping but you're not really escaping it. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Before, when you felt more satisfaction and purpose, did you get up and help the kids off to school?
Client: Yeah, it was so easy. I would just like, you know, I would wake up and I would be like, okay, it's time to get up and get out of bed and get ready to go. I mean, you know, sometimes if I was a little bit tired, it would be a little bit hard, but, you know, it's nothing. You know, as a stay at home mom, I usually get enough sleep for the most part, now that the kids are older and everything. So it's not usually too hard to get up. And I would, you know, it would be another good day. You know, I would be glad to get up and take care of the things that I needed to take care of, and I felt accomplished.
Counselor: So maybe what's going on here? Or maybe we could help remember, you know, over the last few sessions, we talked about. About cognitive behavioral therapy and the different techniques that I'll be using and different things we'll be talking about. Sometimes with behavior, the behavior that's useful, which in this case, I'm assuming we can agree, is the getting up one time behavior that's useful has to come first, even if the feeling doesn't match. So sleeping those extra, I presume, a couple hours, delays you from feeling sad, but it causes other problems. If you were to get up one time, you might still feel sad, right? Because that's why you're oversleeping, because you're sleeping longer, to avoid that. But the functional part of being a housewife, as you identify, would be completed. So maybe some of those feelings of sadness and guilt would, over time, abate, because, functionally speaking, you're completing the task that you want. What's tough about that is that in the moment, it's easy for me to say this now, but in the moment, like, for instance, when you have to get up out of bed tomorrow, you're going to be facing that same challenge, which is, I can get up now and feel depressed or I can wait and feel depressed later. So in that moment, it's hard to act on the behavior that you kind of know you want to move towards. I mean, it sounds like you want to get up and see if the kids are.
Client: Yeah, I mean, I want everything to be normal again. And I guess I never really thought of it like that. Like, I just thought, well, if I'm waking up at the right time and I'm just feeling bad, then, like I said, what's the point? But I guess it makes sense. Like, even if I don't feel like doing it, maybe it'll make me feel better if I do do it, even if it's hard, because nothing's really harder than what I'm already going through.
Counselor: Well, it seems like you're more or less making things worse in an effort to avoid the pain that you're going to suffer anyway. You're making the pain worse. Just delaying it a little bit. Right. What thought? We talked before about automatic thoughts, these thoughts that come up kind of when your belief system meets, these different situations that occur when you have that thought that this is pointless. And I'm going to expand on that thought a little. That what that thought's really getting at is I can avoid this pain if I sleep a little while longer. That's a version of the thought. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah. And also, I guess I thought that, no, it wouldn't really be that beneficial to get up.
Counselor: Okay, so you're also minimizing the benefit.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a couple things going on. Right. I can avoid the pain by sipping in, and there's really no point to getting out because I won't do any good anyway.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: What adaptive response, that self talk. We talked about those things we consciously think to ourselves, could you apply in that moment when you're, you know, whatever time you get up in the morning when you're thinking about this and that thought comes in that it doesn't really matter if I get up anyway.
Client: I mean, I guess I could tell myself, like, I can do this. Like, instead of, you know, when I say to myself, what's the point? Instead I can say, I can do this. I can get out of bed. It'll be okay. I can. I'm strong enough. Even though it's hard to push through the pain and get up now, even though I don't want to, I can say, I can do this.
Counselor: Okay, so that would be your adaptive response. I'm strong enough. I can get through this, but it will be difficult. How about the value of getting up early and seeing the kids off to school? The automatic thought right now is telling you that's not valuable, but I think that you believe it is valuable.
Client: Yeah, I mean, I know it's valuable. I guess what my frustration is is that I know it's valuable. And it used to give me, like, an emotional payoff of, like, pride and satisfaction, and now I'm not getting that anymore. So I guess I need to realize that even though I'm not getting it right now, if I keep trying, maybe it will happen again. Because it did happen before.
Counselor: Well, it seemed logical that you have a higher probability of getting that back. If you do get up, then if you.
Client: I guess that's true. You'll never get the satisfaction of sending my kids off to school. If I never send my kids off to school.
Counselor:
output: So you have a 0% chance of successful successfully moving past this with a sleeping in and you have some other probability greater than zero if you do.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Lucy. Nice to meet you.
Client: Hi.
Counselor: So I understand that you were referred here by your GP because you've been feeling quite down recently.
Client: Yeah, I thought I should. I've been feeling quite bad for quite a while, so I thought maybe it's time to see someone about it because I don't want to feel like this anymore.
Counselor: Okay. So from your notes, I saw that you saw the GP about three months ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how long have you been feeling down altogether?
Client: Quite a few months before that as well, actually. But it's gotten pretty bad these past few months, so that's kind of why I came.
Counselor: Okay. So has it got worse since you saw your GP?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so tell me, how are things at the moment?
Client: Well, it kind of started just feeling a bit low and wound up about things, but, I don't know, just recently I just can't really be bothered to do anything at all. I kind of find it hard to get motivated for things and I want to be. I really want to be better, but it's just kind of reaching the end now where I just. I want to do something about it.
Counselor: Okay, so you said that you're feeling really down, really sad?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you feel like you haven't got any motivation, but. Are you okay?
Client: Yeah, I'm fine.
Counselor: Sorry. Okay, and you haven't got any motivation, but it sounds like you've put quite a lot of pressure on yourself to try and feel a bit better.
Client: Yeah, I just. It's kind of hard as well because there's not really anyone to talk about. So I just kind of stay on my own trying to. I don't like to think about it, but I don't know.
Counselor: So you say you've been. You've been feeling quite isolated. There's not many people around.
Client: Yeah. There's no one I can talk to about it. No one would listen or understand anyway.
Counselor: Okay, so I'm just going to try and find out a little bit more about you. So I understand that you're an english student at uni.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you live away from home with some friends. Is that right?
Client: Yeah, I live here.
Counselor: Oh, okay. So you don't live far from the uni, but you say you feel like you live with your friends, but you don't feel like you can talk to them.
Client: Yeah, I mean, they're lovely. I get on really well with them, but I don't know, recently, whenever they want to go out or stuff, I just. I don't want to bring them down. I can't. They don't understand what I'm going through. They kind of. I don't know, they don't make fun of how I feel, but they don't really understand what it's like. I just. I don't want to go out with them and bring them down or stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds. Do you try and hide the way you're feeling from them?
Client: I guess. I mean, it's easier to hide it than to try and explain it all the time when no one really wants to know.
