Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you've been feeling down, you've been feeling unmotivated, you feel like you want to be better. But actually it sounds like you feel like you can't reach out for help, you can't speak to anybody.
Client: No, I don't really talk to my parents a lot either, so that's kind of hard.
Counselor: Okay. I'm just gonna go back in time a little bit, I suppose. I'm just wondering, when did all of this start? You said it's been going on for quite a few months.
Client: Yeah, I guess it kind of started, actually, when I was revising for my exams. I guess the stress. I put a lot of stress on myself. I think I've always wanted to do well for me and I guess for my parents. So the stress of exams. And it was also kind of hard because my parents were going through a bit of a troubled time then.
Counselor: Okay, so this would be like last March, last April?
Client: Yeah, I think so.
Counselor: Around that time. So about six months ish. And it sounds like a lot was happening. So you had a lot of uni pressure on and you said that your parents were having marital problems. Okay. And it sounds like that was a real shock to you.
Client: Yeah, I guess it was hard as well because I wasn't doing well at uni. I guess I just felt a bit guilty. I know it sounds silly, but I felt like maybe if I could do better, then they would get better, but it just wasn't really happening.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you were trying to work hard and be more successful because you thought that that would make them happier and try and fix things.
Client: Yeah, I wanted to make them feel better, but it just kind of backfired a little, I guess.
Counselor: How did it backfire?
Client: Well, it just ended up with them getting worse, and I've just been feeling worse since then.
Counselor: Okay, so after the summer, after the exam period. And how did that exam period go for you in the end?
Client: Not very well.
Counselor: Okay. That's an awful lot of pressure to put on yourself that you supposed to.
Client: Think it's just annoying because I know I should have done better and I just didn't. And I guess I beat myself up a lot about it.
Counselor: So you say. I know, I know I should have done better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, I suppose hearing it from my perspective, I'm thinking it sounds like you had an awful lot going on at the time. It would be understandable, absolutely. That you wouldn't do as well as normal. I suppose I'm just wondering if you have very high standards for yourself.
Client: Probably maybe more than other people. My parents have always kind of taught me. Not in a loving way, I guess, but that you should do your best, but also get the best. And I agree with that. I think that's the right thing to think. But when I don't do that, I don't know, it annoys me a lot and I worry that it annoys them.
Counselor: So it sounds like you feel you should always do your best. Is that the word you used? Yeah. And that there isn't any kind of exceptions for that, but no. Okay. So I can see then that was a really difficult time for you and that was when your mood started to get lower. And things are still quite bad now. I mean, what's the situation with your parents at the moment?
Client: I think it doesn't sound good. I don't really talk to them a lot, but I don't think they're going through very good. I don't like to talk to them about it because it just makes me feel worse. But I don't think it's getting any better.
Counselor: Were you home over the summer?
Client: For a little bit, yeah.
Counselor: And how was that?
Client: Not very fun? No, it was quite tense all the time. Stress me out more than relaxed me over the summer, I guess.
Counselor: Okay. Okay. So it sounds then like quite a lot has been happening. You've been feeling very low, you've had uni pressure on, and you've had problems with your parents marriage. And sounds like you feel like you can't really reach out to anyone. Like you can't understand, but you can't really reach out to your parents right now. You can't really confide in your friends. So I suppose I'm just wondering if you can tell me a bit more about how you've been feeling. I mean, say this past week.
Client: Really not good, to be honest. I actually. If I don't have to, then I don't really leave the house or get out of. But I just. I can't find the motivation for the things I used to join. I used to love doing sports or going out. And now I just prefer to lie in bed and not really do anything.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I missed a few lectures this week that I should have gone to.
Counselor: Right. So I suppose I'm just wondering then let's see if we can think about one thing. Say a lecture. What kind of thoughts do you have about going to that lecture before it happens?
Client: I don't really see the point anymore. If I can't do as well as I should be doing, then what's the point in putting myself in those positions? I can't be bothered anymore to try. It just stresses me out more than I need to.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like the kind of thoughts you've got in your head are. It's pointless. It's not worth it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Do you have any other thoughts in your head when you're just at that point before you go to the lecture?
Client: I feel like. I don't know. I don't really even deserve to be hear if I can't do well enough. I see all these other students who are doing well and doing better and want to be there. I don't know why I'm here, even at uni, to be honest.
Counselor: So it sounds like you feel like you're not as good as other people here.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. I'm just. Sorry. Is it okay if I take notes as we go through? It's just I'm trying to, I guess, understand what you're telling me and it helps me just to write it down and I'll share this with you later. Okay. So it sounds like those are some quite negative thoughts to have. You're kind of saying, you know, it feels like it's pointless, it's more effort than it's worth, and I don't deserve to be here. I mean, when you have those thoughts, how do you feel?
Client: Very unworthy, probably would be the best way to put it. Kind of, I don't know, lower than normal. Because then it makes me think about all the things that I should have been doing better.
Counselor: Okay, so what you described there, then you said, I'm unworthy. I should be doing lots of things better. Those are kind of what I would call thoughts, actually. I suppose I'm trying to understand what it feels like in your gut. What kind of emotions do you feel happier? Do you feel sad? What kind of emotions are you feeling when you have those thoughts?
Client: Sad. Not happiness? No, sad. A bit of. Kind of anger and frustration as well.
Counselor:
output: Okay. I notice when you're kind of telling me this, and I know this is quite a heavy topic, but you're kind of laughing. And I suppose I wonder a little bit, are you a bit, you know, how do you feel about having these emotions, talking about these emotions, I guess embarrassed.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how are you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well, thank you.
Counselor: Doing well.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: I have family coming into town and I have to go to the airport to pick them up.
Counselor: So you have family flying in?
Client: Yes. That's something that I get very anxious about, having to cross the bridge. I have to cross the Ben Franklin bridge and then get over the bridge that goes to the airport by the stadium. I think that's the Girard point bridge. Yeah. That's two levels there. I have to do that both ways.
Counselor: Going and coming both ways. You have to cross four times?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So what kind of feeling is this bringing up for you?
Client: I get very anxious even just thinking about it right now.
Counselor: So you're anxious right here with me?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I want to try to scale this. We talked about this before with cognitive therapy. So let's say that ten is really the most anxious you're felt about crossing bridges, and one is no anxiety. Where would you be right now?
Client: Right now, probably an eight. Yeah.
Counselor: I don't love anxiety.
Client: Yes. It's worse when I'm at that point on that day, but right now, I think just knowing that I have to do that. Yes.
Counselor: And what's it on that day?
Client: A ten.
Counselor: It reaches a ten, definitely.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. So. But even now, how far away is the. Until they.
Client: Oh, it's a week.
Counselor: So even now, a week out, it's. Nate, this is really hurting.
Client: Yes. I don't like that at all.
Counselor: So for your job and local travel, you don't really have to cross any.
Client: Ten minutes to work every day. And banks. So 20 minutes, shopping centers and everything is just within the vicinity. I don't have to cross any bridges.
Counselor: So no bridges?
Client: No, not at all. I probably planned it that way, too.
Counselor: That worked out well.
Client: That worked out very well.
Counselor: All right. But coming up, pick up the family you will be crossing. So let's look at this at each stage. So, I mean, you're clearly anxious now, as you mentioned. But let's go to, let's try to move forward a week to the day that they'll be flying, what time they fly in.
Client: It's going to be a 04:00 flight. In the afternoon.
Counselor: In the afternoon. So about what time would you have to leave to?
Client: I would have to leave probably at 03:00 because it's only about 20 minutes to the airport. Really?
Counselor: Really.
Client: But I would like to leave earlier. They'll probably take them time. By the time they land and go through, you know, getting their luggages, they probably won't even come out till maybe 430, but I'd like to make sure I'm there at around 334 o'clock.
Counselor: All right, so let's go to that day. Let's go to that day and to that afternoon. So you're still at home. And let's say we're about 15 minutes before you have to get in the car. Car. What are you thinking then?
Client: I have to do this. I have to get up and go. They need me to be there this week. It's my parents coming in and they're elderly, so I don't want them to be stuck at the airport. There's no one else that actually can go pick them up. So I have to get up and go and pick them up.
Counselor: That's what's going through your mind?
Client: That's what's going through my mind. So, you know, there's nobody else that can do this. I mean, it's cheaper than there's no. I probably can't even afford to get a taxi for them because you'd have to cross that's from Philly to. Into New Jersey. So that's going to be very expensive. I can't afford that. When all I'd have to do is pay $5 for the tow and maybe gas up my car for $10 or something. But, um, I. Yeah, I'll be thinking about, I have to do this.
Counselor: I have to do it.
Client: I can do it. Something that I can save money that way. And I don't want to leave them stranded. Definitely someone else can. I mean, they'd be lost. They're not familiar with the airport. And Philly airport is crazy to me.
Counselor: Yeah, it's a big place. A lot going on. So. So you're sitting at home in 15 minutes before getting the cardinal and you're thinking, I have to do this. But your reasons are positive. Like you save money and protect your parents from having to be there alone. So when does the anxiety come in?
Client: Just the thought of the bridge, it's just. I could drive off the bridge. I can fall off. Usually what I do is try to stay in the middle lane. I can't do more than 40 miles an hour. And I just. I'm shaking. I have the radio on and windows down because I can't swim. So if for any reason I'm to fall off, I mean, that's it for me. I even have a little metal one of those. I think it's an instrument that you use in the house for, I don't know, plier or something. Something real hard that I can hit the ground with. It sits right there on my door, on the side of my door. So I'm already, I planned, I have that. I planned ahead of time. I know what I'm going to do as soon as I approach the bridge, but I still feel anxious.
Counselor: So you're anxious before you leave and you're starting to think about the bridge at that point. You already think about it. How about when you get in your car, you start driving toward the bridge?
Client: I say a prayer. I am still anxious. I turn on the radio and the closer I get to, especially the toll point, and I know it's at me. And you see those lights flashing. Last exit before the, you know, the.
Counselor: Toll, you know you're going over once.
Client: Yeah, there's no turning back. There's no turning back.
Counselor:
output: So before that, when you can still exit, what's your anxiety level?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Does the feeling itself, the worry about not being prepared, interfere with preparing?
Client: Yes, it's really hard. So, like, when I'm in the middle of being worried, it's really hard for me to focus. So I can't focus on what I need to do because I feel like my mind is on a lot of different things and I can't focus on, you know, exactly what I should be doing. It's just like I'm worried about, you know, all the different aspects.
Counselor: All right, so your ability to concentrate through the hard work of preparing.
Client: Yeah. To, like, focus my energy on the right things. I'm just, like, wasting time worrying.
Counselor: All right, so this, this excessive worrying and all this interfering and preparing, all this goes on right up until you're getting ready to present.
Client: Yeah. And then, like, while I'm presenting.
Counselor: So let's talk about that. Let's go into the actual day of presenting. So we have the success of work coming in. It's interfered with your ability to prepare. It's distressing for you.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Now it's what in class presentations are in class.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you're in the classroom. Do you, are you the only one to present during that class, or does it rotate through several people?
Client: It depends on the presentation. Sometimes there's, like, one or two other people that have to present that night, depending on, like, how long the topic is.
Counselor: All right, let's use the last time you present that classes as a tempo. What was the order? Like, what order did you go in there?
Client: The one. Well, the one that I really messed up. I think I was first, but usually I'm second, maybe.
Counselor: Okay, so for this example, let's say you do the second. Okay, so you're sitting in the classroom and another student is presenting.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going through your mind then?
Client: I feel like I am totally zoned out. Like, I'm not even paying attention to what that person is saying because I'm so worried about how I'm gonna mess it up. You know, I'm. I'm starting to, like, be sweaty, like, my hands are clammy, my heart starting to race a little bit, and I'm just totally zoned out on what they're doing. I'm just, you know, worrying about what's going to happen when I get up there.
Counselor: All right, so in that moment as you're seated, you're not really watching their presentation. As much because you have these strong or somewhat strong physical symptoms. You have your heart racing a bit. You said sweaty palms. You're zoned out.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Have you ever felt the. The need, desire to run out of the room?
Client: Yes. It's funny you should say that. I was a little bit hesitant to mention that, but I kind of. I do. I feel like I need to find an excuse to, like, use the bathroom or I just need to get out of there.
Counselor: Yeah. So what do you feel is most pressuring you to leave the room? Like, what symptom?
Client: Um, I would say that just, like, my anxiety and my heart rate are starting to increase, and I feel like I just need to get out of there and what.
Counselor: What thoughts going through your mind right then?
Client: Like.
Counselor: So let's take that kind of most severe moment when you're. Let's just say we're still before the presentation.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So you're sitting at the desk, and your heart rate's elevated, and you're not focusing on what they're doing. You're zoned out, your anxiety's high.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What thought is going through your mind right then?
Client: I think. I'm thinking, like, I'm gonna bond this anyway, so I might as well just, you know, not go through the stress of having to do it. Like, I've already. In my head, I know that it's.
Counselor: Gonna end badly, so I've already failed.
Client: Right. So there's no sense in getting up there, and maybe if I don't get up there, you know, I guess it couldn't be any worse, so I might as well just leave.
Counselor: Are you embarrassed that the professor or other students will see that you were really anxious?
Client: Yeah, I don't want. I figure if I leave, then people won't. We'll just maybe think I was sick or whatever, and it'll be a better situation if I just left than having to see me up there, you know, sweating and all this. These other symptoms that I have when I actually get up there. It would be better just to leave before that starts.
Counselor: Okay, so. So better to be thought ill that you just had to leave because you're sick.
Client: Yeah. Or have them wonder what happened than to just be up in front of.
Counselor: Everybody, you know, to have that severe anxiety in front of everybody, and then they can see.
Client: Very embarrassing.
Counselor: Yeah. That would be. That would be a very undesirable outcome for you.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So as you're debating that thought, like, if that's coming to your head and you're thinking, I just need to.
Client: Yeah, flee. I just gotta get out of here.
Counselor: What happens there? So we're maybe, what, 15 minutes before you present? So tell me about that. So you have that thought. You want to flee, right?
Client: And I'm looking at the clock and saying, you know, like, how much more time in this presentation before I have to go? Like, should I go? Should I not go? What are the consequences of running out? You know, and kind of playing out, which would be worse?
Counselor: Have you ever had to run out?
Client: Once I went to the bathroom to try to, like, calm myself down or talk to myself or, you know, like, cool off my face, but I came.
Counselor: Back and you presented.
Client: Yeah. And then I presented.
Counselor: All right, so you. You survived one of the more stressful.
Client: Yeah. I almost felt like I was gonna be ill. I was so stressed that day.
Counselor: That was very, very tough one, yet.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: That particular day, you did survive it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Which is very unpleasant.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So now we're. Now we're right about to where it's time to get up and present. Right. So let's say in this scenario, you haven't fled, but you had those thoughts.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you're anxious, and you have some physical symptoms going on. You get up and it's time to present. What's the sequence from this point on?
Client: So typically, like, I go to load my presentation at this point. Like, I have my note cards or whatever in front of me. I am, like, shaking at this point. I'm so. I don't know if it's scared or worried or maybe a combination of everything. And I'm just, like, sweating. My heart is racing. Like, I almost feel dizzy. I'm just so stressed out about what's going to happen then, you know, I'm starting to speak, and then the presentations are usually, like, 20 minutes or so.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So I have to stay up there for the duration, and I'm just, like, you know, sweating, and I'm wondering, like, are people looking at me or people. Can people see it? You know, am I gonna forget something?
Counselor: So the. So the thoughts are, I wonder if they can see how anxious I am.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: I wonder if I'm going to do poorly on the presentation.
Client: Right. Or they think I'm lazy and I didn't prepare, or are they going to think that, you know, I'm dumb or I don't know, you know, what I'm doing. What are they going to think about me?
Counselor: So they might think less of you as a person.
Client: Right. Or, like, be judging me.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a number of concerns that kind of go into your mind in that moment. So when does it start to turn around? So you start presenting is 20 minutes. You initially get up there and get your presentation up on the, like, the projection monitor?
Client: Something like that, yeah.
Counselor: When does it start to turn the corner?
Client: It depends. Sometimes I settle down a little bit, but then usually, like that, I get some sort of rhythm, I think. And then. But then it gets anxiety again until I get my grades. Do you know what I mean? And I'm like, until. Cause I feel like I'm gonna do poorly until that happens.
Counselor: When do you receive the grades?
Client: Sometimes. She usually doesn't give them that day, but often the next day or the day after.
Counselor: So does that intense anxiety that you're having while you're presenting last all the way?
Client: No, it definitely dissipates once I can, like, go sit down.
Counselor: Okay. So the next big drop off for symptoms would be when you're done. The presentation?
Client: Yeah. When eyes are maybe no longer on me, they've moved on to somebody else. So I figure, like, okay, they forgot about me. I'm safe for right then.
Counselor:
output: But then there's this other worry of now we have to see what the grade's gonna be right.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Do you have on your presentation, do you have so many bullet points you want to cover?
Client: Yeah, like an outline sort of thing.
Counselor: Okay. Would it help to time the deep breathing with reviewing each one of those bullet points?
Client: I never thought about that.
Counselor: I don't know how many bullet points you'd have in a presentation. Maybe you'd have ten or 20, something like that. Yeah, depending on how long it is. So maybe you, as you start to review a certain bullet point, as you're trying to get it into your memory and think about it, you breathe in really deeply. And then as you continue on, you just let out that breath really slowly.
Client: Like a rhythm, sort of. Yeah, I can.
Counselor: And then you go to the next bullet point and do the same thing.
Client: Never thought about it that way.
Counselor: I'm just thinking it'd be some way to structure so you would get in so many breaths.
Client: So I wouldn't forget. Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Something that kind of becomes a habit.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Just make sure you keep your bullet points at a length, not a few paragraphs, but just a few seconds each, so you can get a good deep breath. Or you could, you know, if you did have a longer bullet point, you could have, obviously several breaths, but just some rhythm that you could kind of grab onto something concrete.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Because I know that in that moment, things are probably, like you mentioned, zoning out and it becomes very easy to lose your anchors.
Client: Yeah, exactly. And just get really foggy, almost dizzy.
Counselor: Yeah. So if you can remember for a particular bullet point that you want to take three deep breaths, and that might be something you can really grab onto.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And would kind of cut through that fogginess of something you could still do.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: When's the next presentation in that class?
Client: The next one, I believe, is next Friday.
Counselor: Is that the next presentation you have, like, in all the classes is the one?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. And that's next Friday. Do you know where you are in the order, like, for presenting?
Client: Um, I think I'm actually third in this one.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So not first.
Counselor: Not first. And this one's how many minutes?
Client: Um, like 15 or so.
Counselor: Okay. It's a little shorter than the 20 minutes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So 15 minutes. So you have about a half hour, maybe a little more if there's time to switch out of kind of sitting there.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And potential time where you could be anxious.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: But also potential time when you could be reviewing the notes, your bullet points and breathing.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And saying to yourself, that kind of self talk, that they're not really paying attention to me anyway.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Because that might help reduce that. That anxiety.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's one thing you could say to yourself when you're up there?
Client: I guess I could say that, you know, in general, do pretty well. You know, one bad grade isn't going to make me. Doesn't mean that I don't deserve to be here.
Counselor: Okay, so the. So the self talk up there could be. I deserve to be here.
Client: Maybe I've prepared enough. You know that. I know that I've prepared and I'm a good student.
Counselor: Okay. I've prepared enough. I'm a good student. I deserve to be here.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. Is that something it would be helpful to write down and have as part of your notes that you can.
Client: Yeah, I think it would actually.
Counselor: You can recite that.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Internally as you.
Client: Because it's not long. I think I could. It would be easy to remember and I could just like, maybe put it down on one of my note cards in front of me or something.
Counselor:
output: And how much do you believe that those statements are true?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Andrew. How you doing today?
Client: Hey, Doug. Nice to see you.
Counselor: Nice to see you. It's been about a week since I seen you last. I know you're having some different difficulties, particularly at work.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Any changes there?
Client: Not really. I mean, it's pretty much the same pace. I'm very frustrated with the whole system. I'm working with inner city kids, african american kids, males in particular. And, you know, I sit and talk with these kids and I realize that there's not much I can do for them. You know, for the most part, we're talking about, you know, criminal arrest, drug abuse, you know, no education. And, you know, I don't know what I can really do for them anymore. I mean, you know, I sit and talk to them, but really, in terms of their statistics, it's looking pretty bad for them. So, you know, I get pretty frustrated and it's kind of depressing to do this every day.
Counselor: All right, so as you're working with these use, you're looking at their circumstances and you're saying the odds just don't look good for major improvement. That's leading you to lose hope in your ability to help them into different circumstances.
Client: Absolutely, yeah. I mean, it's just their reality. A kid comes in and mom is either dad's incarcerated, rotted, a picture. Mom is either on drugs or not fully engaged. And this kid has absolutely no life skills. None. He's self medicating or smoking marijuana. At the very least, it's marijuana. And he is just totally convinced that, you know, this is who he is the rest of his life. And he's sitting in front of me looking for answers, and I don't know if I have him.
Counselor: What kind of questions do they ask you?
Client: It's not even questions as more as it is just statements of, you know, this is my life, you know, the struggle is real. This is what I do, this is where I am. And, you know, anything other than this is not even, you know, I didn't fathom. So I'm sitting here, just kidding, I'm trying to draw him out of that whole mindset. But we're talking about years of social conditioning, years and years and years of it. And I just don't know if, you know, I have the skills and the tools to really break through that way of thinking.
Counselor: All right, so can you think of a particular case, particular youth that you're working with that, where you're finding the struggle. I just think of one particular individual where you're frustrated, you're making these statements that kind of. This is the way it is. They don't seem like they have much hope. You don't seem like they have much hope for them. Right. So you have one in mind.
Client: Yes, they do.
Counselor: Okay, so what's his self statement? What's he saying to you that you think is getting a reaction from you?
Client: That he's a drug dealer. He's going to continue to be a drug dealer. He's not going to stop. And that he's involved with gang activity, and that's his family. It's the only family he's ever known, and he's loyal to them. And that loyalty is deep. And he has absolutely no. Even the thought of going back to prison doesn't shape this kid.
Counselor: Not afraid of that.
Client: Not afraid of it for them. Gerald is like going to the school courtyard. There's all his boys in jail. So I'm sitting here like, what in the hell am I doing here with this kid? You know, what kind of options do I give him when I don't even believe he has any at this point?
Counselor: So that's really your automatic thought, is I don't believe he has any options. That's what's going through your mind when he says things like he's involved in gang activity and wants to continue dealing drugs? That's your thought?
Client: That's my thought, yeah.
Counselor: There's no way out for him.
Client: I don't see it. I just don't. I really don't see it for him. You know, he's self medicating. He's giving dirty urine to the probation office. He doesn't care. The judge has given them pass after pass after pass. But the kid just seems intent to, you know, to live this life.
Counselor: So in a sense, your mood, the sadness, the frustration is linked to, for example, this use statements and his philosophy. So he's saying that success is not an option, as you would think of success.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And you're reacting to that, and your mood is moving because of that.
Client: Yes. Yes. And I mean, to a certain degree, I understand where he's coming from. I mean, I was raised with the understanding that you were born black. That's one strike. You were born male. That's two strikes. A criminal arrest record, that's it. Life is over. So to a certain degree, his perception is reality. So I can't disagree with him. But at the same time, this is my job. And I'm having a very difficult time trying to give this kidde any glimpse of hope, which I don't even think he really wants.
Counselor: So it's hard for you to give the hope, and I'm sure he's looking for the hope. And you can understand his situation in terms of being african american, being male and having the criminal record and how that seems to stack the deck severely against him.
Client: Severely, yeah. And that's nothing. I mean, there's some truth to that. I don't know. That criminal arrest record, a conviction in this country pretty much relegates you to a certain level of society, in my.
Counselor: Opinion, in terms of employment opportunities.
Client: In terms of employment opportunity and things like that. So to a certain degree, I understand where he's coming from. It's just an absolute sense of hopelessness that comes from this kid. He'll sit in front of me and he'll just laugh. He'll laugh about it like, Mister D, this is my life. Why are you tripping? Why do you care so much? So I'm just starting not to carry.
Counselor: So you're starting to mirror that approach, the approach he's using.
Client: Yes, I am.
Counselor: So what's bothering you in all this? Not only the circumstances, the racism, the discrimination, the circumstances in with the criminal record, that all bothers you, but also you're bothered because you're losing hope for him.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And for others like him.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: Have you expressed that thought? Sentiment?
Client: No, I haven't. Not in so many words. Not, you know, because to do that, I think, gives the kid credibility. I don't want to increase to his way of thinking if I, you know, agree with him on doing that, giving him a license to be an asshole, so to speak.
Counselor: You don't want to let on that his loss of hope is really. You kind of share that, in a way. You get it. You understand that.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: His lack of hope is grounded in a lot of reality.
Client: Yes, exactly.
Counselor: At the same time, you do this work every day. Do you believe there's hope at some level?
Client: Absolutely. I do believe at my core, I do believe there is hope at some level. I believe in resilience. I think once you tap into it, you can pretty much achieve anything. But it's just hard to peel back so many different layers with this particular generation of kids. It really takes a lot out of you.
Counselor: It's hard to get through.
Client: Hard to get through. Hard to penetrate that shell. So I leave work someday saying, I'm not coming back. We've had enough, you know, and it's depressing after all.
Counselor: So let's go back to that automatic thought. When a youth like the one that you were talking about makes a statement like, you know, their life is essentially defined in this and these narrow parameters, drug dealing and maybe other criminality or other behaviors that aren't productive, and you're kind of thinking there's some truth to that and you're kind of thinking there may not be hope. That's kind of the automatic thoughts or something close to the automatic thoughts. You're having much?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Your reaction to that is to not help them or to not say what you feel to them. What's going on?
Client: I don't want to say what I feel because I think they don't possess the filter to be able to understand it, to understand it. So I think for them it's going to be a license to continue the behavior. So I just hit them bullshit for half an hour, 45 minutes. Because what I really want to say, I don't think it would be beneficial to him.
Counselor: Partially because of the message, but partially because of how they would interpret the message.
Client: Very good.
Counselor: There's two levels to that.
Client: Right? That's how they would interpret the message. I think the message is, you know, for the right person with the right kind of filter would be receivable. But I think how they interpret it is going to be the issue.
Counselor: Right. So what is the message? Tell me what you would want to say to them.
Client: That all this, that what you said is real, that, you know, with a criminal arrest record, you know, your circumstances growing up in the city, broken homes, racism. It's real. But at the same time, somebody else made it before you, someone else went through this and someone else made it out. So if that was the case, I wouldn't be sitting in course with you. I came from the inner city, broken homes, the same scenario. So if that were the case for all of us, then how in the hell am I sitting in? Course, I'm no different. There's nothing special about me. I wasn't an a student to get scholarships. So there has to be some quality that we tap into to really sort of center us, you know, as we go, as we go along. That's what I would like to say to them, but I'm just not too sure how it would be this evening.
Counselor: So your concern seems to be that they would hear the first part but not really the second part. So they hear that their concerns are understandable and they've had circumstances stacked against them. They would hear that, yes, but not so much. There's a way to make it out, or there's hope.
Client: Exactly. Exactly. And I would be devastated by that. Mister Don said that I'm right. I didn't get the job because I'm black. I'm right because I didn't. You know, my situation is what it is. Cause of racism. Mister Don. Mister Don said I wouldn't want that. It would taunt the reputation, probably hurt my employment here. So, you know, I bite my tongue.
Counselor: Is there a way to deliver your message, kind of with the same realism and heart, without including a piece that you feel like they could latch onto? It would be negative.
Client: Is there a way? Did you hear the message? Maybe if I switched it around and I put the last part first.
Counselor: I don't know.
Client: I'm just brainstorming here. Maybe I don't tell them at all. Maybe I just. I make reference and have them come to the same conclusion.
Counselor: Give them all the tools to figure it out.
Client: Figure it out for themselves. Well, if that's the case, then how did this happen? Okay, so if that's the case, if you're saying. If what you're saying is true, then how does this happen? How does this person.
Counselor: Ask them to explain your success?
Client: My success is someone else's success who came from the same neighborhood. How do you explain that same scenario? I think that might be a better way of taking this thing out of it, so to speak.
Counselor:
output: So if that's the new message, how likely do you think you'd be able to deliver that message if somebody told you that they wanted to continue in an unproductive lifestyle?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: You've said that when you're in work, you worry a lot about how you come across in social situations.
Client: Yeah, it really makes me feel really anxious, like what I look like and what people are thinking.
Counselor: Yeah. You said that you worry that you visibly shake.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Are there any other things that you worry that people will notice?
Client: I think obviously, the shaking. I think my hands and legs shaking and going really red and sweating and just looking really weird.
Counselor: So it sounds like you have quite a strong mental image of how you see yourself when you're in these social situations.
Client: Yeah, definitely.
Counselor: So you go red, you shake. Is there anything else that you think that you do? I mean, describe yourself. How do you think you look when you're in these situations?
Client: Just like, I think I just look really obviously weird and out of place and, like, really red and just visibly shaking and sweating and kind of not being able to communicate properly with people.
Counselor: Is there anything that you do to try and kind of defend against these things, to manage these problems?
Client: I guess, like, when I'm holding the camera, I just grip onto it really, really tight, or I kind of clench all my muscles and just find something that I can focus on and to kind of try and make myself shake less and not go as red and stuff.
Counselor: So you focus on something, you grip onto the camera. Do you make eye contact with people?
Client: No, I just tend to just look down.
Counselor: Okay. So you also avoid eye contact. Is there anything else that you do to manage the sweating, for example?
Client: I just, as I kind of looking down and wearing all black, so it's less obvious or kind of wearing just more layers and all black, so you just can't tell.
Counselor: Okay. What do you think would happen if you stopped doing these things? If you stopped gripping onto the camera or you started making eye contact and not looking down, what do you think could happen?
Client: I think it would be so much worse. Yeah. I think I just would just shake even more and be more anxious and look more obviously kind of weird and out of place.
Counselor: What I'm thinking now is, how would you feel about if we did an experiment to test out your thoughts on what would happen if you stopped doing these things? If we did a bit of a role play where we pretended to enact a situation at work.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And if you did this maybe twice in the first time, you do all the things that you normally do. Grip onto something, look down. Is there anything else that you do when you're in these situations, these work conversations to try and cope?
Client: I just kind of all just, like, fumble and kind of just clench whatever it is I'm holding just really tight. And just make sure I don't make any eye contact at all. Just kind of get through it.
Counselor: Okay. So in the first time, I want you to do those things as much as you normally would. In fact, maybe even slightly more than you normally would. And then the second time, I want you to drop doing those things altogether. How does that sound?
Client: Try my best.
Counselor: And how would you feel about if we filmed this so you could actually see what you looked like?
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Do you have a camera with you that we could video on?
Client: Yeah. Is my phone okay?
Counselor: Yeah, yeah, we'll use that in just a sec.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Before we do this, then we're just going to fill out this form, because what we're doing now is an experiment. We call it a behavioral experiment to see what happens when you change the way that you're behaving.
Client: Right. Okay.
Counselor: Okay. So the first column says, I need to fill out an experiment to test this thought that you have so that our experiment is going to be that we do a conversation at work. Who should I play? If you're playing yourself in this role play, who should I be?
Client: Maybe like a client at work, I always have to sit down with clients before we do the shoot and kind of get to know a little bit more about what they want.
Counselor: Okay, so would it work if I was maybe having a wedding and I was hiring you to be a wedding photographer?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What kind of problems do you see coming up in this conversation that we have? Like, what we see yourself doing on camera?
Client: Shaking. Like, being really obviously shaking and. Okay, bright red and.
Counselor: Okay, so visibly shaking. So how. How much will you be shaking? If a hundred is, like, shaking uncontrollably and zero is not shaking at all, how visibly shaking will you be?
Client: 90.
Counselor: Okay, sorry. What was the other thing that you just said?
Client: Like, I go really red.
Counselor: Okay, so you're gonna go red?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How red will you go? I mean, if we look around this room.
Client: Probably, like, the chairs.
Counselor: Okay, so you're going to be as kind of brightly pink as these chairs are.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so out of 100, then how pink would you say these chairs are?
Client: 90 out of 100.
Counselor: Okay. What else are you worried is going to happen when we have these conversations?
Client: Just worried I'll be like, say something stupid and not be able to kind of get what I'm trying to say across properly.
Counselor: Okay, and how stupid out of 100? If 100 is ridiculously stupid, probably like, similar.
Client: 90.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I'd say.
Counselor: What else are you worried will happen when we have this conversation. What else might you see on the camera?
Client: I think you'll probably be able to see that I'm sweating and.
Counselor: Okay, and how much will you be sweating.
Client: Again?
Counselor: 90, I think, like, visibly sweating down the face.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. And what do you think will happen the second time around when you stop kind of doing the things you normally do to cope? When you maybe start to make eye contact and you're not gripping onto something?
Client: I think it'll be even worse. I think it'll. Yeah.
Counselor: How much worse? Slightly worse. Like, twice as bad.
Client: Twice as bad.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Right. Can you give me your phone and we'll.
Client: Yeah. Okay.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Should I just use this?
Counselor: Yeah. Yeah.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: Probably best. Okay.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Leigh. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good.
Counselor: You're doing good?
Client: Yeah. Okay. I guess you guessed. Yeah. Um. Well, I guess I'll tell you, but I, I'm kind of embarrassed to tell you, but, so, like, I'm in college, and all my friends are dating, and I'm just really, like, nervous to just tell you, but, like, I really haven't dated before, and I'm really nervous and scared to date, and I just I just don't know how to do it, and I don't know. I'm just nervous.
Counselor: So, nervousness and some anxiety around dating. You said you'd never really dated before.
Client: No, not really. I mean, I just was never, you know, that was never enforced in my family. I was never allowed to really do that. So just the thought of it is, like, like, scary, scary for you? Yeah. So, you know, I mean, I tend to talk to guys, but it was just like, like, you know, real short and bye, like hi bye kind of thing. Because, like I said, that just was never enforced in my family. And just never, I was never, that's never applaud. That was never applauded in when I was growing up, so I never did it, and I was scared to do it for the repercussions, getting in trouble. So.
Counselor: All right, so no dating in high school. And what type of interactions did you have in high school? You said, you said hi a few times.
Client: Yeah, just like in my science class, you know, particularly this one time, I actually sat next to this boy who was super cute, but, you know, we would say hi, and that was it. He would try to ask me stuff about classwork or the assignment, and I would not even look at him and just tell him and look at my schoolwork. And that was the extent of it, you know?
Counselor: So let's talk about your anxiety. You have anxiety and earlier, like, reaction just to thinking about it. Right. You think about dating. It's just, it's a lot for you. Do you think this anxiety comes from a fear of what might happen, or is this something more how you'll be perceived? Like, what do you think is leading to?
Client: I think it's a little bit of both. I definitely always compare myself to my sisters, and they're super pretty, and I just don't feel attractive enough to have somebody be interested in me. And if they were to be interested in me, I'm not allowed to date, you know, so the repercussion would just be, you know, I'd kind of be shunned for doing so. So it kind of just stayed with me, you know, now I'm 24 and I'm in school, and it's just so overwhelming. And I'm kind of envious of my girlfriends because they're able to do it, and I'm like, damn. Like, how did they do that? So.
Counselor: So that process is far from removed from you. You look at that and think, I don't even know how to approach it.
Client: It's like a foreign object. Like, yeah.
Counselor: So how would you say, how would you describe yourself? Like, how do you feel about yourself?
Client: I always do the right thing. I'm really studious, and I like to have fun. When I'm with my girlfriends, we have a great time, and I'm personable with them and my family, but it's just when it comes to interacting with male, it's just super difficult for me. And I can tell you why, but I can't tell you why. You know, it's kind of that, like, it's like a seesaw every time I'm with a male, you know, in a dating aspect anyway, so it's just difficult for me.
Counselor: Is there a particular outcome that you're afraid of? Like, when you're, well, you're in college now, right? So likely interact with males to some extent. Is there when an opportunity comes up when somebody's interested in you? Is there a particular fear that comes to mind?
Client: Yeah, like, I don't even know why you're talking to me. Like, why would you talk to me? I'm not pretty. I'm flipping awkward. Like, you know, why would you even be interested?
Counselor: So you think yourself as unattractive and awkward?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you question why they would be interested in you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So have you ever had evidence presented to the contrary, like, people who thought you were attractive and not awkward?
Client: Um, well, yeah, I mean, yeah, like, people have told me that I'm pretty and, um, you know, fun and stuff like that, so, yeah, I have.
Counselor: Yeah. But there's some, so they're telling you that? But there's something else telling you that you're not?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you think that's coming from?
Client: I guess just from my, you know, my mom and I think just her rules that I guess I just associated, you know, me not being able to date, that I wasn't presentable enough to date. And I just got this idea that that's the reason why she just didn't want me to date.
Counselor: So you think her reasoning for not allowing you to date, I wasn't the pretty daughter? Were your sisters allowed to date?
Client: They were allowed to date, but under certain circumstances, certain rules they had to follow. But just when I would, you know, even suggest it to my mom, it was just like, no, you're not.
Counselor: So you feel like you were, of you and your sisters, you were the one treated the most strictly on that. But was it much more strictly or just a little differently?
Client: I think it was much more strictly, yeah. Because it's so much so now that I can't even talk to a guy. It's just. I mean, the anxiety and the fear is so intense. I just can't explain it. It's horrible that it's not like that for my sisters because now they're married, you know, so they have kids, and it's like, what the heck happened here? And I can recognize it, but I just can't bring myself to do it, like talk to somebody or, you know.
Counselor: So the way you perceive yourself, the self image here is part of this?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, absolutely.
Counselor: So you have evidence that says that men would be interested in going out with you, dating you, but internally, these thoughts you're having say you're just not worthy.
Client: You know what I mean?
Counselor: That's kind of the theme of it, right?
Client: Yeah, absolutely. That's it.
Counselor: And maybe this is tied to a core belief. Like we talked about core beliefs before cognitive therapy. Are there any of those core beliefs in the list I gave you a few weeks ago kind of stood out that you think might be core beliefs you have?
Client: That I'm unlovable.
Counselor: Unlovable, yeah. Any others?
Client: Fear of rejection.
Counselor: So fear of being rejected?
Client: Fear of being rejected. Yeah.
Counselor: So unlovable. And a fear of being rejected. And then when you have interactions in the moment, like, say you're in class and there's a man sitting next to you in class, and they're interested in you, he's interested in you. He says something that expresses that he's interested. You're immediately suspect.
Client: Oh, yeah.
Counselor: That's what you're.
Client: Oh, yeah. That's like. It's like, what is it? Fight or flight kind of feeling like it really is. It's like, oh, you know. Yeah. Just something comes over me where, you know, it's kind of like I'm conditioned because I don't even live with my mom and my dad now, and I'm on my own, but yet I still hold their values. And not just. All I can just think of is being in high school and having. Being told I can't do that or just the rules and having to follow it. And that's really where I feel like I'm there. If someone says something to me, it.
Counselor: Takes you right back there.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. I. So how do your parents feel about now? Have they said anything like, your sisters are married and you're not? Have they pointed that out?
Client: No, they haven't. Not really. No. Because my mom really wants me. She. I guess. Well, maybe it has to do with that. Like, I'm smarter than my sisters, so she really wants me to be a doctor. And my sisters, they have, you know, they have great jobs, but, you know, they just stopped at a bachelor's degree, and I'm really working to be a doctor. And I always had straight a's in high school and my sisters didn't. So I think that my mom wants to hold on to that, you know, that hope that I'm going to be something great. So she doesn't really enforce the dating thing with me. I guess she's for fear that that's going to get in the way.
Counselor: That's different than being unlovable, right? Yeah. I mean, her reasoning, as you're describing her reasoning sounds more like she wants you to reach a higher educational goal.
Client: I mean, I guess. Yeah.
Counselor: What do you want?
Client: I want to be in a relationship with somebody because all of my friends are, and I'm always that. They're real and it's difficult. I mean, yeah, I want the education. Don't get me wrong, I want a great job, but I don't want to do that alone. I want to have somebody with me that I can confide in and just a confidante. And the time is now. I'm ready, you know? And maybe my mom was just protecting me, I guess. I don't know what she was doing, but I really don't care because I really want to try it. I just don't know how.
Counselor: There's opposing forces at work here, right? I mean, you're motivated to try it like it's a goal. You want to be able to date, you want to go out. It's important to you. Do you want to get married like your sisters?
Client: Yeah, I do.
Counselor:
output: You do? So you have these clear goals, and that's one force. And then the supposing force is this. Well, one of them would be this anxiety that comes over you in the moment when a man's talking to you. Like in that way. Right. Like about going out or any topic like that. So a part of you. A part of you is saying, I really want to move forward and date different people and see if I can find a good match. And another part of you is saying I need to run away. Like you said, fight or flight, right? I want to run away and not have this awkwardness, this anxiety.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Do you have on your presentation, do you have so many bullet points you want to cover?
Client: Yeah, like an outline sort of thing.
Counselor: Okay. Would it help to time the deep breathing with reviewing each one of those bullet points?
Client: I never thought about that.
Counselor: I don't know how many bullet points you'd have in a presentation. Maybe you'd have ten or 20, something like that. Yeah, depending on how long it is. So maybe you, as you start to review a certain bullet point, as you're trying to get it into your memory and think about it, you breathe in really deeply. And then as you continue on, you just let out that breath really slowly.
Client: Like a rhythm, sort of. Yeah, I can.
Counselor: And then you go to the next bullet point and do the same thing.
Client: Never thought about it that way.
Counselor: I'm just thinking it'd be some way to structure so you would get in so many breaths.
Client: So I wouldn't forget. Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Something that kind of becomes a habit.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Just make sure you keep your bullet points at a length, not a few paragraphs, but just a few seconds each, so you can get a good deep breath. Or you could, you know, if you did have a longer bullet point, you could have, obviously several breaths, but just some rhythm that you could kind of grab onto something concrete.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Because I know that in that moment, things are probably, like you mentioned, zoning out and it becomes very easy to lose your anchors.
Client: Yeah, exactly. And just get really foggy, almost dizzy.
Counselor: Yeah. So if you can remember for a particular bullet point that you want to take three deep breaths, and that might be something you can really grab onto.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And would kind of cut through that fogginess of something you could still do.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: When's the next presentation in that class?
Client: The next one, I believe, is next Friday.
Counselor: Is that the next presentation you have, like, in all the classes is the one?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. And that's next Friday. Do you know where you are in the order, like, for presenting?
Client: Um, I think I'm actually third in this one.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So not first.
Counselor: Not first. And this one's how many minutes?
Client: Um, like 15 or so.
Counselor: Okay. It's a little shorter than the 20 minutes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So 15 minutes. So you have about a half hour, maybe a little more if there's time to switch out of kind of sitting there.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And potential time where you could be anxious.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: But also potential time when you could be reviewing the notes, your bullet points and breathing.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And saying to yourself, that kind of self talk, that they're not really paying attention to me anyway.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Because that might help reduce that. That anxiety.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's one thing you could say to yourself when you're up there?
Client: I guess I could say that, you know, in general, do pretty well. You know, one bad grade isn't going to make me. Doesn't mean that I don't deserve to be here.
Counselor: Okay, so the. So the self talk up there could be. I deserve to be here.
Client: Maybe I've prepared enough. You know that. I know that I've prepared and I'm a good student.
Counselor: Okay. I've prepared enough. I'm a good student. I deserve to be here.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. Is that something it would be helpful to write down and have as part of your notes that you can.
Client: Yeah, I think it would actually.
Counselor: You can recite that.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Internally as you.
Client: Because it's not long. I think I could. It would be easy to remember and I could just like, maybe put it down on one of my note cards in front of me or something.
Counselor: And how much do you believe that those statements are true?
Client: I think, you know, sitting now. Sitting here now, I believe them in the moment. Sometimes it's a little hard to believe because I convinced myself otherwise, but I think I actually believe that that's true, that I do deserve to be in the program.
Counselor: Okay, so those self talk items, you believe them to be true.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But you recognize in the moment, and I want you to be aware of this. You might note, I believe them as much.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But remember that, you know, we worked on them, you came up with them and you believe them now.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So try to keep that in your mind as you start to doubt yourself.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: And be ready to recite them. It's easy. I realize it's easy to form these plans.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Ann. How you doing today?
Client: Good.
Counselor: Doing well?
Client: Yeah, I guess so. I've been working still on the fear of leaving the home for extended periods of time, like vacation, and it's been a little harder recently because I have this planned trip with a friend of mine coming up in a few months, and that's kind of been weighing on my mind.
Counselor: Where's the trip to Georgia, and how long will you be there?
Client: She wants to go, like, six days, but, yeah, I'm not sure. With work and school and everything, I can make the full six days, and plus, I'm a little nervous to go that long.
Counselor: So that's a long time for you.
Client: It is, yes.
Counselor: So when did you discover this trip.
Client: Was going to be actually last? Just a few days ago. She messaged me and said, hey, you want to go with me? And we'll go golfing and swimming? I love golfing. Like, you know, I want to go, but I just have these, just, you know, a little nervous about leaving.
Counselor: A little nervous. So when she made that call just a couple days ago, what was the first thought you had?
Client: God, I can't go that long. That was my first thought, that's too long. But then it was like, wow, this would be great. I want to go down there golfing so bad and get away from the cold weather. So, I mean, my immediate thought was, no, not that long, but, yes, I want to go.
Counselor: All right, so you had two kind of conflicting thoughts, right. So one. One is, I could never go that long. Six days, way too long. And the other one is, that would be enjoyable. You enjoy that?
Client: Absolutely, yeah.
Counselor: So which way are you leaning right now?
Client: I want to go to go, but maybe not for six days. Maybe just like a long weekend.
Counselor: Three, four days.
Client: Two would be ideal, but two would probably be idea, but two or three days. Yeah.
Counselor: So what do you think is causing this worry about being gone more than two days?
Client: I don't know. I mean, I've always, as a late teenager in my twenties, I've always had just nervous to leave home. As much as I love being home, I love to travel, too, and do different things. It's just, I guess I'm just afraid something to happen when I'm not around.
Counselor: So you're afraid something will happen to your house or.
Client: Well, I have pets, so I worry about them. My parents are getting older, so I worry about them mainly, like, my immediate family, mainly, I guess, my dad, because he's had a history of heart attacks, and then my pets, that's just worry something will happen. I won't be there.
Counselor: And how about when you were younger, you said this problem's been out for a while.
Client: It's the same thing.
Counselor: The same thing. So mostly family and now some pets.
Client: Well, I had pets then, too.
Counselor: You had pets then, too? Okay, so that's really what's bothering you here, is that you'll be away, and that's when something will happen and it'll be something bad. What about coming back? Like, you can come back?

And somewhere along the line, something changed in you and now you're not happy with it. So what it represents in terms of activities like caring for your children and shopping, now, that's what changed.
Client: Yeah, exactly. Well, I guess, you know, my youngest is eight, so he's only been in school for a couple of years. So I guess, like, it's not super recent, but recently I finally have no children in the home, so it's more. It's more time to myself, and I kind of filled that gap a little bit with other things. Like, I did Cub scouts with the boys for a while, and like I said, I had some friends around the neighborhood, so that kind of, like, filled that time. But now that stuff, it's just not really happening anymore. So now I kind of feel like it's not boredom. You know, it's not like I don't have enough to do. It's like I don't want to do anything, but then at the same time, I feel frustrated because there's nothing to do.
Counselor: All right, so you're frustrated with your situation, maybe with yourself a little bit?
Client: Yeah, I think a lot more with myself because I know that I would feel better if I had, you know, maybe found more friends or found something to do with my time, but I don't want to at the same time. So I'm frustrated with myself because I kind of know what would help, but then I don't really have the, like, the volition to do it.
Counselor: You're not motivated?
Client: Yeah, I'm not motivated.
Counselor: Have you received any feedback from other people about this meeting? Has anyone else noticed that you're down?
Client: Yeah, I mean, obviously my husband has noticed because he has to get the boys ready in the morning. He's really supportive. I know he can tell that I'm not feeling the same, but, you know, he works, and then he has to come home and pick up my slack. So he is getting frustrated, which I understand. And, you know, my mom has said to me that, you know, she thinks I'm not doing as much, and so it kind of hurts. It feels like everybody's trying to tell me I'm lazy and that I'm not doing enough. And it's always that, like, feeling, you know, like nobody really understands how much work goes into being a mother. But then, at the same time, now that I'm doing less and less, I feel like they're all right, you know? I am lazy. I'm not doing anything.
Counselor: They use the word lazy?
Client: No, not that I can remember. You know, I think my mom said, like, you're not doing as much as you used to. And I kind of took offense to that, even though it's kind of true. It's like. I don't know. It hurt.
Counselor: Okay. That was painful for you what about what your husband said? What's he been saying?
Client: You know, I think at first we didn't really acknowledge it. It was like, you know, I took a break here. He picked up the slack, and it was fine. But now that it's been more and more, he's kind of getting frustrated. And, you know, he's been asking me about how I feel and why I'm not doing as much. But at the same time, like, even though he knows that, not motivated, it's still frustrating because it's my responsibility. So I think he's. You know, he's been saying, like, I need you to do more around the house, pretty much is what he said. I need you to do more.
Counselor: What was your response to that? When he said, I need you to.
Client: Do more, I started crying because I know he's right. And that's what I tell myself every day. I need to do more, but I don't have the motivation to do it. And so I'm so frustrated with myself, and, you know, I know that he needs that from me, and I don't know why I'm not motivated to do it.
Counselor: Okay, so you're frustrated for feeling down.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you're frustrated for lacking motivation, and just as little as a few years ago, you didn't feel it this way at all.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I actually think, you know, I've been feeling this way more, like, in the past, like, six months or something like that. Like, I. It was hard for me when my youngest son went to school, but more in, like, the natural way that it is hard, but this is something else. This is more consuming. It's, you know, like, the difficulty of him going away to school almost was motivating. Like, it was hard, but at the same time, it was freeing because I had other opportunities to do stuff. This is just, like, stunting.
Counselor: Okay, so let me shift gears a little bit. Can you tell me about your. Well, a recent day. It's kind of typical of what you're telling me now. Meaning not motivated. Down.
Client: Sure. On Wednesday, I was having a really hard time getting out of bed, so my husband just got the kids ready in the morning, and I felt really bad about that. So I just stayed in bed for a couple more hours, probably until, like, 1030, and I got up, you know, and made myself something to eat. And then I thought, you know, I should probably go to the store because we're almost out of milk and, you know, and I think the boys need shampoo. But I just. I just sat down and I just sat there, and I think I sat for. I don't even know how long the boys came home from school. It was like, you know, 330, and I hadn't even gotten up. And so then I said, okay, the boys are home. I should probably get started on dinner soon because my husband will be home soon. And I. I found something in the fridge to make, and I made dinner. And, you know, after that, everybody, you know, just sat down. We just watched tv, and I just sat there until it was time to go to bed.
Counselor: You said this was recently, right? What would the ideal day have looked like? Take that same day and do what you wish you could have done.
Client: I wish that I would wake up and, you know, I would want to wake up when it was time for the kids to get ready to go to school. You know, I could make sure that everything that they had, everything they needed, I could pack their lunches and get the boys dressed and, you know, check if they needed any permission slip sign, that kind of thing, send them out the door, and then I would see if we needed anything from the store. I probably do a little bit of cleaning around the house. I used to, like, have a list of chores that I would do different things on different days and different days of the month and stuff. So bedding would get washed one day of the week and that kind of thing. Probably, like, follow that list. Nowadays, I just, you know, if it gets done, it gets done. And usually my husband helps me with some of the stuff. And, you know, I would do the bathrooms one day a week. That probably gets done, like, once a month now, but I would do that. So do the cleaning. If we. If I needed to go to the store, I would do that. I'd get ready for the boys to come home. I'd probably make them a snack and figure out what was going to be for dinner. I would go ahead and do that, and then probably, you know, sometimes we would watch tv after my husband got home after dinner, or I would figure out something for us to do. We could play a board game, or I'll watch a movie as a family or something like that. But that would be after the kids did their homework and everything like that. And then after we spent some time together, I'd put them to bed.
Counselor: All right, so there's a fairly wide discrepancy between where you are in terms of behavior and where you want to be. So let me ask you a very specific question about one of the first things in the day. You had mentioned that when it was time to get up you didn't. So you were awake and aware of it, but you went back to sleep, I presume. And of course, your husband got up and he took care of things. How did you feel allowing that to happen? Because clearly that's not what you wanted to happen. How did you feel about that? Oversleeping?
Client: It's just like, you know, the alarm goes off and I know it's time to get up, and my husband's getting out of bed, and I just look at the clock and I think, what's the point? And, you know, it's just this instant feeling of. I can't even describe it, like pointlessness of getting up. And so I go back to sleep, but I feel worse for doing it, you know, like it's a catch 22. Like, I don't want to wake up. I just don't want to. But then when I go back to sleep, I feel bad. I feel guilty.
Counselor: Okay, so by not getting up in the time you wanted, you feel guilty. But you also mentioned something that you thought, which was, if I'm not mistaken, you said, what's the point? Can you expand on that?
Client: It just. It's just like, you know, when I'm sleeping, I don't realize how sad I am, and I don't realize how hard it is to function when I'm sleeping. I'm not aware of that. And as soon as I wake up, I am. And so I just have this feeling of, like, what's the point of getting up and experiencing these feelings when I could go back to sleep and not have to?
Counselor: What's the point of getting up when sleeping will keep the pain at bay?
Client: Yes. Yeah.
Counselor: But then when you do get up, you feel sad and guilty about having overslept.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, definitely. Definitely.
Counselor: So really, functionally, what you're doing is you're delaying experiencing the pain. And then in terms of how it affects your relationships and your family, you're not getting your kids off to school, your husband's getting real frustrated, and all you've really bought yourself is a couple extra hours of sleep and presumably without pain because you're sleeping but you're not really escaping it. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Before, when you felt more satisfaction and purpose, did you get up and help the kids off to school?
Client: Yeah, it was so easy. I would just like, you know, I would wake up and I would be like, okay, it's time to get up and get out of bed and get ready to go. I mean, you know, sometimes if I was a little bit tired, it would be a little bit hard, but, you know, it's nothing. You know, as a stay at home mom, I usually get enough sleep for the most part, now that the kids are older and everything. So it's not usually too hard to get up. And I would, you know, it would be another good day. You know, I would be glad to get up and take care of the things that I needed to take care of, and I felt accomplished.
Counselor: So maybe what's going on here? Or maybe we could help remember, you know, over the last few sessions, we talked about. About cognitive behavioral therapy and the different techniques that I'll be using and different things we'll be talking about. Sometimes with behavior, the behavior that's useful, which in this case, I'm assuming we can agree, is the getting up one time behavior that's useful has to come first, even if the feeling doesn't match. So sleeping those extra, I presume, a couple hours, delays you from feeling sad, but it causes other problems. If you were to get up one time, you might still feel sad, right? Because that's why you're oversleeping, because you're sleeping longer, to avoid that. But the functional part of being a housewife, as you identify, would be completed. So maybe some of those feelings of sadness and guilt would, over time, abate, because, functionally speaking, you're completing the task that you want. What's tough about that is that in the moment, it's easy for me to say this now, but in the moment, like, for instance, when you have to get up out of bed tomorrow, you're going to be facing that same challenge, which is, I can get up now and feel depressed or I can wait and feel depressed later. So in that moment, it's hard to act on the behavior that you kind of know you want to move towards. I mean, it sounds like you want to get up and see if the kids are.
Client: Yeah, I mean, I want everything to be normal again. And I guess I never really thought of it like that. Like, I just thought, well, if I'm waking up at the right time and I'm just feeling bad, then, like I said, what's the point? But I guess it makes sense. Like, even if I don't feel like doing it, maybe it'll make me feel better if I do do it, even if it's hard, because nothing's really harder than what I'm already going through.
Counselor: Well, it seems like you're more or less making things worse in an effort to avoid the pain that you're going to suffer anyway. You're making the pain worse. Just delaying it a little bit. Right. What thought? We talked before about automatic thoughts, these thoughts that come up kind of when your belief system meets, these different situations that occur when you have that thought that this is pointless. And I'm going to expand on that thought a little. That what that thought's really getting at is I can avoid this pain if I sleep a little while longer. That's a version of the thought. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah. And also, I guess I thought that, no, it wouldn't really be that beneficial to get up.
Counselor: Okay, so you're also minimizing the benefit.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a couple things going on. Right. I can avoid the pain by sipping in, and there's really no point to getting out because I won't do any good anyway.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: What adaptive response, that self talk. We talked about those things we consciously think to ourselves, could you apply in that moment when you're, you know, whatever time you get up in the morning when you're thinking about this and that thought comes in that it doesn't really matter if I get up anyway.
Client: I mean, I guess I could tell myself, like, I can do this. Like, instead of, you know, when I say to myself, what's the point? Instead I can say, I can do this. I can get out of bed. It'll be okay. I can. I'm strong enough. Even though it's hard to push through the pain and get up now, even though I don't want to, I can say, I can do this.
Counselor: Okay, so that would be your adaptive response. I'm strong enough. I can get through this, but it will be difficult. How about the value of getting up early and seeing the kids off to school? The automatic thought right now is telling you that's not valuable, but I think that you believe it is valuable.
Client: Yeah, I mean, I know it's valuable. I guess what my frustration is is that I know it's valuable. And it used to give me, like, an emotional payoff of, like, pride and satisfaction, and now I'm not getting that anymore. So I guess I need to realize that even though I'm not getting it right now, if I keep trying, maybe it will happen again. Because it did happen before.
Counselor: Well, it seemed logical that you have a higher probability of getting that back. If you do get up, then if you.
Client: I guess that's true. You'll never get the satisfaction of sending my kids off to school. If I never send my kids off to school.
Counselor: So you have a 0% chance of successful successfully moving past this with a sleeping in and you have some other probability greater than zero if you do.
Client: I never thought about it like that.
Counselor: Does that kind of make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So even though getting up early is going to be painful and going to seem like not a practical move, logically, you know that it has a better chance of paying off for you. And I think that with these type of, what you're going through is probably depression. I'd like to talk to you further to make sure that's what's going on, but it seems like you're depressed and sometimes with depression you just have to get one thing going your way each day. Right. So I'm not saying necessarily tomorrow you have to get up on time and then go make new friends and then go find social activities. You don't have to build Rome in a day here. It's more like, can I do this one thing? Can I prove to myself just what I'm saying, which is I'm strong enough to get up, see the kids off and have that one victory for tomorrow and build on that?
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And part of that's going to be playing those adaptive responses back. Right. Thinking those thoughts, whether it's just thinking them, you know, in your mind, you're actually thinking them and saying them. Sometimes it's helpful just to say them out loud.
Client: Yeah. Not letting the negative thoughts take over because that's what I'm thinking. Like, okay, I can get the kids off to school, but after that I'm going to start thinking, you know, what's the point again? Like, why don't I just sit down? There's no point.
